"That was one bout." Lira wrote on the back of her hand with a stub of pencil. "This was nine. And tonight you weren't fighting somebody who wanted you to last. You were fighting me." She looked at what she had written. "I made you spend."

"You made me spend."

She sat back on her heels and looked at the painted floor as if she had just been given it. Then she said, more quietly, "He was right. The Stone. He said the drill was only worth anything against somebody who could see it coming. Everybody here can't see it coming. You can." She stood. "I'm going to want to do this again."

"So am I," said Cael, and found that he meant it.

Brom had finished wrapping his forearms. He stood at the far end of the painted lines with his feet a shoulder's width apart and his weight sunk into them, and he looked, in the lantern light, like something that had been built there and the hall built round it afterward.

"Give," he said.

Cael went down the floor to him and set his own feet and held up his left forearm across his body.

Brom's Path was Iron Skin, and he could go hard, not all at once and not for long, but enough. When he hit something, he hit it with a forearm that had stopped being entirely flesh, and the something knew. Cael had taken one of those forearms on an honest arm once, long ago at Ardenmere, before he had the give. He had not been able to lift a cup with that hand for three days.

Brom hit him.

It came at him like a beam swung on a rope. And it went nowhere. The give took it in the forearm, all of it, as a pocket takes a dropped coin, and kept it. Nothing went up the arm, and nothing went down through the hip into the floor. Brom's forearm stopped against his as if it had struck a sack of wool, and Brom looked at the place where it had stopped with his eyebrows up.

"Again," said Cael.

Brom hit him again, harder, and the give took that one too, and the hum came up in the bone, deep and low, and began to fade.

The third came before the hum had faded. The give took that too, but Cael felt it take it, the way you feel a cup take water when it is already more than half full. The hum did not fade this time; it stayed in the bone and grew a little, and his fingers began to tingle at the ends.

"Again," he said, and Brom looked at him, and hit him a fourth time.

The give took the fourth. It took it the way a full cup takes one more drop: it held, and the surface stood up over the brim, and trembled. The hum went up his arm as far as the elbow and stopped there, waiting. Cael lowered the arm and stood with his teeth together until the elbow let it go.

"That's the edge," he said, when he could. "Not the strength. The speed. It's a cup. I can pour it out again, but not as fast as you can fill it. Space them out and I could take you all night. Four in a row and the fifth goes somewhere."

"Where?"

"I don't know. I'm not going to find out on you."

Brom considered this, unwrapping and rewrapping the end of one forearm, which was what he did when he was thinking. "At Norhold she was filling it with fire," he said. "From across a ring. Faster than me."

"And it went somewhere."

"Mm." Brom set his feet again. "Push, then."

This was the one Cael had shut his hand on in wing three. He set his right palm against Brom's chest, below the collarbone, and Brom set himself to it, the way he set himself against anything, with his weight down in his heels and his knees soft and his whole body arranged to be the thing that did not move.

Cael gave him the push.

Not the flat hand. The real one, the one he had taken from the Bronze at Ardenmere and given to a Gold at Norhold, at fighting load. It went out of his shoulder and down his arm and through his palm into Brom as if he had put the whole of himself behind a cart on a hill.

Brom slid.

His planted feet went back along the boards a foot and a little more, with a long dry squeal of leather on pine, and stopped. He looked down at his feet, and then he looked up, and he was smiling, which Brom did perhaps three times in a year.

"Again," said Brom.

Cael gave him four more. At the fourth his right shoulder spoke, as it always spoke at the fourth. At the fifth it said something else, longer and lower, and he knew he would be counting it on the stair in the morning. Brom slid each time, less each time, because each time he learned a little more about where to put his weight, and at the fifth he slid no more than a hand's breadth.

"Five," said Brom. "Like her."

"Like her."

"Your shoulder."

"Counting it."

Lira, writing on her hand: "Shoulder, five, the fifth counted." She looked up. "Spark?"

He laid two fingers against the iron of Brom's forearm, where the skin had gone hard and dark under the wraps, and gave it the spark. There was a tick like a nail cooling, and the copper smell rose up between them.

Brom looked at his forearm. "Hm," he said, which was a review.

"Now the one we came for," said Lira.

She went to the north end of the painted lines and Brom went to the south, and they stood twenty feet apart with Cael between them in the middle of the floor, among the white crosses. The lanterns at either end threw their shadows long across the boards toward him, so that he stood where two shadows met.

"Both of us," said Lira. "Get past."

He knew the shape of it before they moved. Brom would come straight and slow and would not be where Cael wanted him to be. Lira would come fast and from the wrong side, with three bursts and the four counts and the empty third. Between them there was no room on the floor at all, only the place where their two reaches overlapped.

So he made room.

He asked the air to lean, along a line between them, from where he stood to the gap past Brom's left shoulder. Fifteen feet of it, a third deep, and the air tipped like a board stepped on at one end, and his ears closed and opened. Down at his feet the dust in the cracks of the boards woke up and ran, pale, along the lane toward Brom.

And the read went with it.

He felt it go. He had meant to keep the read on Brom's body, on the heels and the hips and the weight going down. Instead, the moment he laid the lane, the read went into the lane itself. It read the air: how hard it leaned, how far it ran, where it would let go. It was a beautiful read. It told him exactly where the end of the lane was. And it told him nothing at all about Brom.

He stepped into the lane and it carried him, fast, toward the gap past Brom's shoulder.

Brom was not there. Brom had moved half a beat before, and the read had not seen it go, because the read was looking at the air.

The forearm came across Cael's chest like a door shutting in a gale. He went down on the boards on his back, and the lane let go above him, and all the breath he owned went up into the dark of the gallery and stayed there.

Brom stood over him, looking down.

"You weren't looking at me," said Brom.

"No." Cael lay on the painted floor and looked at the shuttered windows. "I was looking at the road."

He had known it. He had written it in the year's ledger at Norhold, in the guesting-house, before the road home: at Gold it will do one or the other and not both. He had learned it in the ring, which was a bad place to learn things. Now he had learned it again on a floor where the worst that could happen was Brom, and he lay there and let the knowing go all the way down into him, past the place where he knew things to the place where he did them.

The read could take a body or it could take the air. It could not take both at once. Not at Gold. Not yet.

He sat up.

"Again," he said. "I'm going to lay it first, before I need it, and then give the read back to you. The lane doesn't need watching once it's down. You do."

Brom went back to the south end without a word, and Lira was already at the north.

The second time, he laid the lane while they were still walking to their marks. It ran from his feet to the gap past Brom's left shoulder, fifteen feet, a third deep, and the dust ran down it and gathered at the end. Then he took the read off it, deliberately, the way you take your hand off a dog you have told to stay, and sent the read to Brom.

Brom came. His weight went down into his right heel half a beat before he moved. The read had it.

Cael stepped into the lane.

It carried him down past the place where Brom's forearm was going to be and was not yet. Lira's burst came off the wrong foot at the wrong angle and met nothing; she had read him going one way and the lane had taken him a third faster than any feet could. He came out of the end of the lane past Brom's shoulder, behind both of them, and stopped.

Then the cost came in.

It was not in the hip and it was not in the shoulder. It was behind the eyes, a heaviness, as if somebody had laid a warm hand over the inside of his skull. And everything else he carried went slow with it. He reached for the Wind, out of curiosity, the way you test a stair, and it came, but it came late: a beat late, the way a dog comes when it has decided to come in its own time. He counted. For ten counts after the lane, everything answered him a beat behind his asking. At eleven it was gone, and the hand had lifted off the inside of his head, and the Wind came when he called it.

Lira had turned round, and Brom had turned round, and they were both looking at him.

"What did that cost?" said Lira.

He told her exactly: behind the eyes, ten counts of everything slow, gone at eleven. She wrote it on her hand under the shoulder and the hip, small, because she was running out of hand. Then she stopped writing and looked up at him.

"You wrote it settled," she said. "The flag. You wrote nothing pulls."

"Nothing does." He had been turning it over himself since the count ran out. "Pull was the wrong thing answering. The push when I called the Wind, the read when I wanted my feet. That's gone. This is the right thing answering late." He thought back to the second floor in the dark, and the long while he had stood waiting for a pull that never came before he called anything at all. "At dawn I stood still after the lane until I was sure. I must have stood through the whole ten without counting them. Tonight was the first time I reached for anything inside them."

Lira looked at her palm. "So the flag's down, and this is the bill."

"The flag's down. This is the bill."

She wrote bill, not flag under the ten counts, and underlined it.

"Ten counts," said Brom, "in a real bout."

"Is a long time," said Cael.

"Is a long time," Brom agreed.

Cael sat on a painted cross and thought about the notice.

He had it by heart. Every notice he had ever had he knew by heart, because each of them had found him somewhere with nothing else to look at, a yard, a stair, a shut room, and the one from Norhold on one knee on a stone floor, with a healer holding his hand. Note: pressure-differential component; corridor-seeding component. Short range. At the time it had read like a clerk's description of somebody else's coat. Tonight he thought he could put his hand on each line of it. The lane was the corridor; he seeded it, and it grew where he put it, and stayed while he left it alone. The tilt of the air, the ears, the dust running downhill, that was the pressure. Short range was fifteen feet. And the notice had said nothing at all about the read going into the air and leaving the body behind, or about ten counts of everything slow. Notices never told you what a thing cost. They only told you what it was. The cost you found out on a floor, with friends, if you were lucky, and in front of eight thousand people if you were not.

They sat down on the floor afterward among the white crosses, the three of them, with the jug of water going round and the lanterns burning low. Lira lay on her back with her taped hands on her stomach and her eyes shut. Brom sat with his legs out in front of him, unwinding his wraps slowly, a turn at a time, rolling each length up as he went.

And in the gap, it came.

He did not feel it begin. He was sitting on the boards with the jug in his hands, and then he was a little less than that, thinner, a place the lantern light slid over on its way to the wall.

"One," said Lira, without opening her eyes.

Hold.

He gave his attention to Brom. To Brom's hands, rolling up the wrap, turn after turn, the big careful fingers smoothing each length down before the next went over it. He watched the wrap grow into a neat tight roll the size of a fist. Watching Brom was not hiding, and the thinness went out of him like breath.

"Back," said Lira, still with her eyes shut.

"How did you know? You weren't looking."

"I didn't need to look. The room went quieter." She opened her eyes and turned her head on the boards. "That's the first this week?"

"The second."

"It's going down."

It was going down. It went down a little every month, and it had never stopped. Rent from waking, every day, spent or not. He had never used it, not once, not even in the last corner of the hardest fight of his life, when it had offered itself to him like a hand held out. It was sealed for a debt, and the debt was to a quiet man who sat at the middle of the bench and cut his bread into squares, and who did not know it was owed, or what for. Nobody had told him yet. The four of them had decided that at Norhold, on the night of the seal. Not yet. When it could be told whole.

Brom set the rolled wrap down on the boards beside him.

"That's what goes up to wing three," he said. "Every Fifth-day. All that. And you take it as far as the door and leave it there and go in with the rest."

"Yes."

"And you'll do it again next Fifth-day, and the one after."

"For as long as the year asks."

Brom picked up the second wrap and began to roll it.

"Then once a week," he said, "you come here. Here, with us, and you take all of it out of the bag and use it, every piece, and we write down what it costs." He pressed the wrap smooth with his thumb. "So you don't forget it's yours. A man who keeps a thing shut long enough starts to think the shut is the thing."

Lira turned her head on the boards and looked at Brom.

"That's the most you've said since Norhold," she said.

"I was saving it." Brom finished the roll and set it beside the first. "Once a week."

"Once a week," said Cael.

Lira held up her hand to the lantern and read it aloud, squinting at the pencil marks running across her palm and down onto her wrist. "Hip, crest to knee, the eighth into the thigh. Shoulder, five, the fifth counted. Forearm: four in a row, the fourth to the elbow; it's a cup, not a wall. Spark: one, on Brom, who said hm. The lane: fifteen feet, a third deep. First time, the read went into the air and Brom put him on the floor. Second time, lane first, read second, through. After: behind the eyes, ten counts slow, gone at eleven." She lowered the hand. "One drift. Held." She looked at her palm. "Karis is going to make me copy this out three times because of my capitals."

"She'll make you copy it out four times," said Brom, "if you tell her the bit about the floor."

"I'm telling her the bit about the floor first," said Lira. "Which thing, then writing." She sat up. "Bed. Somebody's hip is going to send its bill at the first bell, and I want to be awake to hear about it."

The hip sent its bill at the first bell, with interest, as promised.

He took the residence stair one step at a time on Seventh-day morning and went down to the north wall to let the sun get into it. It was a rest day. The house was mostly asleep, or pretending, and the Crown yard lay empty under the long wall, where the porter's boards stood chalked fresh with the year's names. Down in the valley the two coats stood at the foot of the road and the two at the landing, and none of them looked up.

He sat on the coping by the third buttress with his leg out straight, and after a while he noticed Bracken.

The records hall stood across the court from the wall, its long roof and its row of tall windows facing east toward the valley. In the highest window, the one at the north end that lit the stair to Bracken's rooms, a man was standing. He had a small brass glass in his hand, the kind a ship's officer carries, and every so often he lifted it and looked through it down the valley, toward the place where the bluff road came up out of the trees. Then he lowered it, and stood, and lifted it again.

Cael watched him do it four times. Then he got up, and took the long way round the court so as not to come at the records hall from the direction of the wall, and went in by the side door and up the stair.

Bracken was still at the window when Cael reached the landing. He did not turn round.

"Good morning," said Bracken. "Your hip is bad. I heard you on the stair."

"Good morning." Cael stood beside him and looked down the valley. From up here you could see the whole of the bluff road's last two switchbacks, and the bend below them, and a long stretch of the river road beyond the bridge, all of it pale and empty in the early sun. "You were at the lecture range's windows on First-day."

"I was."

"And this is the seventh day."

"It is." Bracken lifted the glass again, looked, and lowered it. Then he said, as if Cael had asked a question, which in a way he had: "The entry they wrote on you at Norhold had one word at its end. Referred. A referral is a letter, in my trade. A letter that has gone up a road gets an answer that comes down one." He turned the glass over in his hands. "I've kept this office for thirteen years. I've never yet seen an answer come down a road that I didn't see coming a minute before it reached the gate. I see no reason to begin now."

"How long do they usually take?"

"Longer than this, for a small question." Bracken put the glass in his coat. "This is not a small question."

They stood together at the high window a while longer, a narrow grey man and a boy with a bad hip, looking at an empty road in the sun. A cart came up out of the trees on the lowest switchback, loaded with hay, a farmer walking at the horse's head. Bracken took the glass out again, and looked, and put it away.

"Hay," he said.

That night Cael wrote it in Hesk's book under the honest floor's costs, which Lira had copied out for Karis three times in capitals and once more for him.

Seventh-day. Bracken at his high window with a ship's glass. Seven days he has watched the road, and he says the question isn't small. I believe him. I have never known him to round a number.

Chapter 5 — Served

The eighth day of the year was a First-day, hot and still, and at the second bell Cael was on the covered walk with a book under his arm and nowhere in particular to be.

The house had found its feet by then. A week was long enough for that. The intake had stopped walking in groups of six and started walking in groups of two. The boards along the walk had filled up with the year's ordinary paper: the research standings, the program's floor hours, the refectory's rota, and a sheet in Ephram's square hand announcing that the captain would hear grievances on Third-day evenings in the common room and would not be held responsible for his answers. The fire-watch boy's slate hung on its nail under the north arch with last night's hours chalked down it in large careful figures, the last of them rubbed out once and made again.

Cael stopped at the slate, because he always did, and then he looked east, because the arch looked east, and saw them.

Three riders, on the last switchback below the gate.

They were coming up at a walk. Two rode a little ahead and to either side, in grey with a badge on the shoulder, and they rode the way men ride who have been told the pace and are keeping it whether it suits the horses or not. The third rode between them. He sat very upright, and across the front of his saddle, strapped tight against the horse's withers so that it could not shift, lay a case of dark leather the length of his forearm.

Couriers trotted. Every courier Cael had ever watched on that road had come up it at a working trot with his eyes on the next bend, because a courier was paid by the day and the road was long. These three walked, and kept step, the way men walk behind something they have been told not to hurry.

He looked up at the records hall. The high window at its north end was empty, and the ship's glass was gone from it. Somewhere inside, a man who had watched that road for eight days had already put the glass in his coat and gone down to his counter.

At the gate the lodge-man came out of his door and stood as straight as he stood for the Chancellor's carriage, and for nothing else. Riders on registry business did not stop for lodge-men. They passed under the arch at the same walk, still in the saddle, and the lodge-man stepped back against the wall with his hat in his hand and let them. They crossed the outer court with their hooves loud on the stones in the heat, and every head on the covered walk turned to follow them, and they went on round the corner of the lecture range toward the records hall as if nobody on the hill had a right to stop them, which was true.

Cael put his book under his other arm and went after them.

He did not run. A boy running across a court after a registry escort would have been a story by noon. He walked fast, at the pace of somebody late for a lecture, and he came round the corner of the lecture range in time to see the third rider dismount at the records-hall steps and unstrap the case from his saddle. The two outriders stayed mounted. They sat their horses at the foot of the steps, one on each side, facing outward.

Cael went past them and up the steps and in. Nobody stopped him. It would not have occurred to him to wait outside.

The records hall was cool after the court, and dim, and very quiet.

Bracken was behind his counter. He had not come down from the window in a hurry; there was no sign on him that he had come down at all. He stood with both hands resting on the counter's edge, a narrow grey man in a grey coat, and when Cael came in he looked at him once and then back at the door.

The rider came in behind Cael with the case under his arm.

On his feet he was a different kind of man from the two outside. He had soft hands and good boots that had not been walked in, and a clerk's grey coat kept very clean, with a small seal of office in dull silver at the collar that Cael did not know. He was perhaps fifty, with thin hair combed close and the careful face of somebody who has set a great many things down on a great many counters and has never once been set down himself. He set the case on the counter and laid his hand on it and waited.

Withrow came in from the inner door thirty seconds later.

She came down the long hall as if she had been sent for about a gutter. Cael had watched her cross courts and corridors for two years and knew the walk as well as he knew Brom's step on a stair, even and unhurried, the walk of a woman who had decided long ago that nothing would ever be allowed to set its pace. With half the hill already talking outside, he understood that she had chosen it on the stair and was holding it now the way a carter holds a nervous horse.

She stopped at the counter beside Bracken, and the officer bowed to her, to a depth that somebody had once measured, and took a card from his coat.

"An instrument of the registry, under seal," he read from the card, in a voice with nothing in it. "For joint service upon the Chancellor of Halcenvane Academy and upon the enrollee of record whom it names, the two together and in their own persons. Service to be acknowledged in both their hands. The seal to stay whole until it is." He lowered the card. "Are both parties present?"

"Both parties are present," said Withrow.

She did not look at Cael. She did not need to. The officer looked at him, once, the way a man checks a figure against the sum he was given, and looked away again.

He unlocked the case with a key from his watch-chain and took out a form first, a single printed sheet with two ruled lines at its foot. Cael had never seen its like. It was headed Acknowledgment of Joint Service, and under the heading there was a paragraph of small type, and under that, two lines.

Withrow signed on the first line. She signed her whole name, slowly, with the officer's pen.

Then she held the pen out to Cael without a word.

He signed beneath her. His hand was quite steady. He noticed that, and wrote it down in his head as a fact, because it surprised him a little.

The officer witnessed both signatures in his own hand, sanded them from a box in the case, folded the form along a crease that was already in it, and sealed it inside the case again. Then he took out the instrument.

It was thick. It lay on the counter in front of the three of them, a sheaf of heavy paper folded once along its length, and across the fold, holding it shut, sat a wafer of grey wax the size of a mark, pressed with a seal Cael had seen before only on the outside of other people's letters. The Compact's.

"Served," said the officer. He bowed to Withrow again, to the same depth, and to Bracken a little less, and to Cael not at all. Then he took up his case and went out. They heard him go down the steps, and a moment later they heard the three horses go away across the court at a walk, and then nothing.

Nobody touched the instrument.

Withrow broke the wax with her thumbnail and read where she stood, and nobody in the hall would have dared to bring her a chair. She read the first leaf once to herself, without a sign. Then she read it again, aloud, for the hall's book: on service, the enrollee must hear it, and the house must be able to say he had.

Cael had never heard the voice she used. Two sentences in, he knew it was not new. It was the oldest she owned. Twenty years of registry windows were in it, a clerk's voice that gives a paper to a room exactly as the paper gives itself and adds nothing, not even breath.

To the Chancellor, Halcenvane Academy, and to the enrollee of record, Caelen Hesk-ward, unclassified, enrolled under the demonstration provision of the assay clause, jointly:

Be it known that the Guilds Compact, by its registry, having convened formal proceedings upon the question of the classification designated SHATTERED and its bearing upon evaluation integrity within chartered institutions, hereby files a formal challenge to enrollment basis against the said enrollment.

The challenge does not allege fraud in the enrollment's execution, nor contest the text of the provision under which it was executed. It asserts that an unclassifiable practitioner's presence within a chartered institution's evaluation architecture presents an evaluation-integrity question which the demonstration provision was not drafted to answer and cannot answer, and petitions the registry for compelled re-evaluation of the enrollee under standard Arbiter protocol, the enrollment to stand or fall upon that evaluation's result.

Proceedings to be convened at the registry seat at Ostrand upon a schedule of one academic year. The respondent institution and the enrollee of record are directed to answer within fourteen days.

Given under the Compact's hand.

She lowered the leaf, and said the last line again without looking at it, in the same level voice.

"Given under the Compact's hand." A pause, no longer than a breath. "I have signed that line myself. Nine hundred times."

The hall stayed quiet. Somewhere below the bluff the escort's hooves went round the first switchback and were gone. Withrow turned the leaf down again, edge to edge with the ones beneath it, and Cael saw her make certain her fingers would not shake before she let them do it.

"Registrar. Three copies under the house's seal: counsel, the enrollee, the reading room. Before dark."

"Before dark," said Bracken.

She turned to Cael. She did not change her voice to do it; the registry voice was the one that would hold, and she meant to keep it until she was alone.

"They've found a new door into the old question," she said. "Go and tell Karis. She'll be furious for about a minute and useful for a fortnight, and I'd like the minute spent before she has the paper, not after."

He took the library stair two at a time, all four flights, with the hip reminding him at every landing that it had been promised a quieter week.

The door at the top was shut. The card was in its brass holder. The new lock was locked.

He knocked, and the key turned on the inside, and Karis opened the door with a pen in her hand and ink on the side of her thumb and the look of somebody who has been interrupted in the middle of a sentence and means to go back to it.

Then she saw his face, and the look went.

"What," she said.

"A registry instrument. Under escort. Served jointly on Withrow and me in the records hall ten minutes ago." He made himself say it in order, the way she would want it. "A challenge to the enrollment basis. Fourteen days to answer. Withrow read the first page aloud. Bracken is making you a copy now."

Karis stood in the doorway and did not move.

He told her the first page. He had it nearly whole; he had been listening the way he listened to anything that would have to be written down later. Does not allege fraud. Nor contest the text. Evaluation integrity. Compelled re-evaluation under standard Arbiter protocol. Stand or fall. She listened to all of it without interrupting, with her pen still in her hand, and when he had finished she looked past him, down the narrow stair.

"Standard Arbiter protocol," she said. "Those words? Exactly those?"

"Exactly those."

She was quiet. He knew what she was seeing, because he was seeing it too. Standard protocol meant a station: a frame in a stone room, a registry officer at its side, a practitioner standing in it while the frame read him. It was how every Path on the continent had been declared since before the registry kept books. The frame read the Path and named it, and set a tier against it, and a rank inside the tier, and the officer wrote down what the frame had said, and that was a person's classification for life. It was how Lira had been declared, and Brom, and Karis herself. It was how the frame at Denvash had been asked, on the morning of his Kindling, what he was, and had answered with one word in brackets and nothing else at all.

The demonstration provision had never asked a frame anything. That was the whole of why it held him.

"They read the hearing," she said. "Every page of it. Every page we won on." Her voice was quite level. "And then they went away and wrote a paper that doesn't touch a single one of them."

She stood a moment longer. Then she was finished with being angry, or had put it somewhere he could not see, and she turned to the table and tore the bottom off a sheet of paper and wrote on it standing, fast, in her finding hand.

"My assistant's in the lower reading room," she said, and gave him the slip. "Give her that."

He read it on the stair going down, because she would have expected him to.

Bracken's press: the four rulings on the clause. Ask him nicely. — The code, all three volumes, the hall's copy, not the library's; the library's second volume is missing a gathering. — The certified Greyvane transcript, on my shelf in the common room, grey card, my initials on the spine. — Tea. — Tell her she won't see her bed.

The assistant was where Karis had said, at a table under the window in the lower reading room with the district digests stacked beside her. She read the slip once and gave it back to him, which he had not expected, and stood, and pushed in her chair.

"The tea first," she said. "She thinks better with it. Then the rest, in her order."

"She says you won't see your bed."

"She always says that," said the assistant, and went out past him at a fast walk. He heard her break into a run on the covered walk outside, and suspected it was the first time she had run anywhere on the hill since the intake.

Nobody told the bluff. Nobody needed to.

An escort had come through the gate at the second bell without dismounting, and ridden to the records hall, and ridden away again without the thing it had brought, and every person on the covered walk had watched it go by and could do that sum unaided. By the noon meal the refectory was full of people sitting close together over their soup and not eating it. Somebody with a cousin who swept the records hall had it that the thing was a summons. A little after the fourth bell a man from one of the Ostrand broadsides was at the gate lodge, asking the lodge-man what had come up the hill that morning, and the lodge-man was telling him that it had been a fine morning for the time of year, and that he had the greatest respect for the press.

Cael sat on the records-hall steps in the heat and waited, because the others would come there, and they did.

Brom came first, from the direction of the kitchens, with a wedge of cheese wrapped in a cloth and an apple in each coat pocket, none of which anybody had asked for. He sat down on the step below and began cutting the cheese with his clasp-knife into four, though there were only two of them.

Lira came a quarter of an hour behind him, still taped at one wrist, with the tape off the other trailing from her fist. "Rooke stopped the drill," she said, and sat. "He walked across the whole floor to my cross and said Records hall. Now. and gave my place to the Force." She took the quarter of cheese Brom held up to her. "So. Tell me."

He told them what he had told Karis. Lira listened with her eyes on the court. Brom ate.

"Fourteen days," said Lira, when he had finished.

"From this morning."

"She built the whole continent on a wall in one term." Lira took one of Brom's apples and bit into it. "Fourteen days is a holiday."

Behind them the records-hall door opened and Bracken came out onto the top step with a sheet of paper in his hand. It was green: a pale grey-green, like the underside of a willow leaf. He held it out at arm's length, away from himself, the way a man holds a thing he has found on his doorstep and is not yet sure is not alive.

"This was on my counter," he said, "when I came back from the press with the rulings. Stamped. Countersigned. In order." He read from it. "Research standing: floor and archive hours, by application. Applicant: K. Dellenmoor. Hours: the records hall, this night, from the eighth bell until the work is done. Purpose: the house's answer to an instrument served this day. Received and entered." He lowered it. "The stamp is the assessment wing's. The hand on the received line is the wing's. The form was built in the recess for an office that had never had a use for it until this morning." He looked down at the three of them on his steps. "Somebody has been expecting us."

Across the court, behind the assessment wing's tall windows, the counter would be open, and a man would be at a copying table with his head down, rising when the queue moved to take the next sheet.

Bracken folded the green sheet and put it in his coat, beside the brass glass.

"The house's answer goes on the board within the hour," he said. "The Chancellor has written it. It is one line long. I'm told that's deliberate."

Ephram found them there a little after, coming round the corner of the lecture range with the captain's file under his arm and the green tape trailing. He stopped at the foot of the steps and looked up at the three of them, and at the cheese, and at the shut door behind them.

"The cohort's asking me," he said. "Forty of them, in the yard, all at once. I'm the captain. They think captains know things." He shifted the file. "What do I tell them?"

"Whatever goes up on the board," said Cael. "Nothing more."

"And when they ask what the board means?"

"Tell them it means what it says."

Ephram considered this. "I'll tell them that," he said. "And then I'll tell them again, slower, because they'll think I've left a bit out." He looked at Cael a moment longer than he needed to, with the same look he had given the empty floor in wing three, and then he turned round and went back toward the yard, already raising his voice to somebody about the proper place to stand when the captain was talking.

It went up at the fifth bell, on the covered walk's middle board, under the north arch, in Bracken's own hand. Half the house came to read it and went away disappointed, because it was not the kind of line you could make anything out of.

Halcenvane Academy has been served, and will answer within the time allowed.

By the sixth bell the man from the broadsides had copied it into his notebook at the gate lodge, and was riding down the hill with it as fast as a hired horse would take him. Cael watched him go from the north wall. The two coats at the foot of the road watched him go too. It was the first time in a week that either of them had turned his head.

Bracken's boy brought the enrollee's copy up to the residence at the seventh bell, in a grey folder under the house's seal, and Cael took it to his window and laid it on the sill and opened it at the first page.

He had heard it read. Now he read it, all of it, every leaf, once straight through from the address to the attestation. He did not stop to think about any of it. That would come later, at the long table, with the others. This was only the first reading, the one a man does to find out how long a thing is and where its weight sits, the way you lift a sack before you decide how to carry it.

Then he turned back to the first page and left it lying there face up on the sill, with the evening coming in over it through the open window.

The fountain ran below in the court. Somebody downstairs had given up on the song and was practising scales on a whistle instead, which was worse. Across the court and over the roof of the east range he could see the long row of the records hall's windows. In the last of them, at the north end, a lamp had been lit already, though the sun was not yet down.

He took out Hesk's book and Hesk's steel pen. The words had been ready since the library stair, and they went down clean.

They filed. After the hearing I won, and the inspection, and a tournament that ran out of numbers for me, they've gone back to the shelf for one more way to ask. Fine. Their text has lost to ours before. Karis has the code open already. Note the date. The season's open.

He sanded it, gave it a full minute by Hesk's clock, and closed the book.

Then he went over what he had written, with the book shut.

He had meant every word. He meant them still. A year ago he had been a boy on a provision, alive because somebody kept writing it down, and a hearing, a panel and the continent's oldest contest had all tried their instruments on him and found they could not make him fit, and every time the text had held him. He had no reason to think this text would not.

But he noticed something, sitting at the window with the book closed on his knee, and he made himself look straight at it, because noticing things was the one work he had never been able to stop doing.

It was the voice. Withrow's registry voice, reading the first page aloud in the records hall. He had thought, while she read, that she was using it because it was the right instrument for service. He thought now that she had been using it because it was the only one she had that would not shake.

He had never once heard Withrow need a voice that would not shake.

Down in the court a lamp-boy went past toward the records hall with his long pole over his shoulder. At the end of the east range, one after another, the records hall's windows were coming alight.

Cael put the book in his coat, and took the folder from the sill, and went down to join them.

Chapter 6 — The Records Hall

The fire-watch kept an oil book. Every lamp lit on the hill after the tenth bell went into it, by building and by hour, so that the bursar could see at the year's end where the house had burned its money in the dark. Bracken signed it himself every morning, and had done for thirteen years, and in all that time the records hall had never once had a line in it.

At a little past the eighth bell he took the book down from its hook by the side door, opened it on the counter at the night's page, and wrote in his small upright hand.

Records hall. Lamps late. On the registrar's authority, and at his charge.

Then he hung it back on its hook and went to light the lamps.

There were six along the long table on iron stands, two on the counter, and one over the door of the locked press. When he had lit them all the hall was a room Cael had never seen: warm in the middle and black at the edges, the tall windows gone blind, the long table laid down the floor like a road with lamps along it.

Bracken took its head, nearest his counter, with the registry code's three bound volumes stacked at his elbow, spines toward him, and the four bound rulings from the press beside them. Karis took the near side, with her copy of the instrument open and her notebook open beside it and her pens in a row along the table's edge like a surgeon's knives. Her assistant sat at her elbow writing whatever she was told until the tenth bell. Just before she was sent to bed she put up her hand, as if the long table were a lecture hall, and asked the registrar a question.

"Why does a code need a word like discretion at all? Isn't the whole point of a code that nobody gets to choose?"

Bracken considered her over his spectacles for long enough that she went pink.

"Because the men who write codes can't see every case coming," he said, "and they know they can't. Discretion is the room they leave for the cases they couldn't see. Most nights it's the kindest word in the book." He looked down at the instrument. "It depends who's standing in the room."

Karis wrote something in the margin of her own copy. Then she sent the girl to bed, and the girl went protesting in a whisper all the way to the door.

Cael had the foot of the table and the observation notebook. Karis had asked him to stay. She wanted the person the paper described sitting in the room while it was read, she said, so that she could look up from a clause and check it against him.

The fourth chair was the counsel's.

She had come up the bluff road at the ninth bell in a hired chaise from Ostrand, with one bag, and Cael had never seen her before. The inspection had brought a counsel up the hill once, a woman who talked by every account from the bridge to the gate and signed for her chests with a face like a cat in a bath; she had been the Compact's. This was the house's own. In eleven years nothing she had advised the house had ever carried her name; that was her price, and the house had paid it gladly. People on the bluff called her counsel and nothing else.

She was small and grey, with very straight shoulders, and she read with a short steel rule of the kind a joiner uses, laid under each line so that her eye could not run ahead. She did not talk while she read. When she talked, it was in short sentences with nothing left over at their ends.

Withrow did not sit at all. She was in and out all evening on the stair from her office, and each time she came down she left something on the table, a pot of tea once, a folder once, and went back up without a word. Near the tenth bell she came down with a small book in brown cloth.

It was a registry book; Cael knew the size and the colour. Every registrar on the continent had been issued one at the start of his service, the procedures volume of the code in a pocket copy for carrying on circuit. Bracken had one in his coat. Withrow's had been carried further.

She opened it where it fell open, near the middle, and laid it beside Bracken's great third volume at the same page.

The page was chapter fourteen, and its margins were full: dates and the names of districts, in pencil and in ink, in a hand that was hers and not quite hers, younger and quicker. One clause had been underlined twice. Cael counted the lines before he read the words. The upper was black and thin and dead straight, drawn against a rule. The lower was brown ink faded to rust, and it wandered, and beside it in the margin stood a bracket with nothing written inside it.

"It was a kind word once," said Withrow, from the table's head. She had seen him counting. "Discretion. When I was new I took it for leave to be merciful."

She came down the table and laid a fingertip in the margin, beside the line. It did not tremble. Cael had expected it to.

"At its discretion," she read. "Part two. Suspension of practitioner status pending review, such review to be initiated by the registry at its discretion." She tapped the black line. "My second year at the registry. With a rule. Very neat." She moved the fingertip to the brown one. "Nine years later, in a coach on a bad road home from a district I'd rather not name, with no rule and not much light. By then I'd seen what it does."

"What does it do?" said Karis.

"Nothing. That's what it does." Withrow straightened. "It names nobody who must begin the review, and no day by which it must be begun. So nobody begins it." She looked at the faded bracket. "A penalty is a thing done to you, and then it is over. This is a place you are put, and the door has no one assigned to open it." She looked up the table. "Registrar. Is there a date anywhere in that chapter? A limit of days? Anything at all that runs out?"

Bracken went down the chapter a line at a time with his finger under the print, and nobody hurried him.

"Not one," he said.

Withrow closed the brown book, put it under her arm, and went back up the stair at her ordinary pace.

For two years his whole place on the bluff had lived because somebody kept writing it down: a stamp, a renewal, a line in the enrollment book in Bracken's upright hand, every one of them a thing an officer was obliged to do on a day the code named. The provision was alive because it had dates in it. Part two had none. It was the same machine run backward, a thing that stayed done because nobody was ever obliged to undo it. Cael realized he had never once thought of a date as a kindness, and that it was the kindest thing on any form he had ever signed.

Cael had counted the instrument at the start of the night, while the others were still arranging their papers.

He began with the three schedules at the back, because they were the longest things in it. Every one ran past a page, and the paragraphs in front of them were short, a few lines each; only the ninth ran long. Then he went through every leaf with a pencil and a stroke in the notebook's margin for each word he was watching, and went through it twice, because a count done once is a guess.

Discretion, nine times. Evidence, three, and two of those three inside the phrase no evidence is required to be adduced. Fraud, once, in the second paragraph, in a sentence that existed only to say there was none. Eight citations of the code by chapter and section; the convening's own minute twice, by date; and nothing else. No ruling. No precedent. No witness.

Then he counted what it was made of. Nineteen leaves of heavy cream paper, written on one side, with the registry's mark pressed into each corner. Thirty-seven numbered paragraphs. On the first leaf it named him as the registry always did, Caelen Hesk-ward, a name nobody who knew him had ever used.

Schedule two was a list of himself, and he read it slowest. It was laid out in the grammar of declarations, as every practitioner's file on the continent was, with a heading for Path, a heading for tier and a heading for rank. Under Path stood the one bracketed word the frame at Denvash had given him. Under tier, a ruled line with nothing above it. Under rank, the same. It was a form built to hold an answer, holding the shape of a question instead.

The file's standing entries ran down beneath, in order: his Kindling at Denvash, the Greyvane hearing and its finding, the provision with the stamp and its renewals, the tournament's entry with all eleven of its words. And between the hearing and the provision, given its full title as if it were the most ordinary line on the page, sat the one he had known was on his file since the inspection year and had never once seen written down.

Suppression-Advisory Watch, Priority Level 4.

No paragraph leaned on it or so much as named it. It sat in its schedule like a stone in a field that the plough has been driven round. He looked at it a long moment and went on, because it was not what the night was for, and Karis was watching him across the lamps, and he did not want her to have to decide whether to ask.

At the foot of the last leaf, above the seal's impression, in type no larger than the rest, stood the attestation. Given under the Compact's hand. Under it, smaller: For the petitioner, the procurator of record, and a name.

Bracken did not know it. He said so when Cael passed him the leaf. He knew every procurator who had stood before a registry seat in this district in thirteen years, and most in the two districts beside it.

"Which is information," he said, and handed it back.

Cael ruled a line under his column. A man building a case writes evidence on every page, because one day he will be standing in front of a seat with his evidence in his hands. This man had written discretion.

They don't expect to prove anything, he wrote under the line. They expect to be agreed with. Then he passed the column down to Karis. She read it, and laid it with her notes, and he understood that he had done a piece of the night's real work.

The counsel began at the end.

She turned the instrument face down, turned it over again from the back, and laid her rule under the first line of the thirty-seventh paragraph. Then she climbed. Thirty-six, thirty-five, the rule moving up the page a line at a time like a man going up a ladder he does not trust, and twice she stopped and made a note. When she reached the first leaf she closed the paper and set the rule across it.

"Why backward?" said Cael.

She looked at him down the table as though he had asked her fee, and seemed to decide he could have this one free.

"The front of a paper is the story the writer tells you so you'll agree with him," she said. "The back is what he wants. If I read his story first, I've half agreed before I find out what for. So I find out what for." She tapped the rule. "Then I read the story and watch him build it."

Bracken had laid the four bound rulings in a row while she spoke.

They read them before midnight, Bracken reading the headings and Karis the findings, the counsel listening with her eyes shut and her rule across her knees.

The first was the longest. A river house far to the south had enrolled a ferryman's daughter whose station had taken a year to settle on what her Path was, and a richer house upriver had gone to law to say that a girl with no classification on her papers had no business being taught while she waited for one. The finding was a dozen lines. The clause said what a house might do; the house had done it; the girl stayed until the station read her, and after.

Cael found he had stopped writing.

He had known about the clause for two years and about the rulings in Bracken's press for nearly as long, and it had never once occurred to him that there were people in them. A girl in some hall in the south, a long time ago, waiting a year for a frame to make up its mind while two houses argued over whether she could be taught in the meantime. He wondered whether she had kept a book, and what had become of her, and knew nobody had written it down, because findings had no room for afterward.

"Her name's on it?" he said.

"Her initials, and the house's." Karis read them out. They meant nothing to anybody at the table. He wrote them at the edge of the page anyway, small.

The other three went quickly: a mason's guild that had put an apprentice into its school by demonstration and been challenged on the form of its panel, and two guild cases so old that the paper had gone brown and soft and the parties had worn down to the names of their trades. All four sustained. Bracken closed each cover as Karis finished and laid it back in its row.

"Every one of them went at the clause," said the counsel, opening her eyes, "and the clause threw every one of them out. Greyvane went at it too, by another road, and the same thing happened." She picked up her rule. "Whoever drafted tonight's paper has read that shelf."

"So they didn't go at it," said Karis.

"So they didn't go at it." The counsel turned the instrument to its first leaf. "And they told no story at the front. Four sentences of recital, on a paper this heavy. I'd expect forty. The front is where a drafter usually gives something away without noticing, and in twenty-six years I've won most of what I've won there." She laid the rule down. "This one knew somebody would read him from the back. He left me nothing to find."

Karis took the first finding standing, as she took anything that was going to be minuted, with the instrument's second paragraph under one hand and the Greyvane transcript open under the other.

"No fraud," she said. "Listen." She read it aloud, the same sentence Withrow had read standing that morning, the one that alleged no fraud at all. She lifted her hand from the transcript. "Last year the broadsides sold a story a week about a trick: a hidden Path, a bought clerk, a staged hearing. Every one of those stories ends at a door Greyvane locked on the record, and this paper hasn't so much as knocked on one. They've read the record. They know which doors are locked." She sat. "That's the first finding. They spend nothing on ground they could lose."

The counsel took the second, in the voice of somebody reading out tomorrow's weather.

"Paragraph six." The rule went under it. "The provision by which the enrollment was made is acknowledged to be valid, and to have survived in law the standardization directive. Neither is put in issue." She lifted the rule. "I came up this hill expecting to spend the year proving exactly that. Whether the clause is still law. Whether the directive killed it. Whether a house may still enroll by demonstration on a clause out of the founding text. They've signed it for me, under their own seal, in the sixth paragraph of their first paper." She set the rule on the leaf. "Nobody has ever done that to me before."

"Is that good?" said Cael.

The counsel looked at him.

"When a man gives you the field," she said, "look at what he has kept for himself."

Karis had already turned the page.

He watched her read the seventh paragraph. Her finger went along the first line and the second and stopped, and her whole body went still around it. He knew that stillness; he had seen it over a shelf at Greyvane, and over the founding articles upstairs, and over a charter at Norhold, and every time it had meant that she had found the thing a page was built to hide. This time he did not count it. He watched her finger, and waited for it to move.

She did not read it out. She turned the instrument round on the table so that it faced the rest of them, put her finger on the paragraph, and took the finger away.

The counsel laid her rule under it and read it aloud.

7. The petitioner notes, and adopts as its own, the advisory entered in the prior year by an evaluator of the Compact upon the fielding clause of the tournament charter, which reads in full: "The clause says what it says. The enrollment is lawful on its face and adjudicated at public record. If the Compact wishes practitioners of this kind not to compete, it should write different rules — not misread the ones it has."

Nobody spoke.

"The clause says what it says," said Karis at last. "I said that. On the bench under the thorn at the first bend, the morning the entry went down the hill. It says what it says all the same. I said it to you, Cael." She laid her palms on the wood, one either side of the paper. "And somebody said it to them, in writing, a year ago. The Archmarshal. Vastin. You told us at Norhold there'd been three sentences of advisory, and none of us ever saw them. There they are."

"And they've taken his advice," said the counsel.

"They've taken his advice." Karis's face changed then.

Cael had watched that face for three years. He had seen it angry and amused and bored and cold, and once or twice, very late, tired enough to be kind, and at Norhold in the moment the stoppage was called. He had never seen it like this. She was looking at a paragraph on cream paper as if the paper had moved.

"He told them how," she said. "Write different rules, he said, don't misread the old ones. So here are the new ones, written, and when the seat asks them by what right, they'll point at him. The honest man's own sentence, for a warrant." She took her hands off the table. "Write it down. This is where I was frightened. The seventh paragraph. Not the fourteenth chapter, not whatever's coming. This."

"Written," said the counsel.

She had a page at her elbow now that had not been there when the night began, headed in a small exact hand: Halcenvane: the Compact's petition. Working minute. Privileged. She wrote Karis's sentence on it word for word, with the time by the hall's clock, and blotted it.

Cael put it in the observation notebook as well, since word for word was the only way that notebook took anything. Then he wrote the other thing under it. It had come while Karis was speaking, plainly, like a sum totting itself up at the foot of a column.

Vastin, in the room full of clocks: the people who want this to stop are not going to use official channels much longer. I have never held a more official thing than this paper. Nineteen leaves, a seal, an escort at a walk, a form of joint service I had never seen. So either he was wrong about the channels, or this is the last thing they'll send through one.

And the warrant on it is his. He warned me in a room where nothing was written down. They answered in a room where everything is, and signed it with his name.

He read the two lines over.

He was not frightened. Not yet. He was something nearer cold. It was the feeling he had had on the morning of his Kindling at Denvash, standing in a frame that had nothing to say about him and was perfectly calm about it. The fright would come later, he knew, at the window, in the dark, where there was time for it; not here, where there was work.

He looked up, and Karis was looking at him across the lamps.

"Go on," he said. "There's more of it. You said so."

"There's a great deal more of it," said Karis, and turned the instrument back round to face herself, and found the ninth paragraph with her finger. "And none of it gets any better."

Chapter 7 — Corridor

It was Bracken who knew the phrase first, and he knew it from the wrong side.

Karis had the ninth paragraph under her finger, the longest in the instrument, and had read it out once, and the four of them sat with it. It said that an unclassifiable practitioner inside a chartered house's evaluations raised a question of evaluation integrity. It said that the demonstration provision had been drafted for practitioners whose classification was only pending, and not for one who had none to wait for, and so could neither foresee that question nor settle it. And it said that the question therefore fell to the registry itself, under its general charge over the soundness of its own evaluations.

"Evaluation integrity," said Karis. "I've never once met that phrase in a hearing. Where does it live?"

"In the second volume," said Bracken, "in a part nobody opens unless something has gone wrong with a frame."

He did not reach for the volume. He sat with his hands folded on the table, looking into the lamp in front of him, and when he spoke again it was in the voice of a man remembering a particular day.

"I filed one once. My fourth year in the office. The district station in Ostrand had a frame that took to reading every Stone who stood in it a rank higher than he was. Not by much. Enough. A month of Stones went out of that station with ranks on their papers they hadn't earned, and nobody noticed until a quarryman's boy came up this hill with a certificate that said Rank Four and couldn't lift what a Rank Two lifts." He turned his folded hands over. "I wrote it up under the integrity provisions, because that's what they're for. They took the frame off its floor and tested it for a fortnight, and found a seam in the casing that let the damp in, and mended it, and read every Stone of that month over again. Then the frame went back on its floor and read true." He looked down the table at Cael. "That's an integrity question, in that volume. A frame that has drifted. You take it off the floor and test it until it reads true."

By then the second volume lay open in front of the counsel. She had reached across Bracken for it while he talked, and found the place, and now she went down the sections with her rule.

"Twelve sections," she said. "Frames. Stations. Assessors suspected of being bought. Panels whose records argue with themselves. Instruments, or the people who keep instruments." She lifted the rule. "I've looked tonight for the case where somebody turned these sections round to point at the man standing in the frame instead of the frame. There isn't one. This is new."

"So they've stopped asking whether a house may teach me," said Cael.

"They've stopped asking that entirely. They gave it away in the sixth paragraph." The counsel closed the volume on her rule to keep the place. "Now they ask whether the registry can read you. Everybody at this table knows the answer. It has been in your file since your Kindling."

"So I'm not wrong," said Cael. "I'm the frame."

"You are the frame." The counsel's voice did not change at all. "And a frame that will not read true comes off the floor."

Cael sat with that. All his life frames had been the things that failed to read him, and he had stood in front of them and been the question they could not answer. Now the paper had turned it round. He was the instrument on the bench, and they meant to open his casing and look for the seam that let the damp in, as Bracken's men had done with the station in Ostrand. He was not afraid of their looking. He was afraid of what they would write when they found no seam at all, because a frame with nothing wrong in it that still would not read was not a thing the second volume had a section for. It was a thing chapter fourteen had.

Karis had turned to the back while the counsel spoke. She had marked the thirty-fourth paragraph with a slip when the counsel first read the paper upward, and she turned to it at once and read it in a voice with nothing added.

34. That the enrollee be compelled to re-evaluation under standard Arbiter protocol, and that the enrollment stand or fall upon that evaluation's result.

She said nothing about it. It had been written so that nothing needed saying.

The counsel turned in her chair then and looked down the table at Cael as if, for the first time that night, he were the subject of it and not the paper.

"What have you got there?"

He turned the observation notebook round and slid it up to her. She looked down the column: nineteen leaves, thirty-seven paragraphs and three schedules; nine discretions to three evidences and one fraud, in the negative; eight provisions cited, two minutes, no rulings and no witnesses. She read it twice, which he had not seen her do with anything else.

"Do you know the difference, in front of a seat," she said, "between a description and an evaluation?"

"A description says what I did. An evaluation says what I am."

"Good. Their whole case will be that your floor is a description: a panel, a figure, a day, witnesses, nothing more. Mine will be that it is an evaluation, and the oldest kind, older than any frame, and I'll make it as well as anybody living could make it." She slid the notebook back. "Then the seat will choose. You've counted how many times they wrote the word it'll choose with." She tapped the column at nine. "Go on counting. Bring me a column like this every week until it's over. A count is evidence. Indignation never was."

The third volume lay shut at Bracken's elbow, and for a while after the counsel had finished he left it there.

Then he drew it to him, opened it at a place he did not need to look for, laid a strip of plain paper under the first line, and put on his spectacles. Cael had heard him read a hundred pages aloud and never one like this; there was nothing in the voice at all, because Bracken would not let there be.

"Registry code. Evaluation procedures. Chapter fourteen." He did not look up. "Where an evaluation conducted under standard Arbiter protocol returns no valid classification, the following shall apply in sequence. One. Nullification of any enrollment, sponsorship, or standing predicated upon the evaluand's practitioner status. Two. Suspension of practitioner status pending review, such review to be initiated by the registry at its discretion. Three."

He stopped. The next word was one he had read a thousand times and never once had cause to say, and Cael watched him find it heavier to lift than to look at.

"Asset-restriction. Section fourteen, part nine. The registry may restrict, freeze, or hold in abeyance any standing, record, sponsorship, endorsement, travel credential, or institutional relationship attaching to an unclassified person, pending resolution of practitioner status."

He took the spectacles off and held them by one arm.

"Clerks have a joke in their first year," he said, "that chapter fourteen is the only page in the code nobody has ever had to stamp. I've stamped every other page in that book. Fees. Transfers. The frame that read Stones high." He looked at the three numbered steps. "Never this one. It wants a frame that reads nothing at all, and frames don't."

He looked up the table at Cael.

"And now one's sitting at my table," he said. "Somebody, a long time ago, sat in a room like this one and imagined you, and wrote down what we should do with you, in three steps, and filed it, and went home to his supper." He put the spectacles back on. "I've always thought of the code as a thing written by careful men. I'd never thought before tonight about what they were careful of."

Withrow had come back down while he read. Cael had not heard her on the stair. She was simply there, behind Bracken's chair, with the brown book under her arm and one hand on the chair's back.

"That's what the code calls it," she said. "Let me tell you what it looks like from the morning after."

She came round the end of the table into the light and spoke to Cael, and to nobody else.

"The morning after it's entered, a practitioner goes down to the ferry as he goes every week, and holds out his pass, and the ferryman has had a letter. A short one, very polite, in the plainest form. The pass is held in abeyance. The ferryman is sorry. The ferryman has a licence of his own and a family to feed." Her voice did not rise at all. "So he goes up to his guild hall, where they've drunk with him for twenty years, and they've had a letter too. It tells them their association with him is under restriction, and the master reads those two words and understands that his own name goes on the next letter if he so much as nods to the man in the street. So he goes to the records office to see his own file and argue with it, and the clerk tells him it's sealed. Kept, every page, perfectly safe, and nobody may open it. Not he. Not anyone he pays. Not anyone who might stand up somewhere and say what's in it on his behalf." She paused. "And every house that ever put its name beside his gets a letter. This house would get one. After that, every question anybody asked about him would reach us already answered."

She looked at him steadily.

"It's expulsion that follows you," said Withrow. "You can walk out of a town. You can't walk out of the post. It's waiting at the next town, and the one after, and nobody is obliged ever to begin the review that would stop it." She took the brown book from under her arm and held it in both hands. "Twice in my registry years I put my name to one. The first I'd sign again tomorrow; he had done worse than the registry ever learned. The second had a daughter." She looked at the book and not at them. "She came to my counter every week for a year to ask whether the review had begun. Every week I told her the truth, which was that nobody had begun it and nothing in the code obliged anybody to. And every week she thanked me, and went home." A pause. "I have never forgotten her name. Put that down."

"Noted," said the counsel, and wrote it, and did not write the name, because none had been given.

Withrow stood a moment longer. Then she laid her hand on Bracken's shoulder, briefly, which Cael had never in two years seen her do to anybody, and went back up the stair.

Bracken took a card out of his coat.

It was the registry's pocket calendar for the year, printed small on stiff card, every day in its own square. Cael had watched him take it out a hundred times across his counter to settle a question about a fee, and put it back without looking at anybody. He laid it under the lamp now and took up his pen. When the weight on the table had grown too great to look at, Bracken had reached for the one thing on any paper that weighed exactly what it weighed, which was its dates.

He made three marks without a word and turned the card round to Karis.

"The first," she read. "The eighth. The twenty-second."

"Dated the first day of the year," said Bracken. "The morning of convocation. Somebody a week's road from here pressed that wax while the Chancellor stood on her platform telling this house to be what its papers say it is. I don't suppose they knew. I don't suppose it matters." He touched the second mark. "Served this morning. Seven days on a road the post does in three, at a walk, with three horses and a man in the middle who'd been told the pace. It wasn't sent to arrive. It was sent to be watched arriving. I watched it for a full minute from my window, and so did the gate, and so did the coats at the foot of the hill."

"And the twenty-second," said Karis.

"Fourteen from service. The code's plain about that much, for once." He laid the pen across the card. "By close of business on the twenty-second our answer lies on the seat's table in Ostrand. Not the twenty-third. On the twenty-third the seat's clerk writes three words in his docket, respondent made default, and in thirteen years I have never seen a seat take those three words back for anybody's lame horse." He looked round the table. "Counsel."

"Minuted," said the counsel.

Bracken put the card away in his coat beside the brass glass.

The hall's clock struck somewhere in the dark at the far end of the long room. Cael had stopped counting bells before midnight and did not know which this was. The lamps had burned down to their last third and gone orange, and the four of them sat in a small close island of light with the tall windows blind on every side. Bracken got up and went down the table with his trimmer, turning each wick a little higher as he passed it, and came back, and sat.

Karis had been writing on small slips of paper.

Cael had watched her do it without knowing what they were for. While Bracken marked his squares she had torn a sheet into six strips and written a single word on each in her finding hand. Now she laid them out on the table in a row, from her own end toward Bracken's, like stepping stones across a stream.

Executed. Valid. Integrity. Re-evaluate. Nothing. Fourteen.

She did not explain them. She touched each in turn and said only its word, and the table, which had spent the whole night on every one of them, needed no more. At the fifth her finger stayed.

"Nobody will argue that one," she said. "Not them, not us. A frame at Denvash had nothing to say about him, and every office since has copied the same nothing into its books." She moved on to the sixth, and lifted her hand.

"Bracken would carry a paper like this," she said. "So would I, if it came across my desk in order. So would every honest clerk between here and the seat, and every one of them would be right to, because there isn't a lie in it anywhere, and no villain either. Look for the trick all night and you'll come up empty, and the end is still the end. It was the end the morning they sealed it."

She looked down at the six slips.

"It's not a question. It's a corridor. Every door in it is real law, and every door opens one way."

The counsel wrote it down, slowly, every word. Bracken's spectacles stayed in his hand. Above them, through the ceiling, a board creaked once, the sound of somebody who has stood still a long time shifting her weight at last.

From the foot of the stair, where none of them had heard her come down again, Withrow said, "The house will answer."

"The house will answer," said Karis. "Because the other choice has its own word in the docket, and the word is fled, and this house is named on that paper, and I won't have fled written anywhere near it while I live here." She swept the six slips into one hand and tucked them into the back of her notebook. "I'll have bones on it in four days. And when the seat reads it, the seat will go through it with a pen and find nothing to mark. If the end's already fixed, I still want our tracks in the record, every step of them exactly where the code says a step goes."

She drew a clean sheet toward her and wrote a heading and ruled a line under it, and when she spoke again it came out sideways, to the paper, with the pen still moving, as if the words had got ahead of her and she was only following them down.

"There's one more thing in it. I can't place it."

They waited, and the pen stopped.

"That clause is why he's never stood in a station since Denvash," she said, to the heading and not to him. "It's never once asked a frame anything. It keeps him on a floor in front of people, where no Arbiter ever comes." She underlined the heading. "Every paper they've sent up this hill has broken itself on that clause. This one hands it back to us whole and asks for one thing only. A station. The provision doesn't interest them at all. They're trying to move him back inside the instrument."

She kept the pen on the line she had drawn.

"I don't know why that distinction feels important. Noting it."

She turned to the inside of her notebook's front cover. Over two years Cael had watched a few lines gather there that belonged to no case: the fielding clause, a line about the squad rule, a few words copied from the founding articles of a charter she had promised herself not to open until the cold term. She wrote the new one under them, small, and closed the cover, and was back at her heading before the ink had dried.

Cael copied her sentence into the observation notebook and gave it a question mark in the margin. She would answer it in her own time. She always did.

Go up, Karis said a little after, without lifting her pen. There's nothing left tonight that you can count.

So he went out into the court with his copy under his arm. The fountain was the only sound on the hill. On his way across he looked, as he always looked, at the assessment wing, and at the far end of its long front, on the ground floor, behind the counter's window, one lamp was burning. At that hour, in a wing where nobody had business before the third bell. He stood in the court and did not let himself guess what the man at the copying table was making. Whatever it was, it would be made properly, and it would arrive without a note.

The residence front was dark except for one window, and he went up the stair toward it.

It was the common room, and it was not empty.

Brom was at the table. There was a pot of tea on the hob of the banked hearth, and from the look of the hearth he had been keeping it hot for hours, feeding the embers a little whenever they sank. There were cups on the table. Four, set out in a row with their handles all turned the same way, and the fourth stood in front of the empty chair at the table's end, where Karis always sat because the lamp fell best there.

Lira was in the window seat with her knees drawn up and the red drill-book open against them, and she had not turned a page in a long while.

They looked at him when he came in. Neither of them asked anything. He understood, standing in the doorway with the copy under his arm, that they had been sitting up for hours, and that it was not for him.

Karis came up a little after. He heard her step on the stair and moved out of the doorway, and she stopped on the threshold with ink to the second knuckle of both hands and her notebook against her chest.

He watched her count the room. She did it all at once, as she counted anything: a lamp lit at an hour no lamp should be, a fire kept in that should have been let die, two people awake with no work to do, a drill-book open and unread, four cups with their handles turned. He watched her reach the fourth cup, in front of her own chair, and stop.

She went to the table and held the cup while Brom filled it, and drank half of it standing.

"Four days," she told the room, and finished the cup, and set it back in front of her chair.

She went to the stair. On the first step she stopped with one hand on the rail, and did not turn round.

"Thank you for the tea," she said to the stairwell, and went up, and they heard her door.

Brom looked at the empty cup in front of her chair.

"She counted the cups," he said.

"She counted us," said Lira, and put the drill-book face down on the window seat.

"Well," she said. "Tell us."

He sat in Karis's chair because it was nearest, and Brom pushed a cup across to him, and he told them.

All of it had taken nine hours, and he did not give them all of it. He gave them what had moved the table. The frame at the Ostrand station that read every Stone too high, and what the integrity sections were for. The honest man's three sentences, quoted whole and made a warrant. The ferryman's daughter whose initials he had written down. Chapter fourteen in Bracken's voice. The ferry pass, and the guild hall, and the daughter at Withrow's counter every week for a year. Three marks on a calendar card. Six slips of paper laid out like stepping stones.

When he came to the corridor he said it in Karis's words, every one of them.

Brom had been looking into his cup, and he went on looking into it after Cael stopped. Then he said one word to the cup, quietly.

"Corridor."

Cael told them the rest: the answer anyway, the four days, and last the thing Karis had said sideways with her pen still moving, that the paper did not want the clause at all. It wanted him back in front of a frame.

The embers ticked on the hearth.

"Then what's the answer for?" said Brom at last. "If the doors only open one way."

"Because the text has held every time." Cael turned the cup in his hands. "Every time somebody on that side failed, a warden who wanted me gone, a provost who was frightened, a tournament that didn't want me on its roster, the paper caught me when they dropped me. Karis is going to read this paper the way she read those. Somewhere in it there's a place where they read their own text wrong."

Lira had not moved from the window seat. She was looking at the dark glass, not at him, and when she spoke she said it carefully, the way she set one foot on a floor she did not trust before she put her weight on it.

"And this time?"

He waited.

"Every time you've told me that, it's been people dropping you and the paper catching you." She turned her head. "What if the people didn't fail this time?"
