He opened his mouth and found the answer already there, whole and certain.

"Then there's a place where they read it wrong," he said. "There always is. Karis will find it."

Lira looked at him and did not argue. Then she swung her feet down off the window seat, took her drill-book, and went up the stair.

Brom gathered the four cups onto the tray with their handles turned the same way, and carried the tray to the hob, and banked the fire properly at last. At the door he stopped with his hand on the frame.

"Corridor," he said, once more, to nobody, and went up.

Cael did not light his lamp. The records hall's long east front was still lit from end to end across the court, and that was light enough.

He sat on the sill with Hesk's book on his knee and Hesk's steel pen in his hand, and laid his copy of the instrument open beside him at its first page. The entry was finished before the pen touched paper. He wrote it down the way you copy a thing out fair.

I can work within the system. I have the receipts: a hearing, a provision, a stamp renewed four times, a tournament their own clause put me in. The system has text, and text has held me every time the people failed. This is more text. We'll read it better than they do. We always have.

He did not change a word. Every clause had been earned on a floor or in a hearing room or across a counter, with people he loved watching. He sanded it and gave it a full minute by Hesk's clock. It looked like the truth, because, as far as he could see from that window, it was.

Across the court, the records hall began to go dark.

He knew its lamps. Six on the long table, two on the counter, one over the door of the press. The counter's pair went first, together. Then, after a pause, the table's, two at a time, from the far end toward the head, somebody walking back up the room with a trimmer and in no hurry about it. Cael knew the pace. The last pair at the table's head went, and for a moment there was only the one lamp over the press, alone at the end of the long front.

Then that one went too.

The court was dark, and the fountain went on in its basin below. Beside him on the sill the copy lay where he had put it, first page face up to the night, Given under the Compact's hand at its foot in type no larger than the rest. He did not close it. He left it there, open, waiting for better light.

Chapter 8 — Keel

He slept past the first bell for the first time since the road, and woke with the copy still lying on the sill where it had spent the night.

The light had come for it in the end. It lay across the first leaf in a long pale bar, and the fountain was running in the court below, and somewhere along the residence front a door banged and a voice called for somebody's other boot. The ordinary morning of an ordinary house. He lay a while and listened to it, and counted what he could hear, and found that the counting did not help.

Fourteen days. Thirteen, now.

He got up and dressed and put the copy in its folder under his arm, because he did not want to leave it on the sill for the porter's boy to read, and went down.

Karis was not at breakfast. Her chair at the end of the table stood pushed in, and her cup was gone from the rack, which meant she had been down before the bell and taken it up with her. Lira sat across from his place with her elbows either side of a bowl of porridge she was not eating. Brom ate for two, steadily, as if somebody had told him he would need it.

"She's been up there since the third bell," said Lira. "Brom heard her on the stair."

"I heard the key," said Brom.

"Did she sleep?"

"She says she slept." Lira pushed the bowl an inch away. "She also says the floor in her room has a slope to the west, and she's going to have it measured. So no."

He ate, because Brom pushed bread at him until he did, and then he went up.

Two porters were carrying a table across the top landing of the library when he reached it.

They had the door of the old lumber room propped open with a broken chair, and they were working the table through it on its side, sweating and grumbling at it in the low courteous voices porters used on the library stair. Behind them the room itself stood half empty. It had held, for as long as Cael had known it, the house's spare benches and a map case with no maps in it and two rolled carpets nobody would admit to owning. Now the carpets were out on the landing and the benches gone, and somebody had already swept the floor in long straight strokes and left the broom against the wall.

"Registrar's orders," said the older porter, when Cael held the door for them. "Table, two chairs, a shelf for big books. He says big books." He looked at the shelf, which was very big. "He says a girl's to sit in here and nobody's to go past her who hasn't been asked for."

"Which girl?"

"Second-year. Ink on her." The porter set his end of the table down. "She's already been and moved the chairs twice."

By supper the house would have a name for the two rooms together, the reading room and the cleared one facing it across the landing. Ephram would use it first, to a knot of curious first-years at the foot of the library stair, and it would stick: the annex.

Across the landing the reading-room door stood open for the first time Cael could remember. Karis was inside at the long table with her back to the window and her sleeves pushed above her elbows. She had the code's three volumes laid out on her left, open, one above another like steps. On her right lay something he had not seen before.

It was a sheaf of paper, bound along its edge with tape, thirty-odd leaves. It had no cover and no title and no note. He came round the table to see it the right way up. Every leaf was ruled into two columns. In the left column, one paragraph of the instrument at a time, in order, stood the paragraph's number and its first words. In the right, under each, ran every section of the code the paragraph leaned on, by volume and chapter and section, and under each section a line in very small print saying where else in the registry's history that section had been used, and by whom, and how it had come out.

The hand was a copying hand. It was so even that it might have been printed, and it made no letter larger than any other.

"It was under the door when I came up," said Karis. "At the third bell. Pushed through flat, so it wouldn't crease." She turned a page of the code. "The porter's boy was sweeping this stair at the second bell. He says the wing's teaching assistant came up it with something under his arm, and went down it again without, and wished him good morning on the way."

Cael looked down at the sheaf. Thirty-odd leaves. The paragraphs of a paper served at the second bell yesterday, mapped against a code of three volumes, with the history of every section underneath. It would have taken a clerk with a good lamp a week.

"Thank him," said Cael.

"He'd hate that." She turned another page. "I'll use it instead. He'll know I've used it, because he'll see the shape of it in what goes down the hill, and that's the kind of thanks he'd let me give." She looked up at him at last. Her eyes were red at the rims and perfectly clear in the middle. "Sit down. You're going to be told the rules once, and then you're going to read."

The rules took less time than breakfast.

Four days to the answer's bones, said Karis. After that, the flesh, and then Bracken and the house's counsel and the weighing, and then it went down the hill with time in hand. Every leaf of the code that left the records hall came back to it at night, because Bracken would not sleep with the press unlocked and she would not ask him to. Brom would carry. Brom had already been told and had already said yes, in one word, at the foot of the stair at the second bell.

"Twice a day," she said. "Up in the morning, down at night. The volumes weigh more than I do. He says that's no trouble. He says it in the voice he uses when something is going to be no trouble for a month."

"And Lira?"

"Lira is in charge of the door." Karis wrote a section number on a slip and tucked it into the second volume. "Not this door. That one has the girl. The records hall's. The intake found out this morning where we sat last night. There were nine of them on the records-hall steps at the second bell, looking at the windows as if the code were going to come out and wave."

He did not ask how Lira was going to keep a whole intake off a set of steps. He found out at noon.

She had gone to Ephram. Ephram, as captain, still held the meal rota the two second-years had drafted on the first night, the one with a column of names and a table chosen for watching how Cael held a spoon. Lira asked him for it. She took it to the common room, crossed out the heading, and wrote a new one above it in her large capitals. RECORDS HALL STEPS. ONE PAIR AT A TIME. NOBODY SITS. NOBODY ASKS. ANYBODY ELSE IS SENT TO THE FRAMES. Then she gave it back to Ephram to sign, and he signed it, and pinned it up on the covered walk beside the house's one-line answer from the day before.

By the first bell after noon there was a pair of second-years on the records-hall steps, standing very straight. One was the Mire boy who looked at ceilings. The other was the girl from the short table with her small notebook, and she was writing in it.

"She's on both rotas," said Lira, at the rail of the covered walk, very satisfied. "Karis's and mine. She won't sleep for a week."

"She's watching who comes."

"Of course she is. I told her to." Lira looked at the steps. "Somebody might as well."

He read the keel that afternoon, because Karis put it in front of him first.

It was the Greyvane ruling. She had laid it down before anything else, before the paper she was answering had a single paragraph answered, on the bare table in the middle of three cleared feet of wood. The ruling, the certified transcript under it, and Prynn's own copy of the provision on top of both, in that small exact archivist's hand Cael had first seen on a high desk in a room that smelled of cold paper.

"Keel," said Karis.

He had watched them build barges on the slip below Ostrand bridge. He had stood on the bank on the house's free afternoons for whole hours, because the work had an order in it and he liked orders. The shipwrights did not start with the sides you could see. They laid one long timber down the middle of the slip first, end to end, and squared it, and pinned it, and nothing else went on until it was true. Then the ribs went up from it on both sides, and everything that came after hung from the ribs. A barge could lose a plank and float. If the keel was wrong, nothing you nailed to it afterward would keep the river out.

"Everything else hangs from this," said Karis. "Every argument in the answer comes back to one fact: a seat has already heard this question and settled it on the public record, and the paper we're answering doesn't say otherwise. It doesn't even try. So the first thing on the table is the place where the question was settled." She put her palm on the transcript and left it there. "And then I don't move it."

She uncapped her pen and drew a sheet toward her, to write the heading.

Then she stopped, and Cael watched her stop.

It was a small thing. Her pen came down an inch over the paper and stayed there. She looked across at the instrument lying open on the table's far side, at its first leaf, and he knew what she was looking at, because he had looked at it himself all night. To the Chancellor, Halcenvane Academy, and to the enrollee of record, Caelen Hesk-ward, unclassified.

"You answer a paper in its own words," said Karis. "Always. If they call a thing a carriage, you don't call it a cart. You make them argue with the word they chose, not with yours." She did not look at him. "They've given you your registry name. So the answer goes back to the same address. Halcenvane Academy, respondent, with the enrollee of record, Caelen Hesk-ward, unclassified, answers jointly. Do you mind?"

Nobody had asked him that about the name before. Not at Denvash, where Pellin had stamped it on his card; not at Greyvane, where it had been read out over his head; not on any form since. Once, at Ardenmere, he had asked Vell to put it in her book the right way round, which was the nearest he had come. The registry gave him the name the way it gave a ledger a number. People said Cael.

"No," he said. "It's my name in that building. Write it the way they spell it."

She wrote it. He watched it go down in her finding hand, every letter, his own name on a heading he had not written, and found it did not feel like being named. It felt like being entered.

She ruled a line under it, and the keel was laid.

On the second day she put up the ribs.

There were three of them, and she explained them once, to the counsel, who had come up the hill again before noon with her steel rule in her coat pocket and sat at the table's end with her hands folded on it, listening.

The first was Karis's own finding from Greyvane, the long one, the one she had built from the standardization directive's repeal schedules a line at a time until she could say, flatly, in front of a seat, that nobody had ever repealed the clause. It had been left behind, like a child at a fair, when everything round it was swept up and carried off. The second was the house counsel's reconstruction, made the year after, by another road, through the registry's own index of surviving provisions, without reading a word of Karis's first. The third was Prynn's copy and the note on its cover, from the archive at Greyvane, which showed the clause standing in the founding text with nothing written against it in two hundred years of hands.

"Three roads to one town," said the counsel.

"Three roads to one town." Karis laid the three bundles side by side and pinned them together along their edges with brass fasteners, through the margin, three thicknesses of paper made into one. "Any one would do. I'm not going to let the seat find out which. If they knock one down they'll find the other two standing in exactly the same place."

"And if they don't knock any of them down?"

"Then they've conceded the clause twice." Karis capped her pen. "Once in their paragraph six. Once by silence in front of these."

The counsel looked at the fastened bundle the way Cael had seen Brom look at a lift before he took it.

"That's not a rib," she said. "That's a wall."

At noon Brom came up the library stair with the second volume of the code on his shoulder, the way a miller's man carries a sack, and set it down on the shelf in the lumber room without a sound. The girl at the outer table stood up when he came in. She sat down again when he went out. Then she got up and moved the volume an inch along the shelf so that its spine stood level with the others, and sat down once more and went on writing.

Cael read everything that day. That was the arrangement: Karis wrote, and he read. Not for approval, she said; because it was about him, and she did not put her name to documents about people who had not read them. He read at the window with the light behind him and the pages on his knee, and when he had read a leaf he laid it face down on the sill, and Karis took it back without asking what he thought, because if he had thought anything he would have said.

Near the end of the afternoon she did something he did not understand.

She was deep in the provenance, with the directive's schedules open in front of her and her finger on a line, and the finger stayed where it was. She reached behind her with her free hand to the pile of finished leaves and drew one out from near the bottom and held it over her shoulder toward him without turning round.

"Tonight," she said. "First."

He took it. It was the renewals table.

He looked at it, and then at her back, and waited for a reason. She turned a page of the directive and gave him none.

The renewals table was a single leaf, ruled in Karis's hand into a grid, and it had three rows.

He read it at his own window that night, with the fountain going in the court and the copy of the instrument shut in its folder on the bed behind him. Across the top of the grid ran the columns: the sitting, the panel, the day, the finding, the seal. Down the side ran the three times his place on the bluff had been written down by somebody obliged to write it. The grant at Greyvane, from the hearing. The first renewal, at Halcenvane, in the inspection year, before the Compact's delegation. The renewal at the mill town, last year, on the road.

Three rows. Every cell filled. Each day was entered in the form the registry used, and each finding was set down in the panel's own words.

He read it twice and found nothing. He had not expected to find anything; Karis did not make tables with things in them to find. He laid it on the sill and began to undress, and then stopped with one boot off and looked at it again.

Why first? Why tonight?

He sat down on the bed with the boot in his hand and thought about the inspection year.

He remembered the room by its east wall, because that was where the strangers had been. Four chairs set out by Bracken at a guest's distance from one another. The delegation's counsel in the nearest, untying a folder's ribbon with her teeth. Ilsev beside her, sharpening a pencil into a fold of paper on her knee. Havel with a board across his knees, writing the date. And in the fourth chair the Archmarshal, with nothing in his hands at all. Three hours of instruments on the oak under those four chairs: the frames, the board, the pendulum ticking in its case. Then Gault reading his note aloud at the trestle, and the Ash instructor signing, and the Mire instructor adding her four lines about the faulty frame, and the clerk bringing the stamp down on the house's copy. Renewed. That had been the day, and the house's copy had been stamped on it.

But the house's copy was not the only one. Bracken had told him so at the counter two days afterward, when the line went into the enrollment book. The delegation's counsel had asked, in writing, that the registry's own copy of the note go up the road under the delegation's countersignature before the registry sealed it into his file, and Bracken had objected on both sides of a sheet, and lost. So that copy had waited. And when it came back down, sealed and dated, so that the enrollee of record could initial its receipt before it went up again for good, Gault had called him into his office to do it.

He put the boot down and went to the drawer and took out the old volume of the Log.

It was full; there was no room in it for one word more. But every word that was in it was still there, and he knew roughly where in its thick back half the inspection year began. He turned the pages under the lamp, past fights and figures and the names of rooms, to the long entry for the evaluation day, the one that ended on wondering. Then he turned forward a page at a time, counting the days between entries by the bells and the weekday names, until he found two short lines he had nearly forgotten writing.

Gault's office. Initialled the registry's copy of the renewal, back from the delegation under seal, dated today. Up the road again in the noon bag.

Nine days.

He went back to the table on the sill. Its first renewal's row gave one day, the day of the trestle, which was the day the house's own enrollment book carried in Bracken's small upright hand, because that was the day the house had seen it happen. The registry's file, wherever it sat, would carry the other day, the day its own copy was sealed. The house had never kept a copy of that one. It had gone back up the road the same afternoon. The only place on the continent where both days stood side by side was a book he had filled himself and shut in a drawer.

He sat a long time with the two volumes open on his knees.

Then he looked at the table again, very closely, under the lamp. In the margin beside the first renewal's row, so faint that he had to tip the leaf to the light to be sure of it, sat a single pencil dot.

He took it up at the third bell, with the old volume of the Log under his arm.

Karis was already at the long table. She held out her hand behind her, palm up, the way she had held out the leaf, and he put the renewals table into it.

"Nine days," he said.

"Show me."

He opened the old Log on the table beside her elbow at the evaluation day, and laid his finger beside its last word without touching it, and then turned forward to the two short lines and did the same. She read both, the way she read anything with a date in it, once for the words and once for the numbers.

"Under the delegation's countersignature," she said. "Their counsel asked for that?"

"In writing. Bracken objected in writing. She won."

Karis took the whole leaf out of the answer and drew a clean sheet toward her.

He watched her rule the grid again from nothing, column by column, and thought that a footnote would have cost her a minute. A small number in the cell, a line at the foot, and the nine days were explained. She was going to spend an hour instead. She had told the counsel the day before that she had no hours to spare that week.

"You're thinking a footnote," said Karis, without looking up.

"I was."

She went on ruling. Every row this time gave two days, the trestle and the seal, and the first renewal's row gave the reason for the gap in a single line. Under the grid she wrote where each day could be found: the house's enrollment book for the trestle; the registry's own file, to be produced on request, for the seals; and for the gap, the enrollee's contemporaneous record, available to the seat. Then she reached across the table for the instrument, opened it at schedule two, and laid it beside the old table she had just taken out.

"Read them together," she said. "The way he will."

He read them together. Schedule two listed his file's standing entries by the registry's own dates, and the registry dated a renewal by its seal. Her old table dated it by the trestle. Two papers on one desk, about one afternoon, nine days apart.

"Now you're the seat," said Karis. "One of these two was drawn up by people who are careful. Which?"

He did not answer. He did not have to.

"There is no such thing as a small error in a document about a person." She blotted the new leaf and laid it in its place in the pile. "Nobody would have called it a lie. They'd only have called us careless, once, in one line. And after that, every leaf of ours the seat turned over, it would be turning over looking for the next one."

He looked at the old leaf, lying out of the answer on its own. The pencil dot sat in its margin.

"You saw it the first morning."

"I saw that two papers disagreed. I couldn't see why." She did not pretend otherwise. "I could have spent a morning in the inspection's papers. Or I could hand the table to the one of us who was in Gault's office that afternoon, and not say what I was looking for." She did look at him then. "If I'd told you there was a mistake on it, you'd have found one. You'd have found one on a clean leaf. I wanted to see what you'd find if you were only reading. Gault is a signature now. The Archmarshal is a chair. You're the one witness who can't be replaced, and witnesses see more when they don't know what they're being asked."

She went back to the schedules.

He stood by the table with the old Log under his arm. She had not been testing him. She had used him, the way she used the code's third volume and Prynn's copy and the sheaf with no note on it: as the best source she had on one question. It was the most useful he had ever been to her, and he did not mind the method in the least.

And on the way down the stair he remembered the counter, and the four sentences Seln had spent on him in a queue on the third day of the year. Standing papers on the provision come up for the ledger's half-year check. Keep the documentation current. The renewals table was the provision's standing papers, set out in a grid. Whatever went down the hill this week would sit in the registry's file beside the registry's own dates when the half-year check came, and a table that disagreed with them by nine days would have been the first thing the check found. Karis had not heard Seln say it. She had kept the documentation current anyway, because that was what she did with documents.

On the fourth day, which was a Fifth-day, he went to wing three at the second bell, because the provision's hours did not stop for the registry.

It was a short bout and he fought it at the band. The Mire across from him was an Iron Rank Four who sank the boards in front of her a hand's depth at a time, so that wherever Cael meant to plant his foot the floor had turned to something nearer porridge. He read the boards before she softened them, and stepped where she had not yet been, and burst twice, and gave her the third exchange because the rotation's line for that day said the third. Two to one. The rib from the Shield had gone yellow and then gone, as he had told himself it would. Gault added the three cards on the back of his hand and gave the clerk twenty-four and two-thirds, and Ephram at the rail wrote it in his soft-folded chart and drew no question mark beside it.

Walking back across the court, he noticed what it had cost.

Not the burst, nor the exchange given away. Those were the band's ordinary prices, and he paid them every Fifth-day without looking at the bill. It was the hour. Up the library stair, Karis was spending a week of her life laying his name on a table one true day at a time, and he had spent this morning in front of three cards making sure the house's book held a slightly smaller version of him than the one she was writing down. The band had always been a daily expense. He had never before had to pay it in the same week as somebody else paid for the truth.

He had no column for that. He went in to supper without making one.

Karis came down to supper that night for the first time in four days.

She came in late, when the refectory was half empty and the porters had begun stacking the benches at the far end. She had washed her hands and the ink had not come off. She sat down at the end of the middle table in her own chair, and Brom, without being asked, pushed the dish of beans down the board to her, and Seln, at the middle of the bench, moved his cup out of its way by exactly the width of the dish.

She ate three mouthfuls. Then she put down her spoon.

"Bones," she said.

Nobody cheered. Lira put her elbows on the table and her chin on her fists and looked at her.

"And the rest?"

"Seven days." Karis picked up the spoon again. "Bracken inside them. And the scales."

"The scales?"

"Bracken weighs things," said Karis. "He's going to want the number." She ate another mouthful, slowly, as if she had just remembered that food was a thing a person did. "So am I."

Across the table, Seln cut his bread into exact squares, and buttered one, and did not look up. But when Karis said bones, his knife had stopped for a moment above the board, and Cael, who had been watching for it, had counted the moment, and it was a long one.

Chapter 9 — Eleven Pounds

On the thirteenth night of the year the fire-watch's oil book took another line in Bracken's own hand.

Library, top floor. Lamps late. On the registrar's authority, and at his charge.

Cael saw it in the morning, on his way past the hook by the records-hall side door. Bracken signed that book every morning and almost never wrote in it. Now he had written in it twice in a week. He stood and looked at the page longer than a page of lamp-hours deserved, and then he went up to the top of the library and found out what the lamps had been burning for.

Karis had written the integrity section in a night.

She was asleep when he came in. She was sitting upright in her chair at the long table with her arms folded on the wood in front of her and her head on her arms, and the pen had rolled out of her hand and stopped against the inkwell. The lamp at her elbow had burned itself dry and gone out. In front of her, in one stack so neat that it might have been cut with a blade, lay the night's work in her finding hand. The girl at the outer table across the landing had put a shawl over Karis's shoulders and then, apparently, not dared to do anything else. She sat at her own table with her hands in her lap, guarding the door from inside the room.

"Since the eighth bell," the girl whispered. "She didn't stop. I filled the lamp twice. Then I fell asleep, and when I woke up she'd stopped." She looked at the stack as if it might go off. "She said not to wake her unless the building was on fire."

"Is it?"

The girl considered this seriously. "No."

So he sat down at the window and waited, and after the second bell Karis lifted her head off her arms, looked at the dead lamp, looked at the stack, and said in a perfectly ordinary voice, "Ninety-one."

"Good morning."

"Ninety-one." She sat back and the shawl slid off her shoulders, and she did not notice it go. "Every time anybody has ever called on the integrity provisions since the registry began writing it down. I've read every one. I found them in the registry digests. Bracken's press has the oldest digests and the hall has the rest, and Seln's sheaf told me which year each section first appears in, which saved me a week." She laid her hand on the stack. "Eighty-four of them are about things. Frames. Stations. An assessor who took money in a district I won't name. Two panels whose minutes argued with themselves. A records office that lost a whole quarter's declarations in a flood and then tried to pretend it hadn't."

"And the other seven?"

"Seven are about people." She looked at him. "Every one is about something a person did. A false declaration. A bought result. An evaluator who sat on his own nephew's panel. Seven times in the registry's whole history, somebody has pointed these provisions at a human being. Not once was it about what the human being was."

He came and sat across from her. The forty pages lay between them.

"So the paper we're answering is the first," he said.

"The ninety-second. And the first of its kind." She moved the stack an inch toward him. "Read it. Then come down to the counter with me. There's somebody I want to show something to."

Bracken was at his counter, adding the house's lamp-oil accounts for the week with a pained expression, when Karis laid one leaf of the integrity section on the wood in front of him and turned it the right way round.

It was a list. Ninety-one lines, in Karis's smallest finding hand, one invocation to a line, each with its year and its district and the section called on and a few words of what it had been about. She had set them out district by district, as the digests kept them, not by year. She put her finger beside line sixty-three, and took it away.

Ostrand district station; sigil frame reading Stone practitioners one rank above their true rank over one month; integrity provisions, section four; filed by the registrar of Halcenvane in his fourth year in office; frame withdrawn, tested a fortnight, a seam in the casing found admitting damp, repaired, the month's Stones re-read; sustained.

Bracken looked at it for a long time.

Then he put on his spectacles and looked at it again, more closely, and Cael watched the registrar read his own name in a list of ninety-one, in another person's hand, in a document that was going down the hill to answer a petition about a boy who stood two feet away from him on the other side of the counter.

"I'd forgotten I wrote it that way round," said Bracken at last. "Admitting damp. I'd have said letting in now." He was still looking at the line. "In my fourth year I thought a registrar ought to sound like a registrar."

"The original's in the registry's file," said Karis. "I copied the citation from the digest. There's one thing." She took the leaf back and turned it over, to a note at its foot. "In your filing, you spelt casing with two esses. I corrected it in the citation. Silently. It's a convention."

Bracken took his spectacles off.

"Don't," he said.

Karis waited.

"Put it back." He folded the spectacles and held them in one hand. "If the seat goes to my filing, which it may, and finds one spelling there and another in yours, it's one more thing that doesn't match. And it was my mistake. I made it at this counter in my fourth year with the frame's report in one hand and the pen in the other." He looked at her. "I'd sooner the record had it the way I wrote it. Mark it as mine."

Karis took the leaf back to the end of the counter and uncapped her pen. She crossed out the corrected word in the citation, very neatly, with a single ruled line, and wrote the old spelling above it, two esses, and after it, in brackets, the little word every copying clerk on the continent wrote after a quoted mistake, which meant it was like this when I found it.

She brought it back and laid it in front of him.

Bracken read it, and nodded once, and went back to the lamp-oil.

The house's counsel came up the hill at noon and read the forty pages backward.

She did it at the long table in her coat, with the steel rule under each line and her lips quite still, beginning at the last word of the last page and climbing. Karis sat across from her with her hands in her lap and watched her climb. Cael sat at the window. The girl at the outer table across the landing had found a reason to fill the inkwells, all of them, slowly.

It took the counsel most of the afternoon. Near the bottom of the ninth page, on her way up, the rule stopped.

"Never," she said.

Karis leaned across. The counsel turned the page so that she could see it and laid the rule under one sentence. The integrity provisions have never been turned against the nature of a practitioner, as distinct from his conduct.

"You can't prove never," said the counsel. "You can prove ninety-one. A digest can miss a filing. A district can have burned its records. A seat with a mind to be awkward will ask you how you know about the ones nobody wrote down." She lifted the rule. "Say not once in the registry's record. Then it's a count, and it's yours, and nobody can argue with it but a man with a ninety-second filing in his hand."

Karis wrote it in. She did not argue, or explain, or say that she had meant the record. She took the correction the way Lira took a correction from the Stone on the painted floor, all at once, and moved on.

The counsel finished her climb a little before the fifth bell and set the rule across the first page.

"That's all," she said.

"That's all?"

"That's all there is." The counsel stood and buttoned her coat. "I've read a good many answers to a good many petitions. That's the best section on these provisions I've seen written by anybody, and I include my own. Put it in." She picked up her bag. "I'll be back up the hill when the rest of it's done. Send for me early. I like to read things twice."

When she had gone down the stair, Karis sat with her hands folded on the forty pages. Then she tore a strip off the bottom of a used sheet and wrote two lines on it, fast, and pushed it across the table to him.

Best thing I've written. Worth exactly what a record is worth: the seat can agree with every word and turn the page.

He read it and copied it into the observation notebook, both lines, in her section, and slid the strip back. She put it in her pocket.

When he looked up from the notebook, the stack had been turned over. The last page lay on top, where he would read it first, and Karis was standing at the window with her back to the room.

On the sixteenth day Cael took his sheet for the next Fifth-day down to the wing, because the provision's hours were lodged at the counter or nowhere, and the registry did not care what week it was.

The queue had shortened since the first days. The intake had learned the counter's hours and stopped coming in a body. A single Ash first-year stood ahead of him with a form she had filled in twice, once in pencil and once over the pencil in ink. Behind the counter the desk clerk added his column by the window. Gault's door stood shut. And at the copying table, under the shelf with the small unmarked case on it, the teaching assistant rose to take the first-year's sheet and read it from the name to the signature at his even pace, and stamped it, and tore the slip.

Then Cael's turn.

Seln took the sheet. He read it. Name; the Path line blank by rule; evaluator of record; hours; reason. The stamp came down. The slip tore along its rule.

"The Magister signs on Fifth-days," said Seln.

"Karis used the sheaf," said Cael. "All of it. Every leaf."

Seln laid the sheet on the stack at his left hand.

"The office keeps a register of everything that leaves this counter," he said, to the stack. "Forms. Slips. Copies on application. There is no sheaf in it." He set the stack's edge true. "There's nothing to have been used."

"Then I'll tell her that."

"Mm."

Cael had his fingers on the copy-slip. He had turned half away from the counter when Seln spoke again, in exactly the same voice, as if reading the next line of the same form.

"The second volume's own index runs a dozen years behind the volume. The digests are better for the late years." He had already turned back to the copying table. "If anyone should happen to be working from the second volume."

Cael went out through the wing doors and along the covered walk, and did not let himself smile until he was under the north arch.

He had thought, for two years, that Seln did not give things. He saw now that this was wrong. Seln gave things all the time. He gave forms before anybody had asked for them, and a sheaf under a door before dawn, and a correction about an index to a boy at a counter who could carry it upstairs. He gave them in a way that made thanks impossible, because there was no record of the thing and so nothing to thank him for. It was not modesty. Cael did not think it was even kindness, exactly. It was a man who had spent his life on the side of a counter where everything that passed across it was written down, making very sure that the one thing he chose to give stayed off the paper.

He thought about the quiet thing he carried, sealed, and the debt it was sealed for, which the man at the copying table did not know he was owed. He thought that it would be a very hard debt to pay to somebody who would not let anything be paid to him.

He went up the library stair and told Karis about the index. She went straight to the digests without a word. Twenty minutes later she found that one of her ninety-one, a coastal panel that had sat a member short, carried a year she had taken from the second volume's index, and the index had it a dozen years late. She ruled the year through and wrote the right one above it. It changed nothing in the argument. It went in anyway.

Bracken read the whole answer in two nights.

He read it at his counter, every leaf, from the address to the last schedule. The oil book took a third line and a fourth. He did not skim. Cael came past the records-hall windows late on the first night on his way back from the north wall, and saw him through the glass, a narrow grey shape bent over a single lamp, turning a leaf, reading it, initialling its corner, turning the next. A registrar's initials on a leaf were a promise about the leaf. Bracken did not make promises he had not read.

On the second night it rained.

It was the first rain of the year, and it came all at once a little after the tenth bell, out of a sky that had been brass-coloured and heavy since noon. It roared on the long roof of the records hall and came off the gutters in ropes, and the dust in the court turned to a smell before it turned to mud. Cael stood under the covered walk's north arch and watched it, with the fire-watch boy beside him holding his slate against his chest to keep the hours dry. Across the court, in the records hall's one lit window, Bracken did not look up.

Cael went across to him in the end, with his collar up and the rain going down his neck, because the light in that window had begun to look lonely.

Bracken did not seem surprised. He looked up from the leaf under his lamp and pointed with his pen at the stool on the public side of the counter.

"Sit," he said. "You can be useful. The house sends two copies down, one for the seat and one for the petitioner, and I've been checking the second against the first by myself with my finger, which is slow and bad for the eyes." He slid a leaf across the counter, and kept its twin in front of himself. "Read that aloud. Slowly. I'll follow."

Cael read it aloud.

It was the leaf about his Kindling. He had not known Karis had written one. It set out, in her plainest prose, the morning at Weaver's Row in Denvash: the circle of pale wood, the registrar who conducted it, the brass plate that lit late, the one bracketed word on the card, the classification line stamped where it had stood empty for fourteen years. Every fact in it was true and every fact was his, and he had never heard any of it in another person's sentences before. He read it in his own voice to a registrar in the middle of the night with the rain on the roof, and Bracken's finger moved down the other copy a line behind him, and twice Bracken said "Slower," and once he said "Again, that line," and made a small mark.

At the foot of the leaf Bracken initialled both copies in the corner, and blotted them, and set them on the finished pile.

"There was a comma missing in the seat's copy," he said. "Line nine. I've put it in." He took the next leaf off the stack. "Are you all right to go on?"

"Yes."

"Then go on."

They did four more before the rain eased. When Cael went back across the court at last, his own life was lying in two neat piles on a registrar's counter, checked and initialled, and he felt lighter for having read it aloud than he had ever felt for keeping it to himself.

In the morning the court steamed. Bracken sent the porter's boy up the library stair with a message for Karis, and the message was one word long, and Karis read it on the landing and came down at once with the boy still trying to keep up.

The word was Scales.

They weighed it in the post room behind the counter, on the brass beam the house used for parcels going down the hill, where letters were weighed for their postage and nobody had ever weighed anything that mattered. The answer had been bound in two parts, because the binder's thread would not go through it in one, and the two parts lay side by side in a leather document wallet with the house's seal on the flap. Bracken set the wallet on the pan himself. He put on the brass weights one at a time from the box, the big ones first, and then the small, and then the very small ones that lived in their own velvet slots, until the beam came level and stayed.

"Eleven pounds," said Bracken. He bent to read the last weight. "And four ounces."

He took a small book out of his coat and wrote the number in it. It was not the house's book. Cael had never seen it before. It was a pocket ledger in black oilcloth, worn white at the corners, and from where he stood he could see a long column of entries in it, each a single line, each with a date and a figure.

"Every answer the house has filed in my time," said Bracken, to nobody, and put it away. "I like to know what they weighed."

Withrow came in while he was taking the weights off.

She stood in the post-room door and looked at the wallet on the pan, and then at Bracken, who was laying the weights back in their velvet one by one.

"The noon bag goes at the half-bell," said Bracken. "The seat takes the post. I'll put it in myself."

"How many came up our road on the eighth day?"

Bracken put the last weight away. "Three."

"Three, at a walk." Withrow came in and laid one hand on the wallet's flap, over the house's seal. "Then three go down it. The head groom and his son on the greys. Your senior clerk in the middle, with this across his saddle where the town can see it. Fifth-day, the second bell."

"That's three days inside the time."

"Good," said Withrow. "Let them count those as well."

It went down the hill on the nineteenth day, a Fifth-day, at the second bell.

Cael watched from the covered walk with half the house beside him, though nobody had announced anything. The head groom came out of the stable yard on the bigger of the two greys in the coat he wore at convocation and nowhere else, and his son on the other grey looking as if he had been told to sit up straight and was doing it with his whole body. Between them rode Bracken's senior clerk, a long patient man who had kept the enrollment book for nine years and had never in his life been looked at by so many people at once. The wallet was strapped across the front of his saddle under a fold of the house's own cloth, and he kept one hand on it the whole way across the court.

They went out under the arch at a walk.

The lodge-man stood as straight as he stood for the Chancellor. The intake crowded the north wall to watch them take the first switchback, and the second, and the bend above the trees. Lira was on the wall with them, and Brom, and somewhere behind Cael on the walk a third-year said, half laughing and half not, Is that it? Is that the whole answer? and somebody else said, That's eleven pounds of it, and nobody laughed after that.

At the foot of the road the two coats watched the escort go by them onto the river street. Neither turned his head to follow it. They looked at it as it passed, the way they looked at a cart of hay, and then went back to looking at the gate.

Karis did not come down to watch. Cael looked up at the top of the library, at the reading room's window, and she was not in it. She had gone to sleep in her chair the moment the wallet left the counter, the girl at the outer table told him afterward, with her boots still on and her key on its cord in her fist.

He wrote it that night at the sill, with the copy of the instrument beside him and the answer's first leaf lying in his memory where he could read it with his eyes shut.

Eleven pounds four ounces, down the hill at a walk, under our own escort, three days inside the time. The best paper anyone has ever written about me. I read every leaf. I can't find a seam, and I was looking. Karis says it's perfect, and in two years I have never seen her call a thing perfect that wasn't.

I believe her. I also believe the corridor. Tonight I can carry both of them, one in each hand. I haven't yet had to find out what happens when I need a hand free.

The north wall was warm under him from the day's sun, and the valley was going blue, when Lira came along the top of it from the east end.

She walked the coping itself, not the path beside it, as she always did; it was narrower, so it was quicker. Her hands were still taped from the evening drill and she had a heel of bread in one of them. She broke it in two without looking, gave him the larger half, and sat down beside him with her legs over the drop.

"Brom's wearing out a word," she said.

He knew which.

"He says it at the frames. Under his breath, between sets, like a man counting." She bit the bread. "He did it twice yesterday and once this morning, and he doesn't know he's doing it. Brom never says anything twice unless he hasn't finished chewing it." She looked at him sideways. "So you're going to give it to me. All of it. Small."

He gave it to her backward, the way the house's counsel read a paper.

He started at the end, with the morning after, because that was where a person actually lived. The ferryman with a letter, the guild hall with a letter, the clerk with a sealed file and no key. A daughter at Withrow's counter every week for a year, asking whether anybody had begun the review, and nobody ever obliged to begin it. Then the three steps of chapter fourteen in Bracken's voice that would not let itself be a voice, and the third word that nobody had ever had to stamp. Then the six slips of paper laid out down the long table like stones across a stream, each a door, each real law, each opening toward the next and never back the way you had come.

He did not tell it well. He told it in order, which was the only way he knew.

Lira ate her bread and watched the river. When he had finished she brushed the crumbs off her tapes, one hand and then the other.

"Does it have an outside?" she said. "Your corridor."

"Karis says every door opens one way."

"I heard you." She was quiet a moment. "They had a slate at Fenmark."

He waited.

"In the examination hall. Three examiners at a table, and a slate in a wooden frame between them." She held her hands a foot apart. "They chalked it while I fought. Afterward the one in the middle copied it fair onto the form, and wiped the slate with his sleeve so the form would have no crossings-out. I remember thinking how careful that was." She put her hands down. "Every line on that form was correct. Wind. Copper. My name spelt right. Every step in the book, in the book's order. It was the room that was wrong. I've never been allowed to say both of those at once and have anybody listen. I only had angry, and angry's a very poor word. It's all one size."

"Corridor," said Cael.

"Corridor." She tried it slowly, the way she tried a new step on the painted lines. "I could have used that four years ago, near enough."

The ferryman was lighting the lamp on the landing's post. The two coats there turned their faces from it, as they always did when the flame went up, so as not to be blinded for the hour that followed.

"Here's the other half," said Lira. "There was no door out of that hall but the one they pointed at. I went out of it with the form in my pocket, and for a year after that I knocked on guild doors. I asked six of them for a letter and walked to two. One wouldn't let me in the door. The other let me into the hall, and read the form, and was very polite." She turned her head toward him. "Then I came to Ardenmere with nothing left to knock on, and one evening I heard a noise like somebody hitting a boiler with a chain, three streets off, and went to look. Vell's yard. Nobody sent me there. It wasn't on any form. It was round the back of everything, where the town kept what it didn't want to look at, and that turned out to include me."

She stood up on the coping, all at once, the way she came up off a cross.

"So I believe Karis," she said. "Every door opens one way. I've stood in that building. But there's usually a yard out the back." She looked down at him. "Not that anybody draws it on the plan."

She went off along the top of the wall toward the residence, quick and narrow in the dusk, and he sat with the rest of his bread and watched her go until she dropped off the coping at the far end and was gone.

He wrote one line before the light went: Lira: a slate wiped clean, a year of polite doors, then a yard nobody drew.

Chapter 10 — Per Seal

By the time Cael reached the records hall on the twenty-third day, the seat's notice had been open on the counter for a quarter of an hour, and Karis had already read it upside down twice.

She was standing on the public side with her arms folded, the way she stood at a shelf she did not trust. Bracken stood on his own side with one finger resting on the notice's last line, not pointing at it, only keeping it where it was, as a man keeps his hand on a dog. The noon bag lay open beside them with the rest of the house's post still in it. The girl from the annex hovered by the door with a notebook nobody had told her to bring.

"Read the bottom first," said Karis. "Then the rest. The rest is ordinary."

Cael came round beside her and read the bottom first.

The presiding seat: per seal.

Above it, the line he had been half expecting for a fortnight. Appearing for the petitioner as procurator of record: Jent. He had read that name once before, at the foot of the instrument's last leaf, under the attestation, and Bracken had not known it then. Cael looked at the registrar now, and Bracken gave the smallest shake of the head: still nobody he knew.

Then the rest, which was ordinary, as Karis had said. The seat at Ostrand gives notice that it has convened formal proceedings upon the petition served on the eighth day of the year. The seat will sit on its Fifth-days, upon the schedule of the academic year, and will rule before the year's close. Counsel of record will confer with the seat's clerk upon the schedule on the twenty-fifth day. The first sitting will be held on the sixth Fifth-day of the year. Senior evaluators of the district will be called to the evaluation seat on a day to be notified.

Two days to the conference. Seventeen to the first sitting.

"Per seal," said Cael.

"It's in the second volume," said Karis. "Toward the back, in the sections nobody reads unless they're looking for something to be frightened of. Some matters the registry decides belong to the office and not the officer. In those, the seat sits as itself, not as whoever is in it. The code even gives it a hood for the purpose." She did not unfold her arms. "The minute takes the seal's impression and no signature. In law there's nobody under the hood to name."

Bracken nodded once, as a teacher nods at a pupil who has got there first.

"I've read that section a great many times," he said. "A clerk reads everything, in case. I've kept this counter thirteen years and never once seen it called on." He took his finger off the notice. "You'll want to know who it will be. So shall I. I know every registrar who has sat that seat in my time, and which of them likes a long sitting, and which takes his luncheon at the eleventh bell whatever the advocate is saying. None of that is any use. The minute won't tell you, and it won't tell me."

Karis unfolded her arms at last.

"It's very well done," she said.

"It is," said Bracken.

"I hate it."

The girl by the door had been holding her notebook against her chest the whole time. She spoke now, quickly, as if she had been working out the question for a while and was afraid it would go off if she held it any longer.

"If there's nobody to name," she said, "who do you appeal to? If the seat gets it wrong?"

Bracken looked at her over his spectacles, and for a moment Cael thought he was going to send her to her table.

"To the registry," he said. "Which is the seat. Which is the seal." He folded the notice once along its crease. "Go and find the section, and when you've found it come and tell me whether I'm wrong. I should very much like to be."

Karis went out past her. The girl looked at the notice once more, hard, as if to fix it in her head, and went after her.

He copied the notice at the counter in his own hand, and wrote it up at the sill that evening.

Per seal. Jent, the name off the last leaf. Seventeen days.

Every person who has ever decided a thing about me had a face, and I could read it. Pellin at Denvash, with her brass plate. Coss across a desk. Vastin with his frames. The provost who was frightened and couldn't hide it. Umber polishing his spectacles over a sheet he couldn't score. I read every one of them from across a room, and every reading was worth something.

They've filed the face out of it. By a section nobody has used in thirteen years, the seat that rules on my enrollment has chosen to be nobody.

On the twenty-fifth day the coach stopped on Ostrand bridge behind a cart of barrels, and while the carter argued with his horse, Karis told them a story.

"At Greyvane, in my first term," she said, to the window, "an advocate gave me a point at a sitting. A good point. One I'd spent a fortnight on. He stood up and said the archive was right and he wouldn't dispute it, and sat down. I went back to my room and was pleased with myself all evening." The cart lurched forward a yard and stopped again. "In the morning he took the case on a point I hadn't looked at, because I'd spent the whole of the night before being pleased."

"So what do we do?" said Lira.

"When he agrees with us, don't nod. Don't let your face do anything at all." Karis turned from the window. "He's going to agree with us about everything in that answer. All of it. Probably before the clerk has finished the schedule."

"Then where do we look?"

"At whatever he keeps."

The cart moved off, and the coach went on over the bridge.

There were six of them inside. Cael had been told to come. Karis, Lira, Brom and Seln had not, and had come anyway, and Withrow had looked at them at the coach door one by one and told Bracken to enter them on the day's list as the house's attendance. And the house's counsel, who had come up the hill at first light with her steel rule and asked for a seat in the coach instead of in Withrow's carriage, which had gone on ahead. Lira had the red drill-book shut on her knee. Brom sat with his hands clasped between his knees and looked at the floor of the coach as if it were a floor he would have to stand on.

Seln had the end of the bench by the door and a sheaf on his knee, bound along its edge with tape. He was turning its leaves with great attention, and Cael saw it, and saw Karis see it, and saw her look away as she would have looked away from a stranger's luggage. The wing's register had no sheaf in it, and Seln was reading it anyway.

The wool exchange stood where the market street ran out at the top of the hill. It was a long stone hall raised four steps above the street on a plinth, with tall plain windows and a great double door, and in Bracken's grandfather's day, Bracken said, the whole wool clip of the valley had been sold across its floor by the bale. The trade had gone downriver long ago, and the registry, which liked large cheap buildings at the tops of hills, had taken this one, and it still smelled of sheep in the heat. When the coach door opened the smell came in warm and greasy and not at all unpleasant, like the inside of a new coat.

At the side of the building a joiner stood on a short ladder with a mouthful of screws, hanging a door.

It was a new door in an old wall, and the stone had been cut round it so lately that the dust still lay white on the sill. A registry officer stood at the ladder's foot with a ruled board under his arm and watched the second hinge go on as if he would be blamed personally if it went on crooked.

"For the sittings," said the house's counsel at Cael's elbow. "There'll be people on the steps. A great many. The front door belongs to them." She considered the hinge. "They've thought about you. That isn't always a compliment."

Withrow had got down from her carriage and was standing at the foot of the four steps, looking at the new door with her hands folded in front of her. She looked at it for about as long as she would have looked at a notice on a board. Then she looked at Cael.

"When it's finished," she said, "you'll use it as if it had always been there. You won't look at the hinges. You won't look at the front steps on your way past. A door is a door." She turned toward the main entrance. "The registry cut it for you. Let the registry be the only one who remembers that."

The conference was not in the hall. It was up a short stair at the back, in what had been the wool-factors' counting room and was now a district office: a long table, eight chairs, the registry's plain sigil painted over the hearth, and a window at the far end that looked straight down the market street to the wharfs, and over the river to the bluff, with the house along its top.

The first thing Cael saw in it was a hand screwing the lid onto a travelling inkwell.

It did it carefully, a full turn and then a quarter more, so that nothing would spill. Then the hand set the inkwell on the table, and its owner stood up, and came round the table to meet them.

He was not big. Cael had expected size without knowing it, or a voice, or some weight in the way a man came across a room. What came across this room was a man of middle height and middle years in a brown coat that had been good once and had been kept good since, with the cuffs mended in a slightly different brown. A pair of spectacles hung on a black cord round his neck.

"Advocate," said Jent, and it was the third thing he said in that room.

The first two had gone to the others. A name to the house's counsel, which Cael heard and did not catch and which she answered with a short nod, as one tradesman nods to another across a street. A title, and the registry's measured bow, to Withrow. The third went past both of them to the girl behind them with the summary under her arm, and Karis's pen, which she had taken out to make a note of the room, stopped in the air.

Nobody in the house had settled what to call her. The council had needed two sittings to head her line in the accounts. The porter's wall gave her a rank, which said what she could do on a floor and nothing at all about what she did on paper. Cael waited for her to say she was no such thing. She let it stand, and he thought he knew why. It was the first title anybody had ever given her for the work, and not for the room she did it in.

Jent nodded to the three behind her as the house's attendance, and to Cael as a man nods to a party in a matter, and went back to his chair and unscrewed the inkwell.

The seat's clerk came in a minute later, a thin young man with a schedule, and the conference began, and it was dull, and Cael was grateful for every dull minute of it. The clerk read the schedule, and both counsel agreed it, and the clerk wrote that they had agreed it and read back what he had written, and both counsel agreed that too.

Then the lists went across the table.

The house's ran to a hundred and seventy-three items, in Karis's smallest hand. The counsel slid it over with one finger. Jent picked it up, weighed it a moment in his palm the way a man weighs a letter for its postage, opened it at the index leaf and read that, all of it, with his spectacles on. Then he initialled the receipt at the foot and passed it back.

His own was a single leaf. The counsel drew it across and Cael read it upside down.

The registry code: chapter fourteen. The registry code: the integrity provisions. The registry code: the schedule of discretions. The petition as served. The convening's minute. The clause, as the registry certifies it. The standardization directive, with its schedules. The advisory upon the fielding clause. The adjudication office's referral of the enrollee's entry.

Nine. And every one of them, Cael realized, was already somewhere in the right-hand column of Seln's sheaf. Not one was a witness, and not one was a finding about anything that had happened in a room. There was nothing on the leaf a person could be asked a question about, or caught out in, or shown to have misremembered. They were texts, the registry's own furniture, and a man did not bring furniture to prove a thing; he brought it to read aloud from, at the moment of his choosing.

Every one of the nine was there to be cited.

"I'd ask that the respondent's answer go into the record whole," said Jent. "Not the summary. If the respondent has no objection."

"I was about to ask the same," said the counsel.

"Then we're agreed." He took off his spectacles and let them hang on their cord, and turned over a leaf of his own notes. "Your renewals table, Advocate. Two dates to every row, and the gap between them accounted for. I've not seen that before. Somebody was in the room." He let the leaf fall back. "The best-documented enrollment I've reviewed in thirty years. Genuinely."

"Thank you," said Karis, quickly, before he had quite finished, and at the end of the table Lira's eyebrows went up as if somebody had dropped a plate.

Under the table, where nobody could see, Cael let the read go.

He sent it out through his own boots into the old floorboards of the counting room, quietly, as he would never have let it go in a ring with a judge watching, and along the boards under the table to the far side. It came back with the man's weight in his chair. Square. Settled in the middle of the seat as a sack settles when it is set down. In forty minutes it did not once lean forward toward a point he meant to make or ease back from one he would sooner not. It sat where it had been put.

Then the hands. They lay one on each side of the inkwell, square to the table's edge. When one wrote, the other held the leaf; when neither wrote, both went back to where they had been. They did not go to his collar or the cord of his spectacles. They did not tap.

Then the breath, which did not change when the counsel asked him a hard question, or an easy one.

And last the thing Cael trusted most: the little space before an answer that cost something, when a person chose how much of it to give. Every official he had ever sat across from had one. Jent did not. Question and answer followed each other with nothing between them.

"Will the petitioner call any witness?" the counsel asked him, toward the end.

"None."

"Not the evaluator whose advisory you've adopted?"

"His advisory is an exhibit. It speaks for itself. I'd not ask a man to stand up in a room and repeat a paragraph he's already signed."

"Does the petitioner dispute any entry in the respondent's renewals table?"

"No."

"Does the petitioner say the evaluation seat should sit before the integrity question is argued, or after?"

"That's the seat's to say. I'll be content with either."

Four questions. One hard, Cael thought, one sly, two easy, and the counsel had put the sly one second, where a man tired of easy ones might trip. Cael had been counting the clock over the hearth between each question and its answer, and he had the four counts in his head: none, none, none, none. The sly one had cost Jent exactly what No had cost him.

Four measures. Four nothings.

When the clerk asked whether counsel had anything further, Jent was already screwing the lid onto the inkwell, a turn and a quarter.

"Only the order of business." He put the inkwell in his coat and stood. "Enter that the petitioner takes no point on the clause, or the papers, or the renewals, and needn't be heard on any of them. Put me down for the registry's discretion, on whatever days the seat gives me. First, whether there's a question of integrity at all. Then the remedy." He waited while the clerk wrote. "The respondent will want time to answer each. I'd give it to them."

The clerk's pen stopped. Jent looked down the table at Cael and inclined his head exactly as far as a procurator inclines it to a party.

"Hesk-ward."

At the door he turned once more and gave the rest of the room what it was owed. "Chancellor. Counsel. Advocate."

The stair took him. The clerk wrote the hour in his margin, and Cael, reading it upside down, saw that it was the same hour the schedule had given for the conference's end before anybody had come into the room.

The coach was halfway across the bridge before anybody spoke.

"Well?" said Lira, to the house's counsel. "What do you make of him?"

The counsel had her bag on her knees and her rule in her coat pocket, and she took a while.

"I kept waiting for him to want something," she said. "Every man who's beaten me in twenty-six years wanted it badly, and I could find the wanting and lean on it. I leaned on this one the whole morning." She looked out at the river. "There was nothing there to lean on. I've no idea yet what that does to my record."

Seln was at the end of the bench with his eyes shut and the taped sheaf on his knee.

"There's one behind every counter you've ever leaned on," he said, without opening them. "They're called clerks. You've always had the good chair."

Lira laughed out loud, and put her hand over her mouth, and laughed again behind it. Brom's shoulders moved once. Even the counsel's mouth went up at one corner before she stopped it. Seln did not open his eyes. Cael thought that the man might just have made the first joke of his life in front of witnesses, and that he would deny it at the counter in the morning.

Karis had not laughed. She was looking at the summary in her lap without reading it.

"I thanked him first," she said, "so it would be on the minute before he gave everything away. Then it's on the minute that we heard the compliment and didn't bow to it." She folded the summary in half. "He agreed with all of it. In the first minute. I told you he would. And I still had to keep my face still. I'm telling you that so you know it isn't easy."

"It wasn't," said Brom.

Bracken was at his counter when they came up the hill, and he did not ask how it had gone. He asked what the man looked like.

Cael told him. Middle height and middle years. The brown coat, the cuffs mended in a different brown, the spectacles on their black cord, the inkwell with its screw lid. The way he had weighed the house's list in his palm before he opened it.

Bracken listened with both hands on the counter. Then he went to the locked press, and came back with three thin bound books, and laid them side by side: the rolls of procurators admitted to practise before the registry seats of this district and the two beside it, each name with its date and its sponsor and, against some of them, a little ink drawing in the margin by some long-dead clerk with time on his hands.

He went down all three with his finger, a quarter-hour's work. Cael stood and watched him do it, because he could see Bracken wanted it watched.

"Not on any of them," said Bracken at last, and closed the third. "Admitted somewhere, or he couldn't stand at a seat. But not here, and not next door." He put the three books one on top of another. "So he came from further off than the next district to stand at our seat in a matter about our house." He looked at Cael over the books. "Which is information. I don't yet know what it's information about."

The read had told him the man's weight in his chair to the ounce, Cael wrote that night at the sill, and nothing else at all.

Four nothings. I have only ever found a man by what he was afraid to lose, and Jent brought nothing into that room that was his to lose. The compliment he paid Karis the way you pay a fee at a counter, the right amount, honestly. Our whole answer he handed back across the table like a parcel addressed to somebody else.

He's a hand. Somebody else is the arm.

He read it over once. Across the dark court, at the top of the library, Karis's lamp was still burning in the annex, which meant the oil book would have another line in it in the morning.

Chapter 11 — Choosing

Withrow sent for him at the ninth bell that evening, by the porter's boy, with no reason given.

When he knocked and went in she was not at her desk. She was at the glass-fronted case under the framed charter on the far wall, with the key from her chain in its lock, and she did not turn round until she had taken out what she wanted and locked the case again behind it.

It was a buff folder, thick, soft at the spine, with the house's name lettered on the front in a clerk's hand gone brown with age. Every chartered house kept one. Every inspector who came up its road read it before he looked at a single floor. No enrollee ever saw it.

She put it into his hands, and went and sat down behind her desk, and folded her own hands on the blotter, and said nothing at all.

He sat in the visitor's chair with the folder on his knees. He opened it at the back, because that was where the house's counsel would have started.

The newest leaf was the eighth day's. It was in the registry's plain grey type, sent up the road to be pinned in, because a house had to keep its own folder current with whatever the registry entered against it.

Respondent: the academy of Halcenvane, in formal proceedings before the seat at Ostrand. Subject of proceedings: the basis on which it enrolled Caelen Hesk-ward, unclassified, its enrollee of record. Status: pending.

Beside it the right-hand column was ruled, as every column in the folder was ruled, and empty.

He turned back a leaf, and another. The house's placings, a long thin column of meets and figures, and last year's the only one with third in it. Inspections, each with its date and its officer's name and its finding. Near the front he came to the only two leaves in the folder written in two different inks. On each, the left side was an inspector's complaint and the right side was the house answering it, in another year and another hand. He read the right-hand sides first, because he had just been reading one that was empty: a book kept again, and below the house's answer a visiting officer's clearance; an index finished, and below that answer another officer's clearance. Only then did he look across to see what they had answered. A quarter's lamp-hours nobody had written down. A year's declarations nobody had indexed. Both were long before Withrow. Then the charter's grant on its heavier paper, under a seal gone the colour of tea.

He turned forward again to the eighth day. The empty column there was the same width as the columns beside the fire-watch and the records office. It had been ruled by the same machine.

"There's no form for taking a leaf out," said Withrow. "I looked, once, at the registry, for somebody else's house. There's a form for everything else." She did not move her hands. "Suppose the seat is with us on every point. A clerk comes up our road with a stamp, and writes sustained in that column, and I give him tea. That's the best day this folder can have. And the next inspector starts where they're all taught to start, at the grant, and turns forward, and the last thing he reads before he goes out to look at our floors is that this house once stood in front of a seat for what it did with you. If the seat isn't with us, the column says that instead, and he stays a month."

She opened her desk drawer, and took out a paper, and laid it on the folder on his knees. Then another, and another, without a word between them. The program's charter, dated the first morning of the year. The page of the house's accounts with Karis's line on it. The intake's roll, longer than any he had seen pinned to a board. The tournament's sheet with the house's placing on it.

"Four," said Withrow. "You like counting. Count them." He counted them, though he did not need to. "Every one is a thing I asked for, on this desk, in my own hand. When the seat reads your name it will read these too, whether it means to or not." She closed the drawer. "I wanted them on your knees once, so you'd know their weight. After tonight, the adding-up is mine. It's my column."

He had learned that when she spoke in that voice the right answer was to have heard.

"Now the other column."

She took the papers back off the folder, one by one, and returned them to the drawer.

"Karis's doors are real," she said. "I sat with her slips the night she laid them out, and I've walked every one of them since, the way you'd walk a building somebody had asked you to insure. They open one way. She's right."

"And the law on our side?"

"Is good law." She looked at him across the desk. "I don't say that as your chancellor. Before you ever came up our road I had the Greyvane transcript sent from Ostrand, and I went through it with every tool twenty years at the registry gave me, the way I used to go through other people's appeals when I was paid to find what was wrong with them. I came away with nothing. Their paper is the same. Honest work, both of them, and nothing in either to find." She set both hands on the blotter, a hand's width apart. "That's two true things, and they point opposite ways, and I can only stand on one of them. So I've decided which. I'm going to stand on the first, out loud, in front of that seat and the broadsides and every inspector who ever opens that folder, with this whole house on my back, knowing where the second one goes." She did not lower her eyes. "Make a note of the word choosing."

He took out the observation notebook and turned to her pages, two years of small facts in his cramped hand: how she crossed a court, how long she spoke at convocation, how many times she had lifted a page to stop a hall's noise, and at the bottom, from the first morning of this year, load-bearing calm. Under it he wrote the date and the word. Then he underlined it twice, once against the notebook's edge and once freehand, the way she had underlined discretion in her pocket code on the procedure night, and he did not write anything else, because nothing else was needed.

She watched him do it and did not pretend she had not.

"May I ask you something?" said Cael.

"You may ask."

"If you'd known on the morning you signed for me that it would come to this, a folder and a seal and a hood. Would you have signed?"

Withrow did not answer at once. She looked past him at the charter on the wall, in its frame, with the glass a little dusty along the top edge where the porters' cloths did not reach.

"I did know it might," she said. "Not the hood. I'd never have guessed the hood. But a folder, yes, one day, and a column with nothing in it." She brought her eyes back to him. "That's what I meant when I told the hall to leave what it is where anybody can check. Somebody checks. Then you find out whether you meant it." She stood. "I meant it. I'd like that to be the last time either of us asks."

"On the morning of the first sitting, when you get into that coach," said Withrow, "sit up straight. The town watches the coach."

He drew the year that night on a clean page of the notebook: a long ruled line from the first day to the last, with a tick for every Fifth-day.

He put the sittings on it as the notice gave them. The conference, past. The first sitting, the sixth tick. Brom's panel he put at the last tick, because Brom's docket said so. Lira's first meet off the hill he put where Rooke's board in the east hall had it, six weeks on. Then he looked for the re-evaluation and found the notice's words instead of a day: fixed by the seat in its ruling.

Every other mark on the page was a date somebody he knew had written down. That one would be written by a hand under a hood, on a morning he could not yet see. He left a gap on the line for it, and found he had drawn the gap carefully, the way you leave a space at a table for somebody who has not yet come in.

Karis had found the other thing by morning.

She had borrowed Brom's docket out of his left inside pocket to copy its date, and Brom had stood in the annex doorway until she gave it back, which she did inside a quarter of an hour. She had the two dates on a slip, one above the other. Brom's panel, the last Fifth-day of the year, at the district seat in Ostrand. The seat's ruling, before the year's close, and there was only one Fifth-day in the year's last week.

"The same morning," said Cael.

"A street and a half apart." Karis looked at the slip. "Lira will be sure somebody arranged it."

"Did somebody?"

"A calendar did. Some clerk likes his Fifth-days full and his last week tidy, and that's all." She put the slip in the back of her notebook, behind the six from the long table. "It would be easier if somebody had meant it. People who mean things get tired of meaning them. A calendar never gets tired of anything."

She showed it to Brom at supper, because it was his date, and he had a right to it before anybody else made anything of it. He read the slip with his spoon in his other hand and gave it back.

"Then I'll be in town that morning either way," he said. "When mine's done I'll come up the street and sit at the back of yours."

"If you come out of yours Iron," said Lira, "and the seat's still talking, sit where he can see you."
