"I was going to," said Brom, and went back to his beans.

The sittings went up on the covered walk's middle board that afternoon in Bracken's hand, under the house's one-line answer from the eighth day: Sittings at the registry seat, Ostrand, on the seat's Fifth-days. First sitting: the sixth Fifth-day of the year. Underneath it, smaller, Bracken had added a line of his own, which was a thing he never did on a public board. The house will attend.

"How many?" Cael asked at the counter.

"A dozen, if the year runs honest and nobody falls off a horse." Bracken was sorting the noon post into its pigeonholes. "It never runs honest. More."

On the Fifth-day that week he fought in wing three at the band, against a Blade.

She was an Iron Rank Five of the third year, with a long patient guard that liked to make you come to it, and a habit of holding her edge-line a hand's breadth lower than the cohort taught, so that a man who read the line by the cohort's rule stepped onto it. Cael read her weight instead of her line, and went to her slowly in the first exchange and took it with a burst off the left foot when her back heel lifted. In the second she walked him into the corner by the south door, one patient step at a time, and he spent a second burst getting out of it and came out a stride short of where he wanted to be. The third was the rotation's: it went to her, whatever it cost, and it cost him her edge-line laid across his forearm, hard, a sting that went through the wrap and stayed there for an hour. In the fourth he waited for the heel again and it came, and the touch was his.

Twenty-two and a third. Gault gave the clerk the figure. Ephram, at the rail, wrote it in his chart and did not draw a question mark, and kept his eyes on the chart, and Cael was grateful to him for it.

On the twenty-seventh evening, at the north wall, the coats were early.

He had sat at the third buttress for the change of the bell more evenings than he could count, and it had always gone the same way: the bell from the lecture range, and on its last stroke two coats coming along the river street to take the places at the road's foot, and the two who had stood there going off toward the bridge. Tonight the new pair came round the corner of the chandler's a full minute before the bell. They stood a little way off along the river street and waited for it, with their hands in their coats, and only when it rang did they walk the last few yards and take their places.

Men who are early for something are waiting for it to happen.

On the third evening of the year he had written on this coping that men with no questions get sent at the end of something, not the start. He had not known then what the something was. He had a word for it now. The paper served on the eighth day had begun a thing that would end in a ruling, and the ruling would turn him from one kind of entry in a file into another. That was what grey coats of a senior grade were posted to stand beside: not a boy, but the moment the boy's paper changed.

They're waiting for a status change, he wrote on the coping in the dusk. The proceedings will make one.

He told the other two on the residence stair, because they had a right to it, and because he had sat on the coping long enough for the words to have set. Lira listened with her hand on the rail. Brom listened with his eyes on the stair window, which looked the wrong way for the river and showed only the court.

"Early," said Lira. "For the first time."

"A full minute."

"Then they've been told there's a date," said Brom. He did not say what date. Neither of them did. Lira took her hand off the rail and went up, and after a moment Brom went up after her, and Cael stood on the stair a little longer looking at the court, which had nobody in it.

Lira asked for the honest floor on the Sixth-day night, three nights before her trial, and she asked for it in a way she had never asked for anything.

"I want you to be a floor," she said.

They were in the east hall again, at the quarter to the eleventh bell, on Rooke's key. The shutters were drawn along the gallery and the two lanterns stood at either end of the painted lines. Brom had brought the jug. Karis had come this time, for the first hour, with her notebook under her arm. She sat on the gallery stair and said she would take the figures as they happened, counting each one from its start the way Cael had counted on the first night, and that nobody was to break anything she would have to spell.

"A floor," said Cael.

"The Force," said Lira. "The third-year. I'm fighting him on Second-day, in front of the rating table, and I've drilled beside him every morning for two months, and I know exactly how he fights a drill." She was taping her wrists, quickly. "I don't know how he fights me. Nobody's ever made him."

Cael knew the Force a little. A broad-backed young man who laughed when he was surprised; Rank Seven on the porter's wall since the last sitting of the old year, six ranks above Lira's one, and the best fighter the cohort had made in a straight line, without a program, since Ephram. A Force fighter's Path was a shove, and it went on contact. This one put it into the floor through his front foot. He stamped, and a beat later the boards ahead of the stamp, out to a stride, jumped, and went on jumping for a count or two before they settled. Then the shove came back up into him, the way it always came back into a Force fighter along the line it had gone out by, and he had to take it in his knees before he could stamp again.

"He settles," said Lira. "Every time. That's him taking his own push back. Then he stamps again, a stride further on. Settle, stamp, step. By the third stamp the floor in front of him is like trying to cross a cart while it's going." She tore the tape. "I can't get Brom to do that. Brom's a wall. Walls don't move the floor."

"I don't move the floor either."

"No." She looked up. "But you move the air. You lay a road that leans. If you lay one across my line, it's not his floor, but it's a floor that tips under me when I don't expect it, and I can learn what my feet do on it." She stood. "Lay them across me. I'll cross them on the four-count. Brom stands at the end of the line, where the Force would be, and if I get to him I touch him."

Cael looked at Brom. Brom, unwinding his wraps, looked back.

"The lane costs," said Cael. "Ten counts, every time. Behind the eyes."

"I know what it costs. I wrote it on my hand." Lira went to the first cross. "Lay one. We'll write what it costs."

He laid one.

He set it a stride in front of her and across her line, from the north wall toward the south, a road of air fifteen feet long and no wider than his shoulders, tipping toward the south. His ears closed and opened. The dust in the cracks of the painted boards woke and ran south down the lane, a pale thin stream. Then he took the read off the lane, deliberately, the way he had learned on this floor three weeks ago, and gave it back to himself, and stood.

Lira ran the four counts at the lane.

On the first count she stepped. On the second she put her weight on her front foot, the long lie, and her front foot came down inside the lane, and the lane took it. It slid her front foot a hand's breadth south, sideways, out from under her, and her whole lie went wrong with it. She did not fall. She caught herself on the back foot with a grunt and stood there off balance in the painted floor's dust, and the four-count was gone.

"Again," she said.

On the gallery stair Karis had begun to count, quietly, from the moment the dust ran. He tested the Wind at every number. It came late, and late, a beat behind his asking each time, until she said eleven, and then it came when he called it. Ten counts, the same bill as the first night. She wrote it down, and he laid another in the same place, and she began to count again.

She tried the second count outside the lane this time, short of it, and the third count, the empty one, with one foot in the lane and one out. The lane took the foot that was in. She stood through it. She let it slide her front foot, the way a fighter lets a push go by, and on the fourth count she burst off the back foot, the one that was still on honest boards, across the lane and through the end of it, and came out of the burst three strides from Brom with the dust still running behind her.

"Three strides," said Brom.

"Three strides," said Lira. "Short." She was breathing hard. "But I didn't fall. Again."

He laid a third.

She ran it, and it was better: the empty count taken standing, one foot in and one foot out, the lane sliding the inside foot and Lira letting it. She burst on the fourth off the honest foot, and the burst carried her a stride from Brom, and she touched his shoulder. Brom nodded. Lira turned round, grinning, to say something.

And Cael found he had lost the count.

Karis had started it as the third lane went down, as she had started the others, and he had been testing the Wind against her numbers. Somewhere about six he had stopped hearing them. Nothing had happened. The weight behind his eyes had simply stayed, warm and heavy, and the numbers had gone on past him like carts past a man asleep on a bench. He reached for the Wind out of habit, the way you test a stair, and it came late.

"Nine," said Karis, from the stair.

Late.

"Ten."

Late. Lira had turned round. She came across the floor to him fast and stood in front of him and looked at his eyes.

"Eleven."

He reached. Late.

"Twelve."

Late. He felt Lira's hand close on his sleeve.

"Thirteen."

It came on time.

Lira took the pencil stub out of her pocket and wrote on her palm, under the place where the tape stopped. "Ten, ten, twelve," she said. "Clean at eleven, eleven, thirteen." She looked up. "That's the last one tonight."

"I'm all right."

"I know you're all right. It's still the last one." She put the pencil away. "You'd only ever met the ten counts by themselves. Tonight you met them three times in a row and the third ran long. That's a new figure. We don't spend a new figure the night we find it. Rooke says that." She almost smiled. "Rooke says it about me."

Karis, on the stair, read her column back aloud without being asked: First lane, slow through ten. Second, through ten. Third, through twelve; clean at thirteen. Not tested past three. Then she shut the notebook, said she had what she had come for, and went up to bed.

They sat on the boards afterward among the white crosses with the jug going round.

"What did you learn," said Brom, to Lira.

Lira lay on her back with her taped hands on her stomach, looking up at the dark shutters.

"Not to put my weight down on the third count," she said. "I've been doing the lie with a real foot. On his floor the real foot is the one that moves. So I lie with a foot I don't care about, and I keep the one I'm going to burst from on wood that holds still." She turned her head on the boards. "And I go on the fourth. Not the third. Everything I've ever done says go on the third, and against him the third is when the boards are still jumping from the last stamp. The fourth is when he's taking his own push back."

"He'll laugh at you," said Brom. "When you stand there on the empty count."

"Let him," said Lira. "He laughs when he's surprised. I'd like him surprised."

Cael sat with the jug in his hands and the last warmth going out from behind his eyes, and thought about the twelve.

It was the first new thing the lane had told him since the morning it settled. He had believed the ten counts were the price, fixed, like the five free bursts on boards; a thing he could plan around, write in a minute before a fight, and pay. Now he knew they were not fixed. They grew when he spent the lane over and over. He did not know yet by how much, or whether they grew without end, or whether they came back down with rest. He knew only that a figure he had thought was a wall was a slope.

He realized he was glad. Not of the slope, but of where he had found it: on a painted floor at night, with Karis counting from the stair and Lira's hand on his sleeve and Brom standing at the end of the line, and not in front of a crowd with a Gold across the ring. That was the whole reason for the floor. Brom had said it three weeks ago, on this floor. So you don't forget it's yours. It was his, and it had a slope in it, and now he knew where.

They went back across the court in the dark, the three of them, with the lanterns out and the jug empty and Brom carrying both. Lira walked on Cael's left, close, the way she walked when she meant to say something and had not yet decided how.

"Are you going to tell Rooke?" she said at the residence door. "About the twelve."

"It's not his floor. It's ours. He said he didn't want to know what for."

"He said that about the key." She stopped with her hand on the door. "He'd want to know about this. Not to stop it. To know." She looked at him in the dark. "You don't have to. I'm only saying I'd want to, if it were mine."

He thought about it on the stair, and in his room, and at the window with Hesk's book shut on his knee. In the morning he went down to the east hall before the first bell and found Rooke at the trestle with the red book, and told him: three lanes in a night, ten and ten and twelve, and nothing past three. Rooke listened without looking up. Then he wrote one word on the corner of his board, and turned the board so that Cael could not see it, and said, "Good. Now don't do it again until you know why."

Chapter 12 — Admit

The east hall had never held a crowd before, and on the thirtieth morning of the year it held one.

Nobody had announced the trial beyond a line on Rooke's own board, chalked the evening before in his square capitals: PROGRAM TRIAL. SECOND-DAY, SECOND BELL. LIRA AGAINST FORCE THIRD-YEAR. RATED. But the house had read it, and the house knew what rated meant on that floor. It meant the first bout ever fought on the program's painted boards under the program's own seal, with a figure at the end of it that would go into the program's own book. By the half-bell the gallery was full along both sides. By the second bell the porters had opened the shutters on the high windows to let the heat out, and the light came down onto the white crosses in long bright bars, and there were people standing on the gallery stair.

He had found Lira an hour before it, sitting on the east hall's outer step in the grey light with her back against the doorpost and a roll of tape in her lap, doing her wrists. She did them slowly, as she never did on an ordinary morning, a turn at a time, pressing each turn flat with her thumb before the next went over it.

"Brom's way," she said, when she saw him look. "It takes longer. It gives you something to do with your hands that isn't shaking." She tore the tape with her teeth. "They're not shaking. I'm just telling you why it works."

He sat down on the step below her.

"You asked me once not to count your bursts," he said.

"I did. Ages ago." She started the other wrist. "I still don't want you to. I'll know how many. I'll be the one paying for them." She pressed a turn down. "Count his."

"His what?"

"Anything. His stamps. His settles. How long he laughs. You'll see things from the rail I won't see from the floor, and I won't be able to ask you about them till it's over, and I want them all, in order, when I do." She finished the wrist and flexed the hand, and looked at it as if it belonged to somebody she was fond of. "Karis will count my bursts whether I like it or not. That's her business. Yours is him."

Down the walk the Force came round the corner of the range with two of his cohort, all three of them laughing at something, and saw her on the step, and lifted a hand. She lifted one back. Then she stood, and went in to the floor without another word, and Cael went up the gallery stair to find the rail.

Cael had the rail at the north end, where he had stood on the second morning of the year to watch the red book. Brom stood on his left with his arms folded. Karis stood on his right with her notebook shut and her pen in her hand. Ephram was three steps down the gallery stair with the captain's file under his arm, where he could see the whole floor and be seen by the whole cohort, which Cael supposed was the point. The girl from the reading room's outer table had found a place against the far wall of the gallery, with her small notebook open.

Below them on the floor stood the rating table: a trestle under the north windows with three chairs behind it. The clerk with the red drill-book sat at one end. Rooke sat in the middle with his board and his pencil. And at the other end, with a ruled card in front of him and his hands folded on the table, sat the Stone from the river academy, who had asked to come and teach the girl who beat him and was now going to put a figure on her.

Rooke stood up at the second bell and said the rule, once, in a voice that carried to the back of the gallery without being raised.

"Program trial. My rule, not the region's." He held up his board as if the rule were written on it, which it was not. "Four exchanges. Each one, the table gives a flag to whoever took it, or to nobody if nobody did. Most flags takes the trial. Three bursts a bout for the program's entrant, as on every day she's ever stood on this floor. Past three, the table still gives the exchange to whoever takes it, and the card pays for every burst over. The other fighter, what his own Path allows. Level after four, the table rates them both, and the higher figure takes it." He sat down. "The figure goes in this program's book. Not the registry's. Not yet."

Lira stood at the south chalk with her wrists taped and her left arm carried a little close, out of habit. Across forty feet of painted boards stood the Force.

He was a big young man, broad in the back and thick through the thighs, and he stood at his chalk with his feet planted and his hands loose and a pleasant expression, the expression of somebody who has been looking forward to a thing and has decided to enjoy it. He had been drilling beside Lira every morning since the recess. He knew the four-count; he had run it himself, badly, for the practice of seeing it. He had laughed once on this floor when she lied to him on the second count and he went the wrong way. He was Iron Rank Seven, six ranks above her on the porter's wall, and he was the best thing the cohort had built in a straight line since Ephram.

Cael watched his knees.

From the rail there was nothing else to watch. A Force fighter's shove went on contact, and this one's contact was the floor. He stamped with his front foot, and a beat later the boards ahead of the stamp, out to a stride, jumped, as a table jumps when somebody slaps it from beneath, and went on jumping for a count or two before they lay down. Then the shove came back up into him along the line it had gone out by, and his knees gave and his hips dropped a finger's breadth while he took it. That was the settle. Cael could see it from the rail and hear the boards answer it. It was the bill for the last stamp, paid before the next.

"Exchange," said the clerk.

The Force did what Force fighters did. He did not rush. He stamped, and the boards in front of him jumped, and he settled, and stepped up onto them as they lay down again, and stamped once more a stride further on. Stamp, settle, step. He came forward behind a floor that would not hold still.

Lira ran straight at him.

It was the worst thing she could have done, and the whole gallery knew it. She did not run the four-count. She did not lie. She went at him in a plain hard line, burst one off the left hip, the old burst, the one she had brought out of a barn at fourteen and that every fighter on the hill had seen a hundred times. The burst carried her twenty feet and put her down inside his stride.

He stamped as she landed. The boards under her jumped a beat after her heel came down, and her landing went out from under her sideways. She caught herself. She had to; she was on a floor that was trying to put her on her back. And while she caught herself the Force laid his palm on her shoulder, square and plain, and the shove came after the touch, the way it always came after with a Force, and Lira went back a stride and a half and sat down on the painted boards.

The Stone lifted his flag. Red. The Force's.

The gallery groaned.

Rooke wrote nothing at all.

Lira got up. She dusted her palms on her thighs, and walked back to her chalk, and stood there with her hands at her sides and her eyes on the Force's knees. Her lips were moving very slightly.

"She gave it," said Brom quietly.

"Yes."

"On purpose."

"Yes." Cael had seen it from the first stride. Lira did not run straight at a Force fighter. She had not done it since the mill town. "She was counting him."

"Counting what?"

"His settle." He watched her lips. "She needed to watch him stamp and pay for it, start to finish, with nothing in his way. So she gave him nothing in his way."

Karis, on his other side, had opened her notebook. She wrote one line and showed it to him without a word. First flag bought. Price: one flag on the record, in front of the table.

"Exchange," said the clerk.

The Force stamped. Settled. Stepped. And Lira, at her chalk, began the four-count.

The first step was an ordinary step, any fighter's, and the Force watched it come and stamped again. The second step was the lie. She put her weight on her front foot and left it there one count too long, the long lie the Stone had taught her, so that anybody watching for the burst would see it coming and set himself to meet it. The Force saw it coming. He stamped exactly where her burst would land if it came off that front foot, a good hard stamp, and Cael heard the boards jump there a beat later and thought it was the best the man had done all morning.

The third count, nothing happened.

It was the hardest thing in the world to watch. Lira stood on the painted floor with one foot forward and one back and did nothing at all, for a whole count, while a Rank Seven Force stood twenty feet away with the boards still jumping in front of him and his knees bent, waiting. The gallery made a small sound. Somebody laughed, uncertainly. The Force laughed too, from surprise, the way he always did, a short bark.

Then his knees gave, and his hips dropped.

Cael saw it. Lira saw it a hair before he did. The settle was on the man's own fourth count, his own rhythm, the same rhythm he had paid to in the first exchange with nothing in his way. He had to take his own shove back, whether she had given him anything to shove at or not.

And her fourth count was the same beat as his.

She burst off the back foot. Not the front foot she had lied with, which stood on boards that had jumped a moment ago; the back one, which had never left wood he had touched. She burst at the angle the first three counts had sworn she would never take, low and to the right, past the place he had stamped, and came down on still boards two strides from his left hip with her landing beat holding her steady. The Force was still in his settle, knees bent, taking his own push back, with nothing to put it into.

She touched his shoulder. Lightly. Two fingers.

The Stone lifted his flag. Blue.

The noise in the gallery was not cheering, not at first. It was the sound of a great many people realizing at the same moment that the story they had been watching was a different story. Then it was cheering. Rooke, at the table's middle, put his pencil to his board and wrote one word, and Cael could not see what it was and did not need to.

"Two bursts," said Karis, writing. "Two exchanges. One flag each."

The Force stood a moment looking at the place on the boards where he had stamped for a girl who was not there. Then he shook his head, grinning, and went back to his chalk.

He had learned. That was what made him the best the cohort had built. In the third exchange he did not stamp to his own count any more.

He stamped faster, shorter, left and right and centre as he came, two counts apart instead of four, none of them as hard as before but each one coming before the last had lain down, so that the boards a stride ahead of him were jumping across the whole width of his reach. He came on behind them. Within a dozen heartbeats there was no still wood between Lira and him anywhere she could reach in a step.

Cael watched her look for it and not find it.

She tried the four-count once, and the lie on the second count put her front foot on boards that had been still a moment earlier and were jumping now, and her foot went sideways, and she went with it. She did not burst. She scrambled, two ugly running steps and a hop, out of the jumping boards on her own legs, and came up near the east wall beside the striking frames on their thick springs. He came after her. Not fast; Force fighters were never fast. Stamp, settle, step, stamp, a stride at a time, the floor ahead of him jumping like water coming up a beach.

She went back. A stride. Another. The frames were a pace behind her heel.

"She's out of floor," said Brom.

"She's not," said Cael.

She had done it on the honest floor three nights before, at the end of a lane he laid for her, with Brom standing at the end of the line. She had learned it standing in dust that ran. Lie with the foot you don't care about. Go on the fourth.

She stood with her back nearly against the frames and put her left foot forward onto boards that were jumping. She let them. She let them shove her front foot a hand's breadth sideways and did not fight them, the way a fighter lets a push go by. She kept her right foot behind her on the last strip of still wood on the east side of the hall. And she stood there for the empty third count, one foot moving and one foot still, while the Force came up for the stamp that would take the last of her still wood away.

He settled on the count. Even now, stamping fast, stamping in a fan, the man still had to take his push back, and a fighter cannot pay for one stamp and throw the next at the same moment. Two counts now, not four. But a count all the same.

She went on her fourth.

Burst three. Off the right foot, the still one, straight along the line of the frames, not toward him at all but past him, so close to the frames that the nearest post rang as her shoulder brushed it. She came down eight feet on, behind the end of his fan, on boards he had not stamped because every stamp of his had been in front of him. The Force was turning, and a man turning in his own settle turns slowly. He was a beat late.

She touched his back between the shoulders.

Blue.

"Three bursts," said Karis. "Her whole bout." Her pen kept moving. "One exchange to go."

Cael knew what the fourth exchange would cost before the clerk said the word.

The Force had learned twice now. He was not going to give her a settle to burst into. He was not going to chase her into a corner where she could go past him along a wall. When the clerk said exchange he did not come forward at all. He stamped where he stood, to the left, and to the right, and in front, and behind, a stride out on each side, and as each patch of boards lay down he stamped it awake again, turning slowly in the middle, until he stood in a ring of floor that never stopped jumping. It was like a well with the water always moving at its edges. He stood on the still wood in the middle of it and waited for her to come.

There was nowhere near him to land. To touch him she would have to come down on boards that were moving, and anything that landed there would slide.

Rooke's rule was three bursts. She had spent three.

Lira stood at her chalk and looked at the ring of jumping floor. Her lips were not moving now. She was not counting him; there was no count left to find. Cael watched her decide, and saw her know exactly what it would cost.

She went.

Burst four, off the left hip, in one long low flight to the edge of the ring, the old burst, the barn's burst, the strongest thing she had ever owned. She came down on jumping boards. They moved. She let them. She let them slide her landing a hand's breadth and turned the slide into the start of the next thing, as she had learned in the dust on the honest floor, and burst again off the moving boards before they could take her any further.

Burst five.

It carried her over the last stride of the ring and onto the still wood at its middle, a stride from the Force, so close that he could not stamp between them, because there was no floor between them to stamp. He was turning to stamp behind him. He had built a well to stand in, and she had come over its edge.

She did not hit him. She put her taped palm flat on his breastbone and held it there.

Blue.

The gallery came apart.

"Three flags to one," said the clerk into the noise, and wrote it in the red book.

The Stone wrote on his card. He wrote for a long time, longer than a single figure needed. Then he slid the card along the trestle to Rooke, and Rooke read it, and stood up with it in his hand, and the gallery fell quiet to hear it, because nobody on the hill had ever heard a program figure read out on that floor before.

"Execution, ten. Effect, ten." Rooke did not look up. "Control, seven. Twenty-seven."

He put the card down on the trestle.

"Ten is a good ordinary day at the heart of Silver. She was there in two columns." His voice did not change at all. "The seven is the fourth burst and the fifth. Up to three, a fighter owns her bout. Past three she rents it, and the card collects the rent." He looked at the clerk. "Enter it."

Twenty-seven. Cael had her figures in his notebook since the wool town, every one: twenty-five, twenty-six, twenty-seven at her very best last year, the top of what the board called strong Iron. Twenty-eight was the floor of the Silver bracket. She had stood a point short of it before. She stood a point short of it now. But this time the point had a name and a place, and Rooke had just said both aloud in front of the whole house.

Lira walked to the middle of the floor and shook the Force's hand. Her collar was dark through and her chest was going like a bellows, and she was standing on her right leg more than her left.

Rooke came down from the table with his board under his arm. He did not call her over. He went to her where she stood at the edge of the painted lines, and went down on one knee on the boards in front of her, and put his thumb on the outside of her left thigh just below the hip, and pressed.

She hissed through her teeth.

He moved the thumb down a hand's breadth, and pressed again, and again, the way a farrier goes down a horse's leg, and she hissed at each one until he reached the knee, and there she did not.

"From the hip to above the knee, down the outside," said Rooke, to his board, and stood up. "That's four and five. Three never goes there." He wrote. "Two days at half work. No frames. No bursts at all until the leg is quiet, and you'll tell me when it's quiet, and I'll decide whether to believe you." He tucked the pencil behind his ear. "At the meet you don't fight one bout in a morning. You fight one, and eat, and fight again. A fifth burst before noon is a leg that won't carry you after it."

"Yes, Coach."

He went back to the table without another word, and sat, and began writing in the red book in the clerk's place, as if the trial had happened a long time ago.

Ephram came down the gallery stair against the stream of people going up it to leave, with the captain's file under his arm and a pencil behind his ear, and stopped beside Cael at the rail's end.

"I've started her a page," he said. He opened the file a little way, enough to show a sheet folded in four inside it, new, with only three lines on it so far. "I keep one on everybody. You know that. Hers was a line a month. It's going to be longer now."

"What's on it?"

"Today." Ephram closed the file. "Four exchanges, and which ones she bought, and which ones she paid for." He looked down at the floor, where the Force was rolling his wraps at the far chalk. "And his. I've started him a page too. He'll be worth watching after this. Men who get beaten like that either stop or start."

He went off toward the south door to tell the cohort where to stand, and Cael heard his voice go up behind him in the yard, patient and carrying, explaining to somebody that a captain did not have to know why a thing had happened in order to know that it had.

On his way to the south door the Force stopped at the foot of the gallery stair, kit on his shoulder, wraps hanging out of his coat pocket. Lira was on the bottom step by then, unwinding her tapes.

"Two counts was a mistake," he said. "I'll stamp to no count at all by the month's end. You'll see."

"Then I'll have to find something else to count."

He laughed, the short bark, surprised at himself for laughing. Then he shifted the kit on his shoulder.

"The first one. You gave me that."

"Yes."

He nodded, a short honest nod, the way a man nods to somebody who has told him where he left his hat, and went out of the south door. Cael watched him go and knew that by Rooke's next morning drill the man would be stamping to a rhythm nobody on the hill could hear, and that the whole cohort would be the better for having had him beaten.

Lira came up the stair to the rail.

She had her tapes balled in one fist and the other hand pressed against the outside of her thigh where Rooke's thumb had been, and her face had the look Cael had watched on it for two months of mornings and never had words for. She stood at the rail beside him and looked down at the painted floor. The trestle. The clerk back at his red book. The Stone, folding his card in half along a crease he made with his thumbnail, and putting it inside his coat.

"He came from the river to teach me a count," she said. "A man I beat. He wrote and asked." She turned the balled tape in her fingers. "There was a time I'd have thrown that back in his face and called it pity, and walked out to the yard to prove I didn't need it." She watched the Stone go out. "I'm better now. I can admit I want it."

Brom unfolded his arms. Karis, on Cael's other side, closed her notebook very quietly.

Lira looked at the floor a moment longer, and then went down the stair to find her water, walking carefully on the left leg, and did not look back to see how it had been received.

Halfway across the court in the heat, behind the crowd going out, Cael had the observation notebook open on his palm and was writing as he walked, in the working pages at the front where the day's figures went. He had got as far as Lira's name.

Karis reached across without breaking step, closed the notebook on his pencil, turned it over, and opened it again from the back.

"There," she said. "With the things that don't get crossed out. Her word was admit."

He stopped on the flags and wrote it there: the date, and the one word under Lira's name.

At supper Lira asked him, without looking up from her plate, where he had put it.

"The back."

She nodded once and went on eating, and that was all either of them ever said about it.

That same week two envelopes came for Brom.

The first came on the thirty-first day, to Bracken's counter, in the district seat's grey stock with the district's own small seal, and Bracken carried it across to the refectory himself at the noon meal. He did not lay it on the table this time. He stood at the end of the middle table and read it aloud, all of it, which he had never done with anybody's paper in that room.

"Review for advancement of tier. The panel convened under this office's docket of the fourth day is confirmed: three assessors and a sigil frame, at the district seat. The practitioner's record is received and entered as it stands, the title included. Sitting: the last Fifth-day of the academic year." He turned the sheet to the light. "And at the foot. Outcome anticipated: advancement, per title."

He read the last word again, by itself. "Anticipated." Then he turned the sheet round and laid it in front of Karis, not Brom, with his finger beside the foot.

"You've read more dockets than anybody at this table but me," he said. "Have you ever seen that on one?"

Karis looked. "Never."

"Nor have I, and every docket that came up this hill in thirteen years has crossed my counter." He took the sheet back. "A docket gives the day and the room and the panel. Nobody lets it guess at the end. Some district clerk got tired of guessing quietly and wrote his guess where we could all see it." He looked at the word over his spectacles as if it might go away. "I'd like to shake his hand. I'd also like to have him moved. I'll be writing to the district." He held the sheet out across the table to Brom. "Well. They've as good as painted it on the door."

Brom wiped his hands on his napkin and took the sheet, and read it, and folded it twice along the creases the district clerk had put in it. Then he unbuttoned his coat and put it in the left inside pocket, with the first docket and the summons and the Velmere letters, and buttoned the coat again, and pressed the buttons down one after another with his palm.

"Thank you, Registrar."

Bracken's eyes rested on the buttons. He said nothing about where the paper had gone, and went back up the refectory between the long tables.

The second envelope came up with the evening post. Cael saw it on the post-room shelf when he went for his own letters, a square cream envelope with a dark red seal pressed with the bar and the ring, and he knew the seal. Brom took it from the shelf at the eighth bell. He did not open it in the post room or the court. He took it upstairs and shut his door.

Late that night, crossing the court from the north wall, Cael looked up at the residence front, because he always did. Brom's window was lit, and lit wrong. The lamp that had stood on the sill side of the table for two years was over on the far wall now, on the washstand, so that the light fell everywhere in the room except on the table.

Lira was sitting on the stair in the dark when he came in, with her bad leg out straight along the step.

"It's on the table," she said quietly. "On top of the docket. Edges level. Not opened."

"You went in?"

"His door doesn't latch unless you lean on it." She looked at her own hands. "I didn't lean on it. I wanted to." She was quiet a moment. "When he opens it, nobody asks. Not what it said. Not whether he's all right. Tell Karis. I'll tell her too, so she hears it twice."

Karis heard it twice. From the next evening on, the annex door stood open every night until the last bell, with the lamp lit inside and Karis at the long table with her back to the stair, and anybody coming up could have walked in and sat down without knocking. Brom went past it twice the next evening on his way to the stair and did not go in.

On the third evening he opened the letter.

Nobody saw him do it. Nobody at the table learned what it said, because he did not tell them, then or afterward. What they saw was his face, when he came down to supper an hour later than usual and sat in his place and pulled the bread toward him.

It was the face of a man being offered his whole ledger back.

Cael looked at it once, as long as a man looks at a letter that is not addressed to him, and then he looked at his bread.

Nobody asked. Lira passed Brom the beans. Brom took some, and passed them on to Seln, who took some, and passed them on.

Chapter 13 — The Hand

Karis spent the house's money for the first time on the thirty-fifth day, and she made Cael come down to the counter to watch her do it.

"Not because I need a witness," she said on the library stair. "Because I'm going to want to remember what it felt like, and you remember things better than I do when they're not on paper."

The budget line was small. Cael had seen the figure in the house's accounts, on the leaf the council had sat twice to head: a sum for copying and couriers and archive fees, the kind of money a senior instructor spent in a year without noticing where it had gone. Karis had not touched it in five weeks. She had built an eleven-pound answer to the Compact without spending a mark of it, because the answer was the house's, and the house paid for the house's paper. This was the first thing she had wanted for herself.

She laid the request on Bracken's counter, filled in, in her finding hand. It was addressed to the archive at Greyvane, to the keeper of the founding collection, and it asked for certified copies of the signature leaves of the oldest compilation the archive held: the founders' own hands, at the foot of the founding text, as they had set them down before anybody had written a line of commentary over them.

Bracken read it from the address to the signature. Then he took the house's budget book from under the counter and opened it at her line, and entered the sum against it in his small upright hand, and wrote the request's number beside the sum, and blotted both.

"Greyvane," he said. "Prynn, still?"

"Still."

"Then it'll be right when it comes, and it won't come quickly." He sealed the request and put it in the pigeonhole for the Greyvane post. "She has never filled a request of mine in under a month, and she has never once sent me a wrong leaf. Before the midyear recess, I'd say. Not long before."

Karis stayed at the counter with her hands on the wood, looking at the pigeonhole where the request had gone. Cael had seen her ask for things at counters before. At Greyvane she had asked on her own account, for a student's fee, and been made to wait. At Norhold she had asked on the tournament's, and been answered by a clerk who did not look up. She had never asked as anybody's. Now there was a line in a book with her name above it, and a house's seal on her request, and a registrar who had entered it without a word, as he would have entered a request from the Magister.

She took out her notebook and turned it over, and opened it from the back, where the six slips from the long table lived in their pocket behind the last leaf with Brom's two dates beside them. On the inside of the back board she wrote the request's number and Greyvane: the founders' hands, and under it she ruled three short lines and left them empty.

"For what they tell me," she said, before he could ask. "If they tell me anything."

"And if they don't?"

"Then I'll have three empty lines, and I'll know exactly what they cost." She shut the book. "It feels like being trusted with a key by somebody who'll notice if you lose it. I've never been so careful in my life."

Her assistant made the fourth mistake of the month that afternoon, at the outer table, and Cael was at the reading-room window to see what Karis did about it.

The girl had been asked to set out, on a single leaf, which of the integrity provisions' sections a seat could act on of its own motion and which needed a party to ask. She had done it in an hour, neatly, in two columns. Karis read it standing at the outer table, all the way down, and then put her finger beside one line in the left-hand column and took the finger away.

She did not say what was wrong with it.

She went to the shelf, took down the second volume of the code, which Brom had carried up that morning on his shoulder, and laid it on the girl's table, closed.

"Find it," said Karis, and went back into the reading room.

Cael watched the girl through the open door. She looked at the line Karis had touched. She looked at the closed volume. Her face went red from the collar up, and then it set, the jaw first and then the mouth, the way Lira's set on the painted floor when the Stone stood on the cross she should have been on. She opened the volume and began to read. She did not ask anybody anything. She turned pages, went back, turned forward again, went to the index and found the index wanting, went to the digests on the lower shelf without being told they existed.

It took her twenty minutes. Then she crossed the landing with the leaf in one hand and the open volume in the other, and laid both on the long table in front of Karis, and put her finger on a sub-section near the foot of the page.

"Upon a party's motion only," the girl said. "Not of its own motion. I had it in the wrong column. There's a proviso at the end of the section I didn't read."

"Yes," said Karis.

That was all she said. The girl stood there a moment longer, as if waiting for the rest, and there was no rest. Then she went back across the landing with her leaf and her volume and sat down at her own table, and Cael saw her face go slowly pink again, not from shame this time. She had been told nothing at all but yes, and it had been the best thing anyone had said to her since the intake.

Somebody was using the second floor after the eighth bell. Cael saw the lantern from the court on the first evening, one low light behind the middle roof's windows at an hour when the cohort had gone to supper, and went up to see whose it was.

It was two men's. The old striking frames stood in a row along the east wall, padded posts on tired springs, nothing like the program's new frames in the east hall. Brom had the one at the north end. Ephram had the one beside it. Cael stood at the rail by the door, and neither of them looked round, and he stayed.

They did not spar. He waited for them to, that first evening, and they did not. Brom ran his defensive work on his frame from the top: the forearm going hard, the turn, the reset, the drive. It was the long sequence he ran before every road, slow at first and then at fighting pace. Ephram ran Blade work on the next frame at the cohort's speed. The entry line, the cut along it, the recovery. Each of them had his own post. Neither touched the other's.

But they were a hair apart, and they kept the same time.

On the second evening Cael saw the shape of it. Ephram finished a sequence and stopped, and stood with his sword arm down, and watched Brom reset. Watched the turn, and the half-breath after it, and the drive. Then he went back to his own frame. A little later Brom stopped, in the middle of his work, and stood, and watched Ephram's entry line go in: where the feet went, where the weight sat, which way the shoulder came round. Then he went back to his.

On the third evening Lira came up the stair and stood at the rail beside Cael. She watched them, leaning on the rail, and Cael saw her lips move once, counting something, and then stop.

On the fourth evening the lantern burned low, and neither of them trimmed it. Ephram stopped at his frame and watched Brom's reset one more time, the whole of it, top to bottom, with his head a little on one side. Brom finished it. Then Brom turned round from his frame and stood and looked at Ephram, straight, the way he looked at a floor before he stood on it. Ephram looked back.

Neither of them nodded. Neither of them did anything at all. After a while Ephram picked up his kit and went down the stair, and Brom turned back to his frame and finished his work alone, and trimmed the lantern, and put it out.

Cael went down by the other stair with Lira beside him. In the court under the covered walk's north arch she stopped, and looked back up at the second floor's dark windows, and then at him. He had seen it too: two men learning a floor they expected one day to stand on across from each other, each taking the other's measure as thoroughly as either knew how, and neither in any hurry to say what for.

Karis called them to the annex the night before the sitting.

Only the four of them: Lira cross-legged on the window seat, Brom in the doorway because the reading room had three chairs and he would not take one, Cael at the window. One lamp. The girl had been sent to bed and had gone, which she did not always do. On the long table Karis had laid out a sheet on which she had drawn the selling floor of the wool exchange from Bracken's description, with the seat on its platform at the far end and the tables below and the benches behind, and every chair marked in small neat letters.

"Tomorrow is a form," she said. "Filled in, by six or seven people, in a room."

Her finger went to the petitioner's table. "He enters the petition." To the house's. "Our counsel enters the answer." To the platform. "The seat receives both. It rules on neither. It confirms the schedule, and it rises." She took her finger away. "Nothing that happens in that room tomorrow decides anything. Look at it now, here, on paper, so that tomorrow you'll know the room for what it is: the place where the paper gets read."

"Then why are we going?" said Lira.

"Because we said we'd go to every sitting, and the town watches the coach." Karis looked round at the three of them. "And because there's one thing in the room worth watching. Tell me what."

"Jent," said Lira.

"No. You've seen him. He'll be the same man."

"The gallery," said Brom, from the doorway. "Who comes."

"Closer. No." Karis put her finger on the platform, on the square she had marked with a small circle. "The seal. Our counsel is going to stand up and lay eleven pounds of true things on the table under it. Watch what it does when she sits down." She turned down the lamp. "If it does anything at all, I'll take my six slips out of the back of this notebook in front of you and burn them."

At the half-bell on the fortieth day the coach drew up below the market street's last rise, behind Withrow's carriage, in a morning already hot.

Cael counted the steps of the wool exchange through the coach window before the door was opened, because counting was cheaper than deciding what to feel. Four steps, the width of the building. Thirty-one people on them. Nine of them correspondents, with folding boards under their arms and pencils behind their ears and the air of men who had been waiting since first light for somebody to step down from a coach. Two in the dark coats and badges of the river guild. The rest were Ostrand's own: clerks, factors, a woman with a market basket who had plainly stopped on her way somewhere else and forgotten where. They had come early to the top of the town to see a chair with no name on it decide about a boy with none either.

The side door was finished. Its hinges had been blacked, and the dust swept off its sill, and a registry officer stood beside it with a ruled board.

He was young, younger than any registry officer Cael had seen in a doorway, and he had a heavy cold. He held a folded handkerchief in the hand that was not holding the board, and between names he turned his head politely away and used it, and turned back, and found his place on the board with one finger. He did not apologize for the cold or for the door or for the people on the steps. He read the list.

"The Chancellor of Halcenvane Academy."

"Present," said Withrow.

He read the house's counsel next, by her name, which Cael again did not quite catch. Then Karis, as documentary support. Then Brom and Lira, together, as the respondent institution's attendance, and Lira went past him with her chin up as if attendance were a rank. Then Seln, as records support, Halcenvane, and Seln went past him at his even pace without looking at the board at all.

Then the officer came to the last line, and blew his nose, and read it.

"The enrollee of record."

"Present," said Cael.

The officer looked up from the board. "Name for the door log?"

Cael opened his mouth to say his own name, the one people said, and the house's counsel spoke before he could.

"Enter him as the instrument has him," she said. "Exactly."

The officer looked at his list, where the instrument's address had been copied for him by some clerk in a back room, and began to write in the door log's two columns. In the first, for the name, he wrote what the registry had always written: Caelen Hesk-ward. In the second, for the standing in which a person came through that door, he wrote what the paper said he was. The enrollee of record, unclassified.

Cael counted it. He could not help counting it. From the moment the pen touched the first column to the moment it lifted from the second, eleven seconds.

He filed them where the other eleven lived. A circle of pale wood in an office at Denvash, on the morning of his Kindling, and a brass plate at Pellin's elbow that had stayed dark for eleven seconds before it lit, while a fourteen-year-old boy stood in the circle and did not breathe. He had thought then that eleven seconds was the longest any office would ever take to decide what he was.

The side door let them in at the foot of the long room, close by the records table, so that the first thing Cael saw of the proceedings was its paper.

Two officers sat there with their books open in front of them. The senior was a heavy man he did not know. Behind him, at the junior chair, sat a man Cael did know, though he could not have said from where without thinking: a records officer with a careful face and a board, whom he had seen at a desk at Greyvane, and on a chair along the east wall of the evaluation room on the oak, and at other tables before those. The man was writing the date at the head of a leaf. He did not look up.

Cael walked up the strip of floor between the two parties' tables to the house's place, and the old trade went under his boots as he went. The wool-factors had carved their lot numbers into the planking a hundred years ago, row after row, so that every bale had its place and every buyer could find it, and the registry had planed and waxed the boards and set its furniture down on the numbers without troubling to hide them. Nine, ten, eleven. Across the strip Jent was already at the petitioner's table with his inkwell unscrewed; he rose when Withrow came in, to his measured height, and sat again. Cael sat down at the house's table with seventeen under his left foot.

Only then did he look up the room to its end. A low platform. The registry's sigil over it, very large, in plain black. The presiding seat on the platform, and to one side of it a bench of five chairs under grey cloth covers, waiting for evaluators the district had not yet called. Behind him he could hear the public benches without turning: every one of them taken, all the way back to the great double door, and people standing along the wall where there were no benches left.

Cael counted the room, because that was the first thing he did anywhere. Benches, doors, windows, tables, officers. He counted it a second time, and a third. Each time it came out a face short.

The presiding seat was occupied. A registrar sat in it, in the senior grey of the registry, the hood of the seat drawn forward over the head, so that from the house's table there was nothing to see under it but shadow. The hands lay on the bench in front of the hood. They were an ordinary pair of hands, a little lined, neither young nor old, a man's or a woman's, Cael could not have sworn which. The clerk at the side of the platform stood and read into the minute the seat's designation: the seat of the registry at Ostrand, sitting by its seal in proceedings the registry had designated institutional. He read no name. The hood offered none.

So Cael watched the hands, because the hands were all there was.

They kept time with the procedure, and a beat behind it, like a second clock in a house that has been set by the first. When the clerk passed up the minute, the hands took the pen and initialled where the clerk's finger had been, and set the pen down. When the schedule was read, they turned one leaf. The shoulders under the grey did not settle or lift. The hood did not turn toward the respondent's table, or the petitioner's, or the benches. In forty minutes he saw nothing move under that hood that the procedure had not asked to move, and nothing in the hands that the procedure had not put there.

He had spent his life reading people. It came to him, about halfway through, that every one of them had given him something to read whether they meant to or not, because there had been somebody inside the coat doing the giving. There was a coat here, and a seat, and a seal. If there was anybody inside, the seat had been built so that it did not matter.

Havel had his rotation sheet for the Ostrand sittings on a Fourth-day, from a clerk who did not know what was on it, and he read it in his room at the inn by the bridge that evening with the lamp turned up.

Registry seat, Ostrand. Records support, junior chair. Rotation: the seat's Fifth-days, until relieved. There was nothing else. There never was. A rotation sheet told you where to sit and for how long. It did not tell you why, and in all his years of rotation sheets Havel had never once expected it to.

He came to the wool exchange at the first bell on the fortieth day, an hour before anybody else, because the rotation manual said the junior chair would be in its place an hour before the sitting, and he had been in his place an hour before every sitting he had ever been posted to. He laid out the junior chair's things on the records table in the manual's order. First the minute-book, opened to a clean leaf. The receipt book for exhibits. The door log's copy, which the officer at the side door would send in with the porter at the half-bell, to be checked against the list. Two pens. Sand. A clean blotter. He squared each one to the table's edge.

His right hand ached at the web of the thumb, as it did every morning now. He opened it and closed it twice under the table, where nobody could see, and then he trusted it with a pen.

The senior chair came in at the half-bell, a district records officer named on Havel's sheet only by his grade, a heavy, competent man who nodded to him and sat and opened his own book and did not speak to him again all morning. That was correct. The senior chair kept the minute. The junior chair kept the times, the receipts and the door log, and checked the one against the others, and spoke when spoken to. Havel had sat in a great many junior chairs.

The door log came in with the porter. He checked it against the list. Every name on the list had a line in the log, and every line in the log had a name on the list, and against the last line the officer at the door had written the enrollee's registry name and his standing, as the instrument had him. Havel initialled the check and set the log aside.

The respondent's table he left alone.

He had known the boy would be at it. The house had said it would attend every sitting, and the house kept what it said. Havel did not look at him, because the rotation manual's page on courtesy said that an officer of a seat would show the parties ordinary courtesy and no more, and because looking at the boy was not ordinary. He had looked before. On a pump step at Ardenmere, where looking had been the work. Twice at Greyvane, from the recorder's desk below the bench. Three times on the oak at the bluff, from a chair on the east wall: once as the boy came in, and twice when the frame broke, the second quicker than the first. He remembered every one. He did not mean to add to them.

So he kept the times instead.

The seat opened at the second bell. The clerk read the designation; Havel wrote the minute it ended. The petitioner's procurator entered the petition. Jent stood at his table with his leaf in one hand, read the petition's working paragraphs in an even voice that gave no one of them more weight than another, named his nine exhibits and sat; Havel wrote the minute he stood and the minute he sat. Nine minutes. The respondent's counsel entered the answer. She rose, small and grey with a steel rule in her hand, and summarized eleven pounds in a voice that did not hurry and did not linger; twenty-three minutes. Havel took the receipts for both lists of exhibits in the receipt book, nine items and a hundred and seventy-three, and wrote the numbers, and initialled them.

Then the senior chair passed the minute up to the platform for the seat's initial, and it came back down, and Havel saw the seal.

The seat's seal was pressed into the foot of the minute's first leaf, in the grey wax the registry used for proceedings. He gave it the attention he gave every seal that crossed a table he sat at, which was close attention, because looking at seals was part of the work. It was the seat's own. The registry at Ostrand, the old device with the river and the scale. He had seen it on ten thousand minutes. There was nothing in it, or about it, that he had not seen before.

He noted that there was nothing.

He thought, sitting at the junior chair with the minute in front of him, about the five sheets.

They were not with him. They never came to a sitting. They were in his kit at the inn, between the second manual and the third, where they had lived since the night in Norhold when he had written the fifth on a narrow table behind the east tower, with the line he had read upside down on the senior seat's desk at its head. Five entries. The first was a pump step at Ardenmere, and a form with four questions on it, and a mark in the administrative layer of the boy's file that had no office behind it. The last was a sentence closing a door that the first had found open. In between were three more, and every one of the five recorded something that had happened, and nothing that he made of it. That was the rule of the sheets.

He had been told, once, a long time ago, in a room with the door shut, that the mark was not his clearance and he was to let it be. He had let it be. He had only written down that it was there.

He looked at the ordinary seal on the ordinary minute and felt, very faintly, the shape of a sixth sheet, the way you feel the shape of a word you cannot quite remember. And then he looked for the fact to put on it, and there was no fact. A seat sitting by its seal was lawful. A hood was lawful. A procurator who conceded everything was lawful and, in Havel's experience, sensible. The seal was the seal it should have been. Nothing in this room had done anything that was not in the code.

A sixth sheet would need something that had happened. Nothing had happened. A form had been filled in by people in a room.

He went back to the times.

The seat confirmed the schedule. The evaluation seat to be empanelled at a date to be notified. The seat rose. He wrote the minute it rose, and blotted the leaf, and set the receipt book on top of the door log, and did not look up at the respondent's table even when the scrape of its chairs went down the long room.

That evening, at the inn, he took the five sheets out from between the manuals and read them through, every line, in order, the first to the fifth. He read them twice. Then he put them back between the manuals, the same way round, and buckled the kit, and sat at the window over the bridge for a while with his hands folded and the right one aching.

He did not write a sixth. There was nothing to put on it.

The long room stood when the seat rose. Cael was on his feet behind Withrow's chair, and so he saw her bow from behind: the line of her grey collar going down, and stopping, and the back of her neck held straight. He had watched her bow on the house's steps to visiting officers for two years and could have told its depth with his eyes shut. This was the same. It was the registry's own measure, the one she had been taught at twenty and had given across a platform like that one for twenty years from the officers' side, and she gave it now to a hood with no face under it as she would have given it to a registrar she had dined with.

In the stir of the benches emptying, one coat at the far end of the last bench, nearest the side door, stood a fraction after all the others. It was Seln's. Cael had not seen him since the side door. While the others went out to the coach, Cael slipped back in for a moment and stood where Seln had sat, and found that from there a man could see both doors, all three tables and the platform without once turning his head. He went out again before anybody missed him.

Withrow's carriage was waiting at the foot of the four steps, with the correspondents' pencils going on either side of it. She spoke to none of them. At its door she turned, with one hand on the frame, and found Cael with her eyes.

"The same depth," she said. "From this side. I measured."

Then she got in, and the carriage went off down the market street, and the coach went after it.

Brom had his face to the window. Lira was watching Brom.

"You were counting somebody," she said. "All morning. I saw your lips."

"The records officer. The junior." Brom did not turn round. "At Greyvane he sat at the recorder's desk under the bench, and twice he looked up from it at Cael. I was in the gallery. I counted." He was quiet a while. "This morning, none."

"So he's done looking," said Lira, with her boots up on the opposite bench and her back against the coach's door. "Or he's been told to be."

The house's counsel had her bag on her knees. "He tendered nine," she said. "I tendered a hundred and seventy-three. The junior receipted both lists, one after the other. Then the senior chair's minute went up under the hood and came back initialled, without either number changing the pace."

"The pace wouldn't have changed for one or for a thousand," said Karis. "A seal can't count."

"And the seal?" said Lira. "You told us to watch it. Did it do anything?"

"Nothing." Karis kept her eyes on the window. "It initialled where the clerk pointed and pressed where the code said. I watched it the whole time our counsel was on her feet. It didn't so much as turn a page faster." She put her hand on the notebook in her lap, over the back board. "The slips stay."

Seln was at the far end of the bench with his eyes shut. He had not said anything since the wool exchange.

"Under the hood, no man's grade at all," he said, without opening them. "The seat's own. It goes with the seal, whoever is wearing it. A monitoring officer on his rounds behind the senior chair, and the senior chair itself a district man." The coach went over a stone and he did not move. "They keep the minute, all three. None of them has ever decided anything. That's done somewhere else, and they write it down."

At the residence door, when the others had gone in ahead of them and the coach was rolling off toward the stable yard, Seln stopped on the step, and Cael stopped with him.

"The office has written that kind of minute," said Seln, to the door. "Not that one. Others like it."

Then he went in, at his even pace, and up the stair, and Cael stood a moment on the step by himself before he followed.

A morning, he wrote that night at the sill. A hood, two hands, a seal. A procurator with nothing on him. A junior at the records table who wouldn't look. A room doing exactly what the code says a room does.

I keep looking for the person and finding the hand.

He laid the year's dates along the sill two nights later, on the Seventh-day, on slips of his own.

There was one slip for each. Lira's first meet off the hill, three weeks away now, on a road, against Silvers from other houses. Brom's panel, the last Fifth-day of the year, at the district seat in Ostrand. The next sitting at the wool exchange. And a fourth slip with nothing written on it, for the re-evaluation, whose date the seat would fix when it ruled. He set them in a row, as Karis had set out her six on the long table, and sat looking at them with Hesk's book open on his knee, and wrote.

The month closes, and for once the people I came up this hill with have each been handed something fair. Lira has her ladder, a point short, with the point named. Brom has his number, written on a docket a street from the seat. Karis has a shelf, and a key, and a girl to teach, and a line in a book with her name above it. None of it bought. None of it begged. All of it given across a counter, honestly, for once.

Set it down tonight, before it gets complicated. Whatever this challenge costs me, it should not cost them.

Karis came up the stair while he was sanding it, reading her draft aloud to herself as she climbed, the way she did when a sentence would not sit. He heard her in the doorway. The respondent submits that the integrity sections, read with their own proviso, and then nothing.

He did not turn round. He heard the draft's paper stop rustling, and her breath close behind his right ear, and he knew where her eyes had gone. His hand moved to close the book, from a habit older than the bluff, and stopped, and lay on the sill beside it instead.

A finger came past his shoulder, ink on its second knuckle, and rested on the sill beside his last line without touching the page.

"That is not how any of us are built," said Karis.

It was her findings voice.

He took up the pen again and wrote under the line, in the parenthesis the Log kept for things said aloud at the window, and she watched every letter of it go down.

(Karis read this entry over my shoulder and said "that is not how any of us are built." Noted. Filed. Afraid of it.)

When the pen reached the last three words, her finger on the sill tapped once.

"Afraid of it," she said. "Good." She took her finger off the sill. "Then be afraid of it accurately. Not at three in the morning, in general, about everything. Give it dates. Give it a column. Every week, put down what it's cost each of us, in the coin it actually costs, and add it up at the foot." She laid the draft on the sill beside his four slips. "Then on the day it starts costing us more than we can carry, you'll know which day it was. Not some other day. That one." She looked at the blank fourth slip. "That's what the notebook's for. Not for being frightened in. For knowing exactly how much."

She went to the door, and stopped there, with her hand on the frame.

"Read the draft first," she said. "Before anybody else does. That's the arrangement."

"That's the arrangement," said Cael.

She went down the stair. He sat a long while at the window with the four slips and her draft on the sill, and the blank slip at the end of the row, and the fountain going on below in the dark court. Then he turned to a clean page at the back of Hesk's book, past the minute and the costed rule, past the first pole and every entry since, and ruled a column down it, and wrote four names at the head of the column.

He left the rest of it empty, for now.

Chapter 14 — Standing Distribution

The seal had gone in crooked.

Vastin held the petition up to the window and tilted it until the light lay along the wax. The Archmarshal's mark was all there, and the ring of small letters round it, but its left edge was shallow, almost a ghost, where the press had bitten at a slant. It was the press's fault. He had screwed it to the corner of the desk himself on his first morning in this room, nineteen years ago, in a hurry and out of true, and had never straightened it. In nineteen years it had never mattered.

He found he was asking himself whether a seal with a faint edge could be challenged.

It could not, and he knew it could not; he had sat on a hundred inquiries into a hundred seals and never seen a petition refused because a press was old. But the question had come up in him on its own, from somewhere under the morning, and an evaluator who will not listen to a foolish question has only taught himself to stop hearing his instruments. So he put the petition down and went looking for where the question had come from.

It had come from the ninth line of a printed list.

The list was on a slip pinned to the bundle that had come up in the morning file. For the evaluator's file, per standing distribution. Under those words were printed the offices that received such things as a matter of course: the district seats, the stations' office, the archive, the weather clerks, eleven offices in all. The ninth line was his. Senior evaluator, the Compact. Between the stations' office and the weather clerks.

Under the slip was the instrument itself, and at its last leaf, where petitions keep the table of authorities they rely on, there were nine lines. Eight were sections of the code. The seventh, in a clerk's even type, was his. Advisory of the Compact's senior evaluator upon the fielding clause (adopted). He had not needed to turn to the paragraph; he had written those three sentences in this chair. Somebody had filed his title between a section on frames and a section on discretion.

At the bottom of the bundle was the minute of a first sitting at Ostrand. It was dated yesterday.

He had rung for the clerk then, he remembered, and asked whether anything had come up with the bundle: a covering letter, a line from anybody, a question. The clerk had looked through the wallet twice. "No, sir. Only the slip." Vastin had thanked him and sent him down, and sat on with that answer, which was the whole of the matter in four words.

Down in the paved court the porter was folding his paper bag along its old creases. The pigeons had been fed late, and were still walking about on the stones in the sun, as if they suspected there might be more.

His left hand lay on the blotter beside the petition. Some years ago it had begun to dislike mornings; lately it had added evenings, and it did not much care for noon. He opened it and closed it, twice, slowly, and watched it do as it was told. Three trays stood at his right in the order he had kept since before he had a desk worth the name, in, held, done, and the petition belonged in none of them yet.

He opened the lowest drawer at the far end of the long cabinet, where he kept the few things in the room that were his, and took out a letter he had kept for some years without ever deciding why.

Will my father's name ever come off the list?

The hand was careful, and had plainly practised on other paper before it trusted itself to this sheet. Her father had been a district officer on the coast who took money to enter a rank in a station book that no frame had read. There had been one other, before him: a hill-station keeper who let a cracked housing read high for six years and covered it with false returns. Both findings were his, both sound, both sent down this stair; and somewhere below, in an office whose door he had never opened, the rest had followed. He had answered the girl himself, with one word, because a longer answer would only have given her another sentence to wait on.

He put the letter back. The seal on the petition was his own, faint edge and all, and it would carry what was under it. A fear with a name is a thing a man can work beside.

He rang for the clerk.

It was evening before he saw the blot.

He had gone out to the outer office to sign the day's dispatch ledger, as he did each evening. The line for his petition was there in the clerk's tidy upright hand: the date, the number, and in the routing column Registry seat, Ostrand, institutional proceedings. But at the head of the routing column, just before the first letter, there was a small round blot, where a pen had been held over the page a moment too long before it came down.

He remembered the moment. He had been at the inner door. He had seen the pen stop, and had said the route aloud so that the man would not have to ask it, and had given no reason. A reason carried down a stair in somebody's head stops being the Archmarshal's petition and becomes the Archmarshal's quarrel. The pen had come down.

A quarter of an hour later the clerk had come back up with the dispatch slip and laid it by the crooked press, where slips went, and then he had not gone. He had stood with his hands at his sides looking at the slip, and then at the Archmarshal's left hand open on the blotter, and then at nothing. Vastin had waited, and nothing had come, and after a while the man had nodded and gone out to his own desk. But he had left the inner door a hand's breadth wider than he usually left it, and twice before noon Vastin had heard his chair creak as he turned in it. A clerk who watches is a clerk who has noticed there is something to see.

Nine years of that hand, and it had never blotted a line. In nine years the outer office had only ever sent paper out of this room one way, back to whoever had asked for it. A desk like this did not send a finding toward a proceeding that had not called for one, and the clerk's pen had known it before the clerk did.

Vastin signed beneath the blot and went back into his room and took down the letter-book.

He did not need it. He knew what he would find. But he went through it anyway, the way a man going out on a long road checks a buckle he knows is fastened. There they were: four acknowledgments in forty years, pasted in where they had come, each from a seat that had not sent for his finding and had received it anyway. A district's, from a dozen years back, thanking him without rancour for a finding that had cost the district its own petition. A hill station's, whose frame had come out of its housing on his evidence. A guild hall's. A sponsorship quarrel so old the guild's name had faded. Every one of them had answered inside a fortnight.

He closed the book. It had not steadied him. Each of those four seats had wanted to know something.

What steadied him, a little, was the sheet from the east room.

It was in the boy's file in the same drawer, the clerk's ruled page from the room twelve feet by fourteen on the bluff. The first thing his eye went to, as it always did, was not any of his questions but the line near the foot where one was written going the other way, the boy's to him: What is the Compact evaluating? Me, or the provision? The second thing was the line beneath his own eleventh question. He had ruled it himself, before the interview, for a twelfth, the way he always ruled one more line than he expected to use. It was empty.

He knew what would have gone on it. The boy kept a private book of records and had said so: so I can't lie to myself later. The obvious question was what the book said. He had looked at it across four feet of table for less than a second and not asked it, because a private book was not in the record, and an officer of his height who reaches for whatever is in reach has begun to collect. He had once spent ten years helping to take a collector apart.

He took a scrap of paper and wrote a sentence on it, to see whether it was true.

A careful evaluation leaves the proceedings nothing of the evaluator's to use but his manners.

It was true. They had used his manners. They were in the seventh line of a table of authorities.

He struck the sentence through and put the scrap in the stove, and put the ruled sheet back in the file, and went home.

On the third evening there was a pinned note on a copy in his held tray, and he had moved the copy twice.

Second frame reading: within tolerance. The note was in a young man's hand, a hand still deciding what shape it meant to be. It was pinned to the copy of a station's Kindling entry, four years old, for a girl in the northern district: her Path, her first rank, in a station clerk's ordinary writing.

The junior who had pinned it had come up the too-steep stair that afternoon with the girl's file under his arm, nervous and good, and laid it out on the desk because Vastin had made him lay it out himself. Her floor work this season had run on ahead of what her station had written of her, by a margin he had measured four ways and could not make go away. "She doesn't do anything wrong, sir," the junior had said. "That's what I keep coming back to. She does everything her Path says she should. She just does it as if the station had written down somebody a year younger." He had turned his notes round so that Vastin could read them.
