"I measured it with the frame, and by the clock, and by her bouts, and against the tables. It's inside tolerance every way I measure it. I still don't like it."

They had gone through it for an hour: the station's line, his notes, the tolerances for a girl of that age and Path. Everything was sound. She had grown faster than a station had guessed.

Under the station's line, in the junior's hand, was the recommendation they had settled between them: Continue observation. The hand was still deciding what shape it meant to be, and seeing it, Vastin had remembered a smoking stove in a district house a long time ago, and his own file under his own arm, and a senior evaluator, long since a name on a plaque, telling him the thing every evaluator is told once: Write what the instrument says. What you feel about it is information about you. He had handed the same sentence on that afternoon, in other words. It had been easier to say than to hear.

He did not write anything about the copy. He put it back where it was.

He turned down the lamp.

The next morning, because he could not settle to the tray, he went down the too-steep stair and across the paved court to the house's frame shop, which he did perhaps twice a year.

It was a long low room behind the porter's lodge that smelled of oil and cut brass. A station frame stood in the middle of it with its housing off, the way a clock stands with its back off, all its insides showing. The mender was an old man in an apron with a lens screwed into one eye, and he did not stand up when the Archmarshal came in, because he had his hands inside the frame and it would not have been safe.

"From the river station, sir," he said, without looking round. "The one that reads slow in the damp. They want it put right."

"Is it wrong?"

The mender took his hands out, slowly, and wiped them, and considered the question with the respect due to it. "No, sir. It's telling them it's damp. Every reading it gives on a wet morning is a fraction late, and the fraction's always the same, and if they wrote it down they'd know it to the hair." He tapped the housing. "They don't want it to tell them about the damp. They want it to read the same wet or dry. So I'll put a shim in, and it'll stop telling them, and they'll be happier, and it'll be a worse frame." He put his hands back in. "I've said so in my note. They won't read the note."

Vastin stood a while and watched him work. Then he went back up the stair, and did not think about the frame again for most of the day. He found it in his mind that evening as he put the copy back in held one more time: a true instrument, and men who would rather it said something easier.

There was a wrapper in the waste-basket, and he did not remember throwing it there.

It was the outer wrapper of a seat-courier's packet, heavy grey paper stamped across in red, BY SEAT COURIER. BY HAND. He looked at it for some time. Then he looked at the boy's folder lying shut on his blotter, and opened it, and found on top of his own nine leaves a single sheet of registry-seat stock with a seal pressed into it.

He did not remember putting it there either.

He went back for it, a step at a time, as he would have made a witness go back. A tread on the stair that had not been his clerk's tread: single steps, quick, the whole flight, no pause at the top. The clerk in the doorway with the packet held out in both hands. His own face, arranged. Then the two sentences. Then, it seemed, the folder, and the window, and a long while of the porter and the pigeons that had gone into him without leaving any trace at all.

The proceedings' evaluation seat is fully constituted. Supplementary findings are not contemplated by the schedule.

He read it again, to be sure it said what he remembered. It did.

By noon there was a refusal in done that had taken him a quarter of an hour to write, where such things usually took him a quarter of a minute. A guild hall had asked for more time to answer a finding on its own assessors, and he had said no; but he had said it at length, giving the hall the section it had failed to meet, the officer it might apply to instead, and the date by which it should. He had signed it with his name entire.

Under it in the tray lay the first sheet he had started, with a single half-line on it, struck through corner to corner so that it could still be read. The hall's request for further time is not contemplated by

He did not throw that sheet away. He had taught that line to every junior he ever had.

Then he took a slip of paper and wrote a question on it.

Minute of the 40th: evaluation seat, to be called. Refusal of the 44th: fully constituted. Who sat down in those five chairs in four days, without asking this office for the file?

He did not try to answer it. He pinned it to the denial, and closed the folder over both.

"Will you be getting home tonight, sir? It's set in to rain."

The clerk had said it from the doorway at the sixth bell, with the day's wallet against his chest, looking not at the desk but past it at the window, where the evening had gone close and grey. It was the only thing he had ever said in that room in nine years that had nothing to do with paper.

Vastin had looked up from the plain sheets he was writing on. "Later than usual," he had said. "But yes."

The clerk had gone down without another word, and come back a few minutes later, unasked, with a candle already lit in a tin dish, and set it on the corner of the desk by the crooked press. The house put out the lamps on that floor at the half-bell after six. In the morning Vastin found the candle in the consumables ledger, entered in the clerk's tidy hand against the Archmarshal's name and not the floor's. He had not told him to put it there. He left it as it was.

He opened the lowest drawer to see that the folder was in it. It was. It had a tab, and the tab had a heading in his own hand, the only one of its kind he had written in forty years, because every finding he had ever made had come with somewhere to be sent.

Pending a proceeding worth sending it to.

He did not take the nine pages out. He had read them through once last night by the candle, with the rain starting on the glass, and then he had done a thing he did not often do: he had read the last paragraph aloud to the empty room, quietly, to hear whether it would stand being spoken.

"Offered to the proceedings at Ostrand under the code's two provisions; declined without citation as outside their schedule. The schedule itself is not disputed. One thing only is set down. A schedule that leaves no room for the one personal assessment of the subject the Compact holds was drawn for a purpose the evaluator was never told and cannot name from his desk. Where the outcome of an evaluation is settled before the evaluator arrives, it is not the subject who is being measured."

It had stood.

The rest he could have said without the pages. That the proceedings had in their hands already the one honest instrument there was, three years of the record, kept by officers who could see. That a re-evaluation whose answer was known in advance was a procedure wearing an evaluation's coat. That when the standard protocol fell silent in front of this boy the silence was the protocol's own. That the protocol could not read him. Somewhere in the middle was a sentence he had spoken at inquiries for forty years about frames, the instrument is not at fault; it has told you where its reach ends, and last night, for the first time, he had written it about a person, and sat with his pen lifted for a long while before he let it stand.

He had gone home at the ninth bell, later than usual, as he had said he would. The porter had been at the lodge door with his lamp, looking out at the rain, and had said "Late, sir," in the voice of a man noting a thing for the record, and Vastin had agreed that it was. The street had been empty and loud with water. He had walked it without hurrying, with his collar up and his left hand in his coat, and he had found that he was not thinking about the seat, or the five chairs, or who had sat down in them. He was thinking about a boy standing still in a frame that had stuttered and gone dark, three days on the bluff, not moving, not asking what it meant, waiting to be told what the instruments had found. And he was thinking that, of all the officers who had stood in rooms with that boy, he was the one who had written down what that silence meant, and that nobody was going to be allowed to read it.

It was not a theory. He did not hold with theories about subjects. It was only a thing he had noticed, walking, and he let it walk beside him to his door, and left it on the step.

Now he closed the drawer. At the head of the first page, under the subject and the basis and the date, on the line the sheet kept for the name of whoever a finding was meant for, he had written nothing at all.

Chapter 15 — Sideways

On the Second-day Cael went up to the east hall's gallery before the first bell, to watch Lira be taught.

He took the rail at the north end, as he had on the second morning of the year. The high windows were behind him. At this hour the sun came through them low, and laid long bars of light across the painted floor below, over the white crosses and the arrows, so that the whole hall looked ruled like a page in a ledger, with a line for every stride a fighter might take. Lira said she could read it. She said that on a bright morning she could see her own feet a quarter-beat before they landed, because the light told her where the shadow of her heel would fall. She had said it lightly, the way she said most things that mattered to her, and then she had gone out of her way never to train in the afternoon again.

Rooke sat at his trestle with the red book. The Stone sat beside him with his hands folded on his stomach, a broad patient man from the river academy who had come up the hill for the year to teach a Wind fighter to think in courses. Down at the near end, the program clerk had two ledgers open in front of her this morning instead of one. Cael noticed that, and noticed that she wrote in the second only when the gallery door opened, and he did not think anything of it.

Lira ran the four-count against the Current girl.

The girl came at her in long glides, two and a bend, the second glide curving out wide so that the strike came off the end of the curve from a place you had not been watching. Lira watched the bend. On the first glide she lied with her back foot, the one she did not care about, and on the girl's count of four she went. One burst, low, along the line of the bend instead of across it, so that she arrived at the end of the curve a breath before the girl did. She was standing there waiting. Her palm was on the girl's shoulder when the strike should have come.

"Again," said Rooke, without looking up from the book.

They ran it again. And again. On the fourth time the Current girl changed her bend, went short instead of wide, and Lira read the change on the girl's front hip and went anyway, and missed by a hand. She landed badly, caught it on the landing beat, and came round with her chin up and her left arm tucked close to her side out of old habit.

"Better," said Rooke. "Wrong, and better." He wrote one word.

The Stone leaned over and said something to him, and Rooke shook his head once.

That was when Cael saw the two men at the far end of the gallery.

They were not house; he knew every face that came to that rail by now, and these two were strangers. They wore travelling coats and good boots with the road still on them, each with a writing board held against his chest the way a clerk holds a ledger he does not mean to let anybody read. They stood together by the south stair, and they did not lean on the rail the way people did who had come to enjoy a drill. They stood back from it. One of them wrote whenever Lira burst. The other did not write at all. The other watched the gallery.

Cael looked at them, and decided they were scouts. A Silver program meant scouts. Houses all over the region would want to know what Rooke was building on these boards, and who he was building it for, and the answer to the second question was standing below in a sweat-dark shirt with her chin up. He was proud of that, plainly and without reservation. Two strangers had come up a long hill on a cold morning to write Lira down.

He did not see, that morning, that the one who did not write had looked four times at the north end of the rail, where Cael stood. He worked it out the next evening, from something Lira said, and it cost him something to do the sum backward.

Lira finished the line. She bowed to the trestle, the short bow the program used, and looked up and found him at the rail, and lifted two fingers off her strapping: two bursts, clean. He lifted two back.

The Stone came up the gallery stair afterward, which he did not usually do, and stood at the rail a little way from Cael with his hands folded over his stomach, looking down at the empty painted floor as if it were still full.

"She lies with the wrong foot now," he said. "Did you see? The back one. The one she doesn't care about. She learned that somewhere that wasn't here. Somebody laid her a floor that tipped. I'd like to meet them."

Cael said nothing. The Stone seemed to expect nothing.

"She'll be a Silver," he said, "if they let her. It's in her feet now. It wasn't in her when she beat me at the wool town, and it is now." He went back down the stair.

Rooke shut the red book. At the end of the trestle the clerk wrote something in the second ledger, blotted it, and closed that too.

The assistant had printer's ink on both cuffs, and Cael noticed it before he noticed anything else about her, because ink on Karis's assistant was always on the fingers and never on the cuffs.

"I went into the shop," she said. She was standing at the end of the long table in the reading room with the satchel at her feet and a rolled print in her hands, as if the print were the thing she had come up the stair to account for. "The one that prints the weekly. I'd bought the back numbers at the bridge-end and they were short two, so I went to the wharf street to ask for them, and the man gave me them for nothing, and showed me his presses while his boy was inking." She looked down at her cuffs. "He has two. The old one was his father's. The new one he bought this year, because of the enrollee. He said that to me as if I'd be glad to hear it. He said the first weekly was his, and he'd pledged the old press against a cart of paper to start it, and everybody told him it was a fool's trade, and now there are two weeklies and he's thinking of a third." She drew breath. "And I need to give this back."

She held out the print.

"Why?" said Karis.

"I bought it twice. Two stalls, an hour apart. I didn't notice until I was on the road." The girl's face had gone pink from the collar up. "I've put one in the account. I paid for the other. But it's still the house's paper on the house's errand, and I didn't know whose it was."

Karis unrolled it. It was the woodcut that had been in every window since the qualifying year: a boy with a jaw like a spade, standing in a way nobody who had ever fought would stand. She rolled it up again and handed it back.

"Yours," she said. "Keep it where you'll see it. It's the one thing in that satchel that cost exactly what it says."

Brom had come up the stair while they talked, with the code's first volume on his shoulder as he did every afternoon, and he set it on its shelf and stood looking at the girl's account sheets on the table, upside down.

"A carter's year," he said. "Every week."

They all looked at him.

"The weeklies," said Brom. He took the pencil from behind Cael's ear and turned the last sheet over to its clean side, and worked it out the other way round from how anybody else would have, from the answer down to the reasons, the way he checked a load he had already lifted. "That's what it comes to. The bridge-end stall sells three quires a day of each now, by what the girl says, and a quire's twenty-four sheets. The back of the pamphlet says both weeklies sell in three other towns as well as Ostrand, and all three are bigger, so call it four quires each to be safe. Four towns. Two weeklies. A copper a sheet." He wrote the figures in his large slow hand, each line lashed to the one under it before he trusted it with the next, and drew a line, and the total under the line was what he had said before he began. "There."

He went back down for the second volume.

Cael had wanted that figure for two years, and had never had a single number to start it from. His own guess, when he made it now against Brom's, came out low. Brom's had paper in it.

The rest of the girl's sheets he read afterward, and they were only what the money bought: six titles in Ostrand, from the Greyvane hearing in its fourth edition at six marks down to the copper-and-a-half woodcut.

Karis wrote two words on a slip, the printer, and pushed it across the table to him. He knew what she meant. Hers were for things she could cite in front of a seat. That one was for his.

He put the slip in his notebook and wrote the figure under it and nothing else.

Lira came up for the second volume's return trip in Brom's place, because Brom had been waylaid by the cohort, and she read the figure over his shoulder on her way past and stopped.

"A carter's year," she said. "Every week. On you."

"On the question."

"Same thing, to the carter." She hefted the volume onto her own shoulder, which was not built for it, and stood with it there, frowning at the window. "When I was fourteen and walking from guild door to guild door, I'd have given a great deal for a copper. Just one. For bread." She went to the stair. "Somebody in four towns is paying a copper a week to read whether you're a person. I'd like to meet them. I'd like to ask what they'd do with the answer."

She went down. The girl at the outer table had stopped writing to listen, and started again, very fast, when Cael looked up.

"When did he get it?" said Cael.

He said it in Withrow's office before he had sat down or been asked to, as soon as the counsel had given them the two sentences. She had come up the switchbacks at dusk in a hired chaise nobody had sent for and gone straight to the Chancellor's door, and Withrow had sent the porter's boy running.

The proceedings' evaluation seat is fully constituted. Supplementary findings are not contemplated by the schedule.

"He hasn't," said the counsel. "The seat answered him this morning, at Ostrand. His petition went to the seat by courier yesterday: standing to put a finding before it, signed and sealed as his own. The answer went out this morning by seat courier. Wherever the Archmarshal keeps his desk, it's a long road from the river. He'll have it tomorrow at the soonest." Her bag stayed in her hand. "We have it tonight."

"Where?" said Withrow.

"The wharf."

That was all she said about it, and Withrow seemed to need no more. Cael did. He worked it out for himself on the stair later. The seat's clerks ate their noon meal on sitting weeks at the long low inn on the wharf, where he had once seen three of them at a window table with their collars undone; and they were clerks, and they talked about their day. The answer to the Archmarshal had been a joke at an inn before it was a letter on the Archmarshal's desk.

He did not like it at all.

Withrow got up and went to the shelf behind her desk, and took down a thin book bound in faded blue, and opened it near the middle, and laid it on the blotter facing them. It was the registry's drafting book, the one its clerks were given in their second year. The page was a list of model refusals, numbered. Beside the thirtieth, in the margin, somebody had written in a young, very upright hand: the kindest one.

"I wrote that," said Withrow. "I was nineteen." She left the book open. "I taught it to every junior I ever had, from that page."

The counsel watched her. Cael understood that she had come up the hill partly to bring the news and partly to stand in that room while it arrived.

"Should the house write to him?" he said. "Tell him we know? That it's being laughed about before it's reached him?"

It was the counsel who answered.

"No. Think who he is and who you are. He's the Compact's senior evaluator, and he's just asked to put a finding into proceedings where this house is the respondent. A letter from this house on his desk this week, about anything at all, would be on the file by morning; and his finding, if it's ever given, would be read for the rest of its life as something the respondent asked him for." She shook her head. "The kindest thing this house can do for that man is leave him alone."

"He'll find out we heard first."

"And he'll know why nobody wrote. He's spent forty years in rooms where that's the only courtesy there is."

"She's right," said Withrow quietly. "I don't like it either." She took a card from her desk, wrote one word on it, and gave it to him. Choosing. "For the table. It's the second time. They'll know."

He took the card up to the reading room and laid it on the long table, and then the two sentences beside it, written out on a slip in his own hand. Karis read the sentences, and then the card, and was already reaching for the second volume of the code.

She did not read anything aloud this time. She found the two provisions, the old one and the new, and laid the volume open at the old one with her finger beside its last two words, shall receive. Then she got the digest down from the bottom shelf, the one her assistant had found for herself on the day of find it, and opened it at the table of uses at its back, and turned it round so that they could see the line for themselves.

Lira read it out, because somebody had to. "Nine. Received, nine."

"He knocked on the right door twice," said Karis. "Both of them. The old one first." Her eyes went back to his slip. "I was frightened of his three sentences on the night the instrument came. I've been thinking of him since as the man whose words they borrowed." She closed the volume. "He isn't. He's the man who read the code properly, and was told by return that it didn't matter."

There was a card lying on the landing outside the door when they came out, propped against the top stair, and nobody had heard it put there. The house's counsel had gone down the hill by then. It was one of her own cards, with her name on the front in small print, and on the back, in her small exact hand:

He is not yours. Same house, talking to itself. Keep every citation they give you, and a note of each one they don't. Its absence is a finding.

Karis read it twice and put it inside the cover of her notebook, next to the stratum line.

The first-years at the end of the refectory had bought a weekly in town and were reading it aloud to one another in turns, with commentary, and Cael heard his own name in it, and sinister, and a great deal of laughing.

Ephram got up from the cohort's table with the captain's file under his arm, walked the length of the room, and held out his free hand, and the first-year holding the sheet gave it to him without a word. He read it standing, top to bottom, like a man checking a bill he suspects of being wrong, and then turned it round to show them the woodcut.

"This is your enrollee of record. Look at the jaw. You could split kindling on that jaw. I've watched him on more floors than anybody in this room, and I give you my word as your captain that he has never once stood with his feet like that. If he did I'd have him on his back before the glass turned." He folded it in quarters into the file. "Confiscated. You'll have it back when one of you can tell me what's wrong with the stance."

Seln had heard it before supper, at the copying table.

Cael had gone round by the assessment wing on his way from the reading room because the lamp was still lit there, and Seln was still at the table behind the counter with the day's last forms, copying. The desk clerk had gone. Cael stood at the counter and gave it to him in a dozen words, the two sentences and who had been refused, and Seln did not look up. He finished the line he was writing. He sanded it. Then he laid the pen down on the blotter, square to the edge, and sat for a moment with his hands in his lap and his eyes on the form in front of him, which was a request for floor hours from a Mire second-year and had nothing to do with anything.

"Mm," he said.

Then he picked the pen up again and dipped it, and wrote the next line, and Cael went to supper.

When the plates were mostly empty, at the middle of the bench, Seln turned his cup a quarter-turn on the board.

"They benched their best instrument because he measures true."

He said it to the cup, and went back to his bread.

Brom put his spoon down and looked at him, long and slow, and Seln ate through it without appearing to feel it.

On the stair afterward Brom stopped Cael at the turn with one hand, and asked him a question, which he almost never did.

"Who was he talking about?"

"The Archmarshal."

"And?"

Cael stood on the step and thought about it, and about the voice Seln had said it in, as if the sentence belonged to somebody else; and then about fifteen years of true reports going up a chain to an office that wanted something other than true.

"Himself," he said.

Brom nodded once. "Fifteen years," he said. "The best they had." He took his hand off Cael's arm and went on up.

The answer was a joke at an inn before it was a letter on his desk, he wrote at the sill, under the slip that said the printer. Withrow wrote "the kindest one" in a margin at nineteen. Brom asked me a question tonight, so that I'd have to say the answer myself.

Chapter 16 — The Column

The notice on the assessment wing's board was in Gault's hand this week, not the desk clerk's, and Cael read it twice before he understood why.

Sitting week. The provision's supervised hours are moved to the Fourth-day, second bell, wing three. The seat sits on the Fifth-day and the enrollee attends it. Observers enter by the lodge book.

The first two sentences were only sense: the seat sat on Fifth-days, and so did wing three, and the provision would have to give way to the registry and not the other way round. It was the third sentence he read twice. In the two years he had been reading that board, nobody had ever needed a line about observers. The people who watched the provision's bouts were the cohort, and the cohort came in at the south door and wrote its name in nothing.

The desk clerk saw him at the board and leaned over the counter.

"Four," he said, low, like a man passing on what he has been told to keep. "Four names in the lodge book since the First-day, asking to observe. Officers from other houses. The Magister's had the porters clear out the old gallery for them, over the west door." He straightened. "So the room won't surprise you."

Behind the counter, at the copying table, Seln's pen stopped for the length of one word, and went on.

"Thank you," said Cael.

"Mm," said Seln, to his page, and turned it over.

The real errand had been the board, but he had a docket number to ask Bracken about, so he went back by the records hall. The counter's daybook lay open on the brass rail where Bracken had left it to dry, and Cael read the day's line before he could stop himself. It was a page of figures and he had never in his life been able to leave a page of figures unread. Four narrow columns had been ruled across it in the last few weeks, in Bracken's small capitals: HOUSES. SPONSORS. FACULTIES. OTHER. Under OTHER, yesterday, the figure was one hundred and forty-one. The heaviest line on the page, the Fifth-day before the sitting, said one hundred and ninety-six.

Beside the daybook lay a bundle of fair copies tied with green tape, with a label on the tape: Houses. Answered.

Bracken came out of the post room with his sleeves rolled, and answered the docket question. Then he saw where Cael was looking, and untied the tape and turned the top copy round.

Halcenvane's enrollment stands on a provision the registry has not set aside, and has been entered in full on the public record. Each chartered house must read that provision for itself.

"Fourteen," said Bracken, and tied the tape again.

There was one letter on the counter that had not gone into any column. It was sealed in grey.

"The seat," said Bracken. "For the reading room. Those don't go in the baskets. I carry them up."

Cael crossed the fountain court with Gault's third sentence in his head. Holding himself inside the house's rate in front of three cards and a clerk had never been nothing, but it had always been private. Tomorrow four strangers with writing boards would sit over the west door of wing three, and lay what he did beside everything the broadsheets and the tournament books had printed, line for line.

Rooke went down the bluff road at a little before dusk with a satchel on his shoulder, and Cael watched him from the north wall because watching Rooke walk anywhere was unusual; he had business in the town on Third-day evenings, and nobody had ever asked what it was.

At the second switchback below the gate, Rooke stopped.

There was a hat on the milestone there. It took Cael a moment to see that there was a man under it, sitting with his collar turned up and a board on his knee, very still, the way people sit who have been sitting a long time. Lira, who had come up the wall stair with two apples and given him one without asking, said the porter's boy had counted: since the third bell. He had read the board on the gatepost, perhaps. It said in registry type that the house had answered the challenge in its filing, that the filing was public, and that the house had nothing to add to it. He had not come up to argue with the lodge-man. He had simply sat down where a man on the outside of the bend could see the gate and the wall and the whole road up to them, and waited for a boy to come down it.

They watched Rooke say something short. The man looked up the road toward the gate. Then he got up, and tucked the board under his arm, and went down the hill in front of Rooke at a walk.

When Rooke came back up without the satchel, Lira leaned over the wall.

"Coach. What did you say to him?"

Rooke looked up. Cael expected nothing; nothing was Rooke's usual answer. But he gave one.

"That the boy trains before light and eats after dark, and neither of them happens on this road."

He went in at the gate. Lira laughed into her apple.

"Three of them came up to the lodge on the First-day," she said. "Did you hear? They argued with the lodge-man for a quarter of an hour about the board, and one of them tried to give him a coin, and he pretended not to see it, because he said afterward it was a very small coin." She turned the apple round to find the last good side. "I've got eighteen days to the road meet. Rooke says I'm not to think about it. I think about it every time I put my foot down." Then, in exactly the same voice, she said, "How often does the unclassified enrollee come up to watch the Silver drills?"

He looked at her.

"That's what one of them asked the clerk. On the east hall's gallery. Friendly, the way you'd ask about the weather." She threw her apple core out over the wall into the scrub, a long throw. "The clerk told Rooke. Rooke's had her keeping a second ledger since a little after the first sitting. Every name on the gallery, every morning, and their house, and how long they stay. He reads it every night when he locks up. He never said why." She held up four fingers, folded down one at a time. "Rhagen, Rhagen, the lake house, and a place up north she had to ask him to spell. Twenty-six names in a fortnight, and those four are the only ones with no business with us."

He saw them as she said it: the two travelling coats on the gallery yesterday morning, the one who wrote and the one who did not; the one who did not, turning his head four times to the north end of the rail, where Cael had stood being glad for her.

He thought of her coming away from Fenmark at fourteen with nothing, after an examiner had wiped his slate with his sleeve so the form would be clean. Now there was a red book on the east hall's trestle with her figures in it, and a card on the door with her name among the program's seniors, and a ladder somebody had built toward her for the first time in her life. And strangers were sitting at the top of it, watching the stair for him.

"Rooke hasn't stopped the drills," he said.

"Not yet." She pushed off the wall. "He writes it all down first. You'd know."

The schoolroom letter was already lying by itself on the board when Cael sat down after supper.

It was folded very small, on paper ruled for copying, set apart from the three piles at Lira's end of the long table. Nobody was touching it. Lira read it to him, once, in a voice with nothing added.

To the boy at Halcenvane. My teacher read us about you. I am nine and not Kindled yet. Does it hurt, not having a Path written down? I would like to know before it is my turn.

She put it back where it had been, by itself.

Each of her three piles had a slip of paper tucked under its corner, and each slip had one word on it in her hand. Cael had seen them every night for a fortnight. He read them again now, left to right, because he liked how little she had wasted on them.

Kind. Unkind. Unhinged.

He reached across and took one letter off the top of each. The kind one was from a drover on the north road, who had stood on the Concourse's top step for the whole of the Norhold match and wanted it entered somewhere that his knees had held. The unkind one he got as far as the second line of before Lira took it out of his hand, folded it, and put it back, without a word. The unhinged one was a chart of the night sky in four colours of ink, with one star circled, and a note explaining with perfect confidence that this was Cael's Path, and that the registry would understand everything if only it would look up.

"Which star?" said Brom.

"The one with the circle," said Lira.

"It's a good circle," said Brom.

"None of these get answered," said Lira, to nobody in particular. "They all go in my trunk. By pile, then by date. Somebody ought to have a record of this year that wasn't kept by a clerk."

"Good," said Karis, from the end of the table, without looking up from her volume.

Ephram came by on his way up with the captain's file under his arm and a folded sheet in his hand, which he laid on top of the unhinged pile with some ceremony.

"From my cousin at the river faculty," he said. "Their reading list for the second-years. Week nine." Cael unfolded it. Between a ruling about a ferry company and a ruling about a mill race, in a clerk's neat print, it said The Halcenvane matter (pending). "You're on a syllabus," said Ephram. "A file sits in a drawer and nobody reads it. A syllabus gets read aloud by an old man with a pointer for a hundred years." He took the sheet back. "Try to be one of the dull weeks."

"I'll do my best."

"You never have yet," said Ephram, and went up.

The second post came up while she was tying the piles. The porter brought one letter to the table himself, because he had learned the seal: a square cream envelope, a dark red seal pressed with the bar and the ring.

He laid it by Brom's plate.

The last one had come on the thirty-first day, and Brom had kept it two nights on his table before he opened it. This one had come in fourteen. He looked at it. He picked it up and turned it over once in his big hands, and looked at the seal, whole, the bar and the ring. Then he put it, unopened, into the left inside pocket of his coat, where the summons was, and the docket, and the confirmation, and the others.

Nobody asked. That had been the arrangement since the recess, and it held. Lira tied her bundle with a knot she did not usually use. Karis opened her volume again at the page she had just closed. Cael watched Brom's hand come away from the pocket and settle on the board, and then, a moment later, go back to the pocket and rest flat on the cloth over it, and stay there, as if the letter might get out.

On the stair afterward Lira fell into step beside Cael and said, "I'd open it for him."

"I know."

"If he asked, I'd sit with him while he did. I'd read it to him if he wanted, and never say one word about it after." She climbed two more steps. "He won't ask. He's carrying it the way he carries everything, so nobody else has to. And the worst of it is that's exactly what we'd all want him to do, if it were any of us." She stopped at her own landing. "So we don't ask. And he carries it. And the letter sits in his coat getting heavier." She went in at her door and shut it quietly.

Karis had gone up before the piles were tied. When Cael followed her to the reading room at the ninth bell, she was writing, and he read what she was writing upside down before he knew what it answered.

Research standing: enrolled, renewed in the recess by the council of the house in two sittings, entered as Research, enrolled, standing. Budget line: the house's accounts, the registrar's entry of the thirty-fifth day. Renewing officer: the Chancellor.

It was an answer, then. Only afterward did he see the question, printed on the other side of the sheet she was writing on. It was a form from the district fee office at Ostrand, which put its seal on every request a chartered house sent to an archive outside its own district. Her request of the thirty-fifth day, to Greyvane, for the founders' signature leaves, was in order and its fee was paid; before the office would seal it on, it asked the requester to state her standing, its last renewal, and the officer who had renewed it. It cited the section that let it ask.

She finished, and blotted it.

The door from the landing opened, and the assistant stood there in her cloak with her face pale round the mouth and red at the cheekbones.

"I was boring," she said.

Karis put down her pen. "Shut the door. Come in. Start at the end."

The girl shut the door. "At the end she said thank you in a very small voice and went away. Before that she kept looking at the stair." She swallowed. "Before that, I'd told her about the ninety-one. And the paragraph numbers. And that the next sitting's on the Fifth-day, and that the petitioner's conceded the provision is valid and doesn't allege fraud, and that the Compact's own inspection looked at the provision and it stood." She was going backward through it as Karis had told her to, and her voice steadied as she went. "And at the start I told her he's enrolled under a lawful provision, adjudicated at Greyvane on the public record, under seal, with the grant and two renewals on paper. Because she asked me what the enrollee was really like. A Mire girl from the north stair, on the covered walk, after supper. I hardly know her." She stopped. "That was the beginning."

"Then you weren't boring," said Karis. "You told the truth quickly, to a question you weren't ready for, to somebody who came for gossip and got the code. That's the whole work; the rest is decoration. Do it like that for a year, every time anyone asks, and you'll be more use to this house than any clerk on the hill."

The girl stood very still. Then she said "Yes," very quietly, exactly as Karis said it, and went out, and they heard her sit down at the outer table, though there was nothing on it for her to do at that hour.

"Write it in yours," said Karis. "That she came back up the stair to tell me."

Then she lifted her head after all, and turned the fee office's form over, and pushed it across the table to the girl's empty place, as if the girl were still sitting in it. In the morning, when the assistant came up to the outer table, it was waiting there for her, with one line marked in pencil: the section the fee office had cited as its authority to ask. Beside it, in Karis's hand, two words. Find it.

She found it before the second bell. Cael was on the landing when she brought the volume in, open, and laid it in front of Karis with her finger under a sub-clause near the foot of the page.

"It doesn't say shall," the girl said. "Or upon cause. It says the office may, at its discretion. There isn't any condition at all."

"Yes," said Karis.

The girl waited, the way she had learned not to, for the rest. There was no rest. She went back to the outer table and wrote it in her own small notebook, and did not ask what it meant, and Cael did not hear anybody tell her.

The column was at the back of Hesk's book, where he had ruled it at the month's close with four names at its head, his own last. He wrote in it that night for the first time.

Under Lira: Strangers on her gallery, two weeks. One asked how often I come up.

Under Brom: Velmere, a fortnight after the last. Into the pocket sealed. Hand on the pocket.

Under Karis: The fee office wants her standing before it will send her request on. And under that, small, because the girl was not one of the four but there was nowhere else to put it: Her assistant, on the walk. Answered with the code. Came back up the stair to say so.

Under his own name there was nothing to write. He drew a short line at the foot of each of the four columns, the way Karis had told him to, so that each could be added up; and under the first three he wrote a figure, the number of lines above it. Under his own he wrote 0, and looked at it for a long time, and did not write anything beside it.

Then he turned forward to a clean page, because tomorrow was the Fourth-day and there was a line still to write.

He had written one before every bout since the mill town: a single line out of the rotation, saying which exchange he would give away, how many bursts he would let the house see, where the spark would go, and what the figure ought to come to at the end. Seln had told him across a document table that his figures were too tidy. The rotation was the cure: scatter, built on purpose and paid for in advance, so that no one with a pencil and a season's worth of his numbers could find the hand that set them.

Tonight the pen stayed over the page.

The trouble was the strangers. Three cards and a clerk who knew him were one kind of audience. Four officers from four houses, with the broadsheets and the tournament books in their satchels, were another. Rhagen wrote down every exchange of every bout it could see and bound the result and sold it; somebody in an inn that very night would be laying tomorrow's figure beside last season's, line for line. Whatever he did must look exactly like the record, which meant like a strong Iron with a few odd gifts on a good day. And it must not look like the last bout, or the one before, because a record that matches itself has been arranged, and men whose trade is arrangements can smell it.

He went back through the last eight figures in his head. Twenty-three and a third. Twenty-four and two-thirds. Twenty-two and a third. Before those, the season's. He had to land somewhere among them that none of them had landed.

He thought about whom he would draw. The wing's list had a Current third-year on it for the Fourth-day, Iron Rank Four, a long-legged girl from the movement floor who glided. He had watched her in the Crown yard. He had watched Lira beat her pattern two mornings ago, on the painted floor, by going along the bend of her glide instead of across it. He could do that. He could do it in the first exchange and be standing at the end of her curve with his palm out before she got there.

The book would not let him.

He wrote the line at last, and read it over, and did not like it, and left it, because not liking it was a sign that it was honest.

Fourth-day, wing three, the Current. The first exchange to her. Two bursts in the bout, no more. The spark once, and late. Buys: a figure in the low twenties, nothing near the top. Spends: the forearm, probably.

He put the book away and went down, late as it was, to wing three.

Nobody stopped him. The assessment wing was dark except for the lamp at the counter, and the door to wing three had never been locked in his time. He went in and stood on the old pine boards with the high east windows black above him, and then he walked the floor, slowly, from his chalk at the south end to the Current's at the north, counting strides. Fourteen. He walked it again along the line her bend would take. Then he went to the west end and looked up.

The gallery over the door was clean. The porters had swept it that afternoon; he could smell the damp of the swept boards. Somebody had set a row of four chairs along its rail, and a fifth stool, for whoever might not want a chair. From the floor, standing where he would stand, he could see all five of them without turning his head. From the gallery, he supposed, they would see the top of his head and his feet, and whatever his feet did.

Then he went to bed.

Chapter 17 — Under the Gallery

Wing three had a gallery after all.

Cael had fought in the room every Fifth-day for a year without once looking up at the west wall above the door. There had never been anything there worth looking at: a narrow timber balcony, a rail of dark old oak, and behind the rail a stack of spare benches and broken frames that the porters had been putting there since before he came up the hill. The house had built the gallery in the days when wing three was its examination room, so that visiting assessors could look down on a candidate without standing on the same boards. Nobody had visited for a long time. The benches had gone up into it one at a time, the way things go into a loft.

On the Fourth-day morning the benches were gone. The porters had swept the boards up there and rubbed the rail, and in the corners where the broom had not reached, the dust lay in soft grey drifts that showed exactly how long it had been. Four people stood at the rail.

He knew two of them. The pair from the east hall, in their travelling coats, each with his board. The one who wrote stood at the left. The one who did not write stood beside him with his hands behind his back. The third was a woman in the blue-grey of the lake house, with a folding board open on the rail in front of her and three pencils laid out on it in a row. The fourth was an old man in a fur collar who had brought a stool with him and sat on it, so that only his head and shoulders showed above the oak, like a judge at a country fair.

The rest of the room was what it always was. Gault at the trestle in the middle of the north side, with the instrument case set down very straight beside him. The Ash instructor on his right with her book against her chest, the Mire instructor on his left with a pencil behind each ear. The desk clerk at the trestle's end with the wing's book open. And at the east end of the room, at the rail under the high windows, the cohort, more of them than usual, with Ephram in the middle holding his soft-folded chart.

Rooke stood beside Ephram.

He was not on any list for wing three. He had never come to a provision bout in the year Cael had been fighting them. He stood at the rail with his arms folded and his eyes on the gallery over the west door, and he did not look at Cael at all.

Cael went to his chalk at the south end. He did not take Hesk's book out of his coat. The line had been written at the sill the night before, and he had it by heart.

The Current came in from the south door.

She was a third-year from the movement floor, Iron Rank Four by the porter's wall, a tall girl with long legs and a quiet face, who glided the way water goes over a weir: smooth, and a little faster at the end than you expected. He had watched her in the Crown yard. He had never stood across a floor from her.

She came over and shook his hand, and looked up once, quickly, at the gallery.

"Is that for you?" she said.

"I think so."

"Then I'm sorry about the first exchange," she said, "because I'm going to take it." And she went to her chalk.

Gault turned the glass.

"Exchange," said the desk clerk.

She opened the way the textbook said a Current should open, which was the way she always opened: two glides in, the second one bending out wide to his left, so that the strike came off the end of the curve from a place he had not been looking.

He gave her the read.

It went out under thought and came back with her weight. On the first glide she carried it in her back hip, which was right. On the second, half a beat before the bend began, her weight moved into the outside of her front foot, and he knew where the curve would end before she did.

And he could see the other thing, as clearly as he had seen it at the sill: Lira's answer, one burst, low, along the bend instead of across it, and himself standing at the end of the curve with his palm out when the Current arrived.

The book said the first exchange was hers.

He did not burst. He stepped the way an honest Iron steps against a Current, a fraction late, and met the end of her curve with his forearm up. Her strike came off the bend and took him across the forearm, flat and fast, and the give was there, Reydan's give, waiting to drink the whole of the blow into the arm and keep it. He shut it. He let the blow go on up the arm the way it would have gone in anybody, into the elbow and then the shoulder, and felt it arrive there like a door slammed somewhere in a house.

"Touch," said Gault. "Current."

Nought to one.

Up in the gallery a pencil moved. He did not look. He did not need to; the read did not reach that far, but he had stood in enough rooms to know the sound a board makes when a man leans his wrist on it to write.

He walked back to his chalk with the forearm ringing and set his feet.

Now, with the arm ringing, he felt what the line had meant when he wrote it. Every exchange from here would be read twice: once by three cards that had watched him for a year, and once again tonight, by lamplight, in an inn by the river, against a bound book of every bout he had ever fought in public. He was walking across a floor in another man's boots, exactly in his footprints, while the man's tailor watched from the stairs.

"Exchange," said the clerk.

She came in the same way. Two glides and the bend.

This time he used the read and not the burst. As her weight went into the outside of her front foot, he walked, at an ordinary walking pace, to the place where the bend would end. It was three strides. Nobody could have called it anything but timing. When she came off the curve he was already standing there, a little to the side of where she meant to arrive, and she saw him and checked in the middle of her glide, which a Current hates to do, because the whole of their Path is in not checking.

She checked well. She cut the glide short and turned her strike into a sweep, low, at his front knee.

He spent the first burst.

Low and lateral, off the left foot, to her outside; the boards came up under him eight feet on and the landing beat held him there, behind her sweep, at her back. His right hand was on her shoulder blade before the sweep finished.

"Touch," said Gault. "Provision."

One to one.

On the east rail somebody in the cohort let out a breath. Ephram's pencil moved on the soft-folded paper. Rooke did not move at all.

The Current shook her head at herself as she walked back to her chalk, and Cael saw her lips move: counting. She was a good fighter. She was already working out what she would do differently, and she would do it in the third.

She did.

She came out of her chalk without any bend at all. Straight glides, short and quick, one after another, driving forward on a line that pointed at his chest, so that there was no curve for the read to tell him the end of. A Current going straight was a slower Current, and she knew it, and she paid the speed to take the bend away from him. She walked him back. Four strides. Five. He took the ground she asked for, because the line said nothing about the third and because a careful Iron gives ground to a straight Current until the Current runs out of floor.

He ran out of floor first.

The west wall came up behind his heels. He felt it before he saw it, the change in the air at his back, and with it something else: the gallery was directly above him now. He could hear the old man's stool creak. If he looked up he would be looking straight into four faces, and they would be looking straight down at the top of his head.

He did not look up.

The Current set her last glide. He felt her weight go into it through the boards, the read giving him the half-beat before her hip committed, and in that half-beat he could have done any of four things that the house's book had never seen. He did the one the book had seen. He spent the spark.

He spent it late, as the line said: as her lead hand came in, two fingers laid on the back of her wrist for an instant and gone. The copper smell came up off his hand. Her wrist jumped as if a wasp had found it, and the strike went wide, past his ear, into the whitewash with a slap. She was not touched. There was nothing for the cards. But her glide had broken, and she had to step back off the wall to set it again, and while she was setting it the glass ran out.

"Exchange," said the clerk. "Fourth."

Cael came off the wall with the smell of copper on his fingers and the whole front of his left arm aching from the first exchange. Up in the gallery the lake house officer picked up her second pencil.

She had learned twice now, and she came out for the fourth as if she had decided what kind of fighter he was.

She shortened everything. A single glide, and then a step, and then a single glide, so that her weight was never anywhere long enough for the read to give him much. It was clever. It was the cleverest thing anybody had done against him in wing three since the Shield had learned to turn on the ball of his foot, and it took away the timing that a strong Iron would have relied on. A strong Iron would have had nothing left.

He had one burst left in the line.

He stood still and let her come. Glide. Step. Glide. On the third glide her front hip told him which way the strike would go, a quarter-beat early and no more. He went inside it. He did it with the second burst, but he spent it small, a short low burst of a stride and a half, so short that from above it would look like a quick step with good knees behind it and not like a Wind fighter's burst at all. That was a thing he had learned this year and had never written down anywhere except in the rotation's private margins: how to spend a burst so that it looked like less than it was.

He came up inside her strike, beside her, and laid his palm on her shoulder as she turned.

"Touch," said Gault. "Provision. Two to one."

The Current stood a moment with her hand on her shoulder where his palm had been. Then she laughed, short, the way people laugh when a sum comes out right after a long time, and came across and shook his hand again.

"I was sure you'd go round," she said.

"I nearly did."

"No, you didn't," she said, and looked at him a moment longer than she needed to, and went to get her kit.

The four visitors came out of wing three by the west door with their boards under their arms and went across the outer court toward the east hall, to see the afternoon's Silver drills from its gallery, and at the foot of the gallery stair they found Rooke.

He was on one knee on the bottom step, threading a chain through the stair's rail. It was a long chain, the kind the porters used on the cart-shed doors, and he had already run it twice round the newel post. As the four of them came up he drew the last link through, set a padlock in it, and snapped the padlock shut. Then he stood up and hung a card on the chain, square in the middle, where it would be read by anybody who came to the stair. The card was in his square capitals. PROGRAM FLOOR CLOSED TO OBSERVERS. BY ORDER.

Cael saw it from the covered walk, where he had gone with his coat over his aching arm, and he stopped to watch.

The man from Rhagen who wrote things down said something courteous. Cael could not hear it, but he could see the shape of it: a visiting officer's surprise, a question about the house's custom, a slight lift of the board to show that he had signed the lodge book like everybody else. The man who did not write said nothing. The lake house officer looked at the card and then at her three pencils. The old man in the fur collar had brought his stool, and he set it down on the stones and sat on it, as if to see what would happen.

Rooke answered with one word. Cael did not hear that either, but Ephram, who had come out of wing three behind the visitors and was close enough, told him afterward what it was. It was No. The Rhagen man had then asked, very politely, by whose order, since the card said by order, and Rooke had looked at him for a while and said, "Mine," and that had been the second word. Then Rooke turned his back on them and went in at the hall's side door, and a moment later the shutters began to close along the gallery's high windows, one after another, all down the north wall, from the inside.

The four officers stood on the stones for a little while. Then they went away toward the gate, the old man carrying his stool.

By the noon meal the whole house knew. The program would drill under lamps from now on, four of them, set on the painted floor at the corners of the crosses.

It was only then, over his soup, that Cael let himself go back over the end of the bout, because the chain had come first in his mind and the figure second, and he found that he wanted to know why.

Gault had added the three cards in his head, and again on the back of his hand. Twenty-two and two-thirds. Entered. The clerk had written it in the wing's book. Up in the gallery four pencils had written it too, and Cael had heard them. Ephram had come down the room from the east rail with the soft-folded chart and entered it below the Blade, in his cramped square hand, gave her the first, bad arm, and had not drawn a question mark beside it. Then he had looked up past Cael's shoulder at the man from Rhagen.

"They've written the same number I have."

"It's the number."

"I know it's the number." Ephram had folded the chart along its old creases. "Two years I've kept this, and nobody's ever once agreed with me about you. Now four strangers from four houses write down what I write, in the same minute, and I find I don't like it at all." He had tucked the chart into the captain's file. "First time my chart's been right, and I'd give a good deal to have it wrong again."

That was why the chain had come first. The figure was right. Ephram's chart was right. The four strangers' boards were right. It was all exactly right. And it was all going to travel down the bluff road tonight in four satchels to four houses, and be laid beside four bound books, and agree with them; and Rooke, who did not explain anything, had looked at the gallery for the whole bout and then gone and found a chain.

The Current found him first, before Gault did, in the passage behind wing three, with her kit over her shoulder and her face still red from the floor.

"You went short," she said. "On the fourth."

Cael looked at her.

"Nobody goes short off a glide-and-step. You go round it or you take it. I've had that pattern taken off me by a Blade and a Stone and a Shield and once by a girl from the river academy who was much too good for me, and every one of them went round." She shifted the kit. "You went in, and you went short. Like a step. I didn't know you could burst like a step."

"I didn't burst," said Cael. "It was a step."

She looked at him for a long moment with her quiet face. Then she nodded, slowly, the way somebody nods at a figure they have decided not to dispute out loud.

"All right," she said. "It was a step. I'd like to learn that step some time." And she went off down the passage toward the south door. He stood there with his coat half on and felt the cost of the band arrive all at once, from a direction he had not been watching: not the strangers in the gallery, who had seen exactly what he meant them to see, but a third-year from the movement floor who had been close enough to feel it.

Gault came out of his office into the passage behind wing three while Cael was still putting his coat on over the throbbing arm. He had the wing's book under his arm and the instrument case in his hand, and he stopped, which he did not usually do.

"There will be a line about observers in the minute of today's hours," he said. "I have written it. Four officers of other houses present in the gallery, by the lodge book. The provision's demonstration conducted as on every other day." He looked at Cael over the case. "That second sentence is true. I wished it to be on the page in case anyone later wonders whether it was."

"Thank you, Magister."

"Don't thank me for writing down what happened." Gault shifted the case to his other hand. "That is the only thing I am for." He went on down the passage, and then, without turning round, added, "Your forearm. Put cold on it. I have written that down too."

Lira found him on the north wall at dusk without any apples.

"He's shut it," she said. "He didn't tell me why. He doesn't tell anyone why. He told the clerk to keep the book open and write none." She leaned on the wall. "So now there's a ledger in a closed room with none in it, every day."

"How was it under the lamps?"

"Dark. Fine. The crosses are still there; I can find them." She flexed her burst hand. "I just can't see my heel coming any more. You can't read a lamp the way you read a morning."

Rooke came along the wall below them on his way to the gate lodge, and stopped, and looked up, which he did not usually do. He had heard. Cael could tell from his face that he had heard, and that he had expected to hear it, and that he had come along the wall at that hour so that he would.

"Listen to it," he said.

Lira leaned over. "Coach?"

"Your heel. If you can't see it coming, listen to it. Boards talk before a foot's all the way down. Under lamps you'll hear it a quarter-beat early, same as you saw it in the morning." He looked at her a moment longer. "It's a worse way and a slower one. It's also the one you'll have on a floor that nobody's lit for you." He went on toward the lodge.

Lira stayed where she was, leaning on the wall, with her eyes half shut, listening to nothing in particular.

"He shut my light," she said after a while, "and then he came out in the cold to tell me how to do without it." She opened her eyes. "I can't stay angry at him. It's very inconvenient."

He wrote a second line under her name in the column that night. The east hall shut and shuttered by Rooke's order, on account of who was watching me. She trains under lamps. She says it's fine. He looked at the last three words a long while before he blotted them.

There was a knock while the ink was still wet: the porter's boy, to say that Karis wanted them in the reading room, all of them, now, and that she had said now twice.

The first thing Cael saw on the long table was a signature.

It was at the foot of a short covering note, in brown ink, and it was the Chief Adjudicator's own, written large and a little unsteadily, by a hand that had shaken once at a window in the west tower and evidently still did. Karis had the note under her palm and the rest of the courtesy copy beside it: the adjudication office's whole file from Norhold, the match's record, the nine panel charts, and on a sheet by itself the entry Cael had last seen hanging on a nail by the north tunnel. Result: stoppage, Daeva, fourth exchange. Performance rating: unscorable under standard. Referred.

She lifted her hand off the note so that they could read it.

The registry having taken up this office's referral, the office sends the referred file in full, for the proceedings to use. It is the whole of the office's finding. The office has nothing to add to it, and asks that nothing be added to it in the office's name.

Cael read the third sentence first, without meaning to, and then went back for the other two, and thought of four satchels going down the bluff road that afternoon with a figure in each of them that was right.

"Another true number," he said, "going somewhere its maker didn't send it."

"It's a man saying not me," said Brom.

"Not in my name," said Karis. "That's better. Not me is a feeling. This one's under a signature, and it'll be read into the minute with the file, and it'll be there as long as the registry keeps a minute."

"Could he have kept any of it back?" said Lira. "The charts? Any of it?"

"No," said Karis.

She gathered the copy and put it in the reading room's own press, and turned the key.

Karis had told them in the coach what an exhibits sitting was, on the way down the river road that morning, with the house's two cases on Brom's knees because he would not let them ride on the roof.

"Nothing will happen," she said. "That's what it's for. The clerk reads in every exhibit we filed, one at a time, number, title, date, where it came from, the line of receipt. Nobody argues. Jent conceded every one of them before the first sitting. So the clerk reads, and the seat receives, and at the end of it everything we've proved is in the minute." She looked out at the water. "I want you to watch the room, not the clerk. I want to know whether anybody listens."

"Will they?" said Lira.

"I don't know. That's why I want you to watch."

By the fortieth minute a third of the gallery had gone somewhere else behind its eyes.

Cael noticed it before he noticed anything else about the second sitting, because he had been watching the benches instead of the clerk for some while by then. Halfway along the second row a correspondent had laid his board on the bench beside him and folded his arms and shut his eyes. At the back a woman in a market shawl had got out a half-knitted stocking. Two clerks from the river guild were playing some game on their knees with a stub of pencil and a scrap of paper. Nobody was angry and nobody had stopped believing anything. They had come down the market street to see a case and somebody was reading them an inventory. At the front benches not one pencil had moved for nine minutes.

He looked down at his knee, where his own pencil had been keeping the tally under the table, a stroke for each item and a figure for each minute, and read backward what the room had stopped listening to.

It was the house's exhibits, all of them, read into the minute by the seat's clerk in the order the counsel had asked, each with its number, title, date, where it came from and its line of receipt. The clerk had one pace and kept it for everything. A short item, eight or nine seconds; one with a certifying officer's line to recite, twenty or a little more. Bracken's index to the enrollment file, with Bracken's name in its certifying line: fourteen strokes' worth. The Greyvane ruling, the hearing that had kept Cael on his feet in a city he had never wanted to see: twenty-one. Karis's renewals table, rebuilt in a single silent hour with two dates on every row: eleven. The integrity section, forty pages, a night without sleep, ninety-one invocations each traced by hand to its own page: eight seconds. Its title had taken longer than its reading.

And in among the strokes, a mark he had made when Jent rose, the only time Jent rose all morning, to enter one exhibit of his own by its number: the file from Norhold. The clerk had read the covering note into the minute with it, all three sentences, in the registry voice, exactly as Karis had said he would. Cael had watched the third one go into the record. Asks that nothing be added to it in the office's name. The hood had received it, as it received everything. Jent had sat down.

When the clerk read the last number and its line of receipt, Cael had the total on his knee before the senior chair did. A hundred and seventy-three items. Fifty-one minutes and a little over. All of it unopposed. Not one word disputed by any person in the room, because Jent had conceded in writing before the first sitting that every exhibit was what it said it was.

He thought of three sheets he had seen on Bracken's counter that morning before the coach went down. Each had Withrow's name at its foot and the ink still wet: releases of the house's answer, entire, to three faculties of registry law that had written to ask for it to teach from. Across the bottom of the top one, under her signature, she had added a line in her own hand, For teaching. Let them argue. Under that, smaller, in Bracken's upright capitals, someone had written REGISTRAR'S RESERVATION NOTED, and then, smaller still and in the same hand, and overruled.

He looked at the correspondent asleep on the second bench, and thought of three lecture rooms full of second-years being made to read every page of it, and found that it helped.

They read the whole truth about me into the record this morning, he wrote that night, and nobody stood up to argue with a word of it, and a third of the room went to sleep. It was the dullest hour of the year.

Gault's minute for yesterday says the demonstration was conducted as on every other day. Umber's note says nothing is to be added in his name. Withrow wrote "Let them argue" across the bottom of a release. Three people, three lines, none of them meant for this year. Somebody is going to open those minutes long after the seat has ruled and the weeklies have stopped printing, and find that every honest person in the room left one sentence there for them.

I'd like to know who that reader is. I'd like to be worth their trouble.

Chapter 18 — Fifteen Words

The first thing Bracken laid on the table was the receipt.

It was a narrow slip of the seat's buff paper, printed and filled in, with a pin through one corner where it had been fastened to something else. He set it down beside the house's counsel's plate without a word, as if the receipt were the thing that mattered and whatever it had been pinned to could wait. The counsel had come back up the hill in the coach after the sitting and stayed to eat. She put down her fork.

Received at the registry seat, Ostrand, in the matter of the enrollee of record, Halcenvane: one statement, under the head Statements entered (Silver and above). Filing fee, four marks. Paid by the filer.

"Silver and above," said Karis, reading it upside down from across the table. She said it slowly, the way she said a citation she had not expected to need. "That's a fossil. Nobody's filed under that head in—" She stopped.

Withrow, at the table's head, had reached out and turned the slip a little toward the lamp with one finger. Under the printed lines the clerk had written the filer's rank in the space left for it, in a careful hand that had clearly never written it in that space before. Withrow read it, and her finger stayed on it.

"Gold," she said. "Rank Three."

Nobody at the table needed telling who that was. There was exactly one.

Lira's cup stopped halfway to her mouth, and went back down to the board still full.

Only then did Bracken take the statement itself from behind his back, where he had been holding it all this time, and lay it in front of the counsel, and step back to the foot of the table. Withrow began to rise to give him her chair.

"Thank you, Chancellor. I'll stand."

The counsel read it aloud, in the voice she kept for papers that would one day be quoted by people none of them would ever meet.

Daeva. Academy of Auremont. Storm Path; Gold, Rank Three. Entered on her own account at the seat at Ostrand, in the matter of Halcenvane's enrollee of record:

I fought him. Your instruments failed him, not the other way around. Classify the instruments.

She set it down.

At the next table somebody laughed at a joke and stopped, and looked round to see why the middle table had gone so quiet.

Brom reached over and took the sheet by its edges, carefully, as if it might be wet. He read it once, slowly, without moving his lips, the way he read things that would cost somebody something. Then he laid it back down, and turned it round so that the writing faced the middle of the table and not him, toward all of them at once. Cael had never seen him do that with a paper.

It was only then that anybody thought to ask what Bracken was doing there.

Because he should not have been. The registrar's counter was open from the first bell to the eighth, and in two years Cael had never known it open with nobody behind it. If Bracken had to be elsewhere, his senior clerk stood in his place; if there was no clerk, the counter shut and a card hung on the grille. But a first-year had come up from the records hall ten minutes ago, white-faced, to report that he had gone down about a lost key and found the counter lamp lit, the baskets half dealt on the trestle, and nobody there at all. Bracken had crossed the fountain court with this sheet in his hand at a pace nobody on the hill had ever seen from him. He had walked the length of the refectory between the benches with a hundred heads turning after him and had not looked at one of them.

He stood at the foot of the table now with his hands clasped behind him, and seemed to be waiting for somebody to tell him what to do with himself.

Ephram had come over from the cohort's table when Bracken went past it, and was standing behind Karis, counting on his fingers under his breath. He got to fifteen, and stopped, and looked at his two hands as if they had done something surprising.

"A long filing gets answered," said Withrow. She had not touched the statement. "A witness doesn't ask to be answered. The highest-ranked practitioner alive was on that floor when the instruments failed, and she has said so. There's no section anywhere that tells a seat what to do with that, because whoever wrote the code never imagined anybody at her rank would bother."

"The seat will do with it what it did with the Archmarshal," said the counsel quietly. "Receive it, enter it, and step round it."

"Very likely." Withrow's eyes did not leave the sheet. "Registrar. In your thirteen years?"

"Never," said Bracken. "Not at Gold."

He seemed to come back to himself, saying it. He looked down the long room toward the court door as if he had just remembered where he was meant to be. "She paid it herself," he said. "Four marks. I thought the house would want to know she paid." And then, in a different voice, "My counter," and he went back down the refectory at his own pace, and out.

Karis went up to the reading room before the lamps went down and came back with the digest. She laid it on the residence table beside the receipt, open at its table of uses, took a pencil, and in the margin beside the line for Statements entered (Silver and above) wrote a small 45, and drew a ring round it.

"What's forty-five?" said Lira.

"Her," said Karis, and closed the digest on the pencil.

Ephram was still looking at his hands.

"It's a captain's note," he said. "When the rota's wrong and the captain can't change it, she writes one line on it in ink and signs it, so whoever looks at the rota afterward knows somebody saw." He looked at Cael. "She can't change this rota either. She's signed it."

He went down to the records hall late that night, because he could not sleep and the lamp was still lit behind the counter's grille.

Bracken was dealing the evening's sacks into the baskets, the ones he had abandoned half dealt when he crossed the court at a pace nobody had seen. He had his sleeves rolled and his spectacles on, and he was going through the letters at his ordinary speed, address and seal and basket, as if to put the evening back the way it ought to have been.

"I left the counter," he said. "Thirteen years and I have never left the counter. A first-year came to ask about a key and found nobody here." He dealt three to OTHER. "I have written it in the daybook. Counter unattended, a quarter of an hour, by the registrar, on the registrar's own account." He dealt one to FACULTIES. "I was not going to leave that out."

"It was a Gold filing," said Cael.

"It was a Gold filing." Bracken stopped dealing, for a moment, with a letter in his hand. "In thirteen years I have carried three courtesy copies of statements entered up to a chancellor. Every one of them a Silver's, about one thing or another. Tonight it was a Gold's, about you, and I found I couldn't let a porter carry it." He dealt the letter. "Go to bed. I'll be another hour."

On the Sixth-day morning Cael went down to the post room before the first bell, because a letter he had been half waiting for all week without admitting it might be in the early bag, and because he could not sleep.

The post room was behind the records hall's counter, a narrow whitewashed room with a long sorting bench under the window and pigeonholes from floor to ceiling along the other wall. The district courier's bag came up the hill in the dark and was opened there at first light. Usually the post porter opened it, a broad slow man who had done the sort for twenty years. This morning the post porter was sitting on a stool in the corner with his left arm strapped across his chest, looking unhappy, and the man at the sorting bench with the bag open in front of him was Seln.

He did not look up when Cael came in. He held out his left hand, without turning his head, with a small bundle of letters in it.

"You may hold that," he said.

Cael took it. It was the house's general post, which would go up to the residence and the halls. He stood at the end of the bench and held it, and watched.

The porter had explained, from his stool, before Cael had asked, that he had done his shoulder in lifting a crate on the Fourth-day. The assistant to the assessment wing had come down on the Fifth-day and offered, and had done the sort ever since, and did it very well, though not, the porter said, the way he would have done it himself. Seln did not answer this, or seem to hear it.

He sorted the district bag into three piles on the bench. Cael had never watched anybody sort post before with any attention, and he found that it was not one act but four, done so quickly they looked like one. Seln took a letter out of the bag. He read the address. He turned it over and read the seal. He laid it on its pile. He did not hold any letter for longer than another; he did not let his eyes rest on any seal more than on any other. A man watching from the end of the bench would have said he was sorting the post.

Cael watched the piles instead of the man.

The first pile was the house's, for the halls and the residence, and it went into his hand as it grew. The second was the assessment wing's: anything addressed to the wing, its counter, its instructors, its office. The third was the registrar's, for Bracken's counter and the records hall.

The third pile was the tallest. That was not strange in itself; Bracken's counter got more post than anywhere on the hill. What Cael noticed, after a while, was the seals on it. Half of the letters in Bracken's pile carried the grey wax of the district seat at Ostrand. In the wing's pile there was not one. Not one grey seal, in a bag that held forty letters from the district.

He thought back. The wing had always had district post. The provision's hours were signed in the wing, and the district seat had written to the wing about them, about observers and schedules and the figures in the wing's book, every few weeks for two years. He had stood at the wing's counter himself and watched the desk clerk open grey seals.
