Seln laid another grey seal on Bracken's pile, at exactly the pace he had laid the last one.

When the bag was nearly empty, Seln held one letter a moment longer than the others, which he had not done with any letter that morning.

"Auremont," he said, and laid it on top of the bundle in Cael's hands, face down, and took out the next.

It had no seal, only a fold tucked in on itself, the way people fold a letter who do not want anybody to think they took trouble over it. Cael did not turn it over in the post room. He carried the house's bundle up to the residence and left it on the hall table. He took the one letter on up the stair and opened it at his own window, where letters were opened in that house, with the light coming up grey over the river and the fountain not yet running below.

They did this to me the other way — built the ladder to my height and called it fairness. Nobody files challenges against a favorite. Don't mistake what's happening to you for procedure. It stopped being procedure the day they couldn't score you.

— D.

The rematch stands. Keep yourself unclassified.

He did not read it again. He got out Hesk's book instead, and a pen, and copied it into the Log word for word, slowly, the way he had once copied the last lines of Gault's note into a letter for Hesk, because copying a thing makes you see every mark in it. Copying, he saw the dash before her initial, and that she had written the last line after the initial and not before it, as if it were an afterthought; and that she had not written Dear or Cael or anything at all at the top.

He had a piece of her. He went on knowing it the whole time he copied, the way you go on knowing there is a stone in your boot. Somewhere under his ribs, settled since the first morning of the year, sat the weight he had taken from her on the floor at Norhold: the lane, the leaning air, the read that at her weight could have the air or his body and not both. He had paid for it on a stone floor with his whole left side, and he paid for it still, ten counts slow every time he laid a lane. She did not know she had given it. She never would. And here she was in four lines, telling him how to keep what she had never known she was giving away.

Under the copy he wrote one more line.

From anyone else, a joke. From her, the only one of us who has been classified all the way to the top and lived up there, it's directions. That's a strategy. Filed.

Then he put the letter itself where nothing else of his lived: inside the back board of Hesk's book, opposite the column, against the page where the costs were kept. It seemed to belong with them. He closed the book on it, and the court below had begun to fill.

Lira found him on the rail of the Crown yard's top tier that evening, with the sun going down behind the north range and the yard empty below.

She had been under the lamps all afternoon, and had come out of them squinting as if the dusk were too bright, with her head held a little forward like somebody still peering at a thing in poor light.

"Everybody at supper last night thought she'd taken your side," she said, before she had properly arrived at the rail. "The first-years. Half the cohort. Daeva stands up for him." She leaned her elbows on the rail. "She didn't. That isn't what fifteen words on the seat's own paper is for. That's a card nailed to a wall, saying where she'll be standing when all this is over, so no office can ever say afterward it didn't know."

"You sound sure."

"Somebody did it to me." She rested her chin on her crossed arms. "At a board, in front of her whole house. Silver bracket, next cycle. Then she turned round and walked off without looking back to see if I'd heard. People called it a challenge. It wasn't. A challenge is I'll fight you. That was I'll be there." She was quiet a while. "It's the most useful thing anybody's ever said to me. Four words. I don't think Zerin meant it kindly, and I don't think she cared whether it was kind."

"And Daeva?"

"Same house, isn't it. Auremont." Lira pushed herself upright. "They turn out strange ones. Good strange, one or two."

They watched the porter come out into the yard below with his long-handled brush and begin to sweep the oak, in long even strokes, from the north end.

"Did she write to you?" said Lira. "Herself. Not the seat."

"This morning."

"Are you going to tell me what she said?"

"Not yet."

Lira nodded, as if that were a perfectly good answer, which from her it was. "Then tell me when it's yours to tell," she said, and went down the tier steps two at a time, and he heard her stop at the bottom and say something to the porter that made him laugh.

That night the lantern was lit on the second floor again.

Cael saw it from the court on his way in, one low light behind the middle roof's windows, and went up the stair as far as the rail by the door. Brom was at the old striking frame at the north end, alone. He was not running the long sequence he ran before a road. He was hitting the padded post, over and over, forearm and turn and drive, at fighting pace, with the post's tired springs groaning, and he was not stopping between them the way he always stopped to reset. The cream envelope was in the coat he had hung on the frame's corner; Cael could see the square of it against the cloth.

After a while Ephram came up the other stair with his kit. He looked at Brom from the doorway. Then he went to the frame beside Brom's, the one he had used every evening of the week before the first sitting, and set his feet, and began his entry line, the cut along it, the recovery, at the same pace as Brom's, a hair apart, keeping time.

Neither of them looked at the other. After a quarter of an hour Brom slowed, and then stopped, and stood with his forearms hanging and his breath going, and Ephram stopped too, at the same moment, as if they had agreed it. Brom took his coat down off the frame and put it on, and his hand went to the left side of it and rested there, and then he went down the stair. Ephram stayed, and trimmed the lantern, and did not put it out.

Cael went down by the other stair and did not write it in the column. It was not a cost. He had no name for it yet.

On the Seventh-day morning Seln came out of the wing at the half-bell before the first, with no papers in his hands at all, and walked across the outer court toward the lodge.

Cael was on the covered walk. He had been on the covered walk, in fact, for some time, with the notion that if Seln came out at that hour he might happen to be going the same way. Seln passed him without turning his head. Three strides farther on he said, to the air in front of him, "The lodge. Bring nothing," and kept walking at his even pace.

Cael brought nothing, and followed.

The code allowed the assessment wing to read the gate lodge's book of arrivals once a week, on the Seventh-day, so that the wing's records of who had come to observe the provision's hours could be checked against the gate's record of who had come through the gate. Cael had known that for two years as a line in a rule-book. He had never once thought about who did the reading.

The lodge was a single room built into the gatehouse wall, with a stove, a high stool, a counter, and a window on the road. The lodge-man was a short square man with a grey beard and a bad knee, who had kept the gate since before Bracken came to the hill. When Seln came in he was already pouring a second cup of tea, and he set it on the counter without being asked and without looking to see who it was for.

"Assistant," he said.

"Lodge-man."

"You'll have heard about that carter," said the lodge-man.

Seln drank some tea. "I heard he scraped the gatepost."

"Scraped. He took a hand's breadth out of it with his near wheel and then he tells me the post was in the wrong place." The lodge-man pushed the book across the counter. "That post has been where it is for three hundred years. I told him so. He said that was a long time to be in the wrong place."

Seln opened the book at the week's first page and began to read it, and went on listening, and said "Mm" at the right places, while the lodge-man told him the whole of the carter. Then he told him about the carter's father, who had also scraped the gatepost, and what he had said to that one in his day, which had been a good deal more than he had said to the son. It took a quarter of an hour. Cael stood by the stove, where Seln had put him with a glance, and drank the tea the lodge-man had poured him too, and watched.

Seln read the whole week. Arrivals by the day and the bell. Carts, couriers, visitors, deliveries; the four observers who had signed in for the Fourth-day, with their houses beside their names; the correspondents who had been turned back, marked with a small t the lodge-man used for turned. Then he turned to the back of each day's page, where there was a second, narrow column that Cael had never known existed.

The lodge-man saw him look at it.

"Road column," he said. "Since the year of the thieves, when I was a young man. Chancellor before last had the lodge keep a line every bell of what was on the road below, so the house would know if somebody was waiting for a cart to come up. Nobody's ever told me to stop." He shrugged. "So every bell I look out of the window and write down what's there."

Cael read it over Seln's arm.

Every bell, all week, the same line in the lodge-man's plain hand. Two at the foot. And every few lines, at the bell the two coats at the road's foot gave way to the next two: Two at the foot. Changed.

Changed at the bell. Every bell that the rotation said they should change. Not once early. Not once late.

He went back over his own week, the way he went back over a bout.

On the First-day he had gone down the river path alone before light, which he had not done since the year began. On the Second-day he had gone down the bluff road with Brom at the fourth bell, an hour nobody went down at, to carry a crate of the reading room's copying paper up from the ferry because the carrier had not come. On the Fifth-day the whole house had gone down to the sitting in the coach, as was known a week ahead. On the Sixth-day he had carried two document cases down into the town for Karis, so that her answer to the fee office would go in at its counter by her own hand and nobody else's. Four times in one week his pattern had broken. Any of them would have been worth a line to a man who was paid to follow him.

The road column did not care about any of them. Two at the foot. Two at the foot. Changed.

Seln shut the book and pushed it back across the counter with a word of thanks. He told the lodge-man that in his opinion the gatepost was in exactly the right place and the carter ought to be made to pay for the stone. The lodge-man said that was what he'd been saying. Seln finished his tea, and set the cup down, and turned it a quarter-turn on the counter before he let go of it.

They walked back across the outer court together, in the first real light, without speaking.

Halfway across, Cael said it, because it had been building in him since the road column and it would not stay where it was.

"A watcher who doesn't move when his man moves isn't watching his man."

Seln walked on.

"They aren't following me any more," said Cael. "They haven't been, not for a while. I went down that road at four odd hours this week and they didn't shift a foot or a minute. They're not on me." He stopped walking. "He is holding a road."

Seln stopped too, a stride ahead, and turned his head a little, not all the way round.

"Mm," he said.

It was the same sound he made at the counter, at the table, at the lodge-man's carter. But this time he held it a fraction longer, and Cael had stood across enough tables from him by now to hear the difference. It was the sound of a man who has set a sum in front of somebody, without a word of explanation, and has just watched him add it up right.

Then Seln went on across the court to the wing at his even pace, and Cael stood where he was in the cold, with nothing in his hands.

Chapter 19 — The Shape

When the plates had been cleared, Seln put four dried beans on the board in a row and said, "Four offices. Ask."

They were the speckled brown beans the kitchen soaked for the Second-day stew. He had taken them out of his coat pocket without any hurry. He laid them a hand's breadth apart, in front of his own place at the middle of the bench, and now he sat back from them with his hands folded and looked at none of the four people across the table.

The refectory went on round them, loud at the far end where the first-years were.

"A drawing can be found," said Seln, to the beans. "These can be eaten. Ask."

Brom asked first.

Cael had not expected that. Brom did not ask questions at table; he answered them, when he had to, in as few words as the question would bear. But Brom leaned forward on his forearms now and put one thick finger on the board beside the second bean from the left, not touching it.

"That one."

"A provincial registry," said Seln. "The one that keeps the Velmere estate's file. Nine days ago. A query on the standing of the household, the tiers of the people in it, and the estate's registered relationships."

Brom did not move his finger.

"Does the query show at the estate's end?"

Seln answered with a question of his own, and for once he looked straight across the table to ask it. "Who reads the post at Velmere?"

"My grandmother," said Brom. "She always has."

"Then she'll read the query book as well. It lies open on the provincial counter for anybody on the estate's file, with every question in it, and who asked, and when."

Brom took his finger off the board. He nodded once. Then he sat back and folded his arms. Cael, who had watched Brom carry everything from code volumes to a hurt friend's kit without once looking as if it weighed anything, saw him look for a moment like a man carrying something he could not put down and could not shift to the other shoulder.

Lira asked second. She did not point. She said, "Which one's me?"

Seln touched the third bean. "The district seat. Twelve days ago. A query on the certification history of a Wind practitioner of this house, Iron Rank One, for completeness of the respondent institution's file."

"Which file?"

"There is only one."

Lira asked Seln one precise question, in the voice she used at a rating table for a figure she suspected.

"Did they ask for the Fenmark sheet by name?"

"They asked for the file."

"Then they got the Fenmark sheet." She looked down at the bean and not at any of them. Everybody at that table knew what was at the bottom of her file, under four years of other people's honest lines, and nobody said it, and she did not say it either. After a moment she looked across at Cael. "Your column. Under my name. That they read it."

"Tonight."

Karis did not ask about hers. She took a folded letter out of her sleeve and laid it beside the bean at the right-hand end of the row, the one nobody had pointed to.

"Mine," she said. "The keeper of the archive at Ternhall wrote to me this morning, privately. Four lines. A district clerk came to her counter six days ago with a sealed request for my transfer file: my old standing, my privileges, the training log from the paired floor." She kept two fingers on the letter, as if it might blow away. "On the Third-day a fee office wanted to know who I was. Now somebody wants to know who I used to be." She was quiet a moment. "That's twice."

That left the bean at the far left, and Cael asked about it, because nobody else was going to.

"This house," said Seln. "Our own counter, three weeks ago. A district office asking for the sponsorship papers, for the proceedings' record; and in the fourth item, a schedule of every tie this house has to you. Sponsorship, floor hours, the standing that hangs on your evaluation, your travel endorsements." He touched that bean lightly. "The registrar answered it in full, and said in his covering letter that it was in full, twice."

Lira had been looking along the row the whole time, from left to right and back.

"You haven't got one for him," she said. "There isn't a bean with his name on it."

"No," said Seln. "That's the way to know it isn't a mistake."

Karis took four slips from the back of her notebook, wrote the four offices on them, one to a slip, and laid each one under its bean. Then she took a fifth slip and laid it at the end of the row, beyond the last bean, with nothing written on it and nothing on top of it.

On the stair afterward Lira asked her what the blank slip was for.

"Whoever's next," said Karis. "So far they've touched people with a seat at that table. Nobody that careful stops at the table." She reached the landing. "I've left room."

Brom had come up behind them, slower. At the turn of the stair he stopped, and Cael, a step below, saw his right hand go to the left side of his coat, where the inside pocket was, and rest there over the cloth. There was a square cream envelope in that pocket with its dark red seal still whole. It had come up with the post four days ago, and he had turned it over once at the table and put it away unopened, and nobody had asked. Now an office in his own province kept an open book with a question in it about his family, and his grandmother could turn its pages whenever she liked.

Brom took the hand away from the pocket and went on up the stair. Nobody asked him then, either.

The evening post came up at the eighth bell, and it was Seln who brought the one letter that mattered into the refectory.

He had been doing the sorts all week for the post porter, mornings and evenings, and he came in from the court with the house's bundle under his arm and one envelope held apart from it in his other hand. He did not give the bundle to anybody. He walked to the middle table, where the four of them were still sitting because none of them had wanted to go up, and he laid the single envelope face up on Karis's blank slip at the end of the row of beans, and stood back.

Cael knew the hand from across the table. Square, upright, the address set out as level as the bubble in a good spirit glass. Denvash.

Cael reached over and took it, and broke the fold, and read it where he sat, to himself, all of it, from the brass to the dog to the third paragraph and the single initial at the end. He read the third paragraph twice. Then he did not trust his voice, and he passed the sheet across the table to Brom, with his thumb under the third paragraph.

Brom read it aloud. He read it slowly, the way he read anything, without any change in his voice for any of it.

Two polite men from the registry came through Denvash asking after my trade licenses and the shop's title. Wanted to know if you had any interest recorded in either. I told them my grandson's interest in this shop is that he grew up in it, and they wrote that down. Whatever they're building, it has a shape. Mind the shape. — H.

Brom laid the sheet down, and Seln put his hand in his pocket and took out a fifth bean and set it on the slip, beside the envelope, apart from the others.

Then Cael took the letter back and read them the rest of it, the first part, the part he had smiled at. He did not quite know why he did it. Perhaps he wanted them to hear Hesk as Hesk was, a man with a bench and a stove and opinions, and not as a line in somebody's inventory.

The brass came up from the coast at last, and it is a third dearer than last year and not as good, and the founder says it is nobody's fault, which I believe, because it never is. I have a surveyor's level on the bench that came back to me after thirty years. I made it for the man's father. The bubble has wandered a hair, and the son brought it in to be put right; and then, when I had it in pieces, he asked me to set it back the way it was, because his father laid out every boundary in the valley with it a hair wrong and the whole valley is built to agree with it now. I spent four days deciding. In the end I did as he asked.

The stove draws well. The shop is the shop. The widow across the lane has a new dog that barks at me in particular, and I have decided to take it as a mark of my character.

It did not work. He heard it not work as he read it. The dog and the stove and the level went out into the room and fell on the table among the beans, and none of them could get Hesk back out of the third paragraph. He stopped reading and folded the letter.

Grew up in it. He had. At five years old he had slept under the long bench in a nest of clean shavings, because the stove ticked there and it was warmer than upstairs while Hesk worked late. He had learned his letters off the brass makers' plates on instruments that came in to be mended. The shop's title was one sheet of the district's paper folded in four, in a tin box under that bench with the receipts, and it had Hesk's name on it and no other. Two polite men had asked whether his was in the tin box too. And on a form somewhere, in a column under a printed heading, a pencil had set down grew up in it.

"Denvash," said Lira, as if she were setting it down on the table with the beans.

Karis took the blank slip from under the envelope and wrote on it, small. Denvash. Provincial registry. Trade licences, and the title to the shop. She laid it back under the fifth bean.

It was Karis who said it first, and she said it as a guess, which she almost never did.

"If I wanted to shut a man out of everything at once," she said slowly, "every door at once, so that he couldn't move a deed or carry a letter or warn a friend before the next one shut, I would want to know where all his doors were. Beforehand." She looked at the five beans. "Is that what this is?"

"Nearly," said Seln.

"Which part's wrong?"

"Beforehand." He turned his cup a quarter-turn. "You've put it before the shutting. It's before the ruling."

Karis's pen lay on the board where she had let go of it. Cael had never seen her let go of a pen with a question still open.

"Go on," she said.

"Shut every door on one morning, yes. That's what it's for. A restriction that runs one office at a time leaks: somebody hears, somebody moves a deed, somebody's cousin carries a letter over a district line before the freeze arrives. So nobody runs one like that." He laid a fingertip on the board beside each bean in turn, not touching any of them. "Every office finds its own door first, and writes it down, and puts what it found in a drawer. Five drawers, here. Each file lawful. Each as dull as a laundry list. All five indexed under one name. And then they wait."

"For the ruling."

"For a ruling." Seln's voice did not change. "Think what five offices' clerks cost for nine weeks. An office spends that only when it already believes it knows the answer. So if the walking has begun, then somebody well above the seat has settled in his mind how the seat will rule, and has started paying for the morning after. The walking is a finding of its own. It's made by people who don't sit in the seat, and made first."

"And if the seat rules the other way? Our way?"

"Take the bad way first, it's shorter. One clerk, one afternoon, five files carried to one desk; every door shut on the same morning; and the enrollee learns what all this was for on a day when there's nothing left to do about it." He turned the cup back. "Your way, the five drawers are simply never opened together. Each office weeds its old papers in due course, as offices do, and nobody anywhere has broken a single rule."

"What do you call it?" said Brom.

"In the office we called it walking the fences." Seln looked at the five beans. "On paper, it's a pre-restriction inventory."

"How long does it take?"

"For a smith with a forge and a wife and a guild, six weeks. Ten, if the wife's people are spread about." He looked at the four in their row and the one apart. "For a boy with friends at three provincial registries, and a house that took him in, and a grandfather with a shop at the far end of the country—" He laid one finger on the board beside the fifth bean. "Nine weeks. They are in the sixth."

Karis reached out and moved the slips: the four office slips she pushed together into one heap under the four beans, and the Denvash slip she drew a hand's breadth further away from them, by itself, with its bean on it.

"They're not freezing him," she said, looking at the one slip. "He has nothing they could freeze. They're finding out what you'd mind." She took her hand away. "Somebody say it, so I know I'm not the only one who saw it."

"Said," said Brom.

He was looking at the letter in Cael's hand, the level address and the old fold. He had never met Hesk. He had heard about him at a hundred tables, the stove and the spectacles pushed up on the forehead and the barometers waiting to come right, and he looked at the letter as if it were something of his own that a stranger had taken out of his coat.

"The question is what we do the day after."

Lira said it before anyone expected her to say anything, with Karis's bean turning in her fingers. Then she put the bean back exactly where it had been and explained herself, evenly, the way she read the true sum off a bout sheet after a loss. "Not whether we win the next sitting. We'll win it. They'll let us win every sitting all year; it costs them nothing. There are men in Denvash asking about a tin box. That isn't about any sitting. That's about the morning after the last one." Her chin came up. "So that's the question."

Cael looked round the table, because looking was what he did when there was nothing to do. Karis with her palm on the notebook's cover. Brom bent forward with his elbows on his knees and his eyes on the board. Lira with the question still lying open where she had put it, and her chin up over it, waiting for one of them to pick it up. And at the middle of the bench Seln, who had walked fences like these himself for years and knew from the inside what the morning after one looked like, sitting with his hands quite still on either side of the five beans, as if the table might tip if he moved them.

The others went up in ones and twos, Brom last, with his hand on his coat. Cael stayed. After a while Seln began to put the beans back into his pocket, one at a time, the fifth last.

"You'll want to write to Denvash tonight," he said, without looking up.

"Yes."

"Write it." The fourth bean went into the pocket. "Give it to the registrar for his pouch, not to the town post. The pouch is locked in Ostrand and opened here, and I open it." He put the fifth bean away. "Letters from a house under inventory are read. Not by anyone wicked. By a clerk, for completeness, who will copy a line of it into a file. Don't give them a line." He stood, and turned his empty cup a quarter-turn on the board, and left it there. "Tell him the stove sounds well. Tell him nothing else he wouldn't want read aloud in a provincial counting-room. He'll understand. He's been minding shapes longer than either of us."

He went out at his even pace, and Cael sat a while longer alone at the long table, where the beans had been.

Withrow did not read the letter. She asked him to read it to her, all of it, and sat at her desk with her pen in her hand while he did, as if she meant to take a note.

He read the brass and the level and the stove and the dog, and she smiled at the dog. He read the third paragraph. Somewhere in its second sentence the pen in her hand stopped moving above the blotter, and it did not move again until he had finished, and then she laid it down very carefully, parallel to the blotter's edge, which was not a thing she did with pens.

"The girl," she said.

It was the last thing he had expected her to say. She pointed him with two fingers to the visitor's chair, and he sat, which was not usual either.

"The one who came to my counter every week for a year. You know about her. What you don't know is that she wasn't the first of that family at my counter." She took the brown pocket code off the corner of the desk and opened it near the back, and turned it round so that he could see the margin of the page, where, beside a short printed list, somebody had written in faded ink two initials and a few words. "Her father came first. On the fourth morning. He had a flour sack."

She told it from the sack outward.

"He tipped it out on my counter, and it was letters, nine of them, and he had put them in the order they'd come to his door so that I could read his week. The bank's on top, because the note on his house named his standing as its surety, and a standing under restriction is no surety. Then the transit office, to say his endorsement had run out, so that the law no longer let him cross out of his district to argue with anybody. Then his guild, which can't keep a contract with an unclassified man. Then the yard, which had given his run to someone else that same morning. And at the very bottom, the girl's school, to say her place was under review because a child's place rests on the parent's. I think he put that one at the bottom on purpose. The other four I won't give you. They were the same letter in other hands."

Cael looked at the margin. The initials were a man's. Beside them, in a younger version of Withrow's hand: two children; the house; Force, Bronze 4; haulage, river district; 31.

"He'd done nothing," said Withrow. "Twenty years before, a station clerk made a slip writing down his Kindling, and the one officer who could have sworn to the true reading was dead, so the slip could never be put right. The registry stood him in a frame again. Twice. Twice the frame had nothing to say. That was all." She touched the printed list beside her old note. "These are the nine headings. Employment, guild, credentials, property, debts, enrollments, travel, office, and other relationships. The district was short of clerks that year and I was good at it. I walked his fences myself. Seven weeks. I was proud of how careful it was."

"What did you say to him? At the counter."

"That he hadn't nine troubles. He had one, which had come to his door nine times in nine coats, and there was no counter anywhere he could stand at to answer it, because nobody had done anything to him. A restriction isn't an act. It's a condition you're left standing in." She shut the code. "That is how it was built."

"And then?"

"The girl kept coming to my counter after there was nothing more of him to file," said Withrow. "Every week, with her mother's people's address written on the back of her hand in case I had news." She was quiet a moment. "Once, I did. A toll paid at the ferry by the last station, eastbound, in his name. I gave her that. It was the last line anybody ever wrote about him."

"What will they do to Hesk?" said Cael.

"Nothing," said Withrow. "Not a hand on the door. A hand on the clock."

She let that stand a moment before she explained it.

"Grew up in it is what he told them, so it's what they wrote, and it's true. It goes under the ninth heading, a true line among true lines, and it waits. On the morning somebody wants the ninth heading, nobody will say a word against him; they won't need to. Any licence held by a man the registry has entered as tied to a restricted person can be called in for review. Nobody refuses it. They review it." She looked at the letter in his hand. "For exactly as long as somebody likes."

She opened the code once more at the nine headings, took up her pen, and wrote one word in the margin beside the ninth, small, under her own old note about the haulier, in the hand she had used to underline that book in her second year. Then she turned the book round so that he could read it. Choosing.

She closed the code, and put it back on the corner of the desk, and said, "Go to bed."

Lira was sitting on the top stair of the residence when he came up, with her back against the newel post and her knees drawn up, waiting, though she would not have said so.

"Well?" she said.

He sat down a step below her and told her about the flour sack. Not all of it. The nine letters in the order they had come, the girl's at the bottom, the ferry toll at the last station. She listened without moving.

"And Hesk?"

"A hand on the clock."

She was quiet for a long time. Then she said, "I wrote to him once, you know. From Greyvane. I asked when you were born. He sent back the date, and thank you, and he won't have told you." She got up. "Put my line in the column. The Fenmark one. And then put a line in for him, too, even though he isn't one of the four. He'd want to be counted properly." She went along the landing to her door. "He'd say a column with a wrong total isn't a column."

Past midnight he turned back through Hesk's book to the page where the first pole was written, on the night of the instrument, and read it through with the pen in his hand, meaning to write something under it.

He sat a long time and wrote nothing under it. Then, at the foot of the facing page, small, he wrote:

A hand on a clock isn't a person, and it isn't text. Withrow's flour sack had both in it and neither. I've never had to know which side of the line a thing stood on before I could fight it. Tonight I couldn't tell. The page with the line on it is still standing, and I don't know how much longer it will bear my weight.

Then, because Seln had told him to and because he could not have slept otherwise, he wrote the other letter.

It was short. He wrote it three times. The first was angry, and he tore it across. The second was frightened, which was worse, and he tore that too, and sat a while with the pieces in his hands before he put them in the stove. The third he wrote slowly, reading every line as a clerk with a pencil would read it in a provincial counting-room, for completeness, and taking out anything he would not have wanted copied into a file.

You were right to set the level back the way the son wanted it. A valley that agrees with itself is worth keeping agreed. You'll have known that before you spent the four days; you spent them to be sure.

The stove sounds well. Tell the widow's dog it has good judgment.

I'm well. The house is good to me. I read your third paragraph at a window, to the people I'd most want to hear it, and they heard it. I'll mind it.

He signed it with the one letter Hesk signed his with, and sealed it, and in the morning he gave it to Bracken for the pouch, and Bracken took it without a word and put it in the pouch himself.

Chapter 20 — Lot Seventeen

Three nights before the third sitting, the honest floor was the only floor on the hill where anybody was allowed to see what Cael was.

They went in at the quarter to the eleventh bell, as they always did, on the key Rooke had lent Lira for the program's dawn drills and had told her he did not want to know about after dark. But the east hall was not what it had been. The shutters along the gallery had been closed since the Fourth-day by Rooke's order, and they did not need to be drawn. The chain still hung across the foot of the gallery stair with its padlock and its card, CLOSED TO OBSERVERS, so that Brom had to step over it to set the jug down on the bottom stair. The four lamps that the program now drilled under all day were standing at the corners of the painted crosses where the porters had left them, cold.

"Well," said Lira, looking round the shut-up hall with her wrists half taped. "The whole floor's honest now. Nobody's allowed to watch any of it."

Brom lit two of the lamps and left the other two dark, because two had always been the number. Karis sat on the gallery stair above the chain with her notebook open on her knee. Nobody had asked her to come. She had come anyway, every week since the first night, and counted.

"What do you want?" said Cael.

"The real one." Lira tore the last strip of tape with her teeth. "Everything you can't show in wing three. I've had six days of drilling under lamps, and I can't see my own heel coming any more, and I keep landing a quarter-beat late on things I could read in my sleep in daylight." She put her hands on her hips. "If I can see you coming at your true rate, in lamplight, I can see anybody coming at anything. So come."

He looked at Brom. Brom looked at the lamps and then at him, and nodded once, which meant I'm holding the room.

So Cael fought her at his true rate, for the first time since the first week of the year.

He let the read go all the way out and come all the way back, without stopping it anywhere short to look like timing. It brought him Lira's weight half a beat early, as it always did, and in lamplight half a beat was a long time. He used the Wind the way it wanted to be used and not the way the house's book had it. One burst, two, the second off the landing of the first; a third, low, along the wall; a fourth to take him round her lie on the four-count before her fourth arrived. On the boards in wing three he stopped at four, and never let a fifth show. Here he went to five without thinking about it, and then to six, and felt the old easy looseness come into his legs that he had not let himself feel on a floor in front of anybody since Norhold.

Lira lost the first two exchanges. She lost them cleanly and quickly and said "Again" both times before she had finished losing.

In the third she came at him with a straight palm, the hardest thing she had, from the end of a burst, and he did not move out of it. He let it land on his forearm. The give was there, Reydan's give, and for once he let it open. It drank her blow into the arm as a dry cup drinks water, and kept it, and her palm stopped against him as if it had hit a sack of wet sand. She stood there with her arm out, looking at it.

"I hate that," she said with great feeling.

"I know."

"I'd forgotten how much." She shook her hand out. "Again. And lay one."

He laid a lane.

He laid it across her line from the north wall, a road of leaning air fifteen feet long and no wider than his shoulders, tipping south. His ears shut and opened again. And on the gallery stair Karis began to count aloud, quietly, from the moment it was laid.

"One."

In the lamplight Lira could not read her heel. She had said so. But Cael, watching her come at the lane on the four-count, saw her find something else. The dust in the cracks between the painted boards had woken as the lane went down, the way it always did, and was running south along the lane in a thin pale stream. In daylight from the high windows you could hardly see it. Under two lamps set low on the floor, it threw a shadow. The whole lane showed on the boards as a faint moving band of dark, like the wake of a fish under still water.

Lira saw it on her second count. He watched her see it. Her lie went onto the back foot, outside the band, and on the third count, the empty one, she did not put a foot into the lane at all. On the fourth she burst along its edge, the length of it, not across, and came out at its end beside him with her palm already on his shoulder.

"Touch," said Brom, from the dark beyond the lamps.

"Seven," said Karis, on the stair.

Cael reached for the Wind. It came late. It came a beat behind his asking, the right thing answering slow, as it had answered every time since the first night on this floor. He stood in it. Bill, not flag. Lira, beside him, breathing hard, was looking down at the boards where the dust was settling out of the band and the band was fading.

"The dust," she said. "Under the lamps the dust makes a shadow. I can see the lane by its shadow."

"I saw you see it."

"Ten," said Karis. "Eleven."

The Wind came when he called it.

"Ten counts," said Karis, and wrote it down. "Same as the first night."

Lira had gone down on one knee by the end of the lane, and was looking along the boards at the last of the dust, with her face close to the floor and the lamp throwing her shadow long behind her.

"I lost my light," she said, to the boards. "Rooke shut it out on account of who was watching you. I've been angry about it for six days, all by myself, under these lamps, and I haven't told anybody, because it was the right thing to do and I knew it was." She stood up and dusted her knee. "And it turns out the lamps show me a thing the windows never did."

"That doesn't make it fair."

"No. It makes it mine." She went back to her cross. "Lay another. Not across this time. Lay it down the line, at me, and let me try to stand in it."

"We said we don't spend a new figure the night we find it."

"It's not a new figure. It's the same lane. I'm the new thing." She set her feet. "Lay it."

He laid it, once more, and she stood in it on the four-count and was pushed off her feet into the dust, and laughed out loud from the floor. Karis counted ten and wrote ten, and then Brom said that was enough for one night in a voice that nobody argued with.

They put out the lamps by the old order, the far one first, and stepped back over Rooke's chain, and Lira locked the door behind them.

On the stair Cael thought about it, the way he thought about everything on stairs.

In wing three, four strangers had written down a figure for him that was exactly right and entirely false: the band, the house's rate, twenty-two and two-thirds. Here, on a floor with the shutters closed and a chain across the stair, there had been nobody to write anything at all, and the figure had been true. Six bursts on boards. The give opened. A lane and its bill. Every true number about him this year had been made in a locked room by four people who would never be allowed to say it aloud. And every false one had gone into a book.

He wrote it in Hesk's book at the sill before he slept. The only honest measurement anybody has taken of me since Norhold was taken tonight, by Karis, on a closed floor, under two lamps. It will never be entered anywhere. Lira found the lane by its shadow. That will be entered nowhere either, and it's the best thing anybody learned on this hill this week.

On the evening before the third sitting the house's counsel came up the hill by arrangement for once, and spent three hours in the reading room with Karis, and Cael was allowed to sit at the window and listen as long as he did not speak.

They did not argue about what to say. That had been settled weeks ago, in eleven pounds four ounces. They argued about the order.

"Text first," said the counsel. She had her steel rule out on the long table and was turning it end over end in her fingers. "It's the strongest. The drafters' list. The seat can't get round a list."

"That's why it should be last." Karis had four slips of paper in front of her and was moving them about like a girl playing at shop. "If you open with the list, the seat spends two hours thinking it's a quarrel about paper. Jent will have given away all the paper before you stand up. He gives it away first; he always does. So start where he can't follow you." She put one slip at the head of the row. "Start with the people. Twenty-two of them, by name. Make the seat sit through every name. Then the preamble, so they hear what the sections were for. Then the shelf. And then the list, last, so the last thing they hear is the thing that isn't there."

The counsel stopped turning the rule. She looked at the four slips.

"From the people to the paper," she said.

"From the people to the paper."

"I'll need to mark my place. Two hours is long for a gallery." The counsel laid the rule on the table, pointing at the window, and turned it a quarter of the way round, and then another quarter, as if she were trying the weight of the idea. "That will do. A turn for each. Anyone who loses the thread can look at the rule."

Karis wrote the four words on a card in her finding hand, one under the other, and put the card in her case for the morning. Then she sat back and rubbed her eyes, and Cael saw that her hands were not steady.

"It won't be enough," she said.

"No," said the counsel. "It will be the best argument that room has heard in a long time, and it won't be enough." She put the rule in her case. "Do it anyway. Somebody reads the minute afterward. They always do."

"That's her," said Lira, behind him, very low.

She was on the attendance bench, close enough to lean forward and say it into his collar, and she said it before Cael had looked toward the evaluation seat at all. He looked. The grey covers were gone from its five chairs, and four district evaluators he had never seen sat upright in four of them, two men and two women, with their files on small lap-desks. The fifth chair stood a little forward of the others. In it sat a broad-backed woman in the registry's grey. Her files were set at an angle he would have known anywhere, never quite square to the desk and never a hair different from the last time: a counter at Greyvane, the east wall of a room on the bluff, the first seat of the Compact's row over the Concourse.

Ilsev did not look up. She was reading.

"They've put the straightest person they own in the middle," Karis murmured on his other side, with her eyes on her own papers. "Nobody's going to look past her at what she's sitting next to."

Behind the evaluation seat, at the records table, the officer with the careful face was writing the time at the head of a leaf. Brom, on the bench behind, leaned forward to Cael's other ear.

"None," he said.

Cael knew what he meant. Brom had counted the man's looks toward the house's table at Greyvane, and at the first sitting here, and he was counting now. None.

The clerk was on his feet before the parties were called, reading a paper into the minute under the heading statements entered: the filer's name and house and Path and rank, the date, the line of receipt, and then the text, in the voice that adds nothing.

I fought him. Your instruments failed him, not the other way around. Classify the instruments.

The hood received it. The clerk laid the sheet on the pile of things received and reached for the next. Eleven seconds.

Cael did not write anything about it in words. On the back of his schedule, under the table, he wrote two numbers one above the other, 44 and 54, the day the Archmarshal had been told the seat was full and the day the best practitioner alive had been laid on a pile. Karis saw them, and looked at him, and nodded once, and went back to her papers.

Everything else that morning he saw only between things. The side-door officer, his cold gone, not needing to ask the last name on his list. Somebody had already copied Caelen Hesk-ward into his door log from the last sitting, so that all he had to write was the enrollee of record, unclassified, which took him nine seconds now that his hand knew the way. Seventeen under Cael's left foot again, the third time, and this time chosen; he could not choose the room, but he could choose where he stood in it. And a slip of paper folded twice that Karis had handed Brom on the ferry, which was in Brom's right inside pocket now, with orders not to be opened until the coach went home. The left pocket was for Velmere, and it had a sealed letter in it.

Jent stopped in the middle of a sentence.

"A record kept under the demonstration provision," he had been saying, "is not a record that this seat could—"

And he stood at the petitioner's table with his empty hands at his sides, in front of forty benches and a hood, and Cael let the read go out across the floor to him while he stood there. It was his oldest habit, older than the band, and in that room it had never once brought him anything. It came back now with the man's weight, settled square on both heels, nothing leaning toward the thing he was deciding or away from it. No want under it at all.

"No," said Jent. "I withdraw that. It overreaches, and it is false. The provision makes a record, and the record can be read; the respondent spent fifty-one minutes at the last sitting reading it in." He turned his head a quarter-inch toward the clerk. "What the petitioner says is smaller. The record is of what the practitioner has done. It isn't, and doesn't pretend to be, a measure of what he is. The petition rests on that difference and on nothing wider. Clerk, take the wider words out of the minute, if you would."

The clerk drew his pen through a line.

Cael found he had lifted his own pencil off the paper and not put it down. Of everything he had seen in that room in three sittings, it was the first thing he had not seen coming.

What Jent had already given away, Cael could read without looking back at his own notes, because the house's counsel had been keeping score of it in the margin of her privileged minute, where he could see it. Three headings stood there in her small capitals, written before the sitting began. EXECUTION. PROVISION. RECORD. Through each of them now ran a single neat line. She had drawn the first in Jent's first minute, when he told the hood the petition had never said the enrollment was wrongly made. The second, a little after, when he called the clause law and took the house's history of it for his own, word for word. The third when he said again, for the minute, that he had never read a better-kept record of an enrollment, and the clerk looked up to ask if that was to go in as spoken, and Jent said, "Every word. I'd decline to soften it if I were asked," and something along the front benches shifted.

Under the three struck headings there was nothing. The counsel had not needed to write what was left, because there was only one thing, and everyone could hear it.

Cael's own notes had what Jent said it was. The registry's confidence in its own evaluations, which the integrity sections were there to protect; Jent had read their first line to show it. If no standard reading, no trust, by that fact and by nothing else, which he had said three times, like a man laying a plank across a ditch and then walking on it. The discretion, whole and undisputed, needing no fault found anywhere first. And then the thing he had just taken back, the overreach, the stop.

Cael sat with it and put it the way Lira would want it on the coach going home, in what happens to people and not in words from a code.

Everything they had spent six weeks fighting about was gone. Whether the clause was law; whether the house's record was honest; whether anybody had done anything wrong. Jent had handed all of it across the floor in his first ten minutes, and it could never be taken back now, because it was in the minute in his own voice. What was left was one question with no paper in it at all: may the registry stand him in a frame? And everyone in the room knew already what the frame would say.

Jent asked for a single word from the seat, cognizable: that this was a question the seat was allowed to pick up. Once it had picked it up, the code already said what came next. A frame. The standard protocol. And the enrollment would live or die by whatever the frame said back.

He gave a page number in the file from Norhold, once, and closed his mouth on it. Karis wrote the page number down and did not look it up; she knew what was on it.

Then he sat, and unscrewed his inkwell, and laid his hands on either side of his clerk's tabbed folder, which he had never once opened.

"I like him," Lira breathed behind Cael, unhappily.

"So do I," said Cael. "That's the trouble with him."

The house's counsel turned her steel rule four times, and each turn did something to the room before anybody in it understood what she had argued.

At the first turn the four district evaluators stopped looking at nothing and began to look at her. At the second, the front benches put their pencils down. At the third, the hood spoke, for the only time that day. At the fourth the rule lay pointing at the platform again, as it had when she rose, and the gallery made the long low sound galleries make when they may not clap.

Karis had slid a card along the table before the counsel stood. NAMES. PREAMBLE. SHELF. TEXT. "She's going from the people to the paper," she had breathed. "Tick them."

It was the names that had made the evaluators look up. Ilsev heard her own read out among them and wrote something small in her file without lifting her head. The counsel read twenty-two of them, one at a time, each with a grade and a house and a day, at the pace at which a person reads names in a room where names matter. The grant at Greyvane and its two renewals on paper, the season's officers under a regional registrar's seal, the tournament's, and three days of the Compact's own senior evaluator on the bluff. At the Archmarshal's name Cael thought the stillness under the hood altered, the way still water alters when something passes under it. It took four minutes. In the quiet he heard a cart's iron tyre grind over the cobbles in the street. More looking, the counsel said when she had finished, than most practitioners get in a working life; and all of it done by people who could see, sealed and minuted, across three years. She turned the rule. Tick.

It was Karis's count that made the pencils go down. Cael felt her go still beside him as the counsel gave it: seven times in the registry's whole record the integrity sections had been turned on a person, every one of the seven for something the person had done; eighty-four times on things; and not once on what a person was. Only after the count did the counsel lay her papers face down and read the room the preamble, ninety seconds of plain old words, so that the benches heard what the sections had been written for after they had heard what they had been used for. The testing of instruments. Frames, stations, records, protocols. So that the registry might know which of them it could trust.

"Only that nobody ever has," the counsel said then, without a pause, and Cael understood from her answer what the hood had asked: whether the sections could never lawfully reach a practitioner, or only had never been made to. "That's enough. In all the years these sections have stood, this seat is asked to go first, and turn them on a person for what he is. A seat that's asked to go first deserves to hear it in plain words. The petition never used them."

Jent rose to say the petitioner had never called the use an ordinary one, and was content for the minute to say it was new. The counsel said it after him, word for word, and this once, the only time all morning, she said it over her shoulder to the benches. Third turn. Tick.

Cael missed the shelf. Ilsev had turned a leaf in her file just then and looked, for the first time all morning, at the house's table, at him, for perhaps a breath; and by the time he had looked back to the counsel the rule had turned again and Karis had already ticked the line. Later, on the coach, he would have to ask Karis which rulings had been on it.

And last, because the whole case ended in something that was not there, the drafters' list. She took up the directive that had standardized the code and turned to the schedule at its back where its drafters had listed every older provision they meant to cancel, and walked the hood down it slowly, item by item. At the bottom she stopped. They had been careful men, she said. They had listed everything they meant to end. The assay clause was not on their list. Care only runs one way.

Twice Karis passed a card forward to her, and Cael, who could never help reading upside down, read both: a page number corrected, which the counsel used in her next sentence without a hitch; and Leave the fifth point. Don't need it. The counsel turned that one face down.

She finished with no flourish at all.

"The petition asks this seat to measure a man with the one instrument that has never once been able to see him, and to call that measuring. Twenty-two officers who could see him have told you what they saw. You have their names. Ask them."

She gave the rule its last quarter turn, and sat.

Ilsev was standing.

The hood had read the ruling and the room had not yet worked out what it had heard, and in that gap Ilsev rose from the middle chair and asked leave, and had it, and did not open her files.

Cael heard the hood's answer before he understood her question. Its keeping to protocol. Not its result. Nor that. Ilsev had asked what her seat was there to do, and whether that included deciding if the standard protocol could read this practitioner at all, and the seat had said no to the second. Now she was asking that its words be minuted exactly as spoken, so that nobody could stretch her chair afterward to cover the question. The clerk wrote. Ilsev sat, and wrote the same words into her own file in her own hand, and set the file back at its old angle.

"She's fencing her chair," Karis whispered. "So they can't say later she sat on it."

A chair whose only work was to watch how a re-evaluation was carried out. Then there was going to be one to watch.

Cael went back to the ruling and made himself hear it again in his head. The hood had read it from its single leaf, in the same unhurried voice it had used for its one question; only now he heard it the other way about, from what the house had kept to what it had lost.

The house has observed its charter in every particular. Its record is entire, and stands untouched. The clause beneath the enrollment is in force; the standardizing directive did not reach it. The enrollment was made lawfully, and the seat so finds.

The correspondent's hat had gone onto the floor of the second bench just there, when he half rose to be first to the doors and knocked it off his own knee; Lira had caught Cael's sleeve; and the hood had read straight on, its voice and speed unchanged.

Argument on the petition to compel the enrollee's re-evaluation under the standard Arbiter protocol is set down for the sittings that remain, and the seat will rule on it before the academic year closes. The matter proceeds in full: how far the integrity sections reach a practitioner is for the registry to determine, and the seat determines that they reach this one far enough to be heard. On the question raised, the seat may take it up.

Karis's hands had gone flat on the table, and stayed there.

Cael made himself say it the coach way, plainly, so that he would have it straight. What they had won, they had for good: no seat would ever again argue whether the clause was law or whether the house's paper was honest; that was settled under seal, in the minute, forever. What they had not won was the only thing that could still reach him. The sittings that were left would argue a single question, whether to stand him in a frame. And nobody in the room, not Jent, not Ilsev, not the four evaluators, not the hood, could pretend not to know what the frame would say.

Withrow bowed to the platform at the registry's depth when the hood rose. Jent did not smile or gather his papers or once look across the floor.

In the passage behind the selling floor, while the porters brought the cases down, Lira caught his sleeve again. She had lost the thread twice from the attendance bench.

"So we won?"

"Every point."

"And he's going in a frame."

"Probably."

She stood with that in the fleece smell of the old sample passage. "Then it's like a bout," she said slowly, "where the judges give you every exchange and write down you won every one, and then tell you the bout goes on anyway, under rules they'll pick later." She let go of his sleeve. "That's both. That's what she wrote on the slip, isn't it."

"I think so."

"I hate it," said Lira, with deep satisfaction at having understood it, and went to help Brom with the second case.

Withrow came through the passage a moment later, pulling on her gloves, on her way to her carriage. She did not stop. As she passed Cael she said, without turning her head, "Sit up straight in the coach. The town watches it," which was what she had said to him on the evening of the charter folder, and went on out to the steps.

Through the far doorway Cael could see the records table. The officer with the careful face had stayed at it. He was squaring the minute-book to the table's edge with both hands, and then, when it was square, squaring it again.

Brom unfolded the slip at the first milestone past the town and held it up so that they could all read it.

One word, in Karis's hand. Both.

Karis was looking out of the window at the river, and did not look round.

Then for a while everybody talked about the steps at once, and nobody agreed on what had happened first.

Brom said the first thing he remembered was the bruise: something had hit him hard on the left hip on the second step, and when he looked down there was a boy's satchel buckle going away from him round the corner by the corn chandler's, and a voice saying sorry over its shoulder. He had not seen the boy's face. He rubbed the hip now, thoughtfully, as if the bruise might tell him more.

Cael asked Karis what the shelf had established. "The clause survived five challenges," she said. "Greyvane was the newest."

Karis said Jent had stopped by her, not the counsel.

"He said, 'Advocate. The ninety-one. Did you count them yourself?'" She was still looking at the river. "I said every one. He said, 'I thought so,' and put on his hat, and walked off up the street as if he were going home to his dinner."

"He'll give more away next time," said the counsel from her corner, writing. "Giving things away is how that man walks forward." She wrote one line more, and Cael read it upside down: Valid: held. To proceed: held. Both. She closed the minute-book on it.

The river went by. Lira kept one hand on the closed drill-book and never lifted its cover. Brom put the slip back in his right inside pocket and left his hand over it.

At the ferry the coach waited its turn on the landing, and Cael looked out at the two grey coats who stood there as they always stood, changing on the bell. One of them was not looking at the coach's door or at the faces in its windows. He was looking at the luggage rail on the roof, where the house's two document cases were strapped, the way a clerk looks at a line he means to copy.

Nobody in the coach said anything about it. All of them had seen it.

The ferry took them across. On the far landing, while the coach was hauled up the ramp, Karis turned from the window at last.

"We won every point that can be won on paper."

Brom took the time he always took. "And?"

"And it's proceeding."

Cael set the night's entry in his head as the wheels found the road. It came out at one line, and he did not try to make it longer.

Part of me is still keeping score. The rest of me has started counting doors.

Seln had not opened his eyes since the town. He did not open them now. When he spoke, it was to the whole coach, and not loudly.

"Now you understand the file I've been reading my whole career."

Chapter 21 — The Landing

"You buying a wagon," said the carter, "or selling one?"

Lira had both hands in the bottom of a crate of oiled springs, counting them by feel, and she did not take them out. "Neither. I'm carrying springs up a hill for a man who thinks I've got nothing better to do."

"Have you?"

"Not this morning."

The carter laughed, which was what she had wanted. She was a broad woman with a man's hat and a leather apron gone black at the knees, and her wagon stood third in the line for the ferry with its canvas laced down and its two horses asleep on their feet. Wool going west to Ostrand's market, she had said, and salt coming back from somewhere east of it. Lira had asked her nothing about the road at all. She had asked about the horses, because they were good horses and because a woman who loved her horses would talk about them to anyone with sense enough to admire them.

So it was the carter who had brought up the road, and that was the point.

It was the second of three, and she had built all three the way Rooke had taught her to build a bout against a builder: one look at each corner, and never the same corner twice.

On a floor, the obvious attack taught the other fighter where to wait. The grey coats had made the landing feel like a floor. Lira had learned to let useful talk arrive sideways, then keep her arithmetic for the climb home.

The first had been an old man with a mule team, three days before. Rooke really had wanted the new frame cord, and the river barge really had brought it down, and she really had been the only one in the program with a free hour on a Second-day morning. She had carried his manifest for him from the barge to his cart while he complained about the mules, and she had asked him, idly, what all the stamps on it were for.

He had shown her. Every station on the east road put its mark on a carter's paper as he passed, he said, and you could read a man's whole journey off the back of his sheet, if you cared to. Some fools carried a fresh sheet and some carried their old one till it fell apart, and he was the second kind. He had turned it over to show her. Stamps in four colors of ink, overlapping, faded, and then, at the very edge of the paper, a gap.

"That's the last one," he had said, with his thumb on it. "Past there nobody stamps anything. You don't even know you've gone by it, half the time. You only find out when you look for the next mark and there isn't one."

"Do you go past?"

"Every trip. There's money out there." He had folded the sheet into his coat. "And nobody with a book."

The grey coats had been on the landing that morning, both of them, the older pair the house had been watching since the start of the year. They had looked at her once as she came down the hill with tape round her wrists and a coil of cord over one shoulder, and then they had looked away again, at the road up to the gate, where the person they were paid to watch was not coming down. She was the program's Wind. She was nobody's subject.

She had been insulted by that for the whole of the walk back. She had been glad of it by the time she reached the gate.

The woman with the good horses had finished laughing and was looking at her sidelong.

"You're from up top," she said. "The fighting school."

"The academy."

"Same thing with a longer word." The carter scratched the near horse under its jaw. "My girl wanted to go there. Wanted to fight. Turned out she's a Mire, and the station said a Mire's no good to a fighting school unless she's rich, so she drives the second wagon now and she's better at it than I am." She did not seem sorry about any of it. "What do you do up there?"

"Wind."

"Any good?"

"I'm getting better," said Lira, which was true, and which she had never once in her life said out loud to a stranger before this year.

The ferry had started back across, a long flat shape on the brown water with a cart on it and a man at the rope. The woman watched it come. Lira asked her, then, the one thing she had come to ask, which was how long the fords stayed passable east of Ostrand when the river was up. She asked it as if a wagon she had never mentioned might one day need to know.

The answer took a while, and was very good. Two fords, the woman said, and then a long climb, and then a ford you could walk across most of the year if you didn't mind your boots. Four days to the last station if you were loaded. Three if you weren't, or if you were in a hurry and didn't love your horses. She told her which waystation had a well that went bad and which keeper would charge you twice for hay, and Lira said huh in the right places and remembered every word.

"And past the last station?"

The woman shrugged. "Same road. Worse. Quieter." She clicked her tongue at the horses as the ferry bumped in. "Nobody wants to see your card. Nobody's got a book to write you in."

That was twice now. Nobody with a book. Lira did not let her face do anything about it.

"Good springs," said the carter, nodding at the crate, and went to lead her horses down.

The third was the one she kept turning over afterward.

He was young, not much older than Brom, with a new wagon and a quiet way of standing beside it, and she found him on the First-day in the slack hour before noon, when the ferryman ate his bread and the line did not move. She had come down with a parcel of the Stone's letters for the river post and a list of tape for the chandler, and both errands were true, and she did them first.

Then she sat on the landing wall beside his wheel and asked him where the Line was.

She asked it straight, because this one was the corner she had saved for last, and she had decided on the walk down that a straight question would sound the least like a plan. Everybody on the river had heard of the Registry Line. It came up at inn tables the way the end of the world came up, as a joke and not a joke. A girl from up top asking where it really was would sound like a girl who had heard it at a table.

He told her exactly. That surprised her. He knew the last station by its shape, a low stone building with a frame-house behind it and a sigil cut over the door. He knew how far it stood past the last chartered waystation, and which side of the road, and what the ground looked like after it, which was the same as the ground before it.

"There's no fence," he said. "No post. Nothing. You'd walk past it if nobody told you."

"Do you go past?"

"No."

He said it to the near horse's ears and not to her, quite pleasantly, and she waited, the way you wait in a bout for a fighter to finish a step he has started. He did not finish it.

"Why not?"

"I turn there," he said.

He looked at the river. He did not look unfriendly, or frightened, or sorry he had told her the rest. He just stood beside his new wagon as if there were a wall across the road at that spot that only he could see, and she understood that she could ask him again and he would say the same three words again, in the same voice, as many times as she liked.

She did not ask him again. She thanked him for the road and took her tape up the hill.

She did the sum on the bluff road, at the second switchback, where the wall hid her from the landing and the gate could not see her yet.

Four days to the last station, loaded. Three if light. Stamps on a sheet as far as the station, and then a gap at the paper's edge. Two people out of three who went past the gap every trip and made money doing it. Nobody with a book, twice, from two people who had never met. And a young man with a good wagon who turned at the gap and would not say why, which was its own kind of fact. She did not know what it meant. She only knew that if she left it off the sheet because it spoiled the sum, she would be doing exactly what she hated every registry clerk for doing.

So it went on the sheet.

She stood with her back against the warm wall and looked up at the gate.

Up there, pinned to the east hall door in Rooke's square capitals, was a card with her name on it for the program's first road meet. Rooke had crossed out its date a week ago and chalked another eight days later, when the confluence's stewards wrote that the meet was put back for repairs to their hall; she had minded for an afternoon and then been glad of the eight days. Up there was a red drill-book with a figure in it that was hers, and a broad patient man from the river academy who had written to ask whether he might come and teach her, after she beat him. Up there was a word she had never had before this year, and had to learn to say: program. Somebody had built a ladder, and leaned it against a wall, and put her name at the foot of it.

And here she was at the second switchback with a road east in her head, priced to the day.

She had always wanted to leave rooms on her own feet. That was the whole of it, if she was honest, and she was trying to be honest this year. At Fenmark she had been walked out of one. In the year after it she had stood outside guild doors waiting to be let in. She had sworn to herself, on the steps of a station that had a correct form with her name on it, that the next time she left anywhere she would do the deciding.

She had not thought, when she swore it, that the next room might be one she loved.

In the morning she wrote the note on the residence board in her large capitals, under Ephram's grievance hours and above somebody's lost scarf. Numbers, not names. Everybody on that board who mattered would know whose five it was.

Cael read it on the Third-day morning on his way to the wing.

SMALL ROOM, FIFTH-DAY, AFTER SUPPER, FIVE.

He stopped and read it twice. Four of the five were a habit by now. The fifth was not a habit; the fifth was a man who sat at the middle of the bench and was never once asked to come anywhere, and came. Lira had asked him. She had asked him by not naming anybody, so that he could read the board and choose, the way the rest of them chose. That was Lira. She could be as subtle as a dropped crate, until it mattered, and then she could be subtler than anybody he knew.

At the wing's counter the morning queue was short. Seln was at the copying table behind it with a ledger open and a pen in his hand, filing the overnight returns, and he did not look up when Cael came round the end of the counter with a form he did not need.

"The board," said Cael.

"I've read it."

"Will you come?"

Seln turned a leaf. "The office keeps the hours it keeps." That was yes. Cael had learned to hear it.

He filled in the form, slowly, because he had come for something else and they both knew it, and he was halfway down the second side when Seln spoke again, to the ledger.

"Five drawers," Seln said. "Full. Shut."

Cael's pen stopped.

"Since when?"

"The last went in two days ago." Seln wrote a figure in the margin and blotted it. "The post knows before anybody. A district office that's finished walking its fences stops sending queries and starts sending acknowledgments. The seals change color." He turned another leaf. "They've had their nine weeks, near enough. They didn't need all of them."

Five offices. The house's own counter, the district seat, the Ternhall archive, a provincial registry that kept the Velmere estate's file, and a provincial registry at the far end of the country where an old man kept a shop. Each with its drawer. Each drawer full of true lines about who would mind what. All five indexed under one name and closed, and now nobody was walking anywhere. They were waiting.

Cael did not ask how Seln knew what color a district office's seal turned when its clerk was finished. He finished the form and handed it over the counter, and Seln took it and stamped it without reading it, which he had never once done before, and put it on the pile.

Lira was on the north wall at dusk, where she usually was when she had something she was not saying. She had her elbows on the coping and an apple in one hand, and she did not offer him the other half of it, which was how he knew.

"Fifth-day," she said, before he had asked anything.

"I didn't ask."

"You were going to." She bit the apple. Down in the valley the two coats at the foot of the road were changing on the bell, one walking up from the town and one walking down to it, and they passed each other on the bend without a word, as they always did. "It's not a secret. It's a question. I want to ask it once, properly, with everybody in the room, and not in bits on a wall to whoever happens to come up the stair."

"All right."

She looked at him sidelong. "You're not going to try to guess."

"I can guess."

"I know you can. Don't." She turned the apple round in her fingers. "Rooke's put the meet back on the door. Eight days on. Their hall wants mending, they say, and they won't say where." She said it as if she were changing the subject, and they both knew she was not. "Eight more days of lamps. I'll be so good under lamps by then I won't remember what a window's for."

"You'll remember."

"Probably." She was quiet a while. The light went off the river below them, one bend at a time. "Does it cost you much? The band. In wing three. Being twenty-two and two-thirds in front of everybody when you're not."

Nobody had asked him that before. Not in a year of it. Karis counted his figures, and Ephram charted them, and Seln had once told him across a table that they were too tidy, but nobody had asked what it cost to make them.

"Every bout," he said. "Not much each time. It adds up."

"Like a toll."

"Like a toll."

She nodded, as if he had confirmed a figure she already had in her book, and finished the apple, and threw the core over the wall into the dark, where it would roll halfway down the bluff and feed some bird in the morning.

"Fifth-day," she said again, and went in.

Cael was first down the dairy step on the Fifth-day, and Lira was already there.

She had the lamp on the table and a stub of the porter's chalk in her fingers, and she was writing on the slate shelf along the back wall, where the old dairy had once stood its cream to cool. She did not turn round. She wrote a column, short, in capitals, and stood back from it, and rubbed one figure out with the side of her hand and wrote it again.

4 LOADED. 3 LIGHT. STAMPS STOP. 2 GO ON. 1 TURNS.

He read it twice and did not ask. She had said Fifth-day.

He leaned on the shelf to read it and felt the cold of the slate come through his sleeve. He had been down here once before, in his first year, hunting a lost boot, and all he remembered of the place was that cold, and the way the slate had taken his voice when he called up the step and handed it back to him smaller.

Brom came down the passage with the common room's one good chair on his shoulder.

He had to turn sideways at the newel post to get the legs by. Lira looked round at last.

"Is that for you?"

"It's for the council."

"There's a bench."

"There is," said Brom, and put the chair at the head of the table, and sat in it. Something clinked in its seat as he did; he reached under himself and brought out a small spirit kettle and set it on the shelf beside Lira's chalk, without comment.

Karis came in with nothing under her arm. That was so unusual that Cael looked twice. She had one sheet of paper, folded long, in her sleeve, and she sat down at the table's far end and did not take it out.

When Cael looked along the bench again, Seln was on it. He was at its middle, with his hands folded and nothing in front of him, and Cael had not heard the step or the door.

"Right," said Lira.

She came and sat on the table's corner, which was not allowed anywhere in the house, and looked at the four of them and then at the fifth.

"Tell me why we're still answering them."

Nobody answered. She had not expected anybody to.

"I'm not asking about the filings. I know what Karis does is the best paper this house has ever sent down the hill. I know we win, every sitting." She put the chalk down on the table. "And I know that a fortnight ago a hood read lawful and proceeding into the minute in one breath, and went on to the next item. Every time we win, it goes on. So I'm putting it on the table. Once. Properly, with everybody here. Then it's been asked, and nobody can say afterward that it wasn't."

"What's that?" said Brom, and nodded at the shelf.

"The road east. Read it after."

Cael had already worked most of it out from the chalk. Somebody who drove that road for a living had told her the days; somebody had told her where a thing stopped; three somebodies, by the strokes at the bottom. She had been to the ferry landing more than once this week, then, on errands he had thought were Rooke's, and had come back up the hill with a sum and kept it to herself.

Karis leaned over and tapped the chalk at the bottom of the column, under 1 TURNS, without smudging it.

"You left that one on," she said.

"I'm not rubbing a man out because he spoils the sum."

Karis did not stand to answer. She took the folded sheet out of her sleeve and held it out down the table, not to Cael, not to Lira, but to Brom.
