"I wasn't wrong, then," the assistant had said.

"You were wrong to leave it off the list," said Karis. "You were right to tell me why. Do the second thing every time and I'll forgive you the first." And she had sent the girl back down to the index for the rest of the afternoon with a new task, and had sat on alone with the green volume open at the struck heading until the lamps were lit.

The house's counsel came up the hill the following Second-day, and Karis put the green volume in front of her without a word, open at the page. The counsel laid her steel rule along the second paragraph first, before she had read the first at all, and kept it there.

"Old law is an old floor," she said. "It'll take your weight once. After that, everyone in the room knows exactly where you stood, and the other side has had a night to find the soft board." She lifted the rule and set it under the first paragraph instead. "So you get one question out of this, and you get it once. And the second paragraph we leave exactly where it is. We do not cite it. We do not mention it. Nobody in this house so much as looks at it in the hearing of anyone from Ostrand." She looked at Karis over the book. "Until the end."

So the card had stayed in the back of Karis's wallet through three sittings: the first, the exhibits, and the preliminary with its two-word ruling. She took it out at night and changed it and put it back. Cael had seen her change one word on it four times on a coach above the water meadows. He had not been allowed to read it, and he had not asked.

On the morning of the fourth sitting, the young officer at the wool exchange's side door had a problem.

He had the ruled board under his arm and the door log open on the stand, as he had had it at every sitting since the first. He wrote Cael's line without needing to look: Caelen Hesk-ward, and in the standing column the enrollee of record, unclassified, nine seconds. He wrote the house's counsel by her name. Then he came to Karis, and stopped, with his pen over the standing column, and looked at a letter pinned to the top of his board.

"The seat has a request from the respondent's counsel," he said, a little helplessly. "To enter this person under a title. I have to look up how it's spelled."

He looked it up. There was a printed slip on the board with it on, in the seat's type, which somebody at the seat had been made to find the night before. He copied it into the log letter by letter, with his tongue between his teeth like the fire-watch boy at his slate.

K. Dellenmoor. Advocate of record for the respondent, under the hearing provision.

Karis watched him write it. Cael watched Karis. Her face did not do anything that the officer would have noticed, but she watched every letter go down, and when he blotted it she let out a breath that Cael heard and the officer did not.

Inside, the long room smelled of lanolin and hot lamp oil, as it always did. The benches were fuller than at the third sitting. Cael crossed lot nine, lot ten, lot eleven, and sat down at the respondent's table with seventeen under his left foot, where he always sat now. Ilsev was in the middle chair of the evaluation seat with her files on her lap-desk at their angle and her four district evaluators upright around her. At the records table behind her, at the junior chair, the officer with the careful face had the receipt book open and his pen ready and his eyes on the leaf.

The hood came in, and sat, and the clerk read the designation.

The production order went first, because the seat had ordered it.

Bracken carried the records up to the clerk's table himself. They were in the house's own boards, as Withrow had said they would be: one volume, half the thickness of a man's hand, bound in the house's dark cloth with the house's seal pressed into the front cover and a contents leaf inside it in the clerk's best copperplate. Every wing-three bout of the year, in order, with its date, its three cards, its figure. Twenty-three and a third. Twenty-two and two-thirds. The band, written out in full, as it had been built to be written.

The clerk received it and passed it back to the junior chair to be entered. The officer with the careful face took it, and looked at it, and for a moment did not open it; he only looked at the binding, at the house's seal on the cloth. Then he wrote the receipt.

Jent, at the petitioner's table, had watched it go past.

"The petitioner notes," he said, when the clerk looked to him, "that it has not before seen a production order answered in boards." He inclined his head a quarter-inch toward Bracken. "The petitioner is obliged to the respondent."

He meant it. That was the thing about Jent that Cael could never get used to. He meant every compliment he had ever paid in that room, and every one of them was true, and not one of them had ever cost him anything.

When the production had been minuted, the house's counsel rose, and left her steel rule lying on the table behind her, pointing at the platform.

Cael saw Karis see it, and put her palms down on the table, one each side of her notebook, and keep them there.

"The respondent's advocate of record," said the counsel, "asks the seat's leave, under the hearing provision, to put one question through counsel to the petitioner's procurator, to be answered on the record."

Nothing happened at the platform for a count of four.

Then the clerk bent to the green volume at his elbow, which was the same edition as the annex's, cracked in the same place, and found the page, and set his finger on it, and passed it up under the hood. The hands under the grey read it without turning a leaf. They passed it back.

"The provision stands," said the hood, in the registrar's voice that could have been anybody's. "The seat permits one question."

The counsel took the card out of her sleeve. She did not read from it. She held it at her side, face in, and said it from memory, and Cael found that he knew it too as she said it, though he had never once been allowed to read it; he knew it the way you know a tune that has been coming through a wall at you for weeks.

"What evidence, if any, would defeat the petition?"

Cael was watching Ilsev, because he had watched her all morning, so he saw it there first.

She had not lifted her head since the seat opened. Through the production, through the receipt, through Jent's compliment, her pencil had gone steadily along her file and her eyes had stayed on the page. Now the pencil stopped. Her head came up. She looked across the floor at the petitioner's table, and kept looking at it, and did not look down again.

At the clerk's table the clerk's pen had stopped too, halfway through a word.

And on the benches nobody moved at all. That was how Cael knew they had understood. Forty benches of people, most of whom wrote things down for their living, correspondents and clerks and junior officers from three districts with their boards on their knees; and in the whole long room, for the space of a breath, not one pencil moving anywhere.

Only one person in the room was writing. At the junior chair behind Ilsev, the officer with the careful face had dipped his pen and was setting down the time.

Jent was on his feet before the breath was finished.

He answered across the floor, not to the seat and not to the counsel but to the young woman at the respondent's table with her palms down beside her notebook. He answered in the voice he kept for everything, the voice of a man reading out the times of the coaches.

"None, Advocate. The petition doesn't turn on evidence. It turns on discretion."

He sat. He unhooked his spectacles from their black cord, folded them, and laid them on the table in front of him.

The clerk's pen started again. Cael heard it scratch across the leaf, word by word, at its ordinary speed, putting the sentence into the minute, where it would stay.

He had a schedule on his knee with notes all down the back of it, and he looked at them now because he could not look at anything else.

They were from the dairy. He had written them on the way down in the coach that morning, out of habit, to have the argument by him in case anybody in that room should ever ask him for it: Denvash and the brass plate; Vell's ledger; the Greyvane hearing; the grant and two renewals on paper; the inspection; the clause at Norhold; Umber's no number goes here. His receipts. He had laid them out a week ago, in order, at full strength, and Karis had called them an induction and he had not had an answer for her.

He read them over now. Every one of them was a piece of paper that proved something.

That was what paper was. That was all paper had ever been, in his life: a thing somebody wrote down that could afterward be shown. A finding was evidence. A stamp was evidence. A ledger was evidence, and an honest referral was evidence, and a true book on a counter was the best evidence there was. He had carried them into that dairy as a man carries his tools into a workshop, and set them out on the bench, and said: look, these have never failed me.

And the petitioner's own procurator had just told the seat, on the record, in one breath, that evidence was not what this was about.

He had brought receipts to a room that did not take them.

He wrote that on the back of the schedule, under the dairy notes, very small. Then he sat and looked at it while the clerk's pen went on across the floor.

Beside him Karis had not opened her notebook. Her pen lay on the table, capped, between her two hands. She did not write anything at all for the rest of the sitting. Cael understood that later, when he saw what she did instead; at the time he only saw her sitting very still while the seat set down its next date, and the hood rose a little after the eleventh bell, and the long room began to empty.

On the four steps outside, in the noise of the market street, Karis stopped and stood with the wallet against her chest.

"Did you hear what he called me?" she said.

She said it to Cael, not to the counsel. He had heard. Everybody in the room had heard.

"Advocate."

"He's called me that since the conference. In the counting room upstairs. Advocate." She turned the wallet a little in her arms. "I let him, because nobody had ever called me anything for the work before, only for where I sat. I thought it was one of his compliments. He gives those away." She looked up at the wool exchange's great double door. "This morning a clerk wrote it in a door log with his tongue between his teeth, and the seat permitted it, and he said it into the minute. It's a title now. It's on the record." She was quiet a moment. "It was true today. I'd like to remember that it was true for one day, whatever happens."

"It'll be true again," said the counsel, beside her. She did not explain that. She had her hands in her coat pockets and her eyes on the street. "Keep the other paragraph where it is, Advocate. In your pocket, not your mouth."

Jent came down the steps behind them at his ordinary pace, with his clerk and his tabbed folder. At the bottom he stopped, and put his hat on, and touched its brim to Karis.

"A good question, Advocate," he said. "I'd have asked it myself, in your chair."

Then he went off up the market street toward the wharf inn, at a walk, a man going to his luncheon.

Karis watched him go until he turned the corner.

"He wasn't even careful," she said.

She said it quietly, almost to herself, and Cael heard what was under it, because he had felt the same thing at the respondent's table with the schedule on his knee. Every other person in that room had been careful all year. The house's counsel weighed every sentence on her steel rule. Bracken read every seal twice. Withrow had ordered the production answered in the house's own boards. Karis herself had changed one word on one card four times. And the man on the other side of the floor had been asked the one question in the whole proceeding that ought to have made him careful, and he had answered it the way you answer a child who asks you which way is north.

Because for him it was as simple as that. There was nothing to be careful of.

In the coach going home, Karis took the plain card out of her wallet, the one with her question on it, the word changed four times. Under the question, in her finding hand, she wrote Jent's answer, word for word. She dated it. Then she opened her notebook and slid the card inside its front cover, in among the things she kept there: the fielding clause in her finding hand, the squad rule, the charter's slip, and the stratum note with its question mark still waiting. She shut the book on all of them.

The house's counsel came up the hill with them that afternoon instead of taking her chaise home. She wanted to go through the morning's minute with Karis in the annex, line by line, while it was fresh, and to check the production against the receipt the junior chair had written, and she said she trusted her memory of neither past a night's sleep. Bracken had the guest room over the records hall made up for her.

She was still there, asleep, when the riders came.

The lodge-man shut his road window.

Cael saw it from the covered walk, a little after the second bell on the Sixth-day morning, on his way across to the wing. It was a small thing. In two years he had never once seen that window shut in daylight. The lodge-man sat behind it on his high stool from the first bell to the last, with his tea and the bluff road in front of him, and talked to anybody who came up it. Now the shutter came across the glass from the inside, and a moment later the lodge door opened, and the lodge-man stood in it without his hat.

He did not go anywhere. He braced his bad knee against the jamb and said something short over his shoulder, and his boy came out past him at a run.

The boy ran straight across the outer court and round the corner of the lecture range toward the records hall, as fast as his legs would take him, without calling out to anybody and without looking back.

Cael looked at the gate.

There were four horses under the arch. Good ones. Four riders in plain travelling grey, without livery or badge or anybody's colors, were getting down.

He did not go to the wing. He went to the wall stair and up it.

It came out at the top onto a short stone walk along the gatehouse, over the arch, where the house had once hung its bell. The bell was long gone, but its frame was still there: two great uprights of black oak and a crossbeam, gone silver where the weather had got into it, with a waist-high parapet in front of them on the court side. Cael put his back to the nearer upright and sank down until he was sitting on his heels with his shoulders against the wood. From the court below, the frame's timbers would hide everything of him but the top of his head, and the top of a head on a gatehouse is only a stone among stones.

From there he could see the whole of the outer court.

It was flagged in old grey stone, fifty feet from the gate to the covered walk and seventy from the lecture range to the stables, and every flag in it sloped a little toward the gutters at its edges, to carry off the rain. Every flag but the ones in the middle. There the old farm's well had been capped, when the house was built, with a single great slab, and the flags round the slab had been laid dead level. On a wet morning you could feel it underfoot as you crossed: slope, then flat, then slope again. Cael had crossed it a thousand times.

The riders were dismounting the way people dismount who have stood in a great many yards. Three of them did it together without looking at one another. The fourth did it last.

She was a woman, compact and unhurried, of no age he could have put a figure to, in the same plain grey as the rest. She took the rein over her horse's head and led it three paces in from the arch, and stopped, and let the rein hang slack, and did not move again.

He read her. He did it without deciding to; it was the oldest habit he had. He let the read go out across the court to her, the way he let it go out across a floor before a bout, and it came back with her weight. Settled. Even. Square on both feet, with nothing in it leaning anywhere at all.

That was the first time he read her, and it gave him nothing.

Withrow came round the corner of the lecture range at the pace she used for every corridor in her house, with Bracken a half-step behind her and the house's counsel a step behind him, buttoning her coat, with her hair not quite pinned.

She did not hurry across the court. She walked to the lodge and stopped beside the lodge-man in his doorway, and before she said a word to anybody, she lifted her eyes to the board on the lodge wall.

The lodge-man had painted it himself in white on black, years before Bracken came to the hill, and he went over the letters once a year with a fine brush. CARTS — ROUND BY THE LANE. CALLERS — SIGN AND WAIT. POST — THE BAG ON THE HOOK. ANYTHING SEALED — FETCH THE REGISTRAR. Cael watched Withrow find the last line with her eyes and stop on it. The lodge-man had done exactly what his board said. Anything sealed had come up the road, and he had sent his boy for the registrar, and he had shut his window so that he could stand in his own door and see the whole of it.

She gave the lodge-man a small nod, the kind she gave her senior staff, and he stood up straighter against his jamb.

"You have something for this house," she said to the lead rider.

He was a man of forty or so, weathered, with an attentive face that gave nothing away and missed nothing either. He held out a folded paper with a seal on it.

"For the Chancellor. And for the enrollee of record."

"My registrar will take it from you," said Withrow, "when you have read it out." She did not put out her hand. "All of it, please, aloud, from the top. My lodge-man has kept this gate longer than I have kept this house, and in all that time he has never once heard one read."

The rider looked at her for a moment. Then he looked at the lodge-man. Then he opened the paper, and held it at his chest, and read it out in a level voice that went off the walls of the court and came back off them, so that Cael heard every word of it twice.

In the matter of Caelen Hesk-ward.

To the Chancellor of the chartered academy at Halcenvane, and to the enrollee of record therein named. The registry, in support of the proceedings presently convened at the seat at Ostrand, directs the attendance of the said enrollee at the registry facility at the district seat for pre-evaluation assessment, transport and escort provided, effective on presentation. The academy is directed to produce the enrollee to the bearers of this order. Given under the Compact's hand.

Cael counted it as it came back off the walls. Eighty-one words, from the name to the hand.

He sat on his heels behind the bell-frame and heard the name at the top of it go round the court. Caelen Hesk-ward. Nobody who knew him had ever said it to his face. It was the name the registry kept for him, the way a shop keeps a number on a parcel, and here it was coming up off the flags of his own gate in a stranger's voice, with an order underneath it. Attendance. Transport and escort provided. Produce the enrollee. And at the bottom, the five words he had first read on the morning of the eighth day at the foot of a challenge's first page, and had read at the foot of every registry instrument since, and had never heard spoken by anybody at all.

"Under whose seal?" said Bracken.

The rider gave him the paper.

Bracken did not look at the seal first. He looked at the paper. He weighed it on his palm as if it were a letter he was going to charge postage on, and ran his forefinger once along the fold, and held the edge up to his eye to see the deckle. Registry stock came from two mills, Cael knew, because Bracken had once told him so at the counter with enormous pleasure, and Bracken could tell the two apart by their edges.

Then the glass came out of his waistcoat pocket, the smallest of his three, and he held it over the seal without moving.

Then he did a thing Cael had never seen him do. He shut his eyes and laid the ball of his thumb on the impression and moved it slowly round the seal, once, the way a blind reader reads raised letters with a fingertip.

Four riders, a chancellor, the house's counsel with her hair coming down, the lodge-man in his doorway, and up on the gatehouse a boy behind a bell-frame, all of them stood and waited while the registrar read a seal with his eyes shut. It took him a minute and forty seconds. Cael counted it. It was a long time to stand still in a court; Bracken had earned every second of it at his counter, and the riders seemed to know that, because none of them shifted.

While he waited, Cael read the fourth rider a second time.

He did not look at her face. Faces were the last thing he read on anybody. He looked at where she stood, and asked the floor about it.

She had come three paces in from the arch. Not two, which would have left her on the sloping stones of the gate's apron, where everyone who came up that road stopped. Not four, which would have put her in the way of the others. Three. And the third pace had set her down square in the middle of the level flags round the capped well, on the one stretch of dead-flat stone in the whole court.

She had found it on arrival, in three steps, without once looking down.

That was the second time, and it gave him one strange thing, and he did not yet know what to do with it.

Bracken opened his eyes and took his thumb off the seal.

"The paper's from the registry's south mill," he said, in the driest of all his counter voices. "The die is cut to the registry's pattern. Both of them are exactly what they say they are." He looked at the seal a moment longer. "The office isn't. Or it isn't one I've ever met. In thirteen years every office that sends paper into this district has sent some of it across my counter, and this one never has."

"Facilities," said the rider. "An office constituted this year, for the proceedings."

"Then the district seat holds whatever constituted it. I'll write today."

"The order is effective on presentation."

"I don't doubt it's been presented." Bracken looked up then, over his spectacles, at the rider and the three behind him. "I don't doubt you, either. But my book has a column for the office that issues an instrument, and I have never yet left that column empty, and I can't write four riders in it." He held the order out toward the rider at the length of his arm, on his open palm, the way he held out a form at his counter that had been filled in on the wrong side.

He did not let go of it.

Chapter 27 — Measure the Door

The lodge-man wrote the hour on the back of his hand.

He did it with the stub of pencil from behind his ear, standing in his own doorway, while the last of the four horses was still going down the bluff road below the gate, because his book was on the counter behind him and he did not want to lose the minute in the turning round. Cael saw him do it from the wall stair, coming down. Then the old man went in, and took the book off the counter, and copied the figure off his hand into it, and licked his thumb and rubbed the hand clean.

By the time Cael reached the lodge door, Bracken was at the counter beside him with his senior clerk, and the house's book was open between them, and Bracken was giving the morning to the book in the order the book would want it.

Withrow had told him how, before she went in. Cael had heard her from the gatehouse. All of it in the book, Registrar. Now the registrar stood with his spectacles on the end of his nose and dictated in an even voice. The senior clerk wrote it in the hand he kept for the enrollment book, and Cael stood in the lodge door and listened to the morning come back to him one ruled line at a time.

Arrived at the second bell. Four, mounted, in travelling grey, no livery. Departed at a quarter before the third.

An order presented, under a seal of the registry's pattern, naming an issuing office unknown to this counter. Read aloud in the court at the Chancellor's request, in full, by the lead rider.

He had sat behind the bell-frame for that. He had counted it as it came back off the walls. Eighty-one words, and his registry name at the top of them.

The Chancellor declined the order pending verification, on four grounds, as follows.

Bracken did not give them in her order. He gave them in the order a registrar would want to find them in a hurry, with the person first, and the clerk numbered them down the margin as they came.

One. The young man named is enrolled here in good standing and is a party before the seat, and he is produced where the code says and when, and not otherwise.

Two. This counter cannot place the office that sealed the order.

Three. Nothing served on this house since the eighth day of the year speaks of moving him anywhere.

Four. The seat's own schedule has no assessment in it.

Cael had heard her give them the other way round, from the schedule up to the young man, so that the last of them landed on him. On the page they began with him. He thought both orders were right, for the different rooms they were said in.

"Next," said Bracken, and stopped, and took his spectacles off.

The clerk waited with the pen lifted.

"An offer was made by the lead rider to the enrollee," said Bracken. "In these words." He gave them exactly. Cael could have given them himself. "The order is addressed to two parties. The second may come with us of his own accord. If he comes voluntarily, nobody here need refuse anybody anything, and we can all be gone before the third bell."

The pen went along the line.

"The offer was spoken upward, toward the gatehouse roof," said Bracken. "There was nobody on the gatehouse roof."

The clerk wrote that too. He did not look at Cael in the doorway, and neither did Bracken.

Gault was in the lodge doorway beside Cael. Nobody had seen him come across the court; he had his case clamped under one arm and a small black notebook in his other hand, and he had evidently been standing there for the last two entries.

"Registrar," he said. "If you would add that the evaluator of record was not told of any assessment proposed for the enrollee. Before it was proposed, or since."

Bracken gave it to the clerk, and the clerk wrote it. Gault opened his own notebook on his forearm and wrote in it too, standing in the doorway, a short line, and closed it on the pencil.

"I have written that down," said Gault, to nobody in particular, and went away across the court toward the Magisters' stair.

Withrow's eyes had stayed on the rider the whole morning. "You are speaking to me, Officer," she had said. "There is nobody else in this court you have any business speaking to. If your office wants something from a student of mine, it writes to me." That was not going in the book. Bracken did not dictate it. It had not been addressed to the record.

The last entry Bracken gave the clerk was the shortest. No refusal in writing was requested. The clerk wrote it and sanded the page.

Withrow had not gone straight in. Cael saw her stop at the lodge door on her way across the court, where the lodge-man stood with the book under his arm and the hour still faintly grey on the back of his hand, and look up once more at the board he had painted.

"Anything sealed, fetch the registrar," she read aloud. "You did, and you shut your window, and you stood where you could see the whole of it." She nodded to him, the nod she gave her senior staff. "Your board did very well this morning. Put a fresh coat on it in the spring, if you would. I should like it to last."

The lodge-man said he would, Chancellor, and stood straighter against his jamb than Cael had ever seen him stand, and did not sit down again on his high stool until she had gone round the corner of the lecture range.

There was nothing in the house's book about the woman.

There was no line in the house's book for her and no reason Bracken should have thought of one. She had said nothing and done nothing and handed nobody anything. Cael stood in the lodge door while the clerk sanded the page, and gave her the lines himself, in his head, because nobody else was going to.

He had read her four times. The first two he already had: three paces in, onto the one level patch in the court. The third time he had asked the court what she could see from there, and the answer had been the arch. The gatehouse was twelve feet deep. From almost anywhere in the court you saw only a slice of the road through it, the left side from the covered walk, the right from the lecture range. There were a few feet of flag from which the whole opening lay open end to end, road and verges and the first bend below the gate. She had stood in them with her back three-quarters to the arch, and never once turned to look.

The fourth time he had drawn lines. One to the arch behind her; one to the lodge door; one into the corner where the covered walk ran through to the quadrangle; one round the end of the lecture range; one into the stable passage, which had never had a door on it and never would. Every line went past her. Three went within a stride of her boots. And her shoulders had been squared, a hand's breadth, to the last of them: the one way out of that court the house itself could not have closed.

And all that while she had laid nothing. He had run the read at her at full depth across forty feet of stone, at the moment the word went up, when anyone standing in a court with a refusal going on in it lets go of a fraction of something. She let go of nothing. It was not hiding; hiding has a grain to it, and he had learned that grain from two years of Seln at a counter. There was simply nothing there. She was a person standing in a court, in exactly the right place.

An hour after the riders had gone he went up to his sill and took out the observation notebook, and went past two years of the Crown yard, eleven Paths and every fighter on the hill, to the first clean leaf at the back. He wrote a heading the notebook had never needed before.

The fourth rider. A woman. Unnamed. Path: not shown.

He did not write down the four times he had read her. He had them already, and the page was for what they meant.

Guess: the whole craft is where she stands. A Shield guards a person. This guards ground, and whatever has to cross it. If she can do anything from where she stands. I never saw her do anything.

Not known: how far she reaches. How fast. What it costs her. Nothing is free, so it costs her something, and I can't see what. A shape and no numbers.

Then he wrote one more line at the bottom, by itself, because there was only one person on the hill who might know.

Query for Seln: what Path holds people?

At noon he took the guess into the refectory and found it waiting for him.

The third-years' long table under the west windows was full from end to end, as it was every noon, elbows touching. There was one place empty at it, and it was the place on Cael's left. Somebody had been going to sit there. Somebody had come to it with a tray, and looked at who was sitting next to it, and found a place somewhere else.

He sat down and looked at the empty place the way he had looked at the court that morning. One spot in a full room where nobody would stand. Every line in the room went round it.

Rooke sat down in it.

He came with a full plate. He put his elbows on the table and began to eat, steadily, and between mouthfuls he talked across the board to the Current girl about hips. Her hips, and Lira's, and the whole program's. He told her the inside of a landing hip was the first thing to go on a planked floor and the last thing anybody thought to strap, and that Lira's had come back quiet after two days and she was to make it three before she believed it.

Behind Cael two first-years at the bread were telling each other that there had been ten riders, with swords. Further along, a boy who had heard it from the urn said the lodge-man had been struck and his window broken. The two second-years nearest had it best and worst: the Chancellor had sent Ostrand away from her gate, and Ostrand would shut the house for it, and one of them had a cousin who knew the date.

Rooke talked about hips through all of it. He talked about hips for a whole meal, to a table of third-years who had never once heard him say more than a sentence about anything, and the rumours went past him on both sides like water past a post.

Ephram put his tray down on Cael's right, halfway through. Then two of the cohort moved up from the far end. Then the rest of them shifted along, without anybody saying a word, until the table was the table again with no gap anywhere in it. "Grievances are Third-day evenings," Ephram said to nobody in particular, reaching for the bread. "I'm not taking any at lunch."

Rooke wiped his plate with his bread and took it away. He had not mentioned the gate once.

Karis had Bracken's middle glass and the clerk's pencil rubbing of the seal on the long table in the records hall, with the fair copy of the order beside them, when Cael came in at dusk. The others were already there. Seln was at the middle of the bench across from the copy, with his hands folded and his cup at his elbow.

Karis did not look up.

"Before anybody says anything about her," she said, "I want the words straight, because they're going to blur if we're not careful, and I'll be the one keeping the notes." She held up one finger. "Ternhall's anchors are mine. Three footholds I plant in a floor, in their order, so that the heat of a contact runs down into the boards and not back up my arm. Ternhall calls the whole frame a lattice." A second finger. "Which has nothing to do with the Lattice Path. That's lines you can't see, strung across a space, that you find by walking into them." She lowered the hand. "And then there's whatever stood in our court this morning. It wasn't either of those. It didn't plant anything and it didn't string anything. I haven't got a word for it."

"Anchor Path," said Seln.

They looked at him. He had not opened his eyes.

"You won't find it on a meet card," he said. "You find it on a posting roll. I've filed from three towns where one of them was billeted, and I never once saw one on a floor. It's rare at any station. The service writes to the family in the week the station enters it, and most of them go, because nobody else has ever written to them about anything. It holds people. That's what the system keeps it for."

"Holds them how?" said Brom.

"I've never stood near enough to one at work to say, and I won't guess." Seln opened his eyes and looked at the copy. "I know where they're posted, and it isn't escort. Escort is for clerks on good horses. One at that grade, standing where she stood, is enforcement." He laid one fingertip on the table beside the order, not touching it. "Whoever wrote that paper is done assessing."

Seln turned his head toward Cael without opening his eyes.

"Her horse," he said. "When she mounted. Did it shift?"

"No."

"Then she's the best they had to spare this morning." Seln faced the copy again. "Nobody keeps a horse like that for escort work."

Cael wrote Anchor Path in the notebook under the morning's page, and under it Karis's three words in her order, and ruled a line beneath them.

Bracken came in at the hall's side door with a sheet in his hand and his pen behind his ear. He had been at his counter since the riders left. He did not sit; he never sat in that room when there were enrollees in it.

"The letter to the district seat," he said, and read it to them; he read aloud everything the house was going to send. The date; the instrument as presented, quoted whole; the issuing office as named; the registrar of this house is unable to place the said office in any register available to him, and respectfully asks that the instrument constituting it be supplied, together with the seal under which that instrument was itself issued. He lowered the sheet. "It goes down with the morning bag. They will answer inside the week, because they must."

Karis opened her notebook near the back and wrote NO NAME. Then she turned to the date a week ahead and entered DISTRICT REPLY, leaving the intervening leaves blank. Brom told her she was scheduling paper she had not seen. "I'm keeping room for it," she said.

Bracken looked at the blank leaves. "Leave me one more leaf after those." He folded the letter once. "The query should stand beside whatever answer it earns." He looked round the table, a little over his spectacles. "It is not much. It is what a true book is for."

He went back out to his counter.

Karis turned the rubbing over and looked at the grey circle of the seal, the registry's pattern standing up white out of the pencil.

"It's a good die," she said. "Somebody cut it properly." She put her palm on it. "The faceless layer has learned to write paper."

She did not go on. She looked at the side door Bracken had gone out by, and then up, at the ceiling, toward the Chancellor's rooms on the floor above, and Cael watched her count something on the two of them and not say what it came to.

It was Brom who stood up.

"Show me," he said, to Cael. "Where she stood."

Brom was already standing in the chalk ring when Cael got up off his knees.

They had come out to the Crown yard with two lanterns and a lump of the porter's chalk. At the yard gate Cael had looked back and found that Seln had come too, unasked, a few steps behind them, with his coat buttoned to the chin and his hands in its pockets. Seln had not come onto the oak. He stood at its edge by the porter's boards, where the year's names stood chalked pale in the lamplight, Ephram's at the head of the Iron column, and watched.

Cael had drawn the outer court at its own size, fifty feet by seventy, paced once by him and once by Brom until they agreed. The arch as two long lines, twelve feet apart. The lodge door in its cheek. The covered walk's corner. The mouth of the lane. The stable passage, with no door drawn across it. In the middle, a square for the capped well and a ring round it for the level flags; and Brom, before the chalk was out of Cael's hand, had walked into the ring three paces from the arch and turned his shoulders a hand's breadth toward the stable passage.

"Here?"

"A little left. There."

Brom moved, and stood. "Now walk out."

Cael walked out. Middle to the arch, and back; middle to the lodge door; to the covered walk's corner; to the lane; to the stable passage; chalking each road on the oak behind him as he went, the way he chalked a fighter's footwork before a bout. Five lines out of one court.

Every one went past Brom. Three went within a stride of him. One went straight through the place he stood, and he had to step aside to let Cael by. The line to the stable passage started almost under his boots.

"Try it," said Brom. "Get out past me. The doorless way."

Cael went from the lodge door's mark toward the stable passage at a walk, and Brom took one step, only one, sideways off the ring, and was standing in the line. Cael went the long way round, by the covered walk's corner, and Brom took one step back, and was in that line too. He had not hurried. He had hardly moved his feet.

"One step," said Brom. "From there it's one step to anywhere you want to go." He looked down at the chalk. "And that's me. I can't hold anything. I'm just a big man standing in the right place."

The long wall threw their voices back late and thin, so that everything said on the oak was said twice, the way the rider's voice had come back off the court that morning. Without agreeing to, they had all three begun to speak low.

Brom paced the drawn arch once, heel to toe, then looked back at the ring.

"They came to measure the door," said Cael.

Brom considered the chalk arch, twelve feet deep, and the open stable passage. After a while he said, "I'd stand there too, if I was holding it. I'd never have found it in three steps."

"What would she do from there?" said Cael. "If somebody walked."

"I don't know."

"Nor do I." Cael looked at the five chalk lines running out from under Brom across the oak. "I don't know how far she reaches. I don't know that she reaches at all. I've drawn where she stood and where everybody else would have to go. It's a floor with nothing on it about the fighter."

"Then that's what it is," said Seln, from the edge.

They both looked round.

"Count what you've got. Five lines and a place to stand. Write those down." He took one hand out of his pocket and moved it a little, at the bare oak round the chalk. "Leave the rest blank, where you'll see it every time you open the page. A blank you can see is worth something. It's the blanks you've forgotten that get people hurt."

Brom stayed where he was a while longer, on the drawn flags with the lanterns at his feet. Then he stepped out of the ring carefully, the way a man steps out of a place he means to remember. They left the chalk for the porter to wash off in the morning, and picked up the lanterns, and went back.

The cup had not moved.

That was what Cael saw first when they came back into the records hall: Seln's cup, at his elbow on the long table, exactly where it had stood when they went out. Karis and Lira were still at the table, Karis copying the evening into her notebook, Lira with her landing leg along the bench and her eyes shut. Seln sat down at the middle of the bench where he had sat before, and did not touch it.

Seln turned his cups. He always had. A quarter-turn when he sat down, a quarter-turn back when he had said what he meant to say, a quarter-turn on the counter when he had finished a cup of the lodge-man's tea. Cael had watched him do it for two years without ever once remarking on it. Tonight the cup had stood at his elbow for a whole evening, through Anchor Path and the rubbing and Bracken's letter, and he had not turned it once.

Cael thought, at first, that the man was tired. It had been a long day for everyone, and Seln was older than any of them and had been up before the bell to do the post-room sort. Cael sat down across from him and put the lantern on the table and said the thing that had been in his head since the oak.

"Is there any way to find out how far she reaches? Without standing in front of her?"

Seln did not answer.

He was not tired. Cael saw that as soon as he had asked. Seln's two hands were on the table, flat, one on each side of the fair copy of the order, close to the paper but not touching it, and his eyes were on the paper, and they had been on it, Cael understood now, since the moment he sat down.

Karis finished her copying and set down her pen. Lira opened her eyes. Brom sat with his elbows on his knees. And Seln went on looking at the order, longer than any of them, with his hands flat and still on either side of it.

"Fifty-one minutes," said Brom, to the floor between his boots. "That clock room at Norhold. And you came out of it with one sentence for us."

He did not say which sentence. He did not need to. Every one of them had carried it home from Norhold and up this hill, and Cael heard it again now in the Archmarshal's dry voice, among forty clocks: Because the people who want this to stop are not going to use official channels much longer. The sentence no longer ended in the clock room. In Cael's mind it went on down the bluff road, past the arch Withrow had held that morning, toward doors where no chancellor would be waiting.

Seln moved.

He took his right hand off the table and reached for his cup, and Cael thought he was going to turn it at last. He did not. He picked it up and set it down again a full hand's breadth further away from the order, on the far side of his own reach, as if it had been standing too near something; and he put the hand back flat beside the paper, where it had been.

Cael said it aloud, because it was true, and because somebody at that table had to.

"Whatever we're going to do, the schedule isn't ours anymore."

Nobody answered him. And Seln, at the middle of the bench, with his hands flat on either side of the paper, went on looking at it.

Chapter 28 — Where the Mark Sat

Bracken wound the counter clock every Seventh-day before the first bell, and nobody had ever been allowed to talk to him while he did it.

Seln knew that, so he waited.

The paper itself was a day gone. It had ridden down the bluff road in a saddlebag yesterday morning, after a minute and forty seconds at the lodge window in front of one man with a glass, and whatever it had to say about itself it had said then, to him, and to nobody since. Seln had worked that out at about the fire-watch's second round, sitting up in the wing with the senior clerk's fair copy under the lamp and getting nothing from it but the words, which was all a fair copy on the house's own stock could ever give.

So the question had to go to the man with the glass.

The records hall was dark except for the one lamp on the counter. Rain had not come yet, but it was in the air, and the tall windows along the east side showed nothing but grey. Bracken stood on the little step he kept under the counter for the purpose, with the clock's glass door open and the key in his hand, and turned it eleven times. He always turned it eleven times. Seln had counted it on perhaps eighty Seventh-days and had never once heard a twelfth. Then the registrar shut the glass, stepped down, put the step away with his foot, and looked up.

"Seln."

"Registrar." He had his hands in his coat pockets. He took them out. "One question, if you have a minute for it. It's about the paper at the gate."

Bracken's spectacles came down off his forehead onto his nose. He did not say anything, which was his way of saying yes.

"When you held the order up to the light in the lodge," said Seln, "where did the mark sit?"

He had chosen the words in the night, and he had chosen them so that there was only one way to answer them. Bracken was a man who answered the question that was asked. You did not have to tell him why you wanted something. You only had to ask it narrowly enough that the answer could not wander off.

Bracken took a moment. He did not look at anything while he took it. Then he put two fingers on the counter, side by side, as if the sheet were lying there under them.

"Low," he said. "A sixteenth of an inch, against our own stock. I laid the rule on it in the lodge window." He moved the fingers a fraction. "Everything that comes up the hill from the south mill carries the mark the same distance from the deckle. I've put a rule on perhaps four thousand sheets. That one sat a sixteenth low."

"Thank you."

"It's in my book," said Bracken. "Under the seal. Mark a sixteenth low against house stock. I didn't know what to make of it, so I wrote it down."

"That's the right thing to make of it."

Bracken looked at him over the spectacles for a little while. Seln let him look. Then the registrar nodded once, the small nod he gave to a form that had been filled in properly, and opened the day-book, and dipped his pen. He did not ask why. In two years he had never once asked Seln why about anything, and Seln had never once stopped being grateful for it.

He went back across the court to the wing in the half dark. The lodge-man's window was open again. The rain had got at the board beside it in the night, and somebody had already chalked ANYTHING SEALED in fresh.

A sixteenth of an inch was nothing. It was the width of a pencil line.

It was also a whole story, if you knew how paper was made. The mark in a sheet was a wire. Somebody had bent it into a shape and sewn it onto the face of the mould, and when the pulp was lifted on the mould the wire made the paper thinner there, and the thin place showed against the light. A mould lasted for years. A mark, once sewn, stayed where it was sewn. If the mark on a mill's registry stock had moved a sixteenth of an inch, then the wire had broken, or worn through, and somebody had cut it off and sewn it on again by hand. Nobody sews a wire twice in the same place.

So every sheet with the mark a sixteenth low had come off the mould after the mending. And the mould had been mended this year, or Bracken would have laid his rule on a low mark before.

A second run: sheets from the same mill and the same mould and the same pulp, for the same customer, only later.

He had sample leaves of the registry's stock pressed flat in the back of his second manual, one from every posting, because he copied things. He took them out when he reached the copying table, and held the newest to the window. The mark sat where it had always sat. He put the leaves away again.

He had the shape now. He did not have the answer.

There were four favours owed to him in the world, and he had never spent one.

He knew exactly where each of them was. A man in his trade kept that list the way a carter keeps his water barrels, full and lashed down and never once opened on the easy stretches of the road, because the one time you need water is the one time there is none to be had. A favour was not money. It could not be lent or broken into change. You spent it whole, once, and afterward the person who had owed it knew something about you that they had not known before: that you had wanted something enough to ask.

That was the price of a favour, and it was the reason he had kept four.

He went down them in his head, as he went down them perhaps once a season, to be sure they were still where he had left them. A man who kept a mould room at a paper mill in the south. A woman who kept ledgers in a store-house in the west. A ferry-master on a coast he would never see again, who owed him a crossing and would have given him a boat. And an old officer of his own service, retired to a garden, who owed him the largest thing of the four and would have paid it gladly and been ruined by paying it. That one he would never spend. He had known that since the day it was owed. Some debts are only worth keeping so that the other man can sleep.

Two, then, the mill and the ledger, because they were the only two who could answer the only two questions he had.

He sat at the copying table with the wing empty round him and the rain beginning at last against the windows, and he wrote two of them out.

The first went to a man who kept the mould room at the south mill. Eleven years ago Seln had filed one true sentence about him instead of a sentence that would have been more useful to somebody else, and the man had never known which office to thank, but he had known whom. The letter asked one thing. Was the registry mould mended this year, and if so, when, and was a run made off it after? It did not say who wanted to know. It did not have to.

The second went west.

There was a woman in the registry's western stores who had kept the issue ledgers for the paper that the whole half of the continent wrote its instruments on. Every lot that left her stores went into a ruled book against the office that drew it, with the date and the lot's number and the clerk's initial. She had owed him for nine years. He thought of her at her ledger sometimes, on bad nights, because it was a comforting thought: a person in a room somewhere keeping something perfectly. His letter to her asked one thing too. The south mill's second run this year: which lots were drawn, and by whom.

He sealed them with plain wax and no device. Then he put them in a clerk's satchel with three letters that were really the wing's, and buttoned his coat to the chin, and went down the hill.

It was the rest day, and the rain had decided to stay. The bluff road shone. At the second switchback he met a porter coming up with a sack over his head like a hood, who wished him good morning and did not look at him twice. That was the whole art of the trade. A man going down a hill in the rain with a satchel and an errand was not anybody.

At the foot of the road the two coats stood under the eaves of the chandler's warehouse, as close to the wall as they could get. They watched him come down. He let them. He had passed them perhaps two hundred times, and they had written him down perhaps two hundred times as the wing's assistant, with the post. He walked past them at the pace of a man who wanted to be dry and said, "Wet one," and the nearer one said, "It is," and that was all.

The drop was behind the counter of a ship's chandler near the bridge, where a woman sold lamp wicks and tarred twine and was not anything else that anybody could have proved. He bought a hank of twine he did not need. He put the two letters on the counter under the coins. She swept all of it into her apron without looking down.

"The quick bag," he said.

"It's Seventh-day."

"I know what day it is."

She looked at him then, for the first time in four years of twine. Then she nodded, and the letters were gone, and she was counting out his change.

The quick bag went faster than the post by a day each way, and it went to places the post did not. It would cost him a favour of its own, he supposed, one day. Everything did.

He stood a moment in the shop doorway with the twine in his hand, out of the rain, and watched the street. A dray going over the bridge with its load sheeted. Two boys with a dog. A woman under a shawl buying eels from a barrow. The bridge-ward in his oilskin at the near end of the parapet, looking down at the water against the old piers and then at the iron rings let into the stone of the middle one, the way a man looks at a clock he expects to be late. There were five rings on that pier, one above the other. The river was at the first.

Seln had lived in nineteen towns, and every one of them had a man like that, who looked at the water for a living and was right about it twice a year.

On the way back up he counted the coats again, and stood a moment at the second switchback in the rain with the twine in his pocket, and let them count him back. Two at the road's foot. Two across the water at the landing, where the ferry was still running, though it was running short, with the ferryman leaning on his pole at every crossing to hold her against a current that had not been there yesterday. The Ost was coming up.

He went in at the gate and did not look at the place in the court where the woman had stood. He had looked at it enough on the night of the gate. There was nothing in that place but flagstones, and the boy had drawn it all on the oak in chalk, and it had been washed off in the morning.

Two favours left.

On the First-day Karis read the year back to herself, one card at a time, and Cael sat at the end of the long table and listened to it.

The seat wanted the maker of the copies to swear to them, and the advocate of record to sign beside his oath. Karis had said at supper that she would not put her name to a page she had not read against the thing it was copied from, and that this was not caution but manners. So the wing's original cards had come up the library stair in two shallow boxes under the porter's oilcloth, with Seln's leave and Bracken's receipt, and the second set of Seln's copies lay open beside them. He had made two of everything. One had gone down to the seat in the house's boards. The other had stayed in the annex, against exactly this.

The assistant read the cards aloud. Karis followed on the copy with her finger.

"Fifth-day, the fourth week," said the girl. "Gault, the Ash, the Mire. Twenty-two, twenty-three, twenty-four. Figure twenty-three."

"Twenty-three," said Karis.

"Fifth-day, the fifth week. Twenty-one, twenty-three, twenty-two…"

It went on like that, and Cael had not expected it to be hard to listen to, and it was, because he knew every one of those afternoons. He had chosen each figure the night before it was earned, on a page at the back of Hesk's book, and spent the bout earning it to the decimal, and walked off the boards afterward exactly as tired as the rotation had said he would be. Hearing them read out in a row, the whole year so far, in the girl's careful voice, was like hearing somebody read your letters back to you. Every one of them was true. None of them was him.

Rain ran down the reading room's two windows. Below them the river had come up in the night. It was brown from bank to bank now, and moving fast in the middle, and there was a line of froth and sticks along the near side where it was pushing at the bottom of the river street.

"Fourth-day, the seventh week," said the girl, and stopped.

Karis's finger stopped too.

"It's different," said the girl. She held the card closer to the lamp. "The copy's got twenty-two and two-thirds. The card's got…" She tilted it. "The card's got it twice. There's twenty-three and a third, and a line through it, and twenty-two and two-thirds written over the top in another ink."

Karis took the card. She looked at it. Then she turned the copy toward the lamp and looked at the margin beside the line, and Cael saw her mouth change.

There was a note in the margin, so small that you would not have seen it unless you were looking for exactly that, in Seln's square hand. Figure corrected on the card in the desk clerk's hand, different ink. Corrected figure copied. Both seen.

"He found it first," said the girl.

"He found it first," Karis agreed. "Four nights ago, copying straight through the night after the road home. And he copied what the card says now, because that's what it says, and he wrote down that it used to say something else, because it did." She set the card back in its box very gently. "Write it on your slip. Seventh week: corrected on the original; the maker noted it. If the seat asks, we show them both, and his margin."

The girl wrote. Then she looked up at Karis with ink on two fingers.

"Is that a mistake?"

"No. It's a correction. A mistake is when nobody wrote it down." Karis turned back to the copy. "Go on. You found it. That's the whole job."

The girl went on. Fifth-day, the ninth week. Cael watched her, and then watched Karis, who had not once looked up at him. She did not need to; the year was in her hands, and she was reading it straight.

He thought about Seln at the copying table in the wing four nights ago, with the rain on the roof, finding a line through a figure on a card and copying the figure and the line both, and saying nothing to anybody, because it was not his to say anything about. Writing it down instead, small, where it would be found by the one person who was going to look.

He thought that Seln had probably been doing that for his whole life.

The notice for the next sitting was pinned to the frame of Cael's window, where he would see it every time he looked up from the sill.

The seat will sit on the Fifth-day following to receive attestation of the records produced. The enrollee of record will attend in person. The maker of the copies will attend.

He had copied it out of Karis's notebook on the night of the fourth sitting, because the seat's notice had gone into the house's book and he wanted it somewhere he did not have to ask for. In person. Every other sitting of the year had been content to have him on its door log. This one wanted his face.

It had been raining for three days. It came against the glass in long soft gusts and ran down it, and beyond the glass the court was all grey water, and the fountain was a noise in the middle of it.

Lira was on his bed with her boots off and her back against the wall and her feet crossed at the ankle. She had come in without knocking, as she always did, and sat down without asking, as she always did. Brom had the chair, which was too small for him, and it had complained when he sat in it, and he had sat in it anyway with great care, the way he did everything to furniture. Karis stood. She had a sheaf of the attestation papers under her arm and had not let go of them since supper.

Lira rolled her left shoulder. She did it slowly, forward and back, with her face turned a little toward the window, the way a person listens for a sound in a house. The rope at the confluence had laid a bruise across both her shoulder blades as wide as a hand, and he had watched it go from dark to yellow at the breakfast table over a week, a little more each morning, the way you watch a river go down.

"Clean," she said. "Both. Rooke had me on the frames this morning, and nothing talked."

"Good," said Brom.

"I'm only telling you because you were going to ask." She looked at Cael. "You were going to ask. You've been looking at my back for a week like it was a bill."

He had been, and he had not known she knew.

"So," said Lira. "What's this?"

He told them.

He had thought about how to say it all day, and in the end he said it plainly, because there was no way to say it that would make it smaller. On the night of the gate Lira had written her question in capitals in her notebook and left it lying open in the middle of the table, what do they try next, when paper won't do it, and nobody had answered it. He did not have an answer now either. But there was one thing he could do about the question before it was answered, and that was to price it.

"If it's her," he said. "If it's anybody like her. If somebody begins a fight with me, in earnest, the way she would begin one. I want it priced before, not after. I want the whole leaf written tonight."

Karis's arm came down slowly, and the attestation papers with it.

"You mean the reach," she said.

"I mean the reach."

The rain went on against the glass.

The covenant was at the front of Hesk's book. He did not need to turn to it to know what it said, but he turned to it anyway and laid the book open on the sill where they could all see it.

Three lines, in his best hand, from a long table at Halcenvane, written well over a year ago. Nothing made to happen. Only inside a fight somebody else begins. The cost on paper first. And under them, in Karis's wording from the last night at Norhold, with four sets of initials after it: Never again in the middle of a fight unless what follows has been priced first, at the weight it will come at.

"At the weight it will come at," said Karis. "We don't know the weight."

"Seln said the best tool somebody owns."

"Seln said that about where she stood. It's not a tier."

"No." He had thought about that, too. "But it's a guess, and it's somebody's guess who knows. Somebody keeping her for the hard ones isn't keeping an Iron. And if it's Gold, I'm wrong, and the leaf says so, and I'll know I was wrong before I start." He took the pen. "Silver. Call it Silver. If anybody's got a better guess, I'll write that."

Nobody had.

He wrote the heading. Priced before. If it is her, or anyone like her, in a fight somebody else begins. Then he stopped, and looked at what he had written, and put the pen down.

"Say it," said Lira.

"It's wanting it. If I write the price down tonight, I'm saying I'd pay it. That's wanting it. On the stair I didn't want anything. At Norhold I didn't know I wanted it until it was in front of me. This is the first time I've ever sat down at a table and wanted one on purpose, a week ahead, in ink."

"Yes," said Karis.

That was all she said, and he looked up at her. She was standing with the papers against her chest, and she did not look frightened, and she did not look as if she were about to argue him out of it.

"The rule says the cost on paper first," she said. "It doesn't say you have to not want it. It says you have to know what you want before you're standing in the middle of it, so it can't decide for you." She came to the sill and put one finger on the page beside the covenant's second line. "That's what this one's for. You don't get to want it until she begins. That's the whole difference."

"And if nobody begins?"

"Then it's a page," said Brom. "We've got lots of pages."

So he wrote it.

Karis gave him the first figure. She had kept a column for the storm since Norhold, the days and weeks and what had leaned in him and when, and she turned to it in her notebook and laid her palm across it while she thought. Eleven weeks at Gold for the flag to clear. The first month the worst. A Silver ought to weigh less, she said; nobody could say how much less, because there was only the one point on her curve that was any good, and one point was not a curve. She drew one anyway, lightly, on the back of an attestation leaf, through the storm and through the ones before it. Each of the earlier ones had its bill written in the old volume, a day or two of quiet in some room while the rest of him moved over to make space, and she knew those bills better than he did, because she had copied them. They were small points, low on the paper, close together. The storm stood up at the far side of the leaf by itself, like a tree in a field, and her pencil went from the little ones up to it in a long uneasy curve that she did not like and said so.

"Nine weeks," she said. "If I had to put a number on it. Something less than a flag, for about nine weeks. I don't believe it. Write it down."

He wrote about nine weeks, Karis's curve, not believed.

Then the first minute.

"At Norhold the wrong thing answered," he said. "In the middle of the floor. I called the Wind and something else came, and I went down. If I reach in the middle of a fight, that minute's going to happen again, or something like it. I won't be standing up for it. I may not know which way is down."

"Then somebody has to be standing over you for that minute," said Brom.

"Yes."

"Then that's me." He said it without moving in the chair, in the voice he used to tell the kitchen how many loaves. "Write it. Brom, for the minute."

Cael did not write it at once. He was thinking of the north rail at Norhold, and five people holding to Rooke's hand over the cap as if it were a rope, and Brom with his left shoulder low beside Lira, not going.

"There was a rule at Norhold," he said. "Nobody over the cap."

"There was." Brom looked at the window, where the rain was. "I've thought about that rule more than you'd credit. It was a good rule. It kept a hall full of people off a floor where a Gold was working. I'd keep it again tomorrow, in that hall." He brought his eyes back. "There won't be a cap. Wherever this is, if it's anywhere, there won't be a rail or a referee or a man with his arms crossed over his head. There'll be you on the ground for a minute, and whoever's standing nearest. I'm asking to be the one standing nearest. Write it."

He wrote it.

The rest went down quickly after that, because it was the kind of thing he had written many times before. A week at least without the band, so wing three to be excused on some true ground. The lane not to be laid, and the read not to be trusted, until whatever came had finished coming. Somebody in the room with him every hour of the first two days, because at Norhold the first two days had been the bad ones. Rooke to be told nothing but what was true and small.

Then he came to the part he could not price, and he did what Seln had told him on the oak. He left it blank where he would see it. He wrote three headings down the margin, Her reach. Her rate. What it costs her., and drew a line after each, and put nothing on any of the lines.

Lira took the pen out of his hand.

She did not ask. She leaned off the bed and took it, and pulled the book toward her across the sill, and wrote one more line under his in her large capitals, pressing hard, the way she always did.

NOBODY GOES IN AFTER HIM ALONE.

She gave him the pen back.

He initialled under it. Karis initialled with her small exact letters, and Brom made his mark, which was a B with a bar through it like a gate. Lira put hers last, in capitals.

Then they sat there in the lamplight with the rain running down the window and the notice pinned to the frame, and nobody said goodnight for a long time.

Priced on the Second-day, before the sitting, with four initials. Three days of rain and the river over the bottom step of the river street. Lira's shoulder: clean, both sides. She saw me counting it.

Chapter 29 — The Catechism

The mould-room man answered first, because the south mill was nearer, and because he was the kind of man who answered a letter the day it came.

It reached Seln on the Third-day in the ordinary post, inside a printer's circular about a new kind of ruled ledger, folded twice and pushed down between the pages where nobody opening a circular would look. It was written in pencil, in capitals, by a man who had learned his letters late and did not trust the small ones.

MOULD MENDED THIS YEAR. WIRE WENT AT THE TOP OF THE MARK. SEWED IT MYSELF. A SIXTEENTH LOW, I KNEW IT WOULD BE, THERE WAS NO HELPING IT. ONE RUN OFF IT SINCE FOR THE REGISTRY. WE CALL IT THE SECOND. PAID IN FULL.

The last three words were the part Seln read twice. The man had added them on his own. He had understood exactly what was being spent, and he wanted it known that the account was closed.

Seln put the circular in the copying-room stove and watched the pencil go brown and then go.

One favour, one fact. The paper that had come up the hill to the gate had been made this year, off a mended mould, in the south mill's second run of registry stock. That was all: it did not say who had drawn it, or where it had gone. It only said that somebody, somewhere, after the mending, had ordered registry paper and been sent it.

The other half was in the west.

Second run, south mould: thirteen lots, every one in the book, every one against an office you could find in a directory.

A fourteenth, drawn the same week, written in above the first ruled line, where nothing is ever written.

In the office column a mark where the word should be. A mark, not a word.

Nobody here wrote it, and nobody here will say so twice.

The sheet was ash in the post room's stove before the bag-strap was buckled again. He stood over the little iron door with the poker until the ash broke, as she would have expected him to, and only then went back to the bench and the half-sorted bags, because a man who stops the sort in the middle is a man somebody remembers.

It was the Fourth-day. The porter's shoulder was still strapped, so the sort was still his, and he had liked it since the first morning. The post room behind the records hall's counter was a narrow place with forty pigeonholes along one wall, a bench along the other, a brass beam for weighing parcels and the stove the porter kept going from the first bell whatever the weather. In half an hour at that bench you knew where every letter in the house was going and roughly why, and nobody watched you learn it. It was the most honest half-hour of his day.

Her envelope had come up in among the house's ordinary post, addressed to the wing in a clerk's hand and no bigger than an invoice, and he had given it the wing's hole and gone on with everything else before he let himself take it out again. In nine years of owing him she had never once written to him, and when at last she did it was four lines and no signature, because a woman who kept the issue ledgers for half a continent knew to a hair what a line weighed.

So that was the paper.

A mould mended in the south, and a second run off it this year. Thirteen honest lots, gone out in the ordinary way to offices with names and doors and clerks who could be written to. And a fourteenth, the same week, off the same run, on the same stock, that had not gone into the ledger at all but over it. Written in above the line by somebody who could reach a store-house ledger in the west and open it and put a thing where nothing went, and leave a mark in the column that was only a mark.

He had seen a great deal of paper in his life. He had never seen that.

That was not true. He stood at the bench and made himself correct it, because the voice he kept for the audit would not let the sentence stand. He had seen it once, twelve years ago, in a press in a records room in an old building. He had seen paper that was entirely correct in every particular, and that sat a little above where it should have sat, and had been put there by somebody who could reach.

He did not think any further along that road. He had not let himself walk down it in twelve years except on the worst nights, and this was a weekday morning, and there was post to finish.

He finished the post.

Back in the wing, with the copying table under his hands and the rain on the long windows, he went down the grades. He had not said them over since he was young enough to need them, and he found they were all still there, in their order, like tools in a rack nobody had touched.

The record. Paper in a subject's file. A query, a designation, a mark in a column. It cost nothing and was never undone, and it was where everything began.

The instrument. A proceeding, in daylight, by the book. A petition and a seat and an answer, and every door in it real law. It cost a great deal and was always lawful, and it was what an office used when it wanted to be seen being right.

The knock. Paper again, but from an office nobody could place, brought to a door and read there. It was not meant to be obeyed; it was meant to see what the door did, how fast, who came, and how long the man with the glass took over the seal.

And the hand. No paper. No faces. A road, at a place where no house stood, at an hour somebody had chosen.

Four, she had said, and struck the floor once with the stick she never leaned on. Learn them in that order, because they come in that order. And when you have seen the third, gentlemen, do not wait for the fourth to knock. The fourth does not knock.

That had been the last morning, in a room over a ship's chandler's on a quay, with six young men on benches who were not yet anything, and a cat asleep in the sun on the window-ledge. She had been old even then. She had opened every lesson by telling them that nobody in that room would ever be told the whole of anything and that the sooner they stopped minding the better; she had spent the weeks between on the craft, how to read a subject, how to write a return that was true and useful and no longer than it needed to be, how to live a year in a town and leave nothing behind but a room that had been let. The grades she had kept for the end, so that they would know what the other side of the table did, and where they themselves stood.

The boy had had the record since before he could read it. He had had the instrument since the first week of the year, in a sealed packet read out by a woman standing in her own hall. Five days ago he had had the knock, at the gate, in eighty-one words, with a woman standing in the one place in the court that could not be got round.

A fourteenth lot was what the knock looked like from inside a ledger. Seln had held its ash on the end of a poker an hour ago.

That left one grade.

She had taught them the catechism on the same morning, after the grades, as if it were the answer to them.

It was four lines. Every man in the service learned them in his first year, and said them under his breath on the first morning of every posting, the way other men touched a doorpost for luck. Seln had said them nineteen times on nineteen first mornings. He had never once said them on any other morning, because there had never been any other morning that needed them.

He said them now.

He stood at the copying table in the empty wing, with the shelf above it at the edge of his sight and the rain loud on the long windows, and said them aloud, once, at the pace she had used, so that the room would have heard them if the room had been listening.

What you carry is worth what it has not done.

A thing kept is a wall. A thing spent is a door, and doors open both ways.

The keeper is invisible. The witness is a location.

Nobody has ever protected a man by believing him.

Then he stood there and listened to them, the way you listen to a bell after it has been struck, to hear whether it is cracked.

What he carried had done nothing for twelve years. It was worth exactly that. He had always thought the line meant that a thing unused kept its whole value, like a coin in a drawer. Standing there he heard what it actually said. It said the value was the not-doing. It had been worth twelve years of nothing, and it was worth nothing still.

A thing kept is a wall. It had been a wall. It had stood between what he knew and whoever would want to know he knew it, and it had kept him safe, perfectly, every day. But it was a wall round the case, not round the boy. The boy was on the other side of it with the rest of the weather.

The keeper is invisible. He had been invisible for fifteen years. The boy's people had never been invisible for a day. All year they had walked about the hill in the open and let themselves be counted, the girl on the walls with her chalk and the big one at the frames and the researcher with her lamp lit in the top window every night where the whole valley could see it. Five days ago, at the gate, the house itself had stood in the middle of its own court and read the paper out loud. Nobody on that side had hidden anything. They had simply been there.

The witness is a location. He had always heard that as a warning: a man who has seen a thing is only a place where the thing can be found, so do not be found. Now, in the empty wing, it sounded like a choice. He would rather be the place the boy could find.

And the last line.

He had believed the last line more than the other three together. It was the one that had kept him clean. You did not protect a subject by believing him; you protected him by counting what he did, and filing it true, and letting the true thing be your only argument. He had never believed anybody in his life. He had counted them.

He had counted the boy for a year. Two slips on a common-room fire. A season of figures that never once settled into a line. An afternoon at Norhold where everything held back went out in one breath, on purpose, in front of eight thousand people. He had counted all of it, and filed none of it, and somewhere in the counting, without asking his leave, it had turned into the other thing.

He believed him.

Nobody has ever protected a man by believing him. It was true. He had never seen it done. He was going to try.

The wing's clock went on with its slow tick over the counter. Nothing in the room changed its note. Seln stood with his two hands flat on the copying table and understood, quite calmly, that this was the largest thing that had happened to him since a green corridor twelve years ago, and that it had happened on a weekday morning between the post and the noon bell, and that nobody would ever write it down.

He reached up and took the case off the shelf.

He carried it across the court at dusk, in the rain, with his coat buttoned over the top of it.

He did not hurry and he did not take the covered walk. A man on the covered walk was a man out of the rain, and people looked at him in a vague friendly way as they looked at anybody sharing a dry place. A man crossing the open court in a downpour was a man with an errand, and nobody looked at a man with an errand.

He counted them anyway, because he could not help it.

A porter with a hand-cart of coal under an oilcloth: one. Two first-years running for the refectory with a coat held over both their heads: two, three. The fire-watch boy with his ladder: four. A Magister of the Ash faculty under an umbrella the size of a cart-wheel, who said, "Filthy, filthy," to nobody: five. The lodge-man's boy, sent across with a lamp: six.

At the residence door a knot of third-years was standing out of the wet arguing about a bout, and he went round the edge of them: seven to twelve.
