On the stair, coming down, the Current girl from Rooke's program with her wet hair in a towel, who flattened herself to the wall to let him by and said, "Sorry, sorry," as if the stair were hers to be sorry about: thirteen. Two more on the first landing. Three in the corridor, one of whom was the captain, Ephram, with his green-taped file under his arm, who nodded to him and went on: eighteen. Five more behind half-open doors as he passed, reading or mending or asleep.

Twenty-three. Not one of them looked at the thing under his coat. Why would they? The wing's assistant was going up a residence stair with something for somebody. It was the most ordinary sight on the hill.

The boy's door was the last on the second corridor. Seln knocked once, and opened it when the boy said to.

He was at the window, at the sill, with Hesk's book open and the lamp lit and the notice still pinned to the frame. He looked round, and his face did what it always did when a door opened, which was nothing, and then it went still in a different way.

Seln unbuttoned his coat and set the case on the sill beside the book.

He kept one hand on the lid and did not sit. The lamp found the brass of the lock and nothing else, because there was nothing else on the outside of it for a lamp to find, and the boy's eyes went to the lock and stayed there a moment and came back up to his face.

"I'm going to open this," he said. "Not tonight."

The boy looked at the case and then at him, and did not reach for it, and did not ask what was in it. Seln had known that he would not. It was why he had climbed the stair. When the boy spoke at last it was quietly, to the case as much as to the man, and it was not quite a question.

"You're sure."

Seln heard what the boy was offering him. It was a way back down the stair. The boy had built it in two words and held it open, so that a man could take his case and go and nobody need ever mention it again. Seln looked at it, and did not take it.

"No. That's how you'll know it's true."

They decided the rest in a quarter of an hour, standing, with the case between them on the sill and the rain going on.

Not here, said Seln. A residence room had a door anybody could knock on, and a corridor full of people who knew whose room it was. Not the wing either. The wing was his, and everybody who watched the wing knew it was his, and a lamp in it after hours was already a thing somebody wrote down.

"A room with a lock," he said. "A name on the card that isn't yours or mine. A reason for people to go up to it one at a time without anybody thinking it's strange. Somewhere a person has to be on purpose."

The boy thought about it for perhaps three breaths. "The reading room."

"The researcher's."

"It has Bracken's card on the door. Assigned: K. Dellenmoor. It has the brass lock and one key, and she wears the key. The old lumber room across the landing has the code on a shelf and the assistant's table, and the house has called the two rooms together the annex since Bracken had it cleared, and people go up and down that stair all day with books." He stopped. "And it's hers. Nobody on the hill would think twice about four people going up to her room. They've been doing it all year."

"Five people," said Seln.

"Five."

"Then the researcher's room." He took his hand off the case at last. "Not before the sitting. Whatever comes out of this, you don't want to be carrying it in your head into a room with Jent in it. He reads nothing, but other people at that table do. The First-day after."

The boy nodded.

"I'll put it in the floor schedule," said Seln.

He saw the boy not understand that, and then understand it, which took about as long as it took the rain to run from the top of the window to the sill.

The wing posted the floor schedule every Seventh-day for the week to come: four floors, their hours, and who had booked each hour, in Seln's fair copy, pinned up on the wing's board and the residence board and the refectory door. Everybody on the hill read it. Nobody on the hill read it for anything but their own name.

"Five lines on the First-day," said Seln. "Five floors, five hours, a quarter apart, each in one of your names. A practice booking. It's the most ordinary thing on the board. Read your own line. The floor means nothing. The hour is when you come up the stair."

The boy took the pencil from the sill and wrote something on the back of his hand, and looked at it, and rubbed it out with his thumb.

"There'll be six names in the First-day column," he said. "There always are. Ephram has the Crown yard from the second bell every First-day."

"Five," said Seln. "The sixth is the captain, and he wants the floor."

The boy almost smiled. Then he did not, and looked at the case again.

Seln wrote his weekly return that night at the copying table, in the old pattern, as he had written one every week for fifteen years.

Subject attended to his course of study. Subject attended the seat's fourth sitting as directed. An instrument presented at the house's gate on the Sixth-day was declined by the house; subject was not seen at the refusal. Subject's floor work within the band of the year. Nothing further to report.

Every word of it was true. He read it over in the voice he kept for the audit, and the voice found nothing wrong with it, which was the point and always had been. He folded it in the old way, with the subject's reference on the outside fold and the posting's mark in the corner, and put it in the satchel for the quick bag in the morning.

Then he made the duplicate, as he always did, word for word, and opened the cupboard under the copying table and put it into the thickest bundle on the end of the row, the one with the name of this hill on its label.

It was not the last of its kind. He knew that while he was tying the tape. He would write another next week, and the one after, and every week until the year closed, true and empty, in the old pattern, because the pattern was what the office expected and a pattern that changed was a thing somebody wrote down. Nothing in his life was going to look different from the outside. That was the other half of the catechism, the half she had never needed to say aloud.

He put the case back on the shelf above the copying table, where it had stood for two years and where nobody had ever once looked for it, and blew out the lamp.

Bracken saw the chain go across Ostrand bridge a little after the fourth bell on the Fourth-day, and came down from his rooms with the ship's glass still in his hand to say so.

He found Cael on the north wall, because it was where Cael always was at that hour, and stood beside him in the rain without an umbrella and gave him the glass. Cael found the bridge. The bridge-ward was at the near end in his oilskin, with a man from the town, hauling a chain across the roadway from post to post. Below them the river was standing up against the middle pier in a long brown hump, and the iron rings let into the stone were gone under it, all but the top two.

"The third ring," said Bracken. "They shut it to everybody at the third. Carts, horses, people on foot. Since the year the middle arch went, which was before my time." He took the glass back. "The ferryman tied up at noon. I watched him do it."

"The sitting's tomorrow."

"The sitting's tomorrow," Bracken agreed. "The seat does not adjourn for weather. I have never known it to, and the house has never in my time asked it to." He looked out at the water for a moment longer. "Come and see the coachman. He's in the stable passage with a map and an opinion."

The house's coachman had driven the delegation coach for as long as Cael had been on the hill. He was a short broad man with grey whiskers who talked to his horses in a low steady voice all day and to people hardly at all. He had a road map of the valley spread on an upturned bucket in the stable passage, weighted at the corners with four horseshoes, and he put one thick finger on it when they came in, as if he had been waiting with it there.

"Up this side," he said. "West, along the bank road. Two hours if the bank road holds, and it will, it's high. To the upper ferry at the narrows." The finger moved. "She runs in any water. Rock both sides, no width for the river to throw her about in. Over there. Then back east down the river road on the far side, two hours more, into the city by the west gate." He looked up at Bracken. "Leave at the hour before light. In by noon. Sitting's after."

"Thank you," said Bracken.

The coachman folded the map along its old folds and put the horseshoes in his pocket and went back to his horses.

That evening, in the refectory, Withrow came to the end of their table on her way out and stood behind Karis's chair with one hand on its back.

"Since the gate, no enrollee of this house leaves the hill alone," she said. "You know that. Tomorrow you are five, and the house's counsel went down to her rooms by the wharf this afternoon while the bridge was still open, and will meet you at the side door." She looked along the table at each of them, the way she looked at a page before she signed it. "I would go with you, if the seat had asked for me. It has not. It has asked for him, and the maker of the copies, and the advocate of record. Go the long way and come back the short one."

She went out.

"The long way," said Lira, to her plate.

"It's only a road," said Brom.

He came up to Cael's room an hour later with his kit bag, all the same, and turned it out on the bed.

It was what he took to every floor that was not the house's own. Two rolls of linen strapping, a roll of the stiff kind that the healers used for wrists, a tin of the porter's horse salve that smelled of tar and worked better than anything the infirmary had, a clean neckcloth, a flask, a heel of bread wrapped in a napkin, and a short length of leather with a buckle at each end that Cael had never seen him use and had never asked about. He went through all of it with his big careful fingers, as he did before a meet, and put it back in a different order.

"It's a sitting," said Lira from the window seat. "They'll want him to say They are mine and sign. Nobody straps for that."

"I strap for the road," said Brom.

She did not laugh at him. That was how Cael knew she had been thinking about the road too.

Karis came last, with the attestation wallet under her arm and her coat already over the back of the chair as if she meant to sleep in it. She checked the wallet's contents leaf against its contents, which she had done at supper and would do again in the coach, and then she sat on the end of the bed beside Brom's kit and looked at the sill.

There was nothing on the sill but Hesk's book and the lamp. The case had gone back down the stair under Seln's coat an hour after it came up.

Cael told them.

He told them in the order it had happened, because that was the only fair way: the knock at dusk, the case set down beside the book, I'm going to open this. Not tonight. What he had asked and what Seln had answered. The reading room. The floor schedule and the First-day after the sitting, five names, five quarters of an hour, and a sixth line that was only Ephram wanting the Crown yard. He did not say what was in the case, because he did not know. Nobody asked.

Karis sat very still with the wallet on her knees.

"My room," she said.

"If you'll have it."

"He asked for my room." She said it slowly, as if she were reading it off a page in a hand she did not know. "Out of every room on the hill." Then she looked up, and Cael saw that she was not frightened, or not only. "Yes. Tell him yes. Tell him I'll have the girl sent home early that day, and the kettle on, and every paper on the table turned over." She stopped. "No. Don't tell him the last part. I'll just do it."

"I'll bring the kettle," said Brom.

Lira was looking out at the rain. When she spoke it was to the glass.

"Two years he's sat at the middle of the bench," she said. "Two years, and never once put anything of his on the table. Not a cup. Not a word he didn't have to." She turned round. "Good. That's all. Good."

Brom stood and shouldered his kit bag. At the door he stopped, and put his hand flat to the left side of his coat, where the letter was, the one he had carried sealed since the forty-fifth day, and kept it there a moment, as if he were checking that the road had not already taken something.

"The hour before light," he said, and went.

Cael wrote it that night with the rain at last beginning to slacken against the glass.

The bridge chained at the third ring. The ferry tied up. One road to the seat tomorrow, round by the upper ferry, four hours. Seln came up the stair at dusk with a case under his coat and set it on my sill. He's going to open it. He isn't sure. I believe him more because he isn't.

Chapter 30 — The Upper Ferry

The clerk from the district seat found Havel at the inn by the bridge on the Third-day, a little before noon, reading the second manual for the fourth time that week.

He was a young man in a wet hat, and he apologised three times on the stair before he got to the door, and twice more inside it. The district seat's records room was a man short, he said. Two men, if you counted the one with the fever. A letter had come in from the registrar of the academy on the bluff, about an order and a seal, and it concerned the proceedings, and the senior records officer had said that the proceedings' own records support was in the town on its days off with nothing to do, and would the junior chair be so good as to check the registers and draft the usual.

"The usual," said Havel.

"The usual, sir." The young man held out a packet in oilcloth. "With the senior's compliments. He says there's no hurry before the Fourth-day evening."

Havel took it. He thanked the young man, who apologised again for the rain and went.

Inside the oilcloth were two things. The registrar's letter, in a clear upright hand that wasted nothing, asking that the instrument constituting a certain office be supplied, together with the seal under which that instrument was itself issued. And a sheet of thin paper with a pencil rubbing on it of a seal, taken carefully, the grey of the lead built up in even strokes until the device stood out white: the registry's own pattern, the river and the scale, inside a beaded rim.

The letter said where the rubbing had come from, in its first paragraph, with the instrument quoted whole: it was the seal off the escort order that the leader of four riders had read aloud in the house's outer court on the Sixth-day morning, and that the house had declined at its own gate and let ride away again down the bluff road.

He laid the rubbing on the table by the window and looked at it for a long time without touching it.

His right hand ached at the web of the thumb, as it had every morning for a year. He opened it and closed it twice under the table, out of habit, though there was nobody in the room to see.

It was a good rubbing, and it was also a good seal. That was the first thing he noticed and the thing he went on noticing all afternoon: whoever had cut the die had cut it properly. The river ran the right way; the scale's beam was level. The beading round the rim was even and close, and in the beading, at the bottom, where every registry die carried its cutter's number, there were four small figures that the pencil had picked out faintly, as a pencil does when it passes over something raised. He took the reading glass out of his kit and bent over them until he was sure of all four.

The usual was a letter of two sentences. He could have written it in his sleep. But the usual came after the registers, and so, because it was the order the manual gave, he went to the registers first.

He checked it three ways, because there were three registers, and he did not think of it as anything more than that.

The first was the district's own impression book. It lived in the records room at the district seat, on a slanted desk of its own under the window, a book as tall as a child and as thick as a door-step. Every die issued for use in the district went into it on the day of issue, pressed into a red wafer and pasted on the page in the order it came, with the office's name and the date beside it in the keeper's hand. Havel turned its pages for two hours on the Third-day afternoon with the clerk in the wet hat hovering at his elbow, offering to help and being thanked. He found the seat's own seal on its page, forty years old, the river and the scale. He found the fee office's, and the bridge-ward's, and a ferry company's, and a hundred and eighty others.

He did not find the rubbing's.

That proved nothing. A facilities office constituted for a proceeding might very well be a continental office and not a district one, and then its die would never have been issued here at all.

So the second was the registry's printed schedule of the seals of office, which was continental. It came out every year in a stiff grey binding, with a plate for every office that had a seal, engraved to the size of the die. The district seat kept the current year and the four before it on a shelf behind the senior records officer's chair. Havel took down the current year and went through it plate by plate, the next morning, with the rubbing beside him on a clean blotter. Then he went through last year's, in case. Then he took down the current year again and went through the index of offices, under F, and under P for proceedings, and under S for seat.

The rubbing was not in it.

The third was the number.

Every die the registry used was cut by one of three cutters, and every cutter numbered every die in the beading of its rim, and every number went into the cutters' issue ledger against the office the die was cut for. The ledger itself was in the west. A copy was kept at every district seat, in the strong-room, and brought up to date every quarter by the post. Havel signed for the strong-room key at noon on the Fourth-day, with the clerk as his witness, and went down with a lamp.

The ledger ran in numbers, in order, one die to a line, every number cut and every number entered. That was the point of it. He found the place where the rubbing's four figures ought to be, and laid his finger on the page.

The number one below the rubbing's stood there against a die cut for a ferry office on a southern river. The number one above it stood against a die cut for a district fee office in the east. And they stood on consecutive lines, in the same ink, as they had been written, the ferry office's line and then the fee office's line directly under it.

The rubbing's number belonged between them. There was no line for it. There was no room on the page for one. The ledger stepped over it as if the cutters had never counted it, and the number on the rubbing, by the registry's own book, was a number the registry had never cut.

He stood in the strong-room with his finger on the page and the lamp hissing for perhaps a minute. Then he wrote the two flanking numbers on a slip of paper, each with its office, and the rubbing's number between them with nothing against it, and nothing else. He locked the strong-room and gave the key back and signed for its return.

The facilities office was in the district's register of offices. He had expected that too. It was entered there in a good clerk's hand: constituted this year, for the proceedings at the seat at Ostrand, by an instrument filed at the district seat under seal. The instrument was in the file. He asked for it, and it came, and he looked at it.

It was registry stock. The seal at its foot was the rubbing's seal, the same die, the same four figures in the beading. Everything about it was correct.

He drafted the usual at the senior records officer's own table, on the district seat's paper, while the senior watched the rain.

The office named in the registrar's letter was constituted on the date entered in the district's register of offices, by instrument filed at this seat under seal. The registrar is respectfully referred to the issuing authority of the said instrument for any further particulars.

Two sentences, and both of them true. The senior read them, nodded, signed, and handed them back for the clerk to copy fair. It would go up the hill with the next bag.

The form of the usual had no line for what Havel had found. There was a line for the office and a line for the instrument and a line for where to write next. There was nowhere on it to say that the seal on the instrument was in none of the registers that seals were kept in. Nobody had ever needed such a line. A seal was a thing that was in the registers. That was what made it a seal.

He did not add a line, because it was not his letter. It was the district's, and the district had a form, and the form was correct.

At the inn that evening the river was louder than he had ever heard it.

His window looked down on the bridge. A chain had gone across the near end of it at the fourth bell, he had watched it go from the strong-room stair, and now the bridge-ward's lantern hung on the chain-post and nobody crossed. Below the lantern the water stood up against the middle pier in a smooth brown hump, as if something large were resting underneath it, and went away downstream with a noise like a crowd a long way off.

He took the five sheets out from between the second manual and the third and laid them on the table in their order.

He read them through. The first went back to a pump step at Ardenmere and a form of four questions, and to the mark in a boy's file that no office would own. The fifth was a sentence on a senior seat's desk at Norhold, read upside down, closing a door that the first had found open. In between were three more. He read them all twice, slowly, the way the manual said a records officer should read anything he meant to rely on.

Then he took a clean sheet of the same kind and dipped his pen, and wrote the date, and under it the sixth entry, in the plain hand he kept for the sheets.

The seal on the instrument constituting the facilities office named in the order presented at Halcenvane, and on the order itself (registrar's rubbing): absent from the district's impression book; absent from the registry's schedule of seals of office, this year's and last; its rim number absent from the cutters' issue ledger, where the numbers one below it and one above it stand on consecutive lines with no line for it between. Checked three ways. Absent from every registry of seals.

He read it back. It recorded something that had happened. It did not say what he made of it. That was the rule of the sheets, and he had kept it six times.

He laid the sixth beside the first.

A mark with no office behind it. A seal with no register under it. They lay side by side on the table in the lamplight, written years apart, in the same hand. He looked at them for a long while, and he did not make anything of them, because there was nothing in the rule that let him. They were two facts. They were on two sheets.

He understood, sitting there, that there would not be a seventh.

It was not a decision; he did not decide it. It was more as if he had come to the end of a ledger and found the last page ruled off. Every one of the six recorded something the registers could not answer, and he had always been able to write it down because the registers answered everything else, and he could lay one against the other and see exactly where the gap was. This one had gone through all three registers and come out the other side. There was nothing left to lay a seventh against. A seventh would have to be something he thought, and the sheets did not hold what he thought. They never had.

He put the six back between the second manual and the third, the same way round, and buckled the kit.

Then he sat at the window with his hands folded, the right one aching, and listened to the river until the bridge-ward's lantern went out.

The coach went down the bluff road in the dark with its lamps lit and the rain gone east in the night.

Cael sat with his back to the horses and watched the house go up behind them into the black, the lodge window first, then the lecture range, then nothing. The wind had come round behind the rain and was drying everything it could reach. It was cold. The coachman had his collar up to his hat and was talking to the near horse in the low steady voice that never stopped.

At the foot of the road the two coats under the chandler's eaves stood away from the wall to watch them turn. Cael saw one of them lift his head to read which way. West, along the bank road. The man did not move after that. There was nowhere he needed to go with it at that hour; he would write it on his board and give it to the next man on the bell, and by noon it would be wherever such things went.

Brom had the two record cases on his knees, one on top of the other, with his arms round them. He had not let them ride on the roof on the day of the exhibits and he was not going to let them ride on the roof today, in mud. Karis sat beside him with the attestation wallet in her lap and her lips moving. She was saying the form over, the questions the seat's clerk would ask the maker and the enrollee and the advocate, and the answers, under her breath, the way Lira counted her bursts before a bout. Lira was asleep against the window with her coat over her like a blanket and her mouth a little open. She could sleep anywhere in a moving vehicle. She said it was the only useful thing she had learned from guilds.

Seln sat in the far corner with his eyes shut and his hands in his lap. He had sat like that in the coach on every road all year. Cael had long ago stopped thinking it meant he was asleep.

Once, near the end of the first hour, Lira woke without moving anything but her eyes.

"You're saying it out loud," she said to Karis.

"I'm saying it so my mouth knows it before the room does." Karis did not stop turning the wallet's leaves. "The clerk asks the maker whether the copies are his and true. Then he asks the enrollee whether the figures are his own, earned on the house's floors. Then he asks the advocate to sign." She looked across at Cael. "That's all it is. Three questions and a pen. You say They are mine, and nothing else, and you sit down."

"They are mine," said Cael.

"Like that." She went back to her leaves. "Not a word after it. Whatever you're thinking, don't think it at them."

Lira shut her eyes again. "He's always thinking it at them," she said, to the inside of her coat, and was asleep before anybody could answer.

Cael sat with his back to the horses and turned the three words over. They were true. Every figure on every card in Brom's two cases had been earned on the house's floors, by him, on purpose, to the decimal. They were his in the way a rotation page was his, because he had written it the night before. He thought that if the clerk had asked whether they were all of him, he would not have known what to say, and he was glad the form did not ask it.

The bank road ran west along the near side of the river, high on its terrace, with the water on the left below them roaring in the dark. Twice the wheels went into standing water to the hub and the coach lurched, and the coachman talked to the horses until they leaned into it and pulled out. Once a fallen branch lay across the road and Brom got down and dragged it off into the ditch and got back in, wet to the knees, and put the cases back on his lap without a word.

The sky over the river began to go grey.

Hesk's book was inside Cael's coat, against his ribs, where it had been every day since the gate. He could feel the corner of it when the coach rocked. He thought about the leaf at the front of it with four sets of initials, and NOBODY GOES IN AFTER HIM ALONE pressed so hard into the paper that you could read it from the back.

He did not take the book out. He knew what it said.

The upper ferry crossed at the narrows, where the river ran between two shoulders of grey rock not much farther apart than the Crown yard was long.

It was a flat chain ferry, broad enough for one coach and its team and nothing else. A great chain ran from an iron ring sunk in the rock on the near side, down under the water, and up again to a winch-house on the far bank, and the ferry hauled itself along the chain by a wheel turned from its deck. The river came through the narrows deep and fast and brown and very loud. But it could not spread. There was no width for it to throw anything about in. It simply went through, as water goes through a pipe, and the ferry sat on top of it on its chain like a cat on a wall.

The ferryman came out of his hut at the coach lamps with a lantern of his own. He was an old man, thin as a rake, in a coat that had been mended so often it was more mending than coat. He looked at the coach, and at the house's mark on its door, and at the river.

"You'll be the academy," he said. "From up the far end."

"We will," said the coachman.

"Thought you might. Town ferry tied up at noon. Bridge chained at four." He went down the ramp to the deck and stood with one hand on the wheel and looked up at them. "Well, come on. She doesn't mind it. She's never minded it."

They led the horses on with their eyes covered, and the coach after them, with all five of them standing on the deck beside it because the coachman said they would ride steadier that way. The ferryman put his weight on the wheel. The chain came up out of the water in front of them dripping and went down again behind, and the deck began to move.

The old man talked to the chain while he turned. Cael could not hear what he said over the river. It was a long steady murmur with no pauses in it, the same sound the coachman made to his horses, and the chain answered it with a clank at every link that went over the wheel.

Halfway across, the ferryman stopped talking to the chain and talked to them instead.

"Road's good your side," he said, nodding at the far bank without taking his hands off the wheel. "Up the hill and through the cut and down the other side, and then it's all flat to the city. It'll be soup on the flat, mind. But the cut's dry." He gave the wheel another turn. "Only stretch that ever is. It's chalk, the cut. Drinks the rain like a sponge and blows dry in an hour, and you'll come out the far end white as millers."

"Thank you," said Karis.

"No trouble." He spat over the side, politely, downstream. "Had a load of hurdles over last evening for the farm on the hill, and that's been my week. You're the most company I've had."

On the far landing the coachman led the horses up the ramp and put them to, and they all got back in, all but one.

Seln stood on the landing with his collar up.

"I'll walk," he said. "There's a path along the bank under the road. A man on foot gets up the hill quicker than a coach does, and a man on foot by a river is a fisherman." He looked up at the coachman. "Where's the next milestone past the cut?"

"At the culvert, the far end," said the coachman. "Seven to the city, it says."

"Then I'll be at the culvert."

He turned and went down off the end of the landing onto a narrow path among the willows, with the river roaring at his left hand, and in about the time it took Cael to look away and back again he was not a thing that anybody would have looked at twice. He was a grey shape among grey trees. Then he was not even that.

Cael put it away with the other things he had counted that morning. Seln had not been asked; he had chosen the road himself.

The road went up from the landing in two long bends, between hawthorn hedges, and then the hill closed in on both sides of it and they were in the cut.

It was a deep straight cutting through a spur of the hill that came down to the river. Somebody a long time ago had decided to go through the spur rather than round it, and had dug a road down into the chalk and carted the chalk away, and the walls were still there, white and steep and streaked with green where the water ran. On the north side, uphill, the bank stood twenty feet over the road. On the south side, toward the river, it was lower, ten or twelve feet. Toward the far end of the cut, a stone's throw short of where it opened out again, the south bank had been eaten away underneath by some flood long ago, before the road had a ditch, so that its lip hung out over a hollow of shadow, like a brow over an eye.

The road itself was twenty-odd feet wide, cambered high in the middle so the water would run off it, with a ditch along the north side. It was dry, as the ferryman had said it would be. The wind came along the cut from the west behind them and lifted the chalk dust off the crown in little white skirls, and the horses' feet sent it up in clouds.

A skein of geese went over, very high, calling.

Cael counted the cut out of the window as they went, because he counted everything. Four hundred and forty yards, near enough, by the coachman's pace and the bends at each end. At the far end, the east end, the road narrowed to cross a culvert where a stream came down a gully off the hill and went under the road toward the river, with a low stone parapet on either side. Beside the near parapet stood a milestone. He could not read it from that distance. It would say seven.

Across the road just short of the culvert stood a cart.

It was an ordinary farm cart with its shafts down on the road and no horse in them, slewed across the crown so that it blocked most of the way. One of its wheels was off and lying flat beside it. There was nobody near it.

The coachman pulled up forty yards short and sat looking at it. Then he said something to the horses and put the brake on.

"Wheel off," he said, through the trap. "I'll see if it'll shift."

"Wait," said Cael.

He opened the door and got down into the white dust before anyone could stop him, and walked to the coach's front wheel on the south side, and bent to it as if to look at the hub. Then he went down on one knee on the road and put his palm on the chalk.

He sent the read down.

It went out of him through the hand into the ground the way it went into a floor, the cheapest thing he owned and the one he trusted most. It did not read chalk the way it read a man. It read weight. The road under him was carrying the coach, four tons of it through the wheels, the horses in front, the cart's dead weight across the crown forty yards on. All of that was ordinary, and he knew the shape of ordinary.

And there were places in the cut where the ground was carrying weight and nothing stood there.

He counted them. He went round the cut with the read as carefully as he had ever gone round anything, and then he went round it again.

Fourteen.

Two on the milestone. One on each parapet of the culvert. Three in the north bank, high, where nobody could reach. Two in the south bank's lip. Three in a line across the road behind them, at the west mouth of the cut, where they had come in a minute ago. And three more in the road itself, between the coach and the cart, in a rough curve.

Each one was a weight with no body, pressed into the chalk at a single point, as if somebody very heavy were standing there on one toe. The coach had rolled over the three at the west mouth a minute ago without a jolt; they lay flush with the road like stones under the dust, waiting for whatever would be strung between them. They did not move. They did not drain anything, the way Ternhall's anchors had drunk the heat out of Karis's contacts into a floor. They were not strung across the air like the Lattice Path's lines, to be found by walking into them. They were points, and they held.

Together they made a frame. He saw its shape as he knelt there, as clearly as he had seen the chalk court on the oak. Both mouths of the cut were closed. The west mouth behind them had three points across it, and the east had the cart and the culvert and the milestone. The north bank was too high. The middle of the road was held. There was one way through the whole cut that the points did not close, and it was a channel along the foot of the south bank, under the overhanging lip, perhaps twelve feet wide, running east past the cart's tail to the culvert.

He took his hand off the road.

"Fourteen," he said.

He said it to the coach door, not loudly. Karis's face was in the window, and he saw her understand it. He saw Lira, awake now, understand it a beat after.

Then they came.

They came all at once and without any noise to speak of. A man stood up from behind the cart, where there had been no man a moment ago, and stood beside its wheel with his hands at his sides. Two more came down the north bank on ropes that had been lying ready in the grass along the top, and dropped into the ditch and stood up out of it. Two came up out of the gully beyond the culvert and walked along the parapet onto the road. Every one of them was in grey road clothes with a hood, and every one had a scarf drawn up over the lower half of the face, so that there was nothing to see of any of them but a band of skin and a pair of eyes.

They carried no blades. Cael saw that at once, because it was the first thing he looked for. They had short staves at their belts, and two of them had coils of soft rope, and the one at the cart had a pair of leather hobbles hanging from his belt, and a hood of dark cloth, folded.

And one walked out of the shadow under the south bank's lip.

She came out of the hollow at an ordinary walking pace and stopped on the crown of the road, halfway between the coach's horses and the cart, on the one flat patch where the camber levelled before it fell away to either side. She stood three-quarters turned from the coach. She had a hood and a scarf like the others. He could not see her face.

He did not need to see it. He had read her four times across forty feet of stone in the outer court six days ago, and drawn her on the oak in chalk, and written her shape in the notebook with no numbers in it. She had stood on the one level place in the court. She stood on the one level place in the cut. Every line out of the cut went past her.

The man at the cart spoke. He spoke to the coachman, not to anybody in the coach, in an even voice that carried along the chalk walls without being raised.

"Stay on the box. Nobody here wants you." He moved his head a fraction, toward the culvert. "The one we want walks east to the culvert. Nobody else is wanted. Nobody else need be touched."

There was no paper. There was no seal. There was no office, and no name, and no reason given, and no place to write any of it down.

Cael stood up out of the dust.

He looked at the hobbles and the folded hood and the soft rope, and the staves that had been chosen because they bruised and did not cut, and the six faces that were not faces. He looked at the channel along the south bank, twelve feet wide, running to the culvert. He thought of the gully beyond it, which he could not see into, and what a man would keep there if he had come to take a person somewhere.

He said it aloud, flatly, the way Rooke read a floor before a bout.

"Custody. Not assault."

He said it to the three in the coach, and he said it so they would all hear the same thing at the same time. They wanted him whole. They wanted him walking, or carried, but whole. That changed what they would and would not do to him. It did not change what they would do to anyone who stood in the way.

Brom came out of the coach on the south side.

He did not hurry. He stepped down into the dust with the two record cases, and set them on the coach step, side by side, squared, and then walked forward along the foot of the south bank, under the lip, into the channel. He stopped in the middle of it. He turned round to face the cart and the culvert and the gully, and set his feet, and stood.

He did not look at Cael. He did not need to. It was one step from there to anywhere a man might want to go.

Lira got down at the coach's tail and stood with her weight on the balls of her feet, looking at the four men by the ditch and the parapet, at their feet, not their eyes. Karis came out last, on the north side, and went to the near horse's head. The horse was standing very still. Too still. Cael saw Karis put out her hand toward its foreleg and stop, a hand's breadth short, as if she had touched a wall in the dark.

The man at the cart lifted one hand.

"On my count," he said, to his own people, and began it.

Chapter 31 — Four Exchanges

The count was slow, and the four men moved on it.

Cael had seen drills like it on the second floor, when Rooke wanted a team to learn to arrive. You did not run at your mark. You walked, and the count told you how long you had, and you timed your stride so that you came onto your mark on the last word, at the same moment as everyone else came onto theirs. Four men arriving together round a coach were not four men. They were a ring. A ring could be drawn tight by one more word.

The lead did not move. He stayed by the cart's wheel with one hand lifted, keeping the time, and sent the other four in. They came from the two ditches and the two ends, one at each corner of the coach, unhurried, with their staves still at their belts and their hands open. One. Their feet touched the chalk at the same instant. Two. The lead's voice went along the cut like a man calling a dance.

Lira went on two and a half.

He saw her go out of the corner of his eye, because he was already moving the other way. She did not go at any of them. She went to the place behind the coach where the nearest man's next stride was going to come down, and she was standing in it, feet set, when his foot arrived. He came onto her instead of onto his mark. It was not a blow. It was worse than a blow, for a man in a drill: it was the wrong ground, a beat early, and he stumbled into her and off her and lost the count.

Three.

Her second burst took her across the coach's tail and up the north camber to the ditch side, low, so fast that the dust she left behind her hung in the air in the shape of the road she had taken. The man coming up out of the ditch found her where his third stride should have been and stopped dead with his hands up.

The lead's voice did not falter. He said four. But there were only two men on their marks for it, and a ring with two men in it is a pair of men.

That was all Cael saw. He did not see the third burst or the fourth. He had his own road to take, and it went straight up the crown at the woman in the hood.

She had not moved since she came out of the hollow.

She stood on the flat patch of crown halfway between the coach's horses and the cart, three-quarters turned, with her hands loose at her sides and her weight even. She was not looking at him. She was looking at a place on the road about a pace in front of him and a little to his left. He did not understand that until later.

He went at her because she was the key. Every one of the fourteen was hers. He had felt them through his palm and he had felt whose they were, the way you can tell, without being told, that all the letters in a bundle are in one hand. If she was down, or moving, or frightened, she could not lay a fifteenth. He did not mean to hurt her. He meant to make her move.

He spent the Wind at ten paces.

It was a good burst. He had been holding the band down so long that the full thing came out of him almost with relief: the gather low in the belly, the hip loading like a drawn bow, and the shove at his back. The road came up under him. Six feet out from the place he had left, it stopped.

Not the road. Him.

He hit something in the air in front of his chest. It was not a wall, because a wall would have had an edge, and a surface, and a feel. It was a single point, about the height of his breastbone, and it did not give at all. The burst went into it and stopped there, all of it, the way a cart stops when its wheel finds a post in the dark. He went back off it onto his heels. His breath went out of him. The landing beat locked his legs where they stood, the same short pause it had always held him in, and for that pause he could do nothing but stand on the chalk with the point six inches in front of him and know it was there.

She had laid it while he was in the air.

He saw now where she had been looking. She had been looking at the place he was going to be.

He went left. He went round the point, low, with his weight forward and his left foot reaching for the crown. And his foot came down a hand's breadth short of where he had sent it, on nothing, on the air above the chalk, and stayed there. The point under it held his boot like a step. His knee took the jolt. He was standing on one leg on the road and on the other leg on air, and the air was harder than the road.

She had not lifted a hand. She had not moved her feet. She had not even turned toward him.

He came off the point and went back. He had to think.

She doesn't hit, he thought. She takes.

That was the first thing. Every fighter he had ever faced had come at him with something, a burst or a course or a lane or a fist. They had put a thing into the space between them and asked him to deal with it. She did the opposite. She took the space away. Every step he meant to take, she got there first and took the place he meant to put his foot, and left him with one less step in the world than he had had a moment before.

She was reading him. That was the second thing, and it made him cold all down his back. In the outer court he had watched her get onto a horse without the half beat, the little gathering of the body that tells you a person has decided to move. Somebody had trained it out of her. And because she had none, she could see it in everybody else. She saw his half beat. She saw where his weight was going before his weight knew it. She laid her point there and waited for him to arrive.

Somewhere at the back of him, in its sealed place, the quiet thing from the stair stirred, the way it always stirred when he was cornered, and offered to take him out of every eye in the cut.

He did not look at it. It stayed where it was.

Behind him something hit something with a sound like a sack of grain dropped off a cart.

He turned his head for the length of one breath. Two of the four had given up on the ring. They had seen where their work was, and it was not at the coach. It was in the channel along the south bank, under the lip, where the frame left its one way open to the culvert, and where Brom was standing in it.

The first of them had gone at him square. He was a heavy man, nearly Brom's height, and he had come down the channel at a run with his shoulder low. Brom had not stepped into him or away from him. He had simply been there, where the man was going, with his feet set and his arms loose and his chin in. The man had arrived. The sound had been the man arriving.

He was on the chalk now, two yards back up the channel, on one knee. Brom had not moved a foot.

That was one.

Cael turned back to her.

He had backed off two steps to think, and the two steps were gone.

He found that out when he went to take a third, and his heel came down against air. There was a point behind him now, at the height of his calf, where there had been nothing when he walked through that place. She had laid it while he was looking at Brom. He had not even felt her do it.

So that was the third thing. She did not take anything back.

Every point she had laid since he came at her was still there. The one at his breastbone. The one under his left foot. The one behind his calf. He could not see any of them. He could feel each one if he moved toward it, the way you feel furniture in a dark room by walking into it. And she was not lifting them to lay new ones. She was laying new ones as well. The space round him was the space round him minus three, and in a moment it would be minus four.

She did not need to hurry. She had all morning. She had laid fourteen before he ever came into the cut.

He tried the push.

He put his right palm flat against the point at his breastbone, where his chest had found it, and leaned, and then did not lean. He gave it the push at fighting load, the thing he had taken from the Bronze at Ardenmere, the thing he had given a Gold five times in one sitting at Norhold.

The point did not move.

He did. He went backward off his own push as if he had shoved at the side of a house. It threw him two yards along the crown to the north, faster than he could have gone on his feet, and that was useful. For a moment he was out of the pocket she had been building round him. He took it. He used the second push the same way, against the same point from a new side, and it threw him again, west, toward the coach. The third threw him back east. The point stayed where it was every time. It was the most solid thing on the road. He was using it the way a swimmer uses the side of a bath.

The fourth push came, and the right shoulder spoke, low, the way it always spoke at the fourth.

He stopped.

Four pushes and she had not taken a step. Four pushes and he was still in the cut, with three points round him and the woman where she had stood from the first, and every push had moved nobody but him.

He tried to make her move them.

He went wide, fast, toward the north ditch, as if he meant to run along it past her to the cart. She laid a point in front of him at the ditch's edge. It was further from her than any she had laid yet, and he saw what it cost her. She was still for an instant. Not the stillness of a woman waiting. The stillness of a woman doing something, the way a person goes still to thread a needle. Half a second. Less. Then she was waiting again.

He turned before he reached the point, and came back, and went wide the other way, toward the south. She laid one there. Half a second.

Range costs her, he thought. Not much. Something.

He went wide a third time, north again, and she did not lay anything at all. She simply watched him go, and when he turned to come back, the place he was turning into had a point in it, close to her, cheap.

She had learned him faster than he had learned her. She had stopped biting.

He had a moment, then, because she let him have it.

He looked round the cut for the length of a breath. Lira was on the ground.

She was at the edge of the north ditch, where the camber fell away into it, sitting in the chalk with one leg out in front of her and her hands braced behind her. She had spent four bursts. He had not seen the third or the fourth, and he did not know which had put her there. He knew only that her right foot was turned at an angle no foot was meant to hold, and that she was holding very still. One of the four stood over her, a yard off, with his stave across his body in both hands. He did not touch her. He did not need to. He stood between her and the coach and looked at her, and she looked back at him.

Custody. Not assault. They did not want her. They wanted her out of the way.

At the near horse, Karis had her right hand flat in the air a hand's breadth above the animal's foreleg, as if she were warming it at a fire.

He knew what she was doing as soon as he saw it, because he had heard her explain the difference on the night of the gate, counting the words off on her fingers. Ternhall's anchors were her own, three footholds that drank the heat of a contact down into a floor. The Lattice Path was lines strung across the air. These were neither. These were points, and they held. But something ran between them. When she had put her hand out to the horse's leg she had found it, the way you find a rope across a dark yard: a line, taut, between the point fixed against the horse's foreleg and one of the fourteen in the bank. And she had put her heat into it.

It frayed.

He could not see it. He saw the horse's leg shift, a finger's breadth, as if somebody had cut one strand of a halter. He saw Karis's face, set and white, and her right hand, and the skin of her fingers going red from the tips down. She moved the hand an inch along the line she could not see and put her heat into it again.

The man Lira had stopped at the ditch stood two yards off from her at the off horse's head, with his stave held across his body in both hands. He had been given the coach, plainly, once the ring was gone: the horses, the driver, whoever stood by them. He was watching Karis's hands. When the second strand went and the horse's leg shifted again, he took one step toward her and then stopped, as if he had remembered his orders, and only watched. Custody. He was not there to touch anybody who was not wanted.

The coachman sat on his box with his reins in his hands and could not let go of them. He was talking to his horses in the same low steady voice he always used. His hands were held where they were, in the air in front of him, as if he were driving a coach that was not moving.

Brom was still in the channel.

The second man came at him while Cael was watching. He was lighter than the first, and quicker, and he had learned from the first. He did not come at Brom square. He came at the left side, low, and at the last stride turned and drove his shoulder up into Brom's left shoulder from underneath, with his whole weight behind it, the way a man drives a post into a hole.

Brom took it.

Cael heard it. He heard Iron Skin hold, a flat dense sound like a hammer on an anvil with a cloth over it. And under that sound, smaller, he heard something else, a click and a give, and saw Brom's left arm drop an inch at the elbow and not come back. Brom's face did not change. His feet did not move. The man came off him and went down on the chalk and stayed down.

That was two.

Brom stood in the channel with his left arm hanging a little and looked at the culvert, and the gully, and the cart. He did not look at his shoulder. He had told the kitchen once that a man who looks at a hurt only teaches it to be looked at.

Cael went at her a third time, because he had one thing left he had not tried, and it was the fastest thing he owned.

He would lay a lane.

He would put it down the north side of the crown, past her, along the camber, from where he stood to the cart, fifteen feet of leaning air. She could lay her points where he was going to be. Let her try it at the speed a lane went. He would be past her before she had finished threading the needle.

He set his feet and asked the air to lean.

It leaned. He felt the whole cut give a little along one line, as a board gives when you step on its end. His ears closed and opened. The chalk dust woke up on the crown and ran in a thin white stream along the line he had laid, east, past her, toward the cart.

And the read went out of him.

He had known it would. It was the rule. At Gold weight the read took the air or the body, one or the other, never both; you laid the lane first and then you gave the read back, and it came back to you in a breath or two if you let it. He had no breath or two. He stepped into the lane's downhill with the read still out in the air somewhere and nothing to tell him where her points were but his own memory of them.

The lane carried him. The road came at him faster than his feet had any right to bring it.

Eight feet on there was a point at the height of his ribs.

He did not feel it until he was in it. He went into it at the lane's full speed on the right side, low, and the whole of his weight and the whole of the lane's went into one place at the bottom of his ribs. It did not give. He did. He heard himself make a sound. Then he was off the lane and off his feet and rolling, across the crown, down the south camber, over and over, with the chalk and the grit coming up at him white, and he put his left arm out to stop himself because there was nothing else to put out.

The road took the skin off it. He felt it go from the wrist to the elbow, a long hot scrape, as if somebody had drawn a rasp up the inside of his forearm. He came to rest on his side at the bottom of the camber, a few yards short of the channel, with his face in the dust and his right side one solid ache.

And then the bill came in.

Ten counts. It always came after a lane, since Norhold, and it came now: everything he owned answering a beat late. The right thing, slow. Bill, not flag, Lira had written in her palm on the honest floor. He tried to get his hands under him and they got there a beat after he asked. He tried to turn his head to find her and his neck turned a beat after that.

One.

She laid a point.

He felt it go in, near his left shoulder, against the chalk.

Two. Another, at his feet.

Three. Four.

He lay there and counted them in as they came, one for each of his slow counts, because counting was the only thing left that came when he called. Five. Six. She was not hurrying even now. She was laying them the way a mason lays a course of bricks, each one on the last, close round him, closer. Seven.

On the eighth count he got his right hand to the nearest of them, flat, and gave it the spark.

It went out of him the way it always did, like a word. The flint smell came up off the chalk. And he felt the point fray, a little, as the horse's line had frayed under Karis's hand: one thread of it, gone. Then the rest of it held. The spark needed something to burn, and the point had almost nothing in it to burn, and he had two contacts in him and no more.

Nine. Ten.

Eleven, and the bill was paid, and everything answered when he called it.

He was on his knees on the south camber, with his left arm on fire from wrist to elbow and his right side not working properly, and he gave the read back to himself, at last, slowly, and let it go down through his knees into the road.

There was a cage round him.

He felt every bar of it. They were not the fourteen; the fourteen were still out in the cut where they had always been, at the mouths and in the banks and on the milestone. These were new. They were close. They stood round him at the height of his knees and his shoulders and his head, a ring of points two feet off on every side, and above him, and on the chalk under him. He counted them twice. Nineteen.

And there was one more, and it was not on the ground.

It was against the front of his coat.

He had been carrying it since the first exchange. He understood that now, kneeling. When his chest had found the point at his breastbone she had not only stopped him. She had laid a second point against him, against the cloth over Hesk's book, so lightly that he had taken it for the bruise of hitting the first one. It went where he went. It had gone with him on every push and every turn and down the camber. It was the first point of the cage, and every other point in the cage was laid from it, and to it, and through it, the way every stitch in a row of knitting is worked through the stitch before.

He could feel the lines now, faintly, through the read. They ran from the point on his coat out to the nineteen round him, and from the nineteen out to the fourteen in the cut, and from all of them, all of them, back to her. She stood on her flat patch of crown fifteen feet away with every line in the cut running into her two loose hands like the reins of a team.

Three more, and it would close. He could feel exactly where. Three gaps, one at his left shoulder, one at his right hip, one over his head. When those three were laid, the cage would stop being a cage and start being a hold. A person inside a closed hold did not walk to a culvert. He was carried there, quite gently, by people who did not need to touch him at all.

She would lay them in the next three breaths. She had all the breaths she wanted.

He went down the line. He did it in the time it took to draw one breath, the way he went down a rotation page before a bout.

One. The conditions are not to be made. He had not made this road. The river had made it, and somebody who read rivers.

Two. A reach only inside a fight the other begins, in earnest, awake, and on purpose. She had begun it. She had been beginning it since before the coach came out of the ferry. Nobody had ever been more in earnest. And he was awake, as awake as he had ever been, on his knees in the white dust with his arm on fire.

Three. The whole cost on paper first. It was on paper. It was in the book against his chest, under her point, on a leaf with four sets of initials and a line in capitals pressed through to the back. At Silver weight. Brom for the minute.

He did it with his eyes open.

He knelt in the cage and held still, all of him, in front of four exchanges of her. That was all it had ever been. Not taking anything. He turned everything he had left toward what he had watched her do, and kept it there, open. Subtraction. The points laid where his half beat said he would go. The stillness of a woman threading a needle at the edge of her reach, half a second's price for range. The accumulation that never gave anything back. The stitch against his coat, and everything worked through it. He had paid for every one of those in his own body on this road, and he knew them now as well as he knew the stair to his own room with the lamps out.

They came together.

It was quiet. It did not come down on him like the storm had come, all at once and too heavy. It came in like a key going into a lock it had been cut for. And then he could see.

Not with his eyes. He could see the lines.

Every course in the cut stood out to him as plainly as the chalk dust had stood out along his lane: taut grey threads in the air, from point to point to point, a great slack net laid down the whole length of the road, closed at both ends, open in one channel where Brom stood. He saw the nineteen round him, each with its line to the next. He saw the one against his coat, the first stitch, with every other line in the cage worked through it. And he saw how it was held. It was held from inside, from where it touched him. It was the same thing as the point at his breastbone and the one under the horse's leg and the ones that held the coachman's hands. It was a thing set against a surface and told to stay.

From inside, he could tell it not to.

He let it go.

It went the way you let go of a breath you have been holding without knowing it. The point against his coat was simply not there any more. And because every other point in the cage had been laid through it, they went after it, one after another, in the order she had laid them, unthreading round him in a quick soft ripple like a row of stitches coming out when the first is pulled. The nineteen went. Their lines went out to the fourteen in the cut, and the fourteen went too. He felt them go down the road behind him like a rope paying out over a wheel: the three across the west mouth, the two in the south bank's lip, the three high in the north bank, the parapets, the milestone.

The near horse threw up its head and stamped, and stood on all four legs again as a horse should. The coachman's hands came down into his lap with the reins in them.

Karis looked at her own hand in the air above nothing, and took it back.

She felt it in her hands.

He saw that. He was still on his knees and he saw her feel her whole morning go out through her fingers, fourteen points laid before light and every one she had laid since, all of them at once. She did not stagger. She did not make a sound. Her two loose hands closed, slowly, as if somebody had pulled a rope out of them faster than she could hold it.

She lifted two fingers of her left hand.

The team broke off in four heartbeats.

He counted them, because it was the last thing he could do. On one the man standing over Lira turned his back on her and went for the north bank, and the one at the off horse's head let go of his stave with one hand and went after him at a run. On two the two men in the channel were on their feet and going, the second holding his own arm, past Brom, who let them past, into the gully beyond the culvert. On three the man at the cart was gone behind it, and the ropes on the north bank were taking weight. On four there was nobody on the road at all but the four of them and the coachman and the horses.

And her.

She was last. She stood on her patch of crown with her hands closed and looked at him.

It lasted one second. He could see nothing of her face but the band of skin between the hood and the scarf and the two eyes in it. They were grey, and steady, and not angry. He had braced for anger. It was not there. It was the look of somebody who has spent her whole life on one craft and has just watched it done backward, in front of her, by a boy on his knees in the dust, and is trying to see how.

Then she turned and went up the north bank on the rope, hand over hand, without the half beat, and over the top into the grass, and was gone.

He knelt in the road. The wind came along the cut from the west and blew the chalk dust off the crown in a long white skirl and carried it away east over the culvert.

Brom was walking toward him down the channel, with his left arm hanging.

The minute was coming. Cael could feel it coming, everything in him beginning to lean toward the new thing, as a crowded room leans toward somebody who has just come in. He did not try to stand. He knelt in the white dust and let it come, and Brom got there first, and stood over him, and did not say anything at all.

Chapter 32 — Road Dust

The minute was exactly as long as Norhold's, and nothing like it.

At Norhold the wrong thing had answered. Here nothing answered at all. He knelt in the dust and called his own legs, out of habit, to get him up, and the calling went out of him and found nobody at home. The Wind did not lift its head. The read lay where he had left it. Everything he carried had turned, all together and very politely, to look at the new thing standing in the doorway, and none of them was listening to him.

It did not hurt. It was like being in a house where every clock has stopped at once.

Brom stood over him with his left arm hanging and his right hand open at his side, and did not say anything, and did not touch him. He stood the way he had stood in the channel. Anybody coming down the road would have had to come through him first. Nobody came. The wind went along the cut and the horses blew and stamped and the coachman talked to them. Somewhere down the bank the river roared through the narrows.

Then, one by one, the things he carried turned round again and looked at him.

The read came first, as it always did. Then the Wind, a stir low in the belly. Then the rest. He called his legs and they came. He got one foot under him, and then the other, and Brom put out his right hand and Cael took it and came up off the chalk onto his feet.

"That's the minute," said Brom.

"That's the minute."

Brom looked at him a moment longer to be sure. Then he let go and went to see to Lira.

He sat down on the lip of the south bank above the hollow, where she had come out of the shadow, because his legs had decided that for him. The chalk was cold through his clothes. Below him on the river side the hill fell away through hawthorn and willow to the brown water, and he could see a long way down the valley toward the city, the flat land shining with floodwater in long strips, and a smudge of smoke on the far edge of it that was Ostrand.

It had been waiting for him since he held still on his knees, as it always waited. It came to the place behind his eyes that belonged to nothing else, and stayed there, patient as a clerk, until he had a moment to look. He looked now.

He read it through twice. Then he counted, because he could not help it.

Eight.

Silver, it said. It was the first notice that had ever said Silver. The guess on the leaf had been right; he had priced it at the weight it came at. Anchor-adjacent, it said, and he thought of Seln at the long table with his eyes shut, saying the name, and Karis counting the words off on her fingers, keeping them straight. Fixed-point binding. That was the thing against his coat, and the thing he had let go of. Lattice-perception. That was the grey net he had seen laid down the whole cut, which he could not see now at all. Contact-to-short range. Close to her, cheap. Further off, at a price he had watched her pay, half a second at a time.

And at the top, where a name went, unnamed.

Every other notice he had ever read had come out of somebody he could have walked up to afterward. Lira, Brom, a Bronze at Ardenmere, Reydan, Karis, Seln on a stair, and Daeva on the stone, holding out her hand. He could have found every one of them, and some of them he had, and thanked them, or not thanked them, or simply known where they were. He had a line in the old volume for every one of those people.

This one had come out of a band of skin between a hood and a scarf, and a pair of grey eyes, and two loose hands, and it had gone up a rope over the top of the north bank and into the grass. He would never know her name. Nobody would ever write to him that she had been posted, or moved, or retired to a garden. Somebody somewhere had a posting roll with her on it, and that somebody had sent her to this road with no paper so that there would be nothing for anybody to find.

He had taken a piece of the thing they sent. That was the plain fact of it, and he sat with it on the chalk a while.

The bills came in round him while he sat there.

Brom was on his knees in the dust at the edge of the north ditch with Lira's foot in his lap. He had the kit bag open beside him, the one Lira had laughed at the night before, and he was strapping the ankle one-handed, with the linen held in his teeth. His left arm hung. Every time he needed to pull the strapping tight he did it with the right hand and his knee, and he did not once ask anybody to help him. Lira lay back on her elbows and watched him do it, white to the mouth.

"Four," she said.

Nobody had asked her. She said it to the sky.

"Four bursts. On chalk. That's the road's whole free budget and not one over it. I counted." She shut her eyes. "The ankle wasn't the bursts. The ankle was the ditch. I came down on the edge of the camber where it falls off, and the edge went." She opened them again. "Write it down that way. I want it right."

"I'll write it that way," said Cael, from the bank.

"Good." She looked at Brom's arm. "And that?"

"Shoulder," said Brom, round the strapping. "Left. It's in. It was out for a heartbeat and it went back in by itself when he came off me." He tied the knot with his teeth and his right hand. "A week. It's had worse." Then he sat back on his heels and, with the same right hand, without thinking about it, reached across under his coat and felt the left inside pocket, where the sealed letter was. Cael watched his face as he found it there. Then Brom took the hand away and put it on Lira's strapped foot and left it there.

Karis had gone down the gully to the culvert. She came back up it with her right hand wrapped in her own wet handkerchief and held up in front of her like something she had been asked to carry and must not drop. The fingers that stuck out of the end of the wrapping were red to the second knuckle and already shining. She sat down on the parapet beside the milestone, which said seven, and took her notebook out of her coat with her left hand, and opened it on her knee, and wrote something with the pencil in her left hand, slowly, the letters going wide and childish.

Cael could read it from the bank. It was one word.

Fourth.

She had kept a count of her hand's ignition margin since Greyvane. Three times before, she had pushed her heat past where the skin could take it, and three times it had healed, and she had logged every one in this notebook in her small exact hand. The fourth was in her right hand, and it was enormous, and it was crooked. She looked at it for a moment and did not try to make it neater.

The coachman had got down off his box. He was walking the near horse up and down the road between the coach and the cart, slowly, with his hand on its neck, talking to it. The horse's foreleg had been held by a point for most of the fight. It was trembling. The coachman walked it, and talked, and kept his eyes on the horse. Once, passing the bank where Cael sat, he said without stopping, "Twenty-two years I've driven this coach," in exactly the tone he used for the horses, and walked on.

Cael sat on the bank and looked at all of them.

They had come for him. Every one of the six had been there for him, and no one else. The hobbles were for him and the hood was for him and the wagon in the gully, wherever it was, had a door that was meant to shut on him. And the four people he had come here with had paid for every yard of the road. Lira had paid in an ankle, Brom in a shoulder, Karis in a hand she would have to write with for a week. Even the coachman's horse had paid, standing there trembling with the coachman's hand on its neck.

He had paid in an arm and some ribs. He had also been given a thing that a Silver had spent her life on. He did not think that came out even.

He did not know yet what to do with that. He put it away, carefully, with the other things, where he would be able to find it.

Seln came up out of the culvert with an iron pin in his hand.

Nobody saw him come. One moment the gully beyond the culvert was empty, a cleft of wet stone with the stream running white down it, and the next Seln was standing on the parapet beside Karis with water to his knees and his coat dark with it. He had a long iron pin in his right hand, the length of a man's forearm and thicker than a thumb, with a ring through the head of it.

He looked round the cut once, at all of them. At Lira's foot in Brom's lap. At Brom's arm. At Karis's wrapped hand and the word in her notebook. At the coachman walking the horse. At Cael on the bank, with the left sleeve of his coat torn open from the wrist to the elbow and the arm under it raw and white with chalk.

"There's a wagon in the gully," he said. "Closed. Barred at the back, with a bench inside and two rings in the floor. They'd tied the horses a little way up the stream, out of sight of the road." He weighed the pin in his hand. "They took the horses when they went. They didn't take the wagon. It won't go anywhere without this."

"The linchpin," said Brom.

"The off-side one." Seln looked at it as if it were a thing he had found on a beach. "I was under the wagon when they came back down the gully. They walked past it. Nobody looked under it. Nobody looks under a wagon." He turned and dropped the pin into the ditch on the north side, where it went into the mud without a sound and did not come up. "I didn't see anything up here. The bank was in the way. I heard it."

He did not say what he had heard, and he did not ask how it had ended. He looked at Cael on the bank for perhaps one breath longer than he looked at anything else.

"Ribs?" he said.

"Right side."

"Then sit there. Don't lift anything."

He went down the road to help the coachman with the near horse.

Cael watched him go. All morning, from the ferry landing to now, Seln had not been in a single place where anybody on the road could see him. He had not been in a single place where the team could see him. He had not been in a single place where Cael could see him either, and Cael had looked, once, during the third exchange, down the bank toward the willows, and found nothing but willows. The six had come to this road expecting five people and a coachman. They had counted four. The fifth had been underneath their wagon with his hand on its pin.

He took Hesk's book out of his coat.

The leather was warm from his body. There was a small mark on the cover, over the place where the book lay against his ribs, a faint dull patch in the grain as if a thumb had pressed there for a long time. He looked at it and knew what had made it. He did not try to rub it out.

He found the pencil and a clean leaf near the back and wrote it on the bank, with the chalk dust drying white on his hand and the wind turning the pages under his wrist.

Eight. Taken from someone the system sent namelessly, to hold me namelessly. No paper. No seal. No office to write to, not even a false one this time. She stood in the road and did the best thing she knew how to do, and I took it off her, and she'll go home tonight to wherever they keep her and nobody will ask her how her day was. A hand and no face. I don't know what I owe someone I can't find. I don't know if owing is the word. Write it down anyway.

He read it back.

Then, under it, smaller:

The bills: Lira, the right ankle (the ditch, not the bursts; she wants it written that way). Brom, the left shoulder, out and in. Karis, the right hand, the fourth. Me, the left forearm, the right ribs. The coachman's near horse. Seln, nothing anyone saw. The leaf said Brom for the minute. Brom was there for the minute.

He shut the book and put it back inside his coat, against his ribs, where it had been.

The coachman had the horses back in the traces. Brom lifted Lira into the coach in his one good arm as if she weighed nothing, and set her on the seat with her foot up on the record cases, and got in after her. Karis climbed in holding her hand up. Seln shut the door behind them.

Cael got up off the bank, slowly, and walked down to the coach while the coachman and Seln saw to the cart.

It took them a quarter of an hour. The wheel had not broken. It had been unpinned and laid down, and it went back on in two minutes, and then the coachman put his shoulder to the cart and ran it back off the crown into the gully mouth beside the culvert, where it stood beside nothing. Cael did not look down the gully. He knew what was down there. There was a wagon with a bench in it and two rings in its floor, and no pin. Seln climbed up onto the box beside the coachman and sat there in his wet coat, looking down the road toward the city, and Cael got in.

They drove out of the east end of the cut, over the culvert, past the milestone. Behind them the white dust settled on the road where it had been.

The first one came a mile short of the city, at the toll-bar.

The bar was a long white pole on a pivot across the road, where the river road came in off the flats to the west gate. The coachman stopped for the keeper to raise it. The keeper came out of his box with his hand out for the toll, and the bar went up, and swung, and came to rest against its post. And as it touched the post, something in Cael said, very quietly and with great courtesy, There?

He did not know at first what it was asking.

Then he did. It was asking whether he would like the bar fixed there, against its post, where it had come to rest. It would be no trouble, and it was a good place. The bar was resting against a surface, and the new thing in him knew exactly how to set a point against a surface and tell it to stay, and it was offering, as politely as a clerk at the elbow, to do so.

No, he thought.

The offer went away at once, without argument, the way a clerk goes away when you shake your head. The keeper took his toll and the coach went under the bar and on.

He sat back against the seat and listened to himself, and found it was not gone. It was quiet, and waiting, and it had found out that he could hear it.

The west gate. The long street of warehouses by the river, every cellar door open and men with buckets. The market street, steep and wet. The four steps of the wool exchange and the side door in its flank. The coachman took them round into the exchange's yard by the stable arch, so that they would not have to get down in front of the steps, and drew up under the wall, and set the brake.

Over the yard's far roof the exchange's clock stood at five minutes before the hour. The sitting was at the hour.
