Nobody moved to open the door.

"We tell them," said Lira.

She was sitting with her strapped foot on the record cases and her back in the corner and her face still white, and she said it before anybody else could say anything. "Six people with hobbles and a wagon with rings in the floor tried to take him off a road this morning, two hours from here. The seat's sitting in there. Somebody in that room should write it down."

"Who?" said Brom.

"The clerk. The hood. Anybody."

"And then what?" Brom did not say it unkindly. "What does anybody in that room do with it? They write it down. Then what?"

Lira opened her mouth and shut it again.

"The coachman will tell the stables tonight," said Seln, from the open trap, without turning round. "The stables will tell the town by the end of the week. That's a record. It's the only one that'll get written that anybody reads."

Karis had her wrapped hand in her lap and her eyes on the clock across the yard. She did not look away from it while she spoke.

"Think how it reads," she said. "Not how it happened. How it reads, on a minute, at a seat, in that room. The respondent arrives at a documentary sitting the seat asked for him in person, with chalk to his knees and his advocate's hand in a wet cloth. He says that on the way here, this morning, on the only road open, six people he cannot name, whose faces he did not see, with no paper and no seal and no office, tried to take him into custody, and failed, and left. His witnesses are the four people who came with him and a coachman in the house's pay." She stopped. "No faces. No names. No paper. No wagon, by tonight, I'd wager, if anybody went to look. On the morning of a sitting, six days after the house turned away an order at its gate and made the order look sinister." She did turn then, and looked at all of them. "It reads as manufactured theater. Jent wouldn't even have to say so. He'd be kind about it. Everybody in the room would be kind about it, and every weekly in four towns would print it by the Fourth-day under a woodcut of the gate."

The clock across the yard moved its hand on.

"She's right," said Brom at last. He said it to his own knees, heavily. "I hate it. She's right."

Lira looked at Cael.

He had not said anything yet. He had been sitting with his arm across his knees and his ribs telling him about the eight feet of lane he had ridden into a point, and listening, and he found that he had known how it would come out before Karis had finished her second sentence. He did not like knowing it. He knew it anyway.

"She's right," he said. "We don't tell them."

Lira held his eyes a moment longer. Then she nodded, once, and looked away out of the window, and he saw her jaw set the way it set when she was holding a count.

The clock stood at the hour less one minute. Four minutes, from We tell them to the nod. He had counted them without meaning to.

"Then we go in," said Karis, "and we do what they asked us to do, exactly, and nothing else."

The young officer at the side door had his door log open on its board, and he had already written the first name on today's page before they reached him, because he had written it at every sitting since the year began. He looked up to write the second and stopped with the pen lifted.

Then he wrote the second, and the third, and did not ask anything. Cael watched him decide not to. It was the most courteous thing anybody did all afternoon.

The house's counsel was waiting just inside, in her grey coat, with her bag and her steel rule. She had come up from her rooms by the wharf in the morning before the water reached the market steps. She looked at them as they came in out of the light, one at a time, the way she read a paper, from the end up: at Lira on Brom's arm with one foot strapped; at Brom's left arm hanging; at Karis's hand; at Cael's sleeve; at the chalk on every one of them to the knee, white as millers.

She asked one thing.

"Is there anybody I need to send for?"

"No," said Karis.

The counsel nodded, once. She turned her steel rule over in her fingers, a quarter turn, the way she did at the end of every part of an argument. Then she went ahead of them into the long room.

It was smaller today. That was what Cael noticed first. The benches were half empty; a documentary sitting drew no correspondents. Up on the platform the five chairs of the evaluation seat stood under their grey covers, as they had stood at the first sitting, before the seat was called. Lot seventeen was carved into the floor under his foot. The hood was in its place.

At the records table Havel sat in the junior chair with the times and the receipts, and wrote the minute they came in.

The seat's clerk read the designation. Then he read the contents leaf of the records the house had produced, bundle by bundle, in the house's boards, from the first card of the year to the last.

"The maker of the copies," he said.

Seln stood. He stood with his wet coat buttoned and his hands at his sides, and the chalk drying grey on his knees.

"Are these copies made by you, and true to their originals?"

"I made them," said Seln. "They are true." And then, because Karis had asked him to on the stair, "On the card for the Fourth-day of the seventh week the original carries a correction in the desk clerk's hand. I copied the corrected figure and noted both in the margin."

The clerk wrote it. The hood did not move.

"The enrollee of record."

Cael stood. His ribs told him about it.

"Are the figures recorded in these copies your own figures, earned on the house's floors?"

"They are mine," said Cael.

That was all it asked. It did not ask whether they were all of him. Nobody had ever asked that, and the form had no line for it.

"The advocate of record."

Karis went up to the clerk's table and signed the receipt leaf with her left hand. Cael watched the pen go. Her name came out wide and slanting and unlike itself. She looked at it on the page, did not try to make it neater, and gave the pen back.

The seat initialled where the clerk's finger pointed. It rose.

Jent had sat at his table through all of it with his spectacles on their black cord and his travelling inkwell shut, and said nothing, because a documentary sitting gave the petitioner nothing to say. As the long room emptied he gathered his single folder and came along behind their table toward the door, and stopped by Cael's chair, and looked at the chalk on Cael's sleeve and on Lira's strapped boot and on all their knees.

He said it pleasantly, in the voice a man uses about the weather across a counter.

"Roads are poor this month."

Cael looked up at him and sent the read.

He did it out of habit, the way he had read Jent at the conference and at every sitting since, four times, and found nothing four times. He found nothing now. The man stood there in his brown coat with the mended cuffs, middle height and middle years, with a pleasant remark about the weather on his face, and there was nothing on him at all. There was no weight laid down anywhere, and no grain of hiding. It was not that Jent was hiding what he knew. It was that there was nobody in the coat for the read to find, only a procurator of record, doing the job he had been sent to do, courteously.

He might have known. He might have had no idea. There was no way, from the outside, to tell which. That was the whole point of him.

"They are," said Cael.

Jent nodded, as if that were the right answer to something, and went out.

He stayed in his chair a moment after the others had stood. Brom was helping Lira up. Karis was packing the wallet one-handed. Seln was already at the door. The long room was nearly empty, the clerk sanding his minute, Havel blotting the last line in his receipt book.

Cael sat with the chalk on his knees and looked at the room.

He had believed in it. He saw that now, sitting in it, the way you see the shape of a thing only when you are about to put it down. All year he had believed in this room. Not the hood, and not Jent, but the room: the text on the clerk's table, and the code in its three volumes, and the provisions with their dates in them, and the minute that went up under the hood and came back initialled. He had written it into Hesk's book on the first night of the year in his best hand. The system has text, and text has held me every time the people failed. He had stood in a dairy with the slate wall behind him and defended it at full strength. He had brought receipts to this room all year, and when the room would not take them he had gone on bringing them, because the room was the system and the system had text.

This morning the system had sent six people and a wagon with rings in its floor down a chalk road two hours from here, and none of them had had a single word of text on them anywhere.

It had not stopped being the system when it did that. It had not stepped outside itself. It had simply used its other hand. The hand with the paper had been in this room all year, initialling where the clerk pointed, and the hand without the paper had been out on the road, and they had been the same body all along, and he had only ever been watching one of them.

The room had never been the system. It had been one room. The system had as many as it liked.

He did not feel anything break. He had expected, if it ever came, that it would break like a bone, with a noise. It went like the cage had gone on the road: one stitch, and then all the rest after it, quietly, in the order they had been laid. Every receipt he had ever counted was still true. Every one of them was still in the book. They simply did not hold anything up any more.

He got up out of the chair. Havel did not look at him. The clerk did not look at him. He went out of the long room after the others, with the chalk on his knees, into the afternoon.

The water was under the second ring by dusk, and the bridge-ward took the chain off.

They came home the short way, over Ostrand bridge and along the river street and up the bluff road, as Withrow had told them to, with the lamps lit and the river still loud and brown beside them but lower, much lower, with a long tide-line of sticks and froth on the stones where it had been. At the ferry landing the two coats stood in their places in the last of the light. One of them watched the coach go by. He was not looking at Cael. He was looking at Lira's strapped boot, which she had up on the seat by the window, and he went on looking at it until the coach had passed.

Withrow heard it in her office, standing, with her back to the fire.

She did not interrupt them. Karis told it, in order, and Cael put in the parts Karis had not seen, and Brom said nothing, and Lira said the thing about the ditch. When they were done Withrow stood a long moment with her hands behind her back. Then she went to her desk and took out a small book bound in black cloth that was not the house's book, and opened it, and wrote one line in it, standing, and blotted it, and shut it.

"That is mine," she said, "and nobody reads it. It will stay there until somebody gives me a better place to put it." She looked at Karis's hand, and at Lira's boot. "Go to the infirmary. All of you. Now. That is not a request."

They went.

The house's healer was a spare grey woman who had strapped every fighter on the hill for twenty years and had long ago stopped asking how anybody had come by anything. She looked at the five of them in her doorway, in their chalk, and sent Seln away at once, because there was nothing wrong with him but wet knees, and set the other four out along her benches in the order she meant to deal with them.

Lira's ankle first. She unwound Brom's strapping, looked at it, said that whoever had done it had done it properly and should have been a healer, and did it again exactly the same way, tighter. Six days, she said, and a crutch, and no floor until Rooke had seen her walk across one without thinking about it. Then Brom's shoulder, which she moved in her two hands in four directions while he looked at the wall, and said had been out and gone back in by itself, which it ought not to have been able to do, and put in a sling. Then Karis's hand, which she held under the lamp for a long time without saying anything, and dressed with something that smelled of honey, and wrapped, and told Karis not to write with for five days, at which Karis only held up her left.

Cael last. She washed the chalk out of the forearm with warm water, which hurt more than the road had, and dressed it and bound it from the wrist to the elbow. Then she put her cool fingers on his right side, low, and pressed in three places, and listened to him not say anything.

"Cracked," she said. "Two, I think. Not through. Eight days in strapping, and you'll know about every one of them." She began to wind the linen. "Chalk," she said, to herself, and that was the only question she asked.

That night, at the sill, with his arm dressed and bound and his ribs strapped and the lamp turned low, he did not write a second pole. He had thought he might. He sat with the pen over the page and found he had nothing to put on it yet, only the one thing, and he wrote that, by itself, under the eighth's line.

The room was never the system.

Chapter 33 — Fixity

Brom brought the floor schedule up with his breakfast, in his head, because he could not carry a tray and a sheet of paper with one arm.

"Seln's put up next week's schedule," he said. "This morning, before the bell. A day early. He's never once put it up early." He set the tray on the end of the bed, carefully, and lowered himself into the chair, more carefully. His left arm was strapped across his chest in a sling the infirmary had made out of a triangle of linen and a great deal of disapproval. "There's one line in the First-day column. Ephram, the Crown yard, from the second bell."

"And the five?"

"Gone over to the coming Fourth-day. Five floors, five names, a quarter of an hour apart, the same as before." Brom took a piece of bread off the tray and ate half of it. "And there's a new line against wing three. Hesk-ward: excused (ribs). In his fair hand. I watched three people read it and not one of them read anything into it but ribs."

"Ephram?"

"Ephram read it twice." Brom finished the bread. "Then he took his chart out of the captain's file and made a mark on it, standing at the board, and put it back. I don't know what mark. A gap, I'd guess. He's a man who writes down gaps."

Cael lay back against the pillow and looked at the ceiling.

Seln had moved it three days, without a word to anybody, the morning after the road. He had read the coach's arrival and the infirmary's lamps and the five of them coming up the stair with chalk on their knees, and he had gone to the wing before the first bell and copied out the coming week's schedule fair a day before it was due, with five lines moved. He had not asked whether Cael was well enough. He had not asked anything. He had simply moved the day to where a man with strapped ribs would be able to climb a stair, and posted it on three doors, where it looked like nothing.

"The coming Fourth-day," said Cael.

"The day after your birthday," said Brom. "Lira will have told him. She tells people things when she thinks it'll save them asking." He looked at the tray. "Eat that. The rota's on the door."

It was; Cael could see it from the bed. Brom had written it on the back of yesterday's floor schedule, in his heavy square letters, and nailed it to the inside of the door with one nail through the top, at eye height, where nobody coming in could miss it.

BROM, LIRA, KARIS, TWO HOURS EACH BY THE CLOCK ON THE SILL, AND THEN AGAIN FROM THE TOP.

And underneath, smaller, as if he had thought of it afterward:

SOMEBODY IN THE ROOM. ALWAYS.

The first one that morning came at the door.

Brom had left it ajar when he came in with the tray, a hand's breadth open, and the door had swung to on its own weight and stopped against its frame without latching. And as it touched the frame, something at the back of Cael said, quietly and with great courtesy, There?

No, he thought.

It went away.

It had been doing that since the toll-bar. All the way home in the coach, all through the infirmary with its basins and its lamp and the healer's cool hands on his ribs, all the night at the sill. There? It never pushed. It never repeated itself once it had been answered. It simply noticed, every time one thing came to rest against another, that here was a surface and here was a thing touching it, and that it knew how to set a point between them and tell it to stay, and it asked whether he would like that done. It was the most polite thing he had ever carried. It was like having a clerk at his elbow who wanted only to be useful and had been told to ask about everything.

It asked about the door against its frame, and the cup on its saucer on the tray, and the tray on the end of the bed, and the bed's foot where it stood against the wall, and the book on the sill and the lamp on the book and Brom's boot where it rested against the leg of the chair, one after another, each as it came to his notice. There? There? There? And he said no to every one.

Each refusal cost him a little, not much, about what it costs to say no to a child who has asked for the fifth time whether it can come too. But they added up, as small things did, and by the third bell his head was tired in a way his body was not.

Karis came at the fifth bell with her notebook and her right hand still wrapped, and sat at the foot of the bed, and asked him how many.

"How many what?"

"How many times it's asked." She had a sheet of squared paper on the notebook's back board and a pencil in her left hand. "You've been saying no under your breath since I came in. I can see your mouth. I want a count."

He had not known his mouth was moving.

"I don't know. A lot."

"Then we'll find out." She drew a line across the top of the sheet and wrote the bell beside it. "Every time it asks, lift a finger. Don't say anything. I'll make the marks." She looked at him. "I can't write well with this hand. I can make marks."

So he lifted a finger, and she made a mark, and he lifted a finger, and she made another. By the end of her shift the first two lines on the sheet each had about forty marks on them, in rows of five with a stroke through, in her slanting left-handed scrawl.

"Forty an hour," she said. "Near enough." She studied the marks. "It's courteous, isn't it."

"How do you know?"

"Because you keep nodding when you say no." She turned the pencil over. "You only do that when somebody's being polite to you and you don't want to hurt their feelings."

Lira saw it before he felt it.

She was in the chair for her shift a little before noon, with her strapped foot up on a stool and her crutch against the wall and Rooke's red drill-book open on her knee, and she stopped reading and looked at the sill. In the corner of it, where the porter's girl never quite reached with her cloth, a little drift of grey dust had woken up and begun to run along the edge of the wood toward the window frame in a thin stream, as if the sill had tipped.

Then his ears closed and opened, and he knew. Something large in him had lifted its head: the great slow weight that had lain quiet since the dawn on the second floor, raising itself to look at whatever had just come into the house. The air in the room changed its weight, not much, the way air does before thunder.

"Is that you?"

"It's the storm."

"Doing what?"

"Moving." He lay still and let it. It was not the pull of the old days, the wrong thing answering, the coat caught on the nail. Nothing answered him at all; he had not called anything. It was more as if a great iron chest in the cellar of a house had begun, very slowly, to shift itself along the wall to make room for another chest beside it, and he could hear the scrape through the floorboards. "It's making room."

She watched the dust run. Then she took a stub of pencil out of her pocket and wrote on her palm, which she had done on the honest floor all year.

"Bill or flag?" he said.

"Bill, not flag," she said, and stopped, and looked at what she had written, and rubbed it out with her thumb. "No. I don't know. It's not answering wrong. It's not answering late. It's not answering at all, it's just moving." She looked at him honestly. "I don't know which. I'll write that."

She wrote don't know on her palm, and the time by the bell.

This first turn was short. The scrape stopped after a quarter of an hour by Hesk's clock, and the dust lay still an inch along the sill from where it had been, and Lira wrote the figure under don't know and went back to her drill-book.

It came back in the afternoon and stayed. He lay flat through it and let his ears close and open as they liked, while the grey dust ran and stopped and ran again along the wood and the chest in the cellar went the rest of the way along its wall, slowly, scrape by scrape, until it had found the place it wanted and the air went back to being the weight of air.

"Forty minutes," said Karis, from the clock, when it was done; she had come up for her shift at the start of it and had not taken her eyes off the dust. "That's longer than the morning's. I think it's sitting down."

It was. It did not move again.

The doorway was in the middle of the afternoon.

Karis had gone, and Brom had gone to the infirmary to have his sling looked at, and for the quarter hour between their shifts Cael was alone in the room for the first time since the road, because the rota said SOMEBODY IN THE ROOM. ALWAYS. and the healer had said that Brom's sling came first. He did not mind. He lay with his eyes shut and said no to the cup on the saucer and the lamp on the book, and counted the bell from the lecture range, and waited.

He heard Lira on the stair before he saw her. Step, crutch, step, crutch, and the crutch's rubber foot on every tread like a soft knock. She came along the corridor. He heard her stop outside his door, and the door, which was still standing a hand's breadth open against its frame, swing inward as she put the crutch's tip to it.

She came to the threshold.

There? said the new thing, about the doorway.

He was half asleep. He had said no to it perhaps four hundred times since the toll-bar. He began to say it again.

It did not wait.

He felt it go. It went out of him as quick and quiet as a breath, without his leave, without his asking, without his having said anything at all but the first sound of the word no. It set a point against the left-hand jamb of the door, at the height of a woman's shoulder, and another against the right-hand jamb, and drew the line between them taut across the opening, and told it to stay.

Lira walked into it.

She walked into air. He saw her do it from the bed, with his eyes open now and his whole body cold. She came forward on her good foot with the crutch swinging ahead of her to take the next step, and the crutch's tip went through the doorway, and her shoulder did not. Her shoulder met the line across the doorway as a shoulder meets a door that somebody has shut in your face, and she stopped dead, and the crutch went on without her. Its rubber foot skidded on the boards, and her weight went after it, onto the strapped ankle, and she made a sound.

Brom caught her.

He had come up the stair behind her, back from the infirmary early, and he caught her under the arm with his good right hand from behind before she was halfway down, and held her up, and did not let go.

"One," said Brom.

Cael was off the bed without any memory of getting off it; his ribs would tell him about it a long while afterward. He was standing in the middle of the room looking at a doorway with nothing in it, and Lira's face on the far side of the nothing, white, with her shoulder still pressed against the air.

"Two," said Brom.

He reached for it, because he knew how, because he had done it on the road: he reached for the point to tell it not to stay, and he could not find anywhere to take hold. On the road the point had been against his own coat, and he had been inside the thing it held, and he had let it go from where it touched him. This one was not against him. It was against two pieces of painted pine, eight feet apart, with Lira on the far side of them. He was on the wrong side of it. He could feel it there, taut, and he could not get his hands round it any more than you can untie a knot from the other side of a wall.

"Three. Four."

Lira had stopped pushing against it. She stood in Brom's arm and put her open hand on the nothing in the doorway, at the height of her shoulder, and held it there, and looked at Cael through it.

"Five," said Brom. "Six. Seven."

He did not try again, because he did not know what else to try. He stood in the middle of his room with his hands open and looked at her, and she looked at him, and the doorway held.

"Eight. Nine. Ten. Eleven."

"Twelve," said Brom.

On twelve it let go.

It let go by itself, without his asking. He felt the point leave the left jamb and the right, and the line between them go slack and simply not be there, and Lira's hand went forward through the doorway into the room as if somebody had opened a door she had been leaning on. Brom held her up. Her crutch lay on the boards inside the room where it had skidded.

Nobody said anything for a long time.

Then Brom bent, slowly, with his good arm, and picked up the crutch, and gave it back to her, and Lira took it. She came in over the threshold, step, crutch, step, looking at the floor, and sat down in the chair, and put her foot up on the stool. Her hands were shaking. She folded them in her lap so they would stop.

"Twelve seconds," said Brom.

"I didn't ask it to," said Cael.

"I know," said Lira.

"I didn't ask it. I was saying no. I was halfway through saying no." He heard his own voice and did not like it. "It wasn't on the leaf. Nothing on the leaf said it would do anything I didn't tell it to."

"No," said Brom. "It wasn't on the leaf."

Lira had her hands folded in her lap. She unfolded them and looked at them, and folded them again.

"I saw your face," she said. "Through it. The whole twelve. You weren't doing it." She said it carefully, as if she were giving a figure to a panel and wanted it written down right. "You were trying to take it off me from the wrong side and you couldn't, and you were frightened, and it wasn't you. I'm telling you because you'll want to put it in the book the other way round."

He would have. He knew it as she said it.

"It was mine," he said. "Whatever did it. It came out of me."

"So does your Wind," said Lira, "and nobody blames you when it knocks a tray off a table on the oak." She settled her foot on the stool. "Write that it was in you and it wasn't you. Both. They're both true, and I was the one in the doorway, so I get to say which goes first."

He shut the door, carefully, all the way, until the latch clicked. Then he sat down on the end of the bed, because Lira had the chair, and they were still sitting so when Karis came at the fifth bell with her squared paper and stopped in the doorway, which was only a doorway, and looked at the three of them, and asked what had happened.

Brom told her, and she listened. Then she came in, and sat on the floor with her back to the wall, and drew a line on her sheet at the bell, and wrote beside it, in her wide crooked left-handed letters, Doorway. Uncommanded. Twelve seconds. Brom counting.

She looked at the line, and then she drew a small box round it.

Rooke came at dusk, which nobody expected.

He stood in the doorway with his hands in his coat pockets and did not come in. He looked at Lira's foot on the stool and at Brom's sling and at the strapping round Cael's ribs where his shirt was open, and at the rota nailed to the inside of the door. He read the rota. Cael watched him read it, all of it, down to SOMEBODY IN THE ROOM. ALWAYS., and then look at the doorway he was standing in, as if it had told him something he did not have words for.

"Ribs," he said to Cael.

"Ribs. The right side. Eight days, the healer says."

That was true, and small, and it was everything the leaf had said Rooke was to be told.

Rooke nodded, and looked at Lira.

"The ankle's six days in strapping," he said. "I've talked to the healer. You're off the frames and off the floor until I see you walk across the east hall without thinking about it. That's three bouts on the card. The Second-day after next, the Fifth-day after that, and the lake house's exhibition." He took one hand out of his pocket and moved it, palm down, as if he were wiping a board. "I'll strike them in the morning."

"Three," said Lira.

"Three. They'll go on your sheet as not fought. That's a loss, on a program sheet. I won't pretend it isn't." He looked at her a moment longer. "It's a good ankle to lose them for. You were standing where a man's foot was going to land. Brom told me." He put his hand back in his pocket. "I'd have stood there."

He went.

Brom had the watch after supper, and by the end of it the house was asleep.

He sat in the chair with his sling across his chest and his feet stretched out and his chin down, and Cael thought he was dozing. The lamp was low. The new thing asked about the cup, and the lamp, and the rota's nail in the door, and the door against its frame, and Cael said no to each one, aloud now, very quietly, because he had found that it was easier aloud. Every time a thing came to rest against a door, his whole body went cold and listened.

"I measured it wrong," he said.

He had not meant to say it; it came out into the dark room by itself.

Brom did not open his eyes. "Measured what?"

"The leaf. I sat at the sill with all of you on the Second-day and priced it. I wrote down everything I could think of, the first minute and a week without the band and the lane and the read and somebody in the room. I left blanks where I didn't know, the way Seln said." He looked at the door. "There wasn't a line for that. There wasn't a line that said it might do something on its own, in a doorway, to Lira, with me lying here saying no. I didn't think of it. I measured it wrong."

"My father had a forge," said Brom.

Cael turned his head on the pillow.

"At the back of the estate, past the kitchen gardens, in a shed with a dirt floor. Not the estate's forge. His. Mother's people had a smith for the horses and the gates and the real work. My father had a shed with a dirt floor and a little forge he'd built himself, because he liked iron, and he liked a thing you could make with your hands that came out the same every time." Brom moved his feet. "He'd let me in when I was small, if I sat on the bench and didn't touch anything. I sat on that bench a lot of afternoons."

"What did he make?"

"Hinges. Brackets. Hooks for the stable. Nails, once, a whole keg, for no reason I ever found out." Brom almost smiled. "He'd measure the stock before it went in. Always. On the dirt floor, cold, with a steel rule and a bit of chalk, three times, and mark it. How long, how thick, where it was going to bend. He'd take as long as it needed. Then it went in the fire."

He was quiet a moment.

"And sometimes it came out of the fire and did something he hadn't measured. It cracked along a grain he couldn't see, or bent where it shouldn't. Once a whole bar went soft at one end and he never knew why. And he'd stand there with it in the tongs and look at it, and he never once went back to the rule and said the rule was wrong. The rule was right. He'd measured it right. The fire does what fire does. Nobody blames the rule for the fire."

The lamp hissed a little.

"You sat at that sill on the Second-day with the rain on the window and measured it cold," said Brom. "Three times. With all of us. You wrote down what you could see and left blanks where you couldn't. Then it went in the fire, on a road, and it did something in a doorway that nobody could have measured, because nobody's ever had this iron before." He opened his eyes at last and looked at Cael across the dark room. "You've measured. That's the part that's yours."

"And the doorway?" said Cael at last.

"The doorway's the fire's," said Brom. "We'll write it down. Next time there's a leaf, it'll have a line for doorways." He shut his eyes again. "Go to sleep. I'm counting."

Before he could read, Hesk had walked him down the long bench in the workshop with a hand on his shoulder, naming the tools in their racks. The scriber. The dividers. The little brass square with the nick in its heel. The burnisher, the pin vice, the files from the coarse rasp down to the fine one that Hesk called the whisper. A small boy at the end of a bench full of points and edges was afraid of all of them until somebody said what each was for, and after that they were a row of friends.

He was thinking about that bench when he woke, a little before dawn, with the window grey and Lira asleep in the chair at the end of her second watch.

His head ached from the inside, behind the eyes, in a place no healer could strap. It was the ache of a clerk who has stamped forty forms an hour since the toll-bar and has another forty on his desk. Rooke's red drill-book lay open face down on Lira's chest and rose and fell with her breathing. Her strapped foot was on the stool. The lamp had gone down to a blue bead.

Somebody had shut the window in the night against the wind, and its latch had dropped into the keeper with a small iron click that he had heard in his sleep.

The new thing asked about it. There?

He had no more no in him. He turned his head on the pillow and looked at the latch in the grey light, a curl of black iron with a thumb-piece worn bright by a hundred years of hands, and he did with it what Hesk had done with the scriber and the dividers.

Latch, he told it. You lift it with your thumb, and the window opens.

The asking stopped.

He lay still and listened for it to start again, the way you listen after a dog has barked once in the night. It did not. Refusing had always sent it off like a clerk with his paper still in his hand, not offended, coming back at the next counter. This was not that. This was the clerk reading the answer on the form, and blotting it, and filing it, and going home.

He tried the door next, cautiously, because the door was the one he was afraid of. Door. You open it, and somebody you know comes in.

Nothing asked.

The cup on the tray that nobody had carried down. Cup, for tea. The lamp with its blue bead. Lamp. The book under it, the chair, the nail in the rota, the stool. And Lira's strapped foot resting on the stool, and the cold went through him from his scalp to his heels, because it had not once crossed his mind that the thing would ask about a person, and it asked, softly, as politely as it had asked about the cup.

Lira, he told it, at once. That's Lira. Leave her be.

It left her be.

He went round the whole room after that, every surface, every thing that rested on another thing, in the grey light, and gave each one its name and what it was for, and each one went quiet and stayed quiet. And somewhere about the washstand he understood what he had found. Saying no had only ever been an answer to a question it would go on asking. It had never wanted to be turned away. It wanted to be told. It knew surfaces and it knew how to hold a thing against one, and it did not know what a single thing in the world was for, and every time something came to rest it asked, because nobody had ever explained.

He priced it, lying there, because that was what he did with anything new. A word a thing. A word cost almost nothing; a word was cheaper than the Wind's landing beat or the read's quiet minute after. But this house alone had more doors in it than he could count from his bed, and there were other houses, and roads with gates on them, and inns, and every door was going to need its word. It would never be paid off. It would be a small coin he put down at every threshold he ever crossed, so many times a day that one morning he would look up and find he had stopped noticing his hand go to his pocket.

Thresholds most; he could tell that already. He had named the door and it had stopped asking, but it had not stopped looking. It was told, and it accepted being told, and somewhere at the back it still leaned toward that frame the way a hound that has been sent to its basket leans toward the kitchen.

Lira opened her eyes and found him looking at the washstand with his lips moving.

"What," she said.

"It's a door," he said. "I told it."

Karis drew the curve that afternoon, sitting on the floor with the squared paper on her knee and the wrapping off her right hand at last, though she still held the pencil in her left.

The marks went down the sheet in their rows: forty in the first hour she had counted, then thirty-eight, thirty-six, thirty-one after the storm moved, thirty, twenty-eight. A line at the doorway with a box round it. Twenty-two through the night, by Brom's count and Lira's, which they had kept on the backs of their hands. Then the dawn, and the naming, and the counts dropped off the bottom of the page all at once: nine, four, two, one.

She joined the points with the pencil, slowly, and looked at what she had.

"Two days, near enough," she said. "From the road to the latch."

"You said nine weeks."

"I said nine weeks and I said I didn't believe it." She turned back through the notebook to the page on the Second-day, the leaf they had all initialled, where about nine weeks, Karis's curve, not believed stood in his own hand. She laid the new sheet beside it. Then she turned back further, to the column she had kept for the storm since Norhold, and further, to the old figures she had copied out of the old volume, the little points low on the paper from the Wind and the read and the rest.

Then she drew one more line on the new sheet, very lightly, from the first of the old points through the storm and down again to the two days.

"Each one's come in faster than the one before," she said. "Not the storm. The storm was heavy and it came in the middle of the floor, and it's off the line. But the others. Every time there's more of you already there to make room, the next one finds its place quicker. The more you carry, the faster you take the next." She looked at the line. "That's what it looks like. That's what it looks like now."

She wrote two words under the line, in her crooked left hand, and drew a box round them.

For now.

"I don't trust a curve with this few points in it," she said. "I don't trust a curve that only goes one way. Somewhere there's a weight where it turns round and comes back up, and I haven't got a point anywhere near it." She tapped the box. "Until I have, it's two words. And they stay in a box."

Bracken came up the stair at the fifth bell with a letter in his hand.

He did not come in, but stood in the doorway, which was only a doorway, and looked at the rota on the door and the squared paper on Karis's knee, and held out the letter.

"The district seat," he said. "Their answer. It came up in the noon bag." He read it out, as he read everything the house received, every word at the same weight. Two sentences. The office was constituted on the date entered in the district's register of offices, by instrument filed at the seat under seal. The registrar was respectfully referred to the issuing authority of the said instrument for any further particulars.

"It's what she said it would say," said Brom.

"It's exactly what she said it would say," said Bracken. He folded it once. "So I shall write to the issuing authority of the said instrument. I've begun the letter." He looked at Karis over his spectacles. "You had it a week early, Advocate. I've written that down too."

He went back down the stair.

That night, at the sill, with the day's tiredness heavy behind his eyes and Karis asleep in the chair for her shift, Cael turned to the leaf with four sets of initials and wrote beside it, in the margin, what it had cost against what they had said it would.

Priced at Silver, and paid at Silver. Priced: the first minute, with Brom standing over me; paid exactly that. Priced: about nine weeks, which Karis didn't believe; paid two days to the idle state, and the idle state is naming. Priced: a week without the band, which I'm paying now. Priced: the lane and the read unsafe, which I haven't tried.

Not on the leaf: the doorway. Twelve seconds, uncommanded, with Lira in it. Brom says that's the fire's and not the rule's. I'm writing it down so the next leaf has a line for doorways.

Not on the leaf either: what the others paid. That has to have a line too, next time. Ankle, shoulder, hand. It was in the cut and it wasn't anywhere on the page.

Chapter 34 — A Good Room

Rooke struck the three bouts before breakfast, standing at the program's board in the east hall's doorway with a stick of chalk, and Cael watched him do it from the foot of the residence stair because his ribs had made the stair a thing to be taken slowly and he had stopped halfway to rest.

The card was pinned at the board's head in Rooke's square capitals, as every card was. Under LIRA there were three lines, each with a date and a floor and a name. Rooke did not rub them out. He drew one stroke through each, level and unhurried, from the first letter to the last, the way a clerk strikes an entry he means to leave legible, and at the end of each line he wrote two words in the margin. Cael could not read them from the stair. He did not need to. He knew Rooke's two words for a bout not fought, because he had read them in that margin on other fighters' cards, and had never once expected to read them under hers.

Not fought.

Rooke stood back with the chalk in his hand and looked at the board. Then he put the chalk in his pocket and went in to the program floor and shut the door behind him, and Cael heard the bolt go home on the inside, which it never did.

He went down the rest of the stair one tread at a time.

Lira was at the long table in the refectory with her strapped foot up on the bench and a bowl in front of her that she was not eating. She looked at his face as he lowered himself onto the bench across from her, and nodded, and pushed the bowl an inch further away.

"Eat," he said.

"In a minute." She looked at him across the table. She had her elbows on the board and her chin on her two fists, the way she sat when she was about to say something she had been carrying round for a while. "You know what day it is."

He did. He had known since he woke, with the grey light on the ceiling and the new thing in him quiet, named, asking about nothing. He had lain there and said it to himself, and then not said it to anybody.

"It's the eleventh of Sowing," said Lira. "Hesk told me. Two years ago. I wrote to him from Greyvane to ask, and he wrote back in three lines, and one of them was the date and one of them was thank you and the last one said he won't have told you." She took her chin off her fists. "You weren't going to say."

"There didn't seem to be a place to put it."

"There's a place tonight. The reading room, after supper. Karis has said yes and Brom's bringing the kettle and I've asked the kitchen for a honey cake, and they said yes because I didn't tell them who it was for." She picked up her spoon at last. "And I've asked Ephram."

He looked at her.

"He's been on the same table as you for two years," said Lira, "and he's never once been in a room with the door shut where you were. He's going to be tonight. He said he's got grievances. I told him to shut them early, and he looked at me as if I'd asked him to set fire to the captain's file, and then he said he would." She began to eat. "Eighteen. You're eighteen today. Somebody should say it out loud at least once before supper, so I've said it."

He sat across from her with his ribs strapped and his left arm bound to the elbow and his hands round a cup of the refectory's tea, and let it be said.

He had been seventeen for a year. It had been a long one. He had been seventeen at Norhold on the stone with a healer's fingers in his hand, and seventeen on the road home in a cart, and seventeen behind a bell-frame on a gatehouse roof, and seventeen five days ago on his knees in a chalk cut with a cage of points round him. And now he was not. Nothing in him had changed in the night. Nothing ever did, on a birthday. It was only a line in somebody's register moving down a row, but it was his line, and it had moved, and Lira had said it out loud across a refectory table before anybody else could.

"Thank you," he said.

"Eat your bread," said Lira.

The parcel came up in Bracken's pouch at noon, among the house's ordinary post, with Cael's name on it in Hesk's hand.

Bracken brought it up himself. He did not have to; the porter's shoulder was mending and Seln was doing the sort, and Seln would have put it in Cael's hole with the rest. But Bracken came up the residence stair with it under his arm at the noon bell, and knocked, and held it out in the doorway, which was only a doorway, and did not come in.

"From Denvash," he said. "Carrier's mark from the far end of the country, nine days on the road. It's been rained on twice. The inside should be dry; whoever packed it knew what he was about." He weighed it on his palm a moment, by habit. "A little under three pounds."

"Thank you."

"Don't thank me. I only carried it up a stair." Bracken looked at him over his spectacles. "Many happy returns of the day, enrollee. I have it in the book. Your file has had your date of birth on its first leaf since the day you came up the hill, and I have never once had cause to say it aloud." He nodded, the small nod he gave a form that had been filled in properly, and went back down.

Cael did not open it.

He set it on the sill beside Hesk's book. It was wrapped in oilcloth and tied with waxed thread in Hesk's own knot, the one that came undone with a single pull if you knew which end and held like iron if you did not. He knew which end. He did not pull it. Lira had said tonight. He thought he would let it be tonight.

The reading room had never had so many people in it.

It had three chairs and a bench and a window seat and the long table, and Karis's shelves along two walls to the ceiling, and the brass lock on the door with its one key on the cord round her neck, and Bracken's card in its brass frame at eye height outside: Reading room. Assigned: K. Dellenmoor. When Cael came up the library stair after supper, slowly, with his ribs, the door was standing open and the lamp was lit and the room was warm.

The table had been cleared.

Not cleared. Karis did not clear a table; there was nowhere to put what was on it. But every sheet on it had been turned face down. Every stack had been turned over where it stood so that only the backs showed, plain and grey and blank, the code's three volumes shut and laid with their spines to the wall, her notebooks closed, the attestation wallet buckled. The whole long table was a field of the backs of things. In the middle of it, on a clean cloth, stood a honey cake on a kitchen plate with a knife beside it.

The assistant was just going. She had carried the cake up the library stair herself, she said, so that nobody would drop it, and she put her head round the door to say so, and wished him a good birthday with ink on two fingers, and went down the stair again before anybody could ask her to stay. Karis had sent her home early. Cael heard her singing to herself all the way down.

Brom's spirit kettle stood on the end of the nearest shelf over its little blue flame, not boiling. Brom himself had the chair by the shelf, with his left arm in its sling across his chest and his long legs out in front of him. Lira had the window seat with her strapped foot up on a stool somebody had carried in from the annex across the landing. Karis stood by the table with her right hand unwrapped.

He looked at the hand. She saw him look, and held it up in the lamplight, and turned it over.

The blisters had gone down. The skin of the fingers was whole again, and pink and new across the tips. But below the new skin, from the tips to the second knuckle, the fingers were a shade paler than the rest of the hand, as if somebody had washed the colour out of them a little, the way linen washes out in the sun.

"The healer says it'll stay," said Karis. "Paler. For good." She looked at it without any particular feeling, as she would have looked at a figure in a column. "It's the fourth. It's the first one that's left a mark. I've written it down."

She put the hand in her pocket and went to see to the kettle.

Ephram came at the half hour, out of breath, as if he had run up the library stair.

He stopped in the doorway and stood there with one hand on the frame, a tall loose young man in the cohort's coat with the green-taped captain's file under his arm, because he went nowhere without it. He looked at the four of them. Then he looked at the room.

"I shut grievances," he said. "There was one waiting. A first-year with a complaint about the meal rota. I told him to come back next Third-day with two complaints and I'd hear them both at once." He looked faintly appalled at himself. "I've never shut it early. Not once in two years."

"Come in," said Lira.

He came in. Then he saw the table.

Cael watched him see it. He watched the captain's eyes go along the long table, slowly, from end to end, over the turned stacks and the shut books and the blank backs of every sheet, the way they went along a floor before a bout, reading it. He saw Ephram understand that every piece of paper in the room had been turned face down, and that it had been turned face down because he was coming, and that nobody was going to say so.

Ephram did not say so either.

He took the third chair from the end of the table, and turned it round, all the way, so that its back was to the table and its front was to the window. Then he sat down in it, with his back to every paper in the room, facing Lira on the window seat and the dark glass behind her, and put the captain's file on his knees, and folded his hands on top of it.

"You can turn round," said Lira.

"I'm comfortable," said Ephram.

He did not turn round all evening.

Seln came last.

He came up the library stair without a sound, as he came up every stair, and stopped in the doorway, and did not come in at once. He stood there with his hands at his sides and looked at the room.

Cael watched him do it. He had watched Seln look at rooms for two years, at counters and sittings and in the long room at Ostrand from the one seat that saw every door, and he knew the order Seln looked at things in, because it was always the same. The door first: the brass lock, the frame, the card in its brass holder at eye height outside. Then the windows, both of them, the one over the window seat and the narrow one at the end, and what they looked out on, which was the dark and the top of the library's roof and, a long way below, the river. Then the landing behind him, and the annex door across it, and the stair going down. Then the table, with its field of turned backs. Then the people in it, one at a time.

He took perhaps a quarter of a minute over it. Nobody hurried him. At the end of it he said, to the room more than to any of them:

"It is a good room. I have been in a great many."

He came in and sat down at the middle of the bench along the table's far side, where the turned stacks were thickest, as he sat at the middle of every bench. Karis put a cup of Brom's tea in front of him. The kettle had boiled at last, while nobody was looking at it, which Lira said was the only way it ever did.

Seln looked at the cup. Then he put out his hand and turned it, a quarter turn, on the table, the way he had turned his cups for two years at every table on the hill.

Cael saw it. He saw Lira see it, and Brom.

It was the first time since the night of the gate.

They sang, because Lira said that you could not have a birthday without, and nobody else on the hill was going to.

Nobody wanted to start. Lira said she could not sing and proved it in two notes. Karis said she knew no birthday songs, only the ones the founders' compilers had written down, and those were mostly about drowning. Ephram said, with his back to the table, that he had a captain's voice and not a singing one, which was the same thing said twice.

So Brom sang.

He sang without getting up from the chair, with his sling across his chest and his eyes half shut, in a low voice that filled the small room easily, as if it were used to filling much bigger ones. It was not a birthday song. It was a harvest song from Velmere, he said afterward, that the estate's people sang at the last load every year, when the cart came into the yard with the last of the sheaves and the old women threw water on the horses for luck. It had a great many verses. Each one was about a field, and what had grown in it, and who had cut it. Brom sang every verse, slowly, all the way through. Nobody joined him, because nobody knew it, and nobody wanted him to stop.

At the last verse the tune changed. It went up, and came round again on itself, and there was a line at the end of it that everybody in Velmere evidently sang together, loudly, very nearly a shout. Brom sang it quietly.

Ephram, with his back to the table, sang it with him.

He sang it wrong. He had picked up the tune from the verses before and he came in at the end with great confidence and got the third line of it wrong, cheerfully, all on one note, and Brom stopped singing and opened his eyes and looked at him.

"Where did you learn that?"

"The first-years," said Ephram. "Somebody on the ground floor has been singing those three lines under the residence windows since the night before the year opened. He's never once got the third line right. I thought it went like that."

Cael sat at the table and looked at the back of Ephram's head and thought of the first night of the year, at his own window, with the house filling below him and somebody downstairs who could not learn a song.

He began to laugh. It hurt his ribs very much. He did it anyway.

Karis cut the cake with her left hand, because she said the right had done enough for one week. While she was cutting it Lira said them.

She had not said she was going to. She sat on the window seat with her foot on the stool and a plate on her knee and did not eat from it, and when Karis put the knife down she said them out loud, to the room, one after another, in the voice she used to give her figures to a panel.

"Next Second-day. The Current girl from Rooke's program, on the east hall's boards, rated. I'd have won it." She stopped, and went on. "The Fifth-day after that. The Ash second-year from the northern house, the one with the long reach. I don't know if I'd have won it. I wanted to find out." She stopped again. "And the lake house's exhibition. Their Blade. The one who beat the Current girl on figures at the confluence. I wanted that one most."

She looked at her plate.

"Three. Not fought. Rooke struck them this morning. They'll go on my sheet as losses, and the sheet will go to the evaluation at the end of the year with three losses on it that I never stood on a floor for." She looked up. "There. Said."

Cael could not look away from her. She had not hidden them. He had expected that she would, a little, the way he would have, writing the bill small at the bottom of a page where nobody need read it unless they went looking. She had not written them anywhere. She had said them out loud, in a room full of people, on his birthday, in order, with the dates.

"I'd have stood there again," she said, more quietly. "In the cut. Where the man's foot was going to land. I'd stand there tomorrow. I'm not saying them so anybody'll say I shouldn't have. I'm saying them because they're mine and they cost something and I want them said where somebody heard." She picked up the cake at last. "That's all."

Ephram, with his back to the table, said, "Noted."

He said it the way Cael said it, exactly, in the log voice, level and kind. Lira looked at the back of his head and laughed, once, surprised.

Then Ephram took the captain's file off his knees and opened it, without turning round, and took out three sheets of close-ruled paper, and held them up over his shoulder without looking, so that Cael could take them.

Cael took them.

It was the chart. He had known it existed for a year and had never seen it close. Every figure he had put up on the house's floors since the qualifying year, in order, in Ephram's square careful hand, one to a line, with the date and the floor and the three cards and the figure, and a little dot beside each one on a running scale in the margin, so that the dots made a line down the three pages. The line breathed. It went up a little and down a little and never once settled, and never once went past the mark at the top that Ephram had ruled across all three pages in red.

At the bottom of the third page, under the last figure, there was a gap. And in the gap, in the same hand, small: Excused (ribs).

"Ninety-one," said Ephram, to the window. "Ninety-one entries since the qualifying year, and one gap this week." He was quiet a moment. "I'm not asking about any of them. I've never asked and I'm not going to start tonight." He held out his hand over his shoulder again for the sheets. "I wanted you to know somebody's been paying attention. That's all. Many happy returns."

Cael gave him the sheets back. Ephram put them in the file and shut it and folded his hands on top of it again, and looked at the window, and did not turn round.

He opened Hesk's parcel last, when the cake was eaten and the kettle had been filled again and had once again refused to boil.

He took the waxed thread's right end and pulled, and the knot came undone all at once, as it always did for him and for nobody else. Under the oilcloth was brown paper, dry, and under the brown paper was a satchel.

He did not look at the outside of it first. He opened the flap and put his hand in, the way he would have put his hand into any bag Hesk had made, to find out what it was for, and against the back his fingers found a pocket stitched flat and close in Hesk's waxed thread.

He knew what it was for before he had measured it with his eyes. He took Hesk's book out of his coat and slid it in. It went all the way down without being pushed and stood there with a quarter-inch to spare on every side, as if the pocket had been cut round it. Hesk had not seen the book since the day he bound it. He had cut that pocket from memory, at the far end of the country, and it fitted to a hair.

Only then did Cael look at the rest. The flap came down over everything. The strap was long enough to cross a man's body and ride on the opposite hip, so that the bag would sit still when he walked and not swing when he ran. And the buckle was not a bought buckle. Hesk's file marks were on the inside of the tongue, where only somebody who had slept in the shavings under that bench would think to look, and the frame had the little bevel Hesk put on everything he made so that it would not catch on cloth. He ran his thumb over the bevel. The leather round it was the heavy brown kind Hesk kept for instrument cases and would not waste on anything that did not deserve it.

There was a note folded small under the flap. It was on a leaf from Hesk's order-pad, in Hesk's small fast hand, with one initial at the foot. He read it to himself first. Then he read it again.

Eighteen. A man's tools should fit the road he's actually on, not the one they promised him. Your grandmother would say I'm being unsubtle. She'd be right. Mind the shape. — H.

He did not read it aloud. He folded it small again and put it in the satchel's pocket with the book, against the book's back board, and buckled the flap.

Across the table Seln was looking at the satchel. He had not looked at anything else since the brown paper came off. He looked at the strap that went across the body, and the buckle that would not catch, and the flap that came down over everything, and Cael thought, though he could not have said how he knew it, that Seln was thinking about roads.

"It's a good bag," said Brom, at last.

"It's a very good bag," said Ephram, to the window.

The evening broke up a little before the tenth bell. Ephram went first, with the captain's file under his arm, backing out of the door so as not to see the table even at the last, and wished Cael many happy returns again from the landing, and went down the stair whistling the third line wrong. Brom took the kettle. Karis stayed to turn her papers face up again, one stack at a time, in the order she had turned them over, which she said was the only way she would ever find anything in the morning. Seln had gone before any of them, quietly, while the bag was being admired.

Lira came down the library stair with Cael, step and crutch, step and crutch, with his good hand under her elbow on the turns and neither of them saying that it was the wrong way round, a girl on a crutch helping a boy with strapped ribs down a stair by letting him help her.

At the reading room's door he had felt it ask. He had felt it on every doorway since the road, and this one was a good door, oak, heavy, set true in its frame, the kind of door the new thing wanted most. There? He had named it under his breath. Door. Karis's. It opens.

Lira had heard him.

She stopped on the landing below with her crutch planted and looked up at him in the light from the stairwell lamp.

"Is it every door?"

"Every door. Doors most. It wants them." He did not know how else to say it. "I name them and it stops asking. But it goes on wanting them, a little, after."

She thought about that, standing on the stair with her strapped foot held clear of the tread.

"Then I'll name them too," she said. "When I'm with you. Out loud. So you don't have to do every one." She went down another step. "Stair," she said, to the stair, quite seriously. "It goes down. People walk on it."

He did not laugh, because she had not said it to be funny. He said it after her, under his breath, stair, and the new thing, which had not asked about the stair at all, was quiet anyway, as if it had been told something it was glad to know.

They went on down. At the foot of the stair, in the library's dark lower hall, she said door to the street door, and he said it after her, and they went out into the cold.

He wrote it at the sill as soon as he was back in his room, with the satchel on the sill beside him and the house going quiet round him, door by door.

The fountain went on in the court below. The glass of the window was cold, and the cold came through it onto the leather of the satchel where it stood against the pane, so that when he put his hand on the flap it was cold too, like a hand that has come in from outside. The ribs were a low steady ache. The arm under its binding itched, which the healer had said meant it was mending. The new thing in him was quiet. Once, when the latch of the window settled in its keeper as the wind moved the frame, it asked; and he told it latch, and it was quiet again.

He took the book out of its pocket and opened it to a clean leaf and wrote the inventory, because a birthday was as good a day as any to count what he carried.

Eighteen. The eleventh. Hesk's satchel on the sill. The book fits it.

What I carry: eight confirmed.

Wind-adjacent — Lira, the burst. Pressure-adjacent — the Bronze from Ardenmere, the push. Iron-adjacent — Brom, the read, which found the fourteen. Compression-adjacent — Reydan, the give. Ember-adjacent — Karis, the spark, two contacts and no more. Shadow-adjacent — the stair, sealed, rent from waking. Storm-adjacent — Daeva, the lane; moved twice this week, a quarter hour and then forty minutes, and settled. Anchor-adjacent — the hand with no face; idle by naming; wants doorways.

Under all eight, the still place I don't count.

Still open. Still real. Patience.

Eight lines and a ninth that was not a line. Seven names he could have written a letter to, and one he never could.

Somebody knocked at the door.

It was the tenth bell; he had heard it go from the lecture range a minute before. He knew the knock. It was one knock, not loud, the way Seln knocked at the wing's inner door when he wanted the Magisters to know he was there without being asked in.

He opened the door. Seln stood in the corridor in his coat, with his hands at his sides and nothing in them.

"The Fourth-day stands," said Seln. "Your line's the fourth on the board."

"I read it."

"I know you did." Seln looked past him, once, at the room: at the sill, and the lamp, and the satchel standing against the cold glass with its flap buckled down. Then he looked back. "I wanted to say it, not leave it on a board. That's all."

"Thank you."

Seln nodded. He did not say goodnight. He did not say happy birthday, or anything about the cake, or the song, or the bag. He turned and went back along the corridor without a sound, the way he went everywhere, and at the corner he did not look back.

Cael shut the door.

He went back to the sill and sat with the book open and the pen in his hand, and the satchel against the glass, and the cold coming through it. He thought of the chalk cut, and the fourteen, and the band of skin between a hood and a scarf. He thought of a case set down on this sill six days ago, beside this book, and a man who was not sure. He thought of a leaf from an order-pad at the far end of the country, and the three words on it that Hesk had now written to him twice, a few weeks apart, about two different things that were perhaps the same thing.

He wrote one more line, under the inventory, and blotted it, and put the book back in its pocket in the satchel, and buckled the flap.

Tomorrow, Seln's annex. Hesk says mind the shape. I think tomorrow is the shape.

Chapter 35 — Three Routes

The new thing asked nothing when he woke.

He lay on his back with the grey of the window on the ceiling and waited for it, the way a man waits for a dog in the next room to bark once it has heard him stir. The ribs told him where they were. The forearm under its dressing itched in a long line from the wrist to the elbow, which the healer said was the skin remembering how to be skin. The latch sat in its keeper and the door stood in its frame, and nothing in him leaned toward either of them.

He named the door anyway, under his breath, before he put his feet on the boards. Door. It opens on the corridor. It cost nothing to say. Lira had said on the stair that she would name them with him when she could, and she was not here, so he did it himself, the way you lock a door you know is already locked.

Then he got up, slowly, and went to the sill, and stood a moment with his hand on the satchel's flap.

Today was the shape.

He did not open the book, because there was nothing to put in it yet. He dressed one sleeve at a time, the right arm first because the ribs preferred it, and went down to find Lira.

The infirmary smelled of vinegar and clean linen and the stove. The house's healer was a spare grey woman who had strapped fighters for twenty years and did not hold with conversation while she did it. She had Lira on the high bench by the window with the right foot across her own knee, and a pair of long-nosed shears working up the strapping from the toes, one careful bite at a time.

Lira did not look round when he came in, because she was looking at her foot as if it belonged to somebody she had not yet decided to trust.

The last of the strapping came away. Under it the ankle was a little thinner than the other, and yellow-green round the bone, and wrinkled from six days in linen like a hand that has been too long in the wash.

"Stand on it," said the healer.

Lira stood on it.

She did it without help, with both hands on the edge of the bench behind her, and then she took the hands away. Cael watched her weight go over onto the right foot, a little at a time, the way you put weight on ice at the edge of a pond. Her face did nothing at all. That was how he knew it hurt.

"Walk to the door and back."

She walked to the door and back as if the floor might have been waxed in the night and nobody had thought to tell her. At the door she turned on the left foot, not the right, and the healer saw it, and said nothing, and wrote something on a card.

"No floor, no frames, and no running, not even for a bell." The healer put the card in Lira's hand. "Your coach knows, and he'll tell you when."

"He says when he sees me walk across the east hall without thinking."

"Then don't think about it where he can see you," said the healer, which was very nearly a joke, and went to wash the shears.

The crutch stood in the corner where she had leaned it on the first morning, and she looked at it and left it there.

"Somebody'll need it," she said to Cael at the door. "Somebody always does." She stopped on the threshold and put her hand on the frame, and said, quite seriously, "Infirmary door. People come in hurt and go out less hurt."

He said it after her. Nothing in him had been asking, and it was quiet anyway.

They went along the covered walk side by side, slowly, at her pace, which today was also his. The frost was still white on the flags wherever the sun had not yet reached, and their breath went up in front of them and hung there while they walked through it.

"What's your line?" she said.

"The fourth."

"I'm the third." She did not look at him. "I'll be slow on the stair, and don't help me."

"I wasn't going to."

"Yes, you were." She stepped round a puddle with a white skin of ice on it, carefully, with the left foot leading. "You've been going to since the road, and I'd rather be slow."

The floor schedule was on the refectory door, where it always was, in Seln's fair copying hand.

It ran down the whole of the door: four floors and their hours for the week, the Crown yard, the second floor, the old frames and the east hall, and against each hour a name or a house or a program, a hundred lines of it in a hand so even that nobody had ever once looked at it twice. On the Fourth-day, after supper, five lines sat a quarter of an hour apart against five different floors. One of them was his. Hesk-ward. Old frames. Under the Fifth-day it still said, in the same hand, Hesk-ward: excused (ribs).

Ephram was reading the board when he came in. Ephram read the board every morning, all of it, from the top, the way other people read a letter from home.

"Ribs?" he said, without turning round.

"Better."

"Good." The captain found his own name and moved his finger to the next. "The chart's got a hole in it, and I don't like holes." He considered the Fourth-day column, Cael's line among the others, a practice booking on a floor nobody wanted after supper. Then he went on down the door to the Fifth-day, as if he had read nothing at all, and Cael could not have said whether he had.

He went to the wing after breakfast because the excused slip wanted a countersign, and because he wanted to see the shelf.

The assessment wing's counter was its usual morning self. The desk clerk had the day book open and a queue of three in front of him: two first-years with floor sheets and a porter with a parcel. The clock ticked over the counter. Behind it, at the copying table under the long window, the teaching assistant sat with his pen in his column and his head bent, as he had sat every morning for two years.

Cael waited his turn. While he waited he looked past the clerk's shoulder at the shelf above the copying table.

It was empty.

Not all of it. The wing's other sealed things still stood there in their row, a box of old sigil cards and two bound runs of the wing's returns and a tin of sealing wafers. But at the end of the row, where the case had stood for two years, there was only a clean oblong of wood, a shade paler than the wood round it, with a soft grey edge of dust on three sides.

He looked at it for exactly as long as a man looks at anything on a shelf while he waits in a queue. Then he looked at the clock.

The clerk countersigned the slip and Cael said thank you. At the copying table Seln turned a leaf, and said, to the column and to nobody, "Mm."

Cael went out through the wing doors into the cold and stood a moment on the step.

Somewhere between the last time he had looked and this morning, Seln had taken it down. Nobody on the hill had seen him do it. Cael had been looking at that shelf every time he stood at the counter for a week, and he had not seen it either.

Nobody had planned the routes. That was the point of them.

Seln had said it once, in Cael's room, with the case on the sill and the rain on the glass. Read your own line. The hour is when you come up the stair. And then, as the boy was writing on the back of his hand: Come the way you always come. A man who changes his road is a man who has a reason.

So they did.

Karis came first, at the seventh bell, from the refectory, by the library's front door and the main stair. She had come that way every evening of the year with her supper still in her and her notebook under her arm. Brom came second. Brom never took the main stair if there was another one. He went in at the library's north end and up the iron stair through the stacks, three flights of open treads that rang under a heavy man, because he said the long way round was the only exercise the library offered. Lira came third, by the front, slowly. And Seln, Cael knew without being told, would come last, up the bindery stair from the yard behind, the way the wing's man always came when he carried returned volumes up to the readers' shelves.

Three ways onto the library's third floor. Then one stair from there to the top, the tight one, where two people could not pass. Everybody on the hill used one of the three. Nobody had ever thought about which.

Cael sat at his sill with his coat on and Hesk's clock in front of him and waited for the third quarter after the bell.

The clock lost time, as it always had. In tournament weeks he had set it an hour fast so that it would come right by accident, and on finals morning he had put it back himself. Tonight he had set it by the lecture range's bell at supper, and it would be a minute wrong by the eighth bell, perhaps two. He watched the minute hand anyway, because it was something to watch.

When it stood at the quarter he got up, and named the door, and went.

The court was dark and very cold.

The fountain went on in the middle of it, as it did all year, with a crust of ice round the rim of the basin and the water going up black and coming down white in the light from the residence windows. He went round it at a walk, past the dark bulk of the lecture range and the records hall with its one lamp burning in the side window, which was Bracken's lamp and burned there every night of the year whether Bracken was under it or not.

At the top of the library, four floors up, the reading room's window was lit.

It was lit the way it was lit every night of the year, a yellow square at the top of the dark building, with the lamp set close to the glass so that you could see it from the north wall and the gate lodge and, Seln had once said, from the ferry landing at the foot of the bluff. The whole valley knew that window. A coat at the foot of the road could have told you the hour by it: lit at dusk, out somewhere between the tenth bell and the eleventh, never once dark before the ninth.

Tonight it was lit exactly the same.

He went in at the library's front door. Door, he told it, as his hand went to the iron ring. Heavy. It keeps the cold out. The lower hall was warm and smelled of lamp oil and old paper and the stove at the far end. Under the green-shaded lamps at the long tables two readers sat with their heads down. One was a fourth-year from the Ash faculty with a code open and his chin on his fist, and the other a girl Cael did not know, asleep with her cheek on her own notes. The night porter sat in his box by the stair with a newspaper. He looked up, saw a student going up to the reading rooms, and looked down.

Three people. Not one of them would remember it tomorrow. He had caught the counting from Seln somewhere in the year without meaning to, and now he could not stop.

The main stair went up in long shallow flights. On the second landing the ribs said what they thought of it. He stopped, and stood with one hand on the rail, and breathed, and went on. On the third floor the stair ended, and the tight one began, the one Karis called the top stair and the porters called worse things. He took it a step at a time. At the turn he passed the place where Lira would have had to stop too. There was nothing there to show it. She had been slow, and nobody had helped her.

The top landing had one lamp on a bracket, and the annex door stood shut across it. The reading room's door had Bracken's card in its brass frame at eye height. Reading room. Assigned: K. Dellenmoor.

He knocked once, and Karis let him in.

The table was bare.

He had seen it covered for a year, and turned face down for one evening, and he had never once seen it bare. Every stack and every box and every volume of the code had gone. The long table stood under its old green cloth with nothing on it at all, and the cloth was faded in squares and oblongs where a year of paper had lain on it and kept the light off.

"The annex floor," said Karis, before he could ask. "All of it, in order, and I'll be a week putting it back."

She had kept the lamp in the window where it always was, turned up as high as every night, so that anybody looking up from the valley saw what they always saw. They were not sitting by it; a second lamp stood at the far end of the table, away from the glass, with a shade of brown paper pinned round it so that its light went down onto the cloth and nowhere else. The window seat was empty, and nobody would sit there tonight. A person in the window seat was a shape against a lit window, and Karis had thought of that before any of them.

Brom had the chair by the shelf, with the sling still across his chest for one more night, and his spirit kettle stood on the end of the shelf over its little blue flame, not boiling. He nodded to Cael. He did not say anything about the stair or the stacks or the ribs.

Lira had the bench, at the end of it, with her right leg out straight in front of her and her boot off, and the foot resting on its heel on the boards, and she saw him look at it.

"It's fine," she said. "It's not fine, but it's better than it was. I came up the top stair on my backside for the last six steps, if you want to know, and nobody saw, because I waited till nobody was on it."

"I didn't help you."

"No, you didn't." She almost smiled. "Sit down. You're making the room smaller."

He sat on the bench beside her. Karis sat across the table from them with her hands in her lap and the cord of her key round her neck and the key itself inside her collar. Nobody had brought anything. That was the strangest thing of all, in that room. Not a notebook, not a pen, not a cup. Karis had sent the assistant home at the sixth bell, she said, with the copying for the morning and a message for her mother, and the girl had gone down the stair singing.

They waited.

Nobody talked much. Brom said the iron stair had a new loose tread on the second flight, the ninth, and he would tell the porter tomorrow. Lira said she had passed the Ash fourth-year on the main stair and he had asked after her ankle, and she had told him it was a horse, and he had believed her.
