Karis said nothing, but sat with her hands folded and looked at the bare cloth, the way she looked at a page before she began to read it.

The kettle did not boil.

The lecture range's bell gave the eighth hour, far off across the court, muffled by the shutters. Before the last stroke had died there was a single knock at the door, not loud.

Karis got up and turned the key.

Seln stood on the landing with his coat buttoned to the throat and something square under it, and he did not come in. He stood in the doorway and looked at the room in the order Cael knew. The door, the lock, the card; the two windows, the lit one with its lamp, the narrow one at the end, dark, with the library's roof below it; the landing behind him, the annex door, the stair; the bare table and the shaded lamp; then the four of them, one at a time.

It took him longer than it had on the night of the birthday. Nobody hurried him.

Then he came in and Karis locked the door behind him and hung the key back inside her collar. Seln went to the middle of the table, on the far side, where he always sat. He did not sit. He unbuttoned his coat and took out the case and set it down on the bare cloth in the circle of the shaded lamp.

It was smaller than Cael remembered from the sill. Dark leather, scuffed at the corners, a brass lock and nothing else. No mark on the outside. There was a stamp inside the lid from the man who made it, Seln had said once, that nobody had ever seen but him.

He took the key from his waistcoat pocket, a small brass key on a loop of black tape. He put it in the lock and turned it, and the lock opened with a sound like a dry twig, and he lifted the lid.

He did it in four movements, the way a man sets out his tools on a bench before a job.

The first was the largest. He took out a deep stack of paper, held flat between his two hands, and began to lay it on the cloth in rows. Each piece was two sheets together with a brass clip at the top, and he laid them ten to a row, edge to edge, without hurrying, squaring each to the one before with the side of his finger. Four rows. Forty. When he had finished they covered half the table in front of the lamp like the squares of a field seen from a hill.

The second was a bundle tied in the wing's pink tape, about two fingers thick. He set it down at the end of the fourth row and did not untie it.

The third was printed. Cael saw that at once from the way the light lay on it, flat and even, the way it never lay on a page anybody had written by hand. Seln laid it in two stacks side by side beyond the bundle. The left stack was yellower than the right.

The fourth was a single leaf.

It was in a sleeve of folded paper, plain and heavy, made to fit it. Seln took it out of the lid's pocket last, with two fingers at its edges. He laid it at the very end of the table by itself, a hand's width from everything else, and took his fingers away.

Then he stepped back from the table and put both hands flat on the wood in front of him, and said nothing.

Cael had no clock, because he had left Hesk's on the sill, and he did not count. Afterward he could not have told anybody how long it was, which had not happened to him since he was small. He knew only what he saw while it went on. The shaded lamp's flame stood up very straight and still in its glass. On the cloth the forty rows lay in its light, and the yellow stack, and the leaf in its sleeve at the end. Lira's hands were in her lap, one inside the other, and Brom did not reach for the kettle. Karis sat with her eyes going along the first row and back, along and back, the way they went along a shelf, and she did not reach for anything either.

Seln's hands lay flat on the wood, and Cael watched them, and they did not move at all.

At last Karis looked up.

"May I?"

"That is why they are on the table," said Seln.

She took the first one from the top of the first row. She drew the shaded lamp an inch nearer and held the two sheets under it, and Cael saw that they were both in the same hand, small and round and perfectly level, the copying hand of the wing that had filled the floor schedule on the refectory door every week for two years.

"The first sheet is a copy of a station's Kindling record," said Karis. She read it in her plain voice, the one she used for a citation, giving each word its weight and no more. "River station, the fourth district. Entry of the twelfth. A girl of the town. Reading at the frame: Current, second rank. Keeper's note at the margin: reads into Mire. Strong." She laid it face up in front of her. "That's the keeper's hand copied. You can see where he pressed."

"The second?" said Brom.

She held the clipped sheet out to him across the table. He took it in his good right hand and held it to the lamp, and read it out in his slow plain way, as if it were a bill of lading.

"Order of reclassification at evaluation. River station, the fourth district. Entry of the twelfth." He stopped, and found his place. "Per corrective classification at Kindling evaluation: enter Current, Rank One. Margin reading not to be entered. Observe nine weeks following entry."

He turned it over. There was a slip pinned to the back, a narrow strip in the same round hand, and he read that too.

"Observed nine weeks. Nothing to report."

Karis took the second pair, and read the record, and Brom read the order. A station in the hill country, a boy. Ash, first rank. Keeper's note: something of Stone in the frame; second family? And the order: Enter: Ash, Rank One. Margin reading not to be entered. Observe nine weeks. And on the back, Observed nine weeks. Nothing to report.

The third was a coastal station, a girl again. Current, second rank at the frame. Keeper's note at the margin: reads into Wind, faint. Enter: Current, Rank One.

Cael listened, and watched the two of them pass the sheets across the cloth, and did not say what he saw.

Every keeper had written something at the margin: a second family, or a note that the frame had reached past the column it was meant to stay in. Reads into. Something of. Faint. And every order took the margin away and wrote down only the column. Twice now a rank had gone too, but the rank was not the thing; the margin was the thing. He could see it as plainly as he could see the clip, and he did not say it. It was Karis's to say, when she had it in order, and she would not thank anybody for saying it first.

Lira had been very quiet all this while. She leaned forward on the bench, carefully, with the right foot still out straight, and turned the third order over with one finger so that the back of it showed.

"Nine weeks of nothing," she said.

"That is my sentence," said Seln.

They all looked at him. He was still standing, with his hands on the table. He said it in the voice he used at the counter.

"Nothing to report. I have written it every week for fifteen years. On the bottom of every return, in that hand." He did not look at the slip. "It is a true sentence. When there is nothing, that is what you write. It is the commonest line in the service."

Cael looked at the narrow strip of paper on the back of the order.

He had been kept by that sentence. He knew it as surely as he knew the ribs. Two years of true, empty weeks had gone up out of the wing with his name on the outside fold, and every one of them had said that nothing had happened. That sentence had stood between him and the people who read returns. And here was the same sentence, word for word, clipped to the back of a girl from a river town. In her case it said that the correction had held. Nothing to report. She had gone home smaller and stayed there, and nine weeks of somebody's careful watching had found nothing in her worth writing down, because the thing worth writing down had been taken off her paper before she was old enough to know it was there.

The same words. One set had kept him, and the other had buried her.

He did not say that either. He put his hand on the edge of the table, and Lira, without looking at him, put her own hand over it and took it away.

They read eleven more pairs before anybody stopped.

Nobody had decided how many to read. Karis read records and Brom read orders, and after a while Lira took orders too, so that Brom could rest his hand. The voices went on across the bare cloth in the circle of the lamp, very low. Reads into. Something of. Second family, faint. Enter. Margin reading not to be entered. Station after station went by, a mill town and a ferry crossing and a district with a name Cael had once seen on a map, a girl and a boy and a girl, and on every back the narrow slip, the nine weeks, the nothing.

At the twenty-third pair Karis stopped.

There was something folded behind it, under the clip. A sheet folded small, in quarters, and then another sheet folded inside that.

"There's a letter," she said.

Lira put out her hand.

Karis looked at her a moment, and gave it to her. Lira unfolded the outer sheet on her knee and smoothed it with the side of her hand. It was Seln's copying hand again, but the copying hand had done something Cael had never seen it do: it had kept the shape of another man's writing inside its own. The lines ran uphill and the capitals were too large. The spelling was a careful man's spelling, a man who wrote seldom and had looked up the hard words.

Lira read it aloud.

"To the clerk of the district office. Sir. I am the father of the girl entered at the river station on the ninth. I do not write to complain and I hope you will not take it so. At the frame the keeper told us she read strong and read into a second family besides, and he said he had not seen it often, and shook my hand. Now the paper has come and it says only the one, and the first rank. I expect there has been an error in the copying, which I know is easy done. I do not mind which it is. She is a good girl either way. Only she asks me, and I do not know which to tell her. If you would write and say which, I would be grateful. Your servant."

There was no name. Seln had copied everything but the name.

Lira laid the sheet on the table. Her hand stayed on it a moment.

Then she unfolded the second sheet, the one that had been inside the first. It was short. She looked at it, and did not read it, and held it out across the table to Cael.

He took it. Four lines, in Seln's hand again, and under them a district office's mark. He read them aloud because she wanted him to, and because he did not think he could have read them silently and kept his face.

"Sir. The entry is the registry's and I am not able to alter it.

"I have looked at the station's sheet. The keeper's reading is on it, and it is not what the registry entered.

"I have asked my office why, and I have had no answer, and I do not expect one.

"I am sorry. I would tell her both."

He put the sheet down on top of the father's.

The lamp burned. Across the court, very faint through the shutters and four floors down, somebody in the residence was laughing at something, the long helpless laugh of a first-year who has been told a joke after the bell and cannot stop.

"He told the truth," said Brom at last.

"He did," said Karis. Her voice was quite steady. "He looked at the station's sheet himself and found the difference. He asked above him, and wrote down that he'd been given nothing. He told a man he'd never met the one honest thing he had." She touched the edge of the clerk's four lines with one finger, very lightly, the way she touched the founders' volumes. "And he sent it up with the letter, because that's what you do with a letter about an entry. You send it to the office that made the entry."

She looked at the case, open at the end of the table.

"And it came here."

Cael sat and looked at the four lines.

He had told himself all year, and the year before, that the room was the trouble and not the hill. He had found out on the Ostrand road that the room had never been the system at all. He had thought that was the bottom of it, and it was not. Here was a man who had sat in one of the rooms and done everything right. He had read the sheet and asked, and written down the answer he had not been given. He had told a father the truth in four lines, which was more than most people managed in forty. And all of it, his honesty and the father's careful spelling both, had gone up a stair into the drawer that held the corrections. It had been filed there beside them, clipped, in order, and kept.

The honest people were in the drawer too.

Seln took his hands off the table at last. He looked at the two sheets lying on top of each other, the father's and the clerk's, and then he looked at Lira.

"That is the only letter," he said. "In forty. I copied it because it was the only one. I have read it more often than anything else in the case."

Lira nodded. She folded the father's letter in quarters along its old folds and put the clerk's inside it, the way it had been, and slid them both back under the clip of the twenty-third pair, and laid the pair in its place in the row.

Chapter 36 — The Leaf in Its Sleeve

Karis untied the pink tape herself, because it was the wing's knot and she had watched Seln tie it on a hundred files across the counter and knew which end to pull.

The bundle opened on the cloth like a book with no spine. It was reports, a few sheets each, folded once lengthwise in the field service's way, the way a man folds a paper to carry it inside his coat on a horse. The hands varied, because Seln had copied each in the shape of its writer as he had copied the father's letter, and Cael could see a hurried man and a careful one, a man who pressed hard and one who barely touched the page. Every one of them was an evaluator writing from somewhere that was not a desk.

Karis read the first one to herself, and then aloud.

It was an evaluator in the east, on a station circuit, about a young man of a carters' guild whose floor work ran a full rank ahead of his file. The evaluator had measured it at a frame and again on a guild floor and again by the clock, and he wrote that the file was plainly wrong, and asked that the young man be read again. At the foot of his report, in another hand, a registry clerk's stamp had been pressed square: Read against file. Enter at file. And under the stamp, a month later, the evaluator again, smaller: Continue observation.

"He gave in," said Brom.

"He did what the stamp told him," said Karis. "That's not the same thing, not quite." She laid it aside and took the next.

There were twenty-three. She read every one, and she read the stamp at the foot of every one, and after the sixth she stopped reading the stamp aloud because everybody in the room could say it with her. A woman in the hill country whose Stone came up too heavy for its column. A ferryman's boy whose Current had something of Wind in it that his station had not written down. A girl at a guild hall in the south who did everything her Path said she should, the evaluator wrote, only as if she were older than her paper. Each report saw the same thing and asked for the same thing, and each came back stamped the same way. Read against file. Enter at file. Some carried Continue observation under the stamp in the evaluator's own hand, and some carried nothing, and one carried a single line that Karis read twice before she read it out: Noted, and I do not like it.

When she had finished she gathered the twenty-three together and laid her hand on top of them.

"Down," she said, "every one. Where the file and the floor disagreed, the floor was corrected to the file, and never the other way."

"Never once?" said Brom.

"Not in this bundle. There's not one report where somebody was read higher than his paper and the paper went up to meet him." She looked at Seln. "Was there one in the press?"

"No," said Seln.

Cael sat on the bench and looked at the bundle under her hand.

He had spent all year writing himself down. Every Fifth-day in wing three he had stood in front of three cards and fought at a rate the house had chosen for him, a smaller man than the one he was, entered in the house's book at a figure that breathed and never rose. He had paid for it every week and called it a cost. But he had chosen it. He had sat at a long table with the people who mattered to him and decided, in ink, how much of himself to show, and he could have stopped any Fifth-day he liked. None of the twenty-three had chosen anything. Somebody had looked at what they were and stamped the page to say they were something less, and they had never even been told there was a page.

The memoranda were heavier than anything else on the table, and Karis turned the first stack over before she touched a word of it.

"Bottom first," she said, "always. The top of a pile is what somebody wanted you to find."

So she started at the oldest, at the yellow end, and worked forward. The sheets were printed, all of them, each a single leaf in a registry circular's form, with a number at the head and a seal pressed at the foot and a line of signatures under the seal. Cael watched her turn them, and the paper changed as she went, from a thick soft yellow stock that had gone brown at its edges to a thinner whiter one, and then to the hard bright paper the registry used now, the paper of the instrument on his own sill. The type changed too. The oldest leaves had heavy letters with long tails, the kind on the founders' volumes Karis kept on her top shelf, and the newest had the narrow even type of every form Bracken had ever put across a counter. The seal at the foot of each changed by small degrees, a ring of letters gone and another come, the river and the scale drawn first one way and then another. The signatures changed with every issue, officer after officer, a new name every few leaves.

The words did not change.

Karis read the heading of the oldest aloud, and then the heading of the newest, and then four from the middle at random, and they were all the same.

"Memorandum to keepers of stations and to clerks of entry. Corrective classification at Kindling evaluation." She put her finger under the line on the newest leaf. "And the body. It's three sentences, and it's been three sentences since this one." She touched the yellowest. "A word changes here and there, and shall became is to. A clause about the post came in when the post did. Otherwise you could lay the oldest on top of the newest and read straight through them."

"How many?" said Lira.

"Nineteen issues, reissued every ten years or so, by the look of the seals, when the officers changed or the paper did. Nineteen times somebody sat at a desk and had it set in type again, and signed it, and sent it to every station in the Compact."

Brom had been looking at the stacks without reading anything. He had his good hand on the table and his chin down, and he spoke to the paper.

"That's a form," he said.

Karis looked at him.

"I don't mean the shape of it," said Brom. "I mean what it is. You don't reissue a thing nineteen times because you're still arguing about it; you reissue it because it's how things are done. The estate had forms like that, the harvest tally and the stable book, and nobody thought about them, because that was what they were for." He moved his hand off the table. "That's a form."

"Yes," said Karis, after a moment. "You make a form so that the next man doesn't have to decide anything. He only fills it in."

Lira had pulled the yellow stack a little toward her along the cloth. She did not pick anything up. She looked at the first leaf with its brown edges and its heavy type.

"The first one wasn't a form," she said. "It can't have been. The first one somebody had to argue for."

"Yes," said Karis. "The first one is the one I want." She drew it back into its place beside the others, very gently. "Not tonight. I want it in order first, all of it, every seal against every other seal. I won't guess at the first one; I'll find it."

Cael had been reading the signatures while she talked.

He could not help it. Under every seal there was a line of them, three or four to an issue, and he went down them the way he went down the names on a bout card, by habit, and without meaning to he had counted. Nineteen issues and seventy-one names, give or take two he could not read in the yellow ones where the ink had gone brown and spread. Officers of the registry, by the titles after them: a chief clerk of entry, a keeper of the rolls, a second secretary, men and women whose offices Bracken would have known and Cael had never heard of. Not one of them appeared on two issues: ten years at a desk, and then a new name.

"Did they know?" he said. "Any of them?"

"They knew what it said," said Karis. "It says it in three sentences. You can't sign three sentences and not know what they say." She looked down the row of names as he had. "Whether they knew what it did is a different question. I don't know how to answer it from here."

"Most of them signed a reissue," said Seln.

They looked at him. He had not moved.

"A reissue is the lightest paper in any office," he said. "The words were settled before you were born. The clerk brings it in with the coal accounts and the lamp-oil order, and you sign where he points, because the last man signed there and the man before him." He looked at the yellow stack. "I have signed reissues, as every officer has. You sign them the way you sign for coal."

Seventy-one names, thought Cael, and he looked for the one that would make it simple, the cruel one, the one who had known and wanted it. There was no such name on the table.

The leaf was last, as it had been last out of the case.

Seln moved for the first time since he had put his hands on the table. He went round the end of the table and drew the sleeve toward the lamp with one finger, and then slid the leaf out of it himself, by its edges, and laid it on the cloth with its face up. He did not let go of it at once.

"Everything else is my hand," he said. "The orders and the records and the reports I copied, at night, over five weeks. The memoranda were spares. The press held three or four of every issue and nobody had counted them in a generation, so I took one of each. This is the only thing in the case that someone else made." He took his finger off it. "A copy of it would have been worth nothing. Everything it says is in what it is."

Karis's hands were already in her coat pockets. She carried thin cotton gloves there all through the cold term, for the founders' volumes on her top shelf, and she drew them out now and worked them on while she kept her eyes on Seln and not on the leaf, as if it would be rude to look at it bare-handed. Only when the second glove was on did she reach across and turn it toward the lamp by one corner.

Cael could see it from the bench. It was small, smaller than any of the memoranda, a single leaf of a thick grey-brown paper that had a faint grain in it like cloth. The writing on it was not printed. It was ink, in a hand Cael had never seen, upright and very old-fashioned and very clear, with a heading and a short paragraph under it. There was no seal. At the foot there was a mark that might once have been a seal before something wore it away, or might never have been anything.

Karis read it aloud. She read it more slowly than she had read anything that night.

"Of the advisory corrections function. The function is appended to the reading and is not the reading. It does not alter what the reading shows. It advises what is to be entered, and the entry is made as advised. It is to be maintained, and its maintenance is the office's charge."

She stopped.

Cael waited for her to go on. She did not. She sat with her gloved hands either side of the leaf and her eyes on the last line, and her face had gone into the stillness he had seen on it once before, at a citation in the seventh paragraph of the instrument on the first night of the year, and he knew she was frightened, and he knew she was frightened accurately.

"Appended," said Lira.

"Yes."

"To the reading."

"Yes." Karis did not look up. "And it's not the reading. It says so, and it goes out of its way to say so." She took a slip of paper from the pocket of her coat and a pencil, and wrote one word on the slip, and turned the slip face down on the cloth before anyone could read it. "I'm not going to say what I think, not tonight. I don't guess past paper, and I won't start in front of the paper that would make me."

"Nobody's asking you to," said Brom.

"I know." She laid the pencil across the face-down slip. "I'm telling myself."

Cael looked at the leaf from where he sat, upside down across the cloth, the old upright hand and the worn place at its foot.

The function is appended to the reading and is not the reading.

He thought of Denvash, which he did not often let himself do. A district office on a cold morning, a chalk circle on boards worn into two shallow places where a generation of feet had stood, and a warden-adjunct with tired grey eyes three feet away at a desk with a brass plate let into it. Something had woken behind his breastbone, small, a point of light at the edge of his sight that he could feel and never point to. He had counted eleven seconds while the plate did not light, and then the word had come, very far away and very close, and the plate lighting late with the same word in it, and the light at the edge of his sight going out like a pinched wick.

All his life since, he had said that his Arbiter had spoken once and gone dark. He had said it to panels and wardens and Magisters, and written it in two books. It had been the one fixed fact at the bottom of every argument he had ever won. It had read him once, and said one word, and the registry had written down that word because it had nothing else to write, and he lived in the gap the word left.

The leaf said there were two things in that office, not one. There was the reading, and there was something appended to it. And there had been eleven seconds.

He did not follow the thought any further. It was not his to follow. Karis had turned her slip face down, and he left his own face down beside it.

Seln said it then.

He did not sit down to say it, and he did not raise his voice. He stood at the middle of the table's far side with the whole of the case laid out in front of him in the lamplight, the forty and the bundle and the two stacks and the leaf, and he said it to the room the way he had once read a form to a man in a doorway at the third hour, one plain sentence after another.

"The registry corrects them. At Kindling, when the station reads them. Downward, by a form, for as long as it has had paper to write the form on. That is what I have carried."

He did not say it again. Nobody in the room said it again that night, in those words or any others. It lay on the table among the paper, said once, and nobody touched it.

Cael watched them hold it.

Lira's hands had come together in her lap, one inside the other, and stayed there. Karis had not taken her gloves off. She sat with them resting on the cloth either side of the leaf, as if she had forgotten they were on. Brom's good hand had gone, very slowly, to the left side of his coat, and lay over the inside pocket where the summons was, and the docket, and the letter from Velmere that he had carried sealed since the forty-fifth day. He did not take anything out. He only kept his hand there, the way a man puts his hand on a wall in the dark.

Seln's hands were flat on the table, as they had been all night.

Far off across the court, the lecture range's bell gave the half hour. It was the same bell that had rung the half hour every night of Cael's life on the hill. It sounded exactly the same.

It was Brom who spoke first, a long while after, with his eyes on the forty rows.

"How many?"

Seln looked at the rows too, and answered them rather than Brom.

"I stopped estimating. Estimating felt like filing."

Brom nodded slowly, as if that were an answer, and it was.

"Where?" said Lira.

"My fourth posting, twelve years ago." Seln put one hand back on the table, as if the wood steadied him. "A district seat in an old building, a records room on its top floor with presses round the walls, the kind with doors. I was looking for a subject's travel endorsements. They were filed where they should not have been, so I opened presses until I found them, and in the fourth press I found these." He moved his eyes over the rows. "The orders were in bound runs, a few years to a volume, with the records bundled behind them, and the memoranda on the bottom shelf in a box. And at the back of the box, loose, under the oldest, that." He did not look at the leaf. "Nobody had opened the press in years; the dust said so."

"And you copied it," said Karis.

"Over five weeks, at night. The posting gave me the room's key because I was a junior who stayed late, and juniors who stay late are trusted with keys." He said it without any pride at all. "One lamp on the floor, so the window stayed dark, and a few sheets a night in the lining of my coat. The case I bought afterward, in another town, from a man who made them for surveyors. I never told him what it was for, and he never asked, and he put his stamp inside the lid because he was proud of his work." He paused. "I did not understand it, and I want that said. I copied it because it was paper that sat a little above where it should have sat, and I had been trained to notice that, and I did not know what to do with what I noticed except keep it. For a year I thought it was a district's bad habit, a careless office."

"What changed?"

Seln was quiet a moment.

"A corridor," he said, "in a district station, a year on, with green distemper on the walls to the height of a man's shoulder, and benches. I was waiting for a file. A keeper came out of the frame room with a mother and a girl, and he was pleased, the way they are when a reading is a good one, and I heard him tell the mother that her girl read strong, and read into a second family as well, and he had not seen it in years." He looked at the father's letter, folded under its clip in the third row. "A week later I was back for another file, and the station's out-tray was on the counter, and her certificate was in it, waiting to go. One family, first rank." He took his hand off the table. "That was when the paper turned into children. It had been only paper for a year."

Lira was looking at him with her chin on her fist.

"And then twelve years," she said.

"And then twelve years."

"Two years on this hill," said Lira.

She said it the way she said a figure to a panel, plain and exact, and she did not take her eyes off Seln while she said it.

"Two years at that counter, and 'Mm,' and your cup turned a quarter on every table. Floor schedules on three doors in that hand, every week, so neat nobody's ever read one twice. Pleasant to every first-year who couldn't fill in a sheet, and to every Magister who wanted a room, and to me, the first week, when I didn't know where the east hall was and you walked me half across the court to show me." She took her chin off her fist. "With that on a shelf over your head the whole time, behind you, where you could feel it." She was quiet a moment. "I'd like to know what that cost, being pleasant."

Seln looked at her for a long time. Cael had never seen anyone ask him a question about himself and wait for the answer, and he did not think Seln had either.

"Nothing anybody would have noticed," he said at last. "That was the price."

Lira held his eyes a moment longer, and nodded, and let it be.

Karis had taken her gloves off and laid them side by side on the cloth beside the leaf. She was looking at the yellow stack again, at the memoranda, and when she spoke it was the voice she kept for craft, a reader asking another reader how he had done a thing.

"You said it sat a little above where it should have, the orders. But they're correct. I've read fourteen tonight, and every one is right: every date agrees with its record, every station is named the way the station names itself, every clip is on the right pair." She frowned at the rows. "There isn't a slip in them anywhere. How did a junior on his fourth posting look at paper that was correct in every particular and know it was wrong?"

"My mother's ledger was always right," said Seln.

Nobody understood him, and he saw it, and he went on, which he did not often do.

"She kept the books for a grain factor on a river quay, twenty years at the same desk with the same scale outside the window. I copied her ledgers from the time I could hold a pen, because the factor paid a boy a copper a page for the fair copies, and I was the boy." He looked at the stack of orders. "Every page of her ledger had a mistake on it, a weight misheard or a sack counted twice or a figure carried wrong. And every mistake was struck through with one line, so you could still read it, and initialled, and the right figure written beside it in the margin. That was what right looked like: a page that had been near something real, and been wrong, and been put right by a person who signed for it." He moved one hand toward the memoranda, the whole two centuries of them. "This has never once been wrong. There is not a struck figure in it, nor an initial in a margin. Two hundred years of paper made by people, and not one of them ever made a mistake." He took the hand back. "It had been made to agree."

Karis sat back on the bench.

"Yes," she said quietly. "Yes, that's how you'd know."

It was past the ninth bell. The lamp in the window would be wanted out within the hour or the valley would notice a difference, and the case had to be somewhere before it was.

"I need it for five nights," said Karis, "to index it. Every seal against every seal, every hand against every hand, the stations on a map, the dates in a column. I can't do it from memory and I won't do it from notes I take out of this room." She looked at Seln. "So it stays here, or it goes back to your shelf, and I come down to the wing every night with a lamp, and somebody writes the lamp down."

Seln looked round the room in his order again, the door and the windows and the landing and the shelves. It did not take him as long the second time.

"Here," he said.

He chose the place himself. He walked along Karis's shelves until he came to the row of her grey document boxes on the second shelf from the floor, the ones with her initials on their spines, which held her Greyvane papers and had not been moved in a year. Two of them stood apart by about the width of a man's hand. He measured the gap with his eyes and then with the case, and it went in between them and stood there, dark leather between grey card, a little shorter than its neighbours. From the door it looked like one more box nobody had labelled yet.

"The room has your key," he said to Karis. "The case has mine." He touched his waistcoat pocket. "Two keys, and neither of us opens it alone."

"The assistant never comes in after the sixth bell," said Karis. "From tonight. I'll tell her I'm working on something that smells."

"Tell her it's glue," said Brom. "She'll believe glue."

They put it back in the order it had come out, and it went back faster than it had come out, because Seln did it and nobody else touched it. The leaf went into its sleeve and the sleeve into the lid's pocket. The memoranda went in, oldest at the bottom. The bundle, tied again in the wing's knot. The forty, row by row, squared. The lid closed and the small key turned with its dry sound, and Seln carried the case to its place between the grey boxes and stood it there and came back.

Brom had begun to stand. He did it the careful way he had done everything for a week, getting his legs under him first and then the rest. Karis was reaching for the shaded lamp to turn it down. Lira had her hands on the bench to push herself up on the good foot.

Seln was buttoning his coat.

"Seln," said Cael.

Seln stopped with his hand on the third button.

"Will you sit down." His voice was steadier than he had expected. "It's my turn to put something on the table."

Lira let go of the bench first and sat back down on it, slowly, and put her right foot out straight again in front of her. Karis took her hand away from the lamp. Brom looked at Cael for a long time, and then he lowered himself back into the chair by the shelf without a word, and reached over with his good hand, and turned the kettle's little blue flame up again under the pot.

They all knew what he meant. They had known since a back room in Norhold on the night before the final, when Lira had told him to cost the seal out loud, and he had.

Seln looked at the three of them, and saw that they knew, and that he did not.

He took his hand off the button. He came back to the middle of the table's far side, and for the first time that night he sat down.

Chapter 37 — Two Files

He had never told it from the beginning.

He understood that only as he opened his mouth to start, sitting on the bench in the circle of the shaded lamp with Seln across the bare cloth from him. Lira had learned it in a yard at Ardenmere with grit in her palms, one piece at a time, because she had been there when each piece happened. Brom had learned it from Lira and from his own three mornings in an alcove, and had asked the rest across a table, and been told. Karis had come to it at Greyvane with most of it already worked out on paper in her own hand, and had asked only for the parts she could not get by reading. Each of the three had it whole now. Not one of them had ever heard it in order, start to finish, in one telling.

Nor had he. He had written it down in pieces as it came, in two books, over years. He had never once said it straight through out loud.

"I'll tell it the way the book would," he said. "In order. With the prices."

Seln nodded once. He put his hands flat on the table and did not move them again.

So Cael began at Denvash.

He told the circle chalked on the worn boards of a district office, and the warden-adjunct three feet away watching the brass plate let into her desk, and the thing that woke behind his breastbone and came up to the edge of his sight. He told the eleven seconds he had counted while the plate did not light, and the one word that came at the end of them, very far away and very close, and the light at the edge of his sight going out like a pinched wick and never coming back when he looked. He told the letter that had made Denvash impossible for Hesk's sake, and the road east. He told Lira next, because Lira had come next: six weeks of bouts in a yard at Ardenmere, with her knocking him down on the boards between them more times than either of them had counted. Then one cold night on a cot under a window, with the Log on his knee, something had been written in the dark place behind his breastbone where the light had gone out.

"I didn't know what it was," he said. "I sat and read it twice. Then the first time I spent it on a floor, Lira saw it, and she knew what it was before I did, because it was hers."

"It was mine," said Lira, from the end of the bench. "I'd know my own burst in a dark room."

He told the others in their order. The Bronze from Ardenmere, who had driven him across a floor with flat hands until something of the push came into his right shoulder and stayed there. Brom and his three mornings, and the read that came out of them, the cheapest thing Cael owned and the one he trusted most. Reydan, on a scored floor, and the give that took a blow into the body and kept it from going further. Karis, at Greyvane, across a formal yard in the cold, with her little fires coming up out of the ground. Hers was the only one he had ever asked for first, and she had said yes in writing, and been asked again the night before he spent it, and said yes again.

He told the notices.

"They come after, every time," he said. "Words behind my eyes, as if somebody were holding up a card: fragment acquired, and the name of the Path with adjacent after it, because it isn't the Path, it's a piece of how the Path is done. Then how long it lasts and how far in it goes, and sometimes a tier, and then how it was taken and what kind of engagement it was." He looked at the cloth. "I don't know who writes them. Nobody's ever been able to tell me, and I've stopped asking out loud. I write them down word for word, every time, and I've never once found one wrong."

Seln did not move.

He told the rule: how the four of them had sat at a long table at Halcenvane, before the stair, and written it in a minute in Karis's hand, and numbered it, and signed it. Nothing made to happen. Only inside a fight somebody else begins. The cost on paper first. And after Norhold, a fourth line under the three, initialled by four: never again in the middle of a fight unless what follows has been priced first, at the weight it will come at.

"Because every one of them costs," he said. "The Wind's bill comes to the hip. The push comes out of the right shoulder, four blows a sitting and no more. The read is cheap, and the give is a cup that fills. Karis's spark burns me too, at the fingers, if I spend it past two contacts. The storm's the heaviest thing I own, and when I lay a lane the whole of me goes a beat slow afterward for ten counts, and if I lay three close together the third costs twelve." He said it in the log's voice, each figure exact. "Those are the prices, and they're all in the book. Nothing's free. That was the first thing I learned, on a cot at Ardenmere with the Log on my knee, and it's still true."

He told Daeva, on the stone at Norhold in front of eight thousand people, and the storm that came out of her into him, and the eleven weeks of it settling, and the morning on the second floor when it settled.

He told the woman on the Ostrand road.

"And under all of them," he said, "there's one I don't count. Session nine, at fifteen: a piece of something like Tide, from nobody. There was no Tide practitioner within a day's ride. There was nothing at stake and nobody against me, nothing the rule says it needs, and it came anyway." He moved his hand on the cloth. "I don't know what it is. I've kept it out of the count for three years, because the day I count it I've decided something I don't know. I've got three words for it. Still open. Still real. Patience."

He stopped.

He had told it all but one, and he had told it in order, with the prices. His hands were steady. He was tired, too, in a way the ribs had nothing to do with. It was as if he had carried something heavy up four flights and set it down, and only now felt how heavy it had been.

Seln had not moved once. He had not turned his cup, because there was no cup. He had not looked away from Cael's face in all that time, and his own face had shown nothing at all, as it showed nothing at the counter. But Cael had watched him listen, and he listened the way Karis read, all of it, to the end, before he let himself think a single thing about any of it.

"Eight," said Seln. "And one you don't count."

"Eight." Cael looked at him. "I've told you seven."

"Yes," said Seln. "I counted."

Seln asked four questions.

He asked them one at a time, and he waited for each answer to finish before he asked the next, and none of them was the question Cael had expected. He did not ask what it felt like, or why, or how far it went, or what it meant. He did not ask about the woman or the storm or the notices. Every one of his questions was the same question asked from a different side, the only question his trade had ever taught him to ask about a thing that mattered: who could find it?

"Who knows?"

"Lira. Brom. Karis." Cael did not look at them. "Now you. Nobody else alive."

"Nobody you told when you were small? The man who raised you?"

"I didn't know what it was when I was small. By the time I knew, I'd learned not to say."

Seln took that, and set it somewhere, and went on.

"Where is it written?"

"Two books. The old volume's full, and it's in my trunk under the bed, locked. The current one's Hesk's book, and it's in the satchel." Cael touched the strap across his chest. "Everything since Ardenmere is in one or the other, every notice word for word and every price beside it."

"Under the bed," said Seln.

"Locked."

"Mm," said Seln, and Lira, at the end of the bench, made a small sound that might have been a laugh if she had let it.

"Can an instrument read it off you?"

That was the one Cael had thought about longest, over the years, at night, and he answered it carefully.

"No frame has ever read anything off me but what I put in front of it. The plates in the wing read what I give them, and I give them the band. The read at Brom's grade is a surface, and I can hold a surface. And my own Arbiter went out at Denvash after one word. It's never lit since. I've not stood in a station since."

"A light that goes out is a reading too," said Seln. "Somebody writes down that it went out."

Karis looked up from the cloth very sharply. Seln did not look at her; he waited.

"I know," said Cael. "They wrote down the word it said first. That's all they've ever had."

"And the last." Seln moved one finger on the wood, very slightly, the first time his hands had moved since he sat down. "Does it ever show where somebody counts? Not in a fight, but after, in a corridor or on a stair or at a table, where a man like me would see it."

"The bills show," said Cael. "The hip, the shoulder. People see a fighter with a bruise and a stiff walk, and they think bruise. Nobody's ever looked at a bruise and thought anything else." He thought of Ephram's three close-ruled pages. "The band shows, and Ephram's charted it for a year, but the band's the thing I chose to show. It breathes because we made it breathe."

"I know," said Seln. "I watched you make it."

He sat on after that with his eyes on the cloth. Brom's kettle had begun to tick on its shelf, the small dry sounds a pot makes before it thinks about boiling. Cael waited, and did not know for what.

At last Seln looked up.

"You may say it to me twice more in your life," he said.

Cael did not understand him. Seln saw it.

"What you have just told me, all of it, in order. Twice more, if there is ever a need, and you will know if there is, but not a third time." He said it as he would have said a rule of the wing to a first-year who had asked about floor hours. "Every telling is a copy, and a thing told three times is a thing on its way to being known. I have kept the case twelve years by never once describing it to anybody, and you will keep this by telling it as seldom as you can bear to." He paused. "I am not ungrateful. I am only telling you the price, because nobody told me mine until I had paid it."

"Twice more," said Cael.

"Twice more."

"There's one more," said Cael. "I've told you seven."

Seln waited.

"It's yours."

He watched that go into Seln's face and not come out. Nothing changed in it. Seln did not move or blink or draw a breath. That was how Cael knew it had gone in.

So he told the stair.

He told it the way he had written it, standing against a wall under a lamp in the covered walk with the notebook held to the stone at the third hour. The archive at Halcenvane on a bad night two years ago, near enough, in the first year he was on the hill. The fire-watch gone the long way round. A man with a bag at the top of the upper flight, in the doorway, with his gloved hand already going into a press he had no business opening. And on the landing above him, in the light, the wing's assistant. He was reading the man a form, one plain line after another, about copying and paper and what a magistrate counted in years, until the man's hand came back out of the press with nothing in it.

"I was on the half-landing," said Cael. "Below you, in the corner behind Brom's coat, in the dark, where I'd sat three nights running."

"I know where you were," said Seln.

Cael stopped.

"I knew there was somebody in the corner on the second night, and I knew who on the third." Seln's voice had not changed at all. "I did not look down the flight. A man in a doorway with a bag looks where the officer looks, so I did not look."

Nobody in the room moved.

Cael went on, because there was nothing else to do. He told the rule counted on five fingers against Brom's coat: earnest, a man spending everything he had in the light and meaning every word; his, begun by him, before Cael knew there was anything to begin; close, one flight; his work, the wing's officer doing the wing's work; and awake, the little finger. He told how he had not done it the way he did a burst, all at once before thinking could catch up, but slowly, on purpose, on the cold stone, knowing exactly what he did and to whom. And the quiet coming down over him like a heavy door swung shut, the stair's sounds gone, the light gone flat, and three seconds or four of the night going on above him without him in it. And then the notice.

He said it word for word, because he had it by heart and had never once said it aloud.

Seln's hands lay flat on the table.

"Adversarial," he said, after a moment. "I was not against you."

"You were against him," said Cael. "In earnest, with everything you had. It was enough."

He told the rest quickly, because the rest was only time. Two years, near enough, since the stair. It had never been used anywhere, by anybody's count. He had never once asked it for anything in front of a living soul, save once on the first night, to get past a lantern, and then it had not come. Rent from waking every day, spent or not, the way a room costs rent whether you sleep in it or not. Drifts in the gaps, never in the work: a thinning at his edges on a stair or in a queue, when he was tired. Lira had counted them for him on the back of a chair with her thumbnail, and the count had fallen every week. Its two halves would not sit together in his hands. To hide moving he had to read the room, and to read the room he had to be the most awake thing in it, and being that awake was what put the hiding out.

"You do both at once," he said. "I've watched you. I still can't."

"A year of it," said Seln. "Before I was a man in a doorway, I glowed." He did not explain that, and Brom, in the chair by the shelf, looked at the floor as if he had heard it before somewhere.

Then Norhold.

"The night before the final," said Cael. "In a back room on the harbour, with the shutter open a crack. We'd costed everything I was going to spend the next day: the Wind past six, the push at fighting load, the give, the spark. Everything that had been held back for two years was going to go out in one afternoon, in front of the whole continent, and be on the record for good." He looked at Lira. "And I said the quiet thing stayed sealed, and Lira said to cost the seal, out loud, and say why."

"I did," said Lira. "I wanted it said."

"So I said why." Cael made himself look at Seln. "Because of who it came from. That fight was going to be written down three times over and gone through for years by people whose whole work is sorting. If I'd used it, somebody sorting would find one loose thread. Where did a fighter with no tier ever see that kind of work, done well, long enough to come away with any of it? It isn't a long thread, and if you pull it, it comes away in your hand at a counter in the wing, at a copying table, where a quiet man has spent his whole life making sure nobody ever looks at him twice."

Seln did not move.

"So it stayed sealed. It was sealed that night for a debt, and the next afternoon, in the last corner, against the barrier, with her lane coming and nowhere left to go, it offered. It always offers when I'm cornered, and it would have hidden me from every eye in the bowl." He let his breath go. "I didn't turn my head."

"We all held the coat," said Lira quietly. "All four of us, not just him."

Brom nodded once, slowly, at the floor.

"He isn't told," said Karis. "That's what we said in the back room. He's never told." She looked across the table. "We were wrong about the second half."

The kettle had stopped ticking. The lamp stood up straight in its glass.

Cael did not watch his face. Two years across a counter had taught him that it was the last place on the man where anything would show. He watched the hands instead, flat on the green cloth, and saw the fingertips pressed down until they had gone pale, the way a clerk presses a ledger open at a page he means to read back through from the top. Cael knew which pages. The counter, the bench and the cup. The slips on the common-room fire. A season's figures that never once settled into a line. An afternoon at Norhold where everything held back went out in one breath, except one thing. Somewhere in all that, a boy had been holding a coat over him and never saying so, and the hands were finding each place.

The colour came back into the fingertips, and he said it to the cloth.

"You kept my file too, then."

Nobody answered him, because it was not a question.

He sat a while longer. Then he took his hands off the table for the second time that night, and folded them in front of him on the cloth. Cael had never seen him fold his hands.

"Is it still sealed?"

"Yes."

"Tonight. Now. With me told."

"It's sealed till somebody unseals it," said Cael. "I don't know who that is now. It was a debt, and you've been told. I don't know what a debt is after it's been told."

Seln looked at the folded hands.

"I am not going to release it," he said, "and I am not going to take it back. I couldn't if I wanted to. It is yours. A notice says so, and I have never yet known one of those to be wrong either." He was quiet a moment. "But I would like to set the terms of the seal. If you will let me."

"Set them."

"While its use can be seen by anyone who could carry the seeing west, it stays where it is." Seln said it slowly and exactly, the way he wrote a line in a return that he meant to be read by somebody careful. "Not for my file, which can look after itself now; it has had practice. For the trade. Somewhere, in a room I will never see, there is a man whose whole work is sorting, and any report of a thing that moves the way I move gives him a thread to pull. Where there is no witness who can carry it west, there is no thread, and then it is yours. Use it or don't, as you judge." He unfolded his hands. "And you will not ask me first. That is the other term."

Cael took Hesk's book out of the satchel.

He opened it on the cloth to the leaf after the birthday inventory, and uncapped Hesk's steel pen, and wrote it there in front of all of them, in the smallest plain hand he had, with the shaded lamp drawn close.

Shadow-adjacent, the quiet thing from the stair. Told tonight, whole, to the man it came from, in Karis's room, the four of us there. The debt is closed. The seal is kept. Grounds revised: no longer a debt kept from him. His terms: sealed from any witness who could carry it west; otherwise mine, and I don't ask.

He blotted it and turned the book round on the cloth so that it faced across the table.

Seln read it upside down without touching it, the way he read everything that came across the counter, twice, and then he nodded once.

"Mm," he said.

Brom got up out of the chair by the shelf, which took him the usual time, and went to the kettle. It had boiled, and none of them had heard it go. It stood over its blue flame with a thin plume coming out of the spout, as if it had been waiting a long while for somebody to notice. Brom made the tea one-handed, which he had got good at in a week, and put a cup in front of each of them on the bare cloth, Seln's last.

Seln looked at his cup.

Then he put out his hand and turned it a quarter turn on the table.

They went down at a little before the tenth bell, one at a time, a few minutes apart, because Seln said that five people coming down a stair together was a meeting, and five people coming down one at a time was the library closing.

Karis stayed, because she would turn the lamp in the window down at its usual hour and not a minute before. Brom went first, by the iron stair through the stacks, and Cael heard the ninth tread on the second flight say what Brom had said it would. Seln went second, by the bindery stair, and did not say goodnight. At the door he stopped and looked back at the shelf, at the dark leather case standing between two of Karis's grey boxes like one more box with no label, and then at Cael, and then he went.

Lira went third, and Cael went with her, because she had said not to help her and he was not going to, and that did not mean he could not be on the same stair.

She went down the top stair the way she had come up it, which turned out to be sitting, one step at a time, with her hands on the tread behind her and her right foot held clear. At the bottom she got up by the newel post and stood on the third-floor landing breathing hard, and looked at him.

"Not a word," she said.

"I didn't say anything."

"You were going to." She put her hand on the newel post's cap, worn smooth by a hundred years of hands. "Post," she told it, seriously. "It holds the rail up. People hold it going down."

He said it after her.

They went down the main stair together, slowly, at her pace. On the second landing she stopped, not for the ankle.

"Two years," she said. "He knew it was you in the corner. All the time we were holding a coat over him, he'd been holding one over you, on a stair, and he never once looked down it."

"Yes."

"I keep thinking about the first week." She started down again. "Walking me across the court to the east hall. Being pleasant." She did not say anything else until the street door, and at the street door she said, "Door," and he said it after her, and they went out into the cold.

He did not write the cache in the book.

He sat at the sill with the satchel on it and the book open and Hesk's pen in his hand, and the court below him dark, and the fountain going up black and coming down white, and he did not write it.

He had written everything for years. Every notice word for word, every price. The book was where a thing went to be true. And Seln had sat across the table and asked where it was written, and when he had answered, Seln had said Under the bed. In a voice that cost nothing, he had said, A thing told three times is a thing on its way to being known. The case had been kept twelve years by a man who had never once described it to anybody. Cael did not think he would last twelve hours if he started writing it down.

So he wrote what he could.

Day 88. Five in Karis's room by three stairs across an hour. The case opened. What was in it does not go into a book. It is in a room with two keys, and the five of us have it, and that is where it will stay.

Lira's strapping off this morning, Brom's sling off tomorrow, and the ribs two more days by the healer's count.

Told the whole of it tonight, in order, to the one person at that table who had never heard it, the first time from the beginning. It's longer than I thought, and shorter. Twice more in my life, he says, and not a third.

Then he turned back three leaves to the birthday inventory, to the line for the sixth, and drew one straight line through sealed, rent from waking so that it could still be read, the way Seln's mother had done in a grain factor's ledger on a river quay, and wrote the new figure beside it in the margin.

Sealed, on his terms. Rent from waking.

He initialled it.

Through the window, down in the court, a man in a dark coat came out of the library's shadow at the bindery end and crossed the flags toward the wing. He went at an even pace, neither slow nor quick. He did not take the covered walk. He went straight across the open court in the frost where anybody could have seen him, and nobody did, because nobody looks at a man going home at the tenth bell with nothing in his hands.

Cael watched him all the way to the wing door. At the door he stopped, and did not look back, and went in.

Chapter 38 — Thresholds

The worst of the next morning was that the hill looked exactly the same.

He had half expected it not to. He had lain awake for an hour after the tenth bell with the satchel on the sill and the court dark below, and some part of him had believed that the house would look different in daylight, now that he knew what he knew. But the frost was on the flags as it had been yesterday. The fountain went up and came down. The porter's boy was chalking the day's names on the Crown yard's boards, and two Mire second-years were arguing at the refectory door about whose turn it was to fetch the bread, and the coats at the foot of the road changed on the bell. Not one thing on the whole bluff had moved an inch to make room for what was on the shelf in Karis's room.

He went to the wing at the second bell for the week's floor sheet, because it was the Fifth-day and he always did.

The queue was four long. A first-year girl stood at the front of it with a folded paper in both hands, holding it the way you hold a thing you have been told twice not to lose. She was small, with a scarf wound three times round her neck against the cold and a Wind badge on her coat so new its pin still shone. The desk clerk was busy with the day book, so it was the teaching assistant who rose from the copying table to take it from her, as he did when the clerk was busy.

"From my station," she said. "They wrote that you wanted it for my file, so my mother sent it on."

"The house's copy," said Seln. "Thank you." He unfolded it on the counter and read it, and Cael watched him read it. It was a station certificate, the ordinary kind, with a registry seal at its foot and three lines of a clerk's writing above. Seln read the three lines once at his counter pace, neither slow nor quick. Then he blotted the foot where the girl's mother had signed for it, though the ink was days dry, and folded it again along its old folds, and wrote a line in the wing's ledger, and put the certificate in the drawer under the counter where enrollees' station papers went.

"Mm," he said, to the ledger.

The girl said thank you and went out into the cold with her hands free and her scarf trailing.

Cael stood in the queue and looked at the drawer.

There would be a certificate in it for every enrollee on the hill, four hundred and thirty of them. There would be one for Lira, from wherever she had been read, and one for Brom from the Velmere district, and one for Karis. There was no certificate in it for him, because the plate at Denvash had lit with a word and no station had ever written him down since. Every other paper in that drawer was three lines in a clerk's hand, and some of the three lines were what a station had read, and some of them were what an order had told it to write. There was no way on earth, standing at a counter in a queue, to tell which.

He could have spent the rest of the year that way. He saw it quite clearly as he stood there. He could look at every badge on every coat, every Ash and every Current and every Stone at every table in the refectory, and wonder what had been taken off its margin. He could read the whole hill as a drawer full of wounds and walk up and down it all year with that in his face, and Seln would see it at the counter in a week, and so would the coats, and so would anybody whose whole work was sorting.

He decided, standing there, that he would not.

It was a decision; he felt himself make it, the way he felt himself set his feet before a burst. He did not stop knowing. He only put the knowing where he put the band, somewhere it could be carried every day without being looked at. The girl with the new badge was a Wind first-year with her scarf trailing. That was what she was this morning. If it was not all she was, that was not a thing he could mend from a queue, and it was not a thing he was going to do to her by looking.

"Hesk-ward," said the desk clerk. "Your sheet."

He took his sheet. Under the Fifth-day, in Seln's hand, it still said excused (ribs). In wing three that morning the band bouts would go on without him, three cards and a figure, the Ash instructor and the Mire and Gault, and somewhere in the residence Ephram would be ruling his chart and leaving a second gap. Cael folded the sheet and put it in his coat.

At the copying table Seln turned a leaf and did not look up.

Brom's sling came off at noon.

He came out of the infirmary with the linen triangle folded small in his good hand and his left arm hanging at his side, and stood in the covered walk opening and closing the left hand very slowly, the way a man tries a hinge that has been painted shut.

"A week of nothing heavy," he said, "and nothing over my head. She says I'm to let it remember where it lives." He opened the hand again and looked at it. "It's forgotten. You'd think it would remember a thing like that."

He went to the old frames all the same, after the noon meal, because Ephram was there. Cael went with him and stood at the wall and watched. Brom did not lift anything. He stood beside the frames with his arms folded, the left one carefully, and watched Ephram work through the long frame's sets one after another without a word, the way they had stood together at those frames all year. At the end of his sets he wiped his hands, and looked at Brom's left arm for one second, and nodded at it as if it had passed some test he had set it privately, and went.

"He measures everything," said Brom, when the captain had gone.

"So do you."

"So do I." Brom unfolded his arms. "I don't mind being measured by somebody who's going to be right."

Lira asked it on the north wall at dusk, as Cael had known for a day that somebody would, and that it would be her.

She had come out along the wall at the slow careful pace the ankle allowed, and sat down beside him on the coping by the third buttress with her right foot out straight along the stone. Below them the valley was going blue. The river had dropped since the flood and run back into its banks, and the ferry was working again at the landing, small and black on the grey water. At the foot of the road the two coats stood apart from each other as they always stood, and while Cael watched, the bell went in the lecture range and two more came up the road from the town and the first two walked down it. Nobody hurried, and nobody looked up at the wall.

"Why are we still here?" said Lira.

She did not say it angrily. She said it the way she had said it once before, in a whitewashed dairy with a slit window, as if it were a question in a lesson that had come up on the board and was owed an answer.

"I'm not asking to be difficult," she said. "I'm asking because I sat on that bench last night and listened to you all read forty of them out, and I've been doing my drills in my head all day, and I can't make them go." She looked at the coats. "That seat down there runs on it, and so does the evaluation. Every sitting we go to, we're sitting in the room and answering it, and it's the thing in the case. They want to read you again. We know now what reads you." She pulled her coat closer. "My carters said the stamps stop four days east, loaded, or three days light. I've been carrying that in my pocket since the dairy. We could be past the last station by the Seventh-day after next if we left on the Seventh-day."

"We could," said Cael.

"So why are we still here?"

He did not answer at once. Brom had come along the wall behind them while she was talking, and stood now with his back against the buttress and his hands in his coat, and did not sit, because sitting on cold stone with one good arm was a thing he said he would do next week.

"Both roads," said Brom. "I said it in the dairy, and I've two boxes roped under my bed, and that's not nothing." He looked down at the ferry. "I'm not saying stay. I'm saying I've been packing for a fortnight and I've not told anybody what for, and I'm tired of it."

Lira turned and looked up at him.

"You've been packing?"

"Since the gate." He did not look at her. "Somebody had to."

Cael sat between them on the coping and looked at the coats at the foot of the road.

"The first thing I believed about all this," he said slowly, "was that the text would hold, that the people failed and the text didn't. I wrote it on the first night of the year, and it died on the Ostrand road. The room was never the system." He moved his hand on the cold stone. "Last night I found out what the system is. It's a form, three sentences that seventy-one people signed for coal. It's not a room I can walk out of, because it's not in a room. It's in every station between here and the coast." He was quiet a moment. "Knowing that doesn't make leaving cheaper. I thought it would, and I don't know why I thought it would. It only makes it clearer what we'd be leaving."

"That's not an answer," said Lira.

"No."

"I'll take it," she said. "For tonight."

Karis came out along the wall at the second bell after dusk, which was when she always came when she came at all, with her coat buttoned wrong and a volume of the code under her arm and her hair coming down at the back. She stopped beside Brom, and looked at the three of them, and saw at once what they were talking about, because Karis always could.

"Don't," she said. "Don't say it again. Not till I've priced it."

"Priced what?" said Lira.

"Leaving. What it costs, to the day and the line; not what it feels like, but what the code writes down." Karis shifted the volume under her arm. "I know what happens if a respondent walks out in the middle of a proceeding, because I read the coastal default to you in the dairy, and you all remember the word. I don't know what happens to the rest of us, or to the house, or whether there's any day in the year when it's different." She looked at Lira. "Give me two days."

"One," said Lira.

"Two."

"One and a half."

"Two," said Karis, "and you can have the half back afterward with interest." She turned and went back along the wall the way she had come, with the code under her arm, toward the lit window at the top of the library.

Lira watched her go. Then she laughed, once, quietly, the first time she had laughed since the infirmary.

"She's going to find it," she said. "Whatever it is."

"She always does," said Brom.

Lira crossed the east hall in front of Rooke on the Sixth-day at dawn, and Cael went with her as far as the door.

She could not drill. She went every dawn regardless and sat at the rail with Rooke's red drill-book and watched the program work under the two lamps, because she said a drill watched was half a drill done, and that she would rather be half than nothing. This morning she did not go to the rail by the wall. She stood a moment in the doorway with her hand on the frame. Then she let go and walked across the painted floor between the white crosses and arrows to where Rooke stood at the far rail with his arms folded, in front of the whole program, at her own pace.

Cael watched her from the door. She did not limp, or do anything a stranger would have seen. But she was thinking about every step, and he could see her thinking about it, in the set of her shoulders and the way her eyes stayed a yard ahead of her feet on the boards. If he could see it from the door, Rooke could see it from the rail.

She reached the rail and stopped.

Rooke looked at her feet, and then at her face.

"Not yet," he said.

"I know," said Lira.

He nodded, and turned back to the floor, where the Current girl was waiting on the four-count with her hands up. "Again. On the four," he said, and the program went on.

Lira walked back across the hall the same way, thinking about every step, and came out past Cael into the grey dawn of the covered walk.

"I knew before he said it," she said at last. "I knew at the third step." She pulled her scarf up. "I wanted him to say it out loud, so I'd stop wondering, that's all. Now it's said, and I can stop."

Bracken brought the Greyvane leaves up the library stair himself on the Seventh-day, at noon, all four flights, which he had not done since the birthday parcel.

He came into the reading room with a flat packet under his arm wrapped in oilcloth and sealed with the Greyvane archive's grey wax, and stood in the doorway in his spectacles and weighed it on his palm out of habit before he held it out.

"Nine days on the road," he said. "Registered, under seal, with the archive's compliments and an invoice for the copying that I have paid and entered. The first spend on the house's first budget line for an enrollee's research." He gave it to her. "It came before the recess, as they promised. I note it because the archive at Greyvane has never in my thirteen years kept a promise about a date, and I wish it to be on the record that it has kept one."

Karis signed his receipt with her right hand, the pale fingers steady on the pen. Then she broke the seal and folded back the oilcloth and looked at what was inside without touching it, as she had looked at the leaf.

Nine sheets, each with a seal impression taken in fresh wax from an old die and a line of signatures copied under it in an archivist's careful hand. The founders' hands, and the registry seals that had been set beside them on the charter, one for every year the charter had been renewed.

She took out the grey notebook and turned to the page near the back where she kept the things that were not finished, and found her own heading, Greyvane: the founders' hands, with three blank lines ruled under it that had been blank since the day the budget was voted. She filled them in, one line at a time.

Received, the house's ninety-first day. Under seal, entire.

Nine leaves. Seals of known years, one to a renewal.

Paid.

She drew a single straight line through the heading, so that it could still be read.

Bracken had watched her do it from the door. He had a way of watching a form being filled in properly that Cael had seen at the counter for two years, a small stillness, as if the room had briefly come into tune.

"Registrar," said Karis. "May I borrow the enrollment book? The old volume. The one before yours."

Bracken looked at her over his spectacles.

"For a citation," said Karis.

"I don't ask what for," said Bracken. "I ask when it comes back."

"Tomorrow. Before the second bell."

"Then it's lent." He nodded the small nod he gave a form that had been filled in properly, and went back down the stair, and twenty minutes later the porter's boy came up it with the old volume in his arms like a baby he had been told was valuable.

She found it that night.

The five of them sat in the reading room under the shaded lamp, with the case on its shelf between the grey boxes and the lamp in the window turned up as high as every night, and Karis laid it out for them on the bare cloth in the order she had found it. She had the code's second volume open on the left and the old enrollment book open on the right, and a single sheet of her own between them with five lines on it.

"Three things," she said. "Then the door. Then the price."

She put her finger on the code.

"First. A respondent who leaves the jurisdiction while a proceeding is pending is absent. You remember the coastal letter. The seat doesn't need him to have run. It needs him not to be there. The code doesn't count missed sittings; it counts days from the close of the fourth sitting, the one that put the record, and if he's out of the jurisdiction on the fortieth of them, it enters him." She did not need to read the line. "Respondent absent from the jurisdiction; entered as fled. That's Cael. The fourth sitting closed on the seventy-fifth day. If he were gone, it would enter on the hundred and fifteenth, long before any ruling."

"Second." She turned two leaves. "A chartered house whose enrollee is entered as fled, during a proceeding brought against his enrollment, is entered as having harboured the flight. It's one line on the house's charter. It doesn't close the house; it sits on the charter for the next inspection, and the inspection reads it." She looked at the table. "Withrow's charter folder, the one with the remedy column."

"Third. The enrolled associates of a respondent entered as fled." She did not look at Lira or Brom. "Every enrollee of this house whose file names him, in a minute or a squad list or a delegation. A note on each file: associated with a respondent entered as fled. No penalty, only a note, on three files." She paused. "His makes four."

Lira's hand had closed on the edge of the bench.

"So we can't go," said Brom.

"Not now. Not without the word on four files and a line on the house's charter, and not without leaving Withrow with that in her folder for the rest of her tenure." Karis turned to the enrollment book. "That's the price of now. Here's the door."

The old volume was open at a page near its middle. The ink had gone brown. The hand was not Bracken's; it was older, rounder, with long tails on the letters.

"A ruled matter is not a pending matter," said Karis. "The code's very particular about it, in a section about enrollees under orders that haven't yet taken effect. Once the seat has ruled, the proceeding is concluded. If the ruling revokes an enrollment, the revocation takes effect on a date, and until that date the enrollee is still an enrollee in standing, under an order. And an enrollee in standing may withdraw." She put her finger on a line in the brown ink. "And the house enters it in these words."

She read it aloud.

"Withdrawn in the week following the district seat's ruling, before the date of its effect. Resigned in good standing."

"Who was it?" said Lira.

"A fourth-year, two registrars ago, in a guild matter ruled against him. He went home to his father's trade, I think, but the book doesn't say." Karis closed her hand over the line, not quite touching it. "It doesn't matter who. What matters is the words. The house has written them before, and nobody questioned them, and they stood."

Cael looked at the brown ink under her hand.

"So there's one door," he said.

"One." Karis looked at him. "It opens on one day, the day of the ruling, and stays open until the revocation takes effect, and then it shuts. And it only opens at all if we lose. If the seat rules for the house, there's no door, because there's nothing to resign from." She sat back. "Until that day there's only the corridor: every sitting attended, every form filed on time, every bout in wing three at the band, and every first-year at that counter handing in a certificate, and you standing behind her in the queue with your face doing nothing." She was quiet a moment. "Perfectly, until the ruling. If we put one foot wrong before it, the door we'd use afterward turns into the word on four files."

"So we don't run," said Lira slowly. "We walk."

"We walk. Perfectly."

"Corridor," said Brom.

Seln had said nothing all evening. He sat at the middle of the far side with his hands flat on the cloth and his cup turned, and when they looked at him he moved one finger.

"I am not enrolled," he said. "My door is a different shape." He did not say what shape. "Walk yours."

Karis drew one more line on her sheet, under the five, and wrote beside it in small letters for now, and provisionally. She closed the enrollment book very gently, so as not to crack its spine, and put it on the corner of the table by the door, where she would see it at the second bell.

They went to the east hall on the First-day night after the tenth bell, the four of them, on Lira's key, to learn what the new thing saw.

Not to use it. Cael wrote that first.
