He wrote it standing at the rail under the first lantern, on a clean leaf of Hesk's book, before anybody had taken a step onto the painted boards, and held it out, and the other three initialled it one after another. Brom's B with its bar through. Lira's L, very upright. Karis's K, written with the right hand, the pale fingers holding the pen as steadily as they ever had.

Perception only. Nothing laid. Nothing fixed. Every There? named, aloud if need be. If anything fixes, Brom counts. If Brom counts past one, we stop.

"And we stop anyway at the first bell," said Lira, "because I'm cold, and I'm not allowed to move about to get warm."

She had the bench by the rail, with Rooke's red drill-book on her knee for something to hold and her right foot out straight on the boards. Karis had chalk and her grey notebook and her coat buttoned right for once. Brom had gone up the gallery stair and drawn every shutter down the length of the north wall, as Lira had drawn them on the first honest floor of the year. Now he stood in the hall's great doorway, with one of the two tall doors standing open a hand's breadth onto the dark of the passage and his right hand on its edge.

Two lanterns. The painted crosses and arrows going away across the planed floor into the half-dark. The frames along the east wall on their heavy springs.

Cael walked out into the middle of the floor and stood there, and shut his eyes, and let it look.

He had never let it look before. Since the road he had spent every waking hour answering it, no and then names, a word a thing at every threshold, so that it would stop asking. He had never once stood still and let it ask about everything at once and not answered any of it, only listened to the asking.

It was like opening a window on a night full of small sounds.

The hall came to him as places where things were resting. The frames along the east wall stood on their feet on the boards, and each foot was a place, a small sure point where weight met wood and stayed. The lantern on its hook by the rail hung, and its hook in the beam was a point, and the point was asking. The bench Lira sat on had four legs, and the legs were four points in a square. The bar across the foot of the gallery stair was two points and a line. The great door had its hinges, three of them, all points, and along its edge, where it stood open against nothing, a long empty place that the new thing leaned toward with its whole attention, the way a dog leans toward a door with somebody behind it.

And between the points, faint, there were lines.

Not lines anybody could see. He could not have said where they were with his eyes open. But with his eyes shut he could feel the hall hung together by them, foot to foot and hook to beam and leg to leg. It was like a scaffold built round a house that has not been built yet, every rest in the room joined to every other rest. It was not a picture of the room. It was a picture of every place in the room where a thing could be held.

He stood in the middle of it and understood the woman on the Ostrand road.

He had fought her for four exchanges and never once seen what she saw, and now he did. She had stood in the cut and seen this, every rest and every line, a whole road strung with places a thing could be held. She had laid her points where his body was about to come to rest, because she could see the rests before he reached them. It was not magic; it was this, done well, for years, by somebody who had learned it as he had learned to read a floor.

He did not like how easy it looked.

"Lira," he said, with his eyes shut. "You're sitting with more weight on the left."

There was a pause.

"I'm sitting on a bench," said Lira.

"You've got your right heel on the boards and almost nothing on it. Everything's on the left foot and the bench." He could feel it, the two points where her feet met the floor, one heavy and sure and one hardly there at all, a point that barely asked. "You told Rooke it was better."

"It is better." Another pause. "It's not that much better."

He heard her shift, and the faint point grew a little heavier, and then went faint again.

"Don't," she said. "That's cheating. You can't read my feet with your eyes shut."

"I'm not reading them. It's asking about them."

"Then tell it to mind its own business."

He laughed, and it hurt the ribs only a little now, and the new thing went on asking about her feet. He named them for it, aloud, very quietly, because she was listening. Lira's feet. One's mending. Leave them be. The asking about her feet stopped.

Brom moved his weight in the doorway. Cael felt it before he heard it: a rest lifting, and another place on the boards, half a pace to the left, where a foot was about to come down, lit faintly a breath before the foot came. He opened his eyes in time to see Brom's boot come down there.

"It knows where you're going to stand," he said. "Before you stand there. A breath early, not more."

Karis wrote it down without a word.

The door was Brom's idea.

He had stood in the doorway all this while with his right hand on the edge of the open door, because somebody had to be in the door, and he had noticed something that Cael had not.

"It hasn't asked about this one," said Brom. "Has it."

Cael turned and looked at him. He let it look at the door.

It did not ask, and that was the strange thing. The great door stood open a hand's breadth, a tall oak leaf on three iron hinges, a threshold, the very thing the new thing wanted most of anything in the world. It had asked about every door he had passed through for a week, and it did not ask about this one at all. It knew the door was there. He could feel the hinges as points and the edge as a long place. But it was quiet about it, the way it went quiet after he had named a thing.

"No," said Cael. "It hasn't."

"Watch," said Brom, and took his hand off the door.

There?

It came instantly, so fast and so hard that Cael's breath caught, the whole of the new thing turning toward the open edge of the door like a needle to north. There? There?

"Put it back," he said.

Brom put his hand back on the door.

The asking stopped, not slowly but at once, the way a dog stops barking when somebody it knows comes through the gate.

"It's already held," said Karis quietly. "That's it, isn't it? It wants to fix the door so the door will stay, but a door with a hand on it is staying already. Somebody's holding it, and there's nothing left for it to do."

"So I'm a doorstop," said Brom.

"You're a very good doorstop," said Lira from the bench.

"I'm the best doorstop on the bluff." Brom took his hand away again, deliberately, and Cael felt the There? come up like a hound's head, and Brom put his hand back, and it went down. "There. I can do it all night, and I've done harder work for less."

Cael stood in the middle of the painted floor and looked at Brom's hand on the edge of the door, the big square hand that had held twelve feet of road against two men on the Ostrand road and held a girl up in a doorway for twelve seconds. Something in him went quiet that had nothing to do with the new thing.

It did not ask about a door somebody was holding; it only wanted to hold what nobody was holding. He did not know yet what to do with that. He wrote it down anyway, after, on the leaf under the rule: A held door isn't asked about. Brom's hand. It only wants what nobody has.

Karis's part came last, because it cost her something and she wanted it measured.

She knelt on the boards between two of the frames with her chalk, and drew a line across the floor from the foot of one frame to the foot of the other, about four feet long, straight and white. Then she sat back on her heels and held out her left hand over one end of the line, palm down, close to the wood.

"Left hand," she said, before anybody could ask. "The right's done enough. These are the smallest I own, a wick's worth, and I'll count them aloud." She looked at Lira on the bench. "You count them too. If I say a number you didn't, tell me."

"One," said Karis.

A point of fire sat on the boards at the line's end. It was no bigger than the head of a pin, blue at its root and yellow at its tip, standing up perfectly still on the bare wood the way a candle flame stands in a room with no draught. It did not spread, or even scorch the board, but simply sat there, burning on nothing.

"Two," said Karis, at the other end.

And the new thing asked about the chalk.

It asked as it asked about a door. Not about the flames themselves, which moved and were not at rest; about the line between them. Two points that stayed where they were put, and a line drawn from one to the other, white on the boards: to the new thing that was a threshold. It leaned toward the chalk line between the two small fires exactly as it leaned toward an open door, with its whole courteous attention. There?

"It wants the line," said Cael. "It thinks it's a doorway."

"Two points and a line between them," said Karis. "That's all a doorway is, to it, isn't it? Jamb and jamb and the space between." She wrote it. "Name it."

Chalk, he told it. Karis drew it. Nothing comes through it but air.

It went quiet.

She put the two flames out with a closing of her hand, and stood, and moved the line. She drew it again two feet further from him, and lit its ends again, and counted three and four, and the new thing asked, and he named it. She moved it two feet further and counted five and six, and it asked a little less surely, as a voice is less sure across a wider room. At ten feet he named it, and Karis wrote 10 in her notebook and drew a ring round it.

At twelve feet she lit the seventh and the eighth, and the asking was very faint, like somebody speaking in the next room with the door shut. At fourteen she drew the line and did not light it, and asked him, and there was nothing at all.

"About ten," she said. "Sure to ten, faint at twelve, nothing at fourteen." She wrote it, and under it, For now. "That's what it can see. That's not what it can reach. Nobody's measured that, and nobody's going to tonight."

"Eight," said Lira from the bench. "You said eight. I counted eight."

"Eight," said Karis. She looked at her left hand, front and back, in the lantern light, and the fingers were their ordinary colour. She wrote in the notebook in her small upright hand, Eight, left, smallest. Not an instance. "Not one. Good."

She went back to the line at twelve feet, to put out the last two flames, and it happened then.

The chalk line at twelve feet lay on the boards between its two small fires, and the new thing, which had been faint about it, was suddenly not faint. It leaned. It leaned the way it had leaned in his own doorway with Lira coming through it on her crutch, when he had been halfway through saying no. Something in him began to go out of him toward the line, quick and quiet as a breath, to set a point at one end of it and a point at the other and tell the space between them to stay.

"One," said Brom from the door.

"Chalk," said Cael aloud, hard, to the whole of it. "Karis drew it. On a floor. Nothing comes through it but air. It's nothing. It's a line."

It stopped.

It stopped where it was, halfway out of him, and came back, and lay down, the way the clerk at his elbow had once read an answer on a form and blotted it and gone home. The chalk lay on the boards. Karis's two small flames stood either side of it, burning on nothing. Nothing in the air between them had been told to stay.

Brom did not say two.

Karis closed her left hand, and the two flames went out, and the hall was only two lanterns and the painted floor and the chalk.

"That's the bill," said Cael, and his voice was not quite steady. "Behind the eyes, like the naming on the first morning. Not bad."

Lira had a stub of pencil out. She wrote on her palm, under the lantern, and turned her hand so that he could see it. Bill. And under it, smaller: Brom, one. Stopped.

"We stop," she said. "We said we would."

They stopped.

Karis wiped the chalk lines off the boards with her handkerchief, all four of them, so that Rooke's program would find the floor as it had left it. Brom went up the gallery stair and opened every shutter again down the length of the north wall. Cael put out the lanterns one after the other and stood a moment in the dark of the hall, where the new thing asked about nothing. He had told it what everything was.

Lira was at the great door when he reached it, with her hand on its edge, holding it open for him.

"Door," she said, before he could. "Rooke's. Oak. It's held. You can go through."

He went through.

Chapter 39 — Two Hundred Years

Karis had five nights, and she used all of them, and on the Second-day she said she was ready.

Nobody saw her work; that was the arrangement. The assistant went home at the sixth bell every evening with a story about glue, and believed it, and told Ephram, who told the refectory, so that by the Fourth-day half the hill knew that the researcher at the top of the library was mending a founding volume with something that smelled, and kept away. The lamp burned in the window at its usual height every night and went out at its usual hour. Behind it, at the far end of the long table under the brown-paper shade, Karis sat with the case open and the two keys in the room, Seln's for an hour at a time while he sat silent at the middle of the bench, and laid the whole of it out again, and again, and again, until it would lie in the order she wanted.

Cael went up on the third night only to bring her bread, because Brom said somebody had to and Brom's shoulder did not like the top stair yet. She did not look up when he came in. The forty pairs were not in four rows any longer. They lay in a single long line down the whole of the table, sorted by something he could not see, with a slip of paper on each in her small upright hand. The memoranda stood beside them in nineteen separate piles, one issue to a pile. Every seal on every one of them had a numbered slip tucked under it, and the nine new leaves from Greyvane lay open across the window end in their fresh grey wax. Seln sat at the middle of the bench with his hands flat and watched her. Karis asked Cael one question, about Denvash, with her eyes still on the seals, and he answered it standing at her elbow, and Seln said nothing at all.

He put the bread down at her elbow and went away again. The next night, when Karis came down to the east hall with the rest of them, she brought the plate back empty, and he did not know whether she had eaten the bread or Seln had.

On the Second-day after supper they came up as they came up every evening of the year, by their three ways, a few minutes apart. The assistant had gone home singing, and the lamp was in the window.

Karis had put everything away.

The case stood shut between the grey boxes on its shelf. The long table was bare again to its faded green cloth. In the middle of the cloth, under the shaded lamp, lay four slips of paper folded once and numbered on the outside in her hand, one to four, in a row. A little apart from them lay a fifth, face down.

She waited until Seln had looked at the room in his order and come in and sat down, and Brom had lit the kettle's blue flame under the pot, and Lira had got her foot up on the stool. Then she put her hands flat on the table either side of the slips, the way Seln did, and Cael wondered if she knew she was doing it.

"Four findings," she said, "and one limit. I'm going to give you them in the order I found them, which is the order they stand on each other in. I'm not going past the case. If anybody asks me to go past it, I'll stop, and I'll stop for good, and I mean that." She looked round at them. "Not because I'm cross, but because the minute I guess at something in front of this paper, the paper's no use to anybody, including me."

"Nobody's going to ask," said Lira.

"You will," said Karis, "all of you, because it'll be the most natural thing in the world. I'm telling you now so you'll know what I'm doing when I don't answer."

She unfolded the first slip.

"The orders don't correct strength," she said. "They correct reach."

She did not have the forty out. She did not need them. She had them by heart, every station and every margin, and she gave them in the order she had sorted them into, which was not the order Seln had laid them on the table.

"I sorted them by the margin," she said, "not by the station or the date, but by what the keeper wrote at the edge of the reading, that the order told the clerk not to enter. And every margin is the same kind of thing. Reads into. Something of. A second family, faint. Not one keeper in forty wrote at the margin that a child was too strong. Several of the forty were weak; a first rank, and a low one, with a second family showing faintly behind it like a face behind a window. They were corrected all the same. And I went through every pair looking for one where the order took strength away and left the rest, and there isn't one. When a rank goes, it goes because the second family went, and the second family was what was holding the rank up." She moved one finger on the cloth. "They don't correct how much. They correct how far."

"Reach," said Brom.

"Reach, how far a reading goes past the one column the station has for it." She looked at the four slips. "Strength they leave alone, because strength they like. Strength's easy; you write it down in a rank and build somebody a ladder. Daeva was read at thirteen, in a garden court, and nobody ever corrected a line of hers. She's the strongest thing on the continent at her age, and they've never once taken anything off her paper. They built her a ladder to her height and called it a cycle."

Cael sat very still.

They did this to me the other way — built the ladder to my height and called it fairness. He had the letter by heart; it lived inside the back board of Hesk's book, in the satchel across his chest. He had never told Karis its words. She had come to the same sentence from the far side of a case.

"And reach is what they can't have," Karis went on, "because reach is what doesn't fit a column. A child who reads Current and something of Mire isn't a better Current. She's a question the registry hasn't got a box for. So the function closes the question before anybody asks it. Margin reading not to be entered. And she goes home with one family on her paper and grows into the paper, because people do."

"Nine weeks of nothing," said Lira quietly.

"Nine weeks of nothing. They watch to see whether the margin comes back, and it never does, not in forty. Of course it doesn't, when nobody's told her it was there."

She turned the first slip over. There was more on the back.

"The second half of the first finding is the mark on Cael's file."

Nobody moved.

"The leaf says the function is appended to the reading and advises what's entered. It doesn't say what happens when the reading gives it nothing to advise, and nothing else in the case says it in words." She looked at Cael. "But your file says it. The petition put it in schedule two by its full title, on the first night of the year, and you read it. Suppression-Advisory Watch, Priority Level 4."

"Advisory," said Seln.

"Advisory, the same word, on a designation nobody at any height has ever been able to trace to an office." Karis drew a breath. "Cael told me on the third night, when he brought the bread. I asked him about Denvash, and he told me: eleven seconds. The plate lit eleven seconds late, and the word came at the end of them."

Cael had not known she had asked for anything but the bread. He remembered telling her, standing at her elbow with the plate in his hand, and her not looking up.

"Eleven seconds is a long time for a reading," said Karis. "Every other reading on the continent is done before you've finished a breath. I think the function had his reading in front of it for eleven seconds and couldn't find a column to put it in, any column, and couldn't take the margin off because it was all margin. So it did what a good form does when it can't be filled in: it failed safe, and wrote the one word it had for a thing that couldn't be written. Then it marked the file, so that whoever came after would know there was something there it hadn't been able to correct." She laid the slip down. "The mark has no office behind it because no office made it. It made itself, the way a stamp comes down when a lever's pulled. And Ilsev sent it up, at the hearing, twice, to every height she could reach, and asked who'd authorized it. Something answered her each time, something that wasn't anybody."

She was quiet a moment.

"She just never knew what was answering."

Brom's kettle ticked on its shelf.

"Ilsev did everything right," said Karis. "She's the most honest seat in the district. And Havel at the junior chair, who looks at the file every time it's on a table, as Brom's counted. He's seen something he can't place, and he's kept looking at it, which is all an honest man can do with a thing like that." She looked at each of them. "I want a rule about them before we go on."

"Say it," said Lira.

"Ilsev and Havel are never told. It would only cost them."

Eleven words. Cael counted them because he could not help counting them, and he was glad there were so few.

"Agreed," said Brom.

"Agreed," said Lira.

Seln moved one finger. "Agreed."

"Agreed," said Cael.

Karis nodded once, and wrote the eleven words on the back of the first slip, under the rest, and folded it again.

The second slip was longer, and she held it a while before she opened it.

"The second finding is about time," she said. "How old each piece of it is. I'm going to tell you how I dated it first, because if I don't you'll think I'm guessing, and I'm not."

The words had told her least, she said. Here and there a word had been swapped for one the founding compilers would never have used, and that put the issues in order and no more. The type gave her two breaks. The stocks gave her three: a soft rag, a harder sheet, and then the bright paper of the instrument on Cael's sill, and the house's own oldest filings ran through the same three in the same sequence, so she could say which issues were older than which. None of it gave her a year. Years had come up the library stair on the Seventh-day, in Bracken's arms.

"Greyvane," said Karis.

She put her hand on the corner of the table where the nine leaves had lain all week.

"Nine renewals of Greyvane's charter, nine registry seals set beside the founders' hands, nine years written under them in the charter's own text. I've never in my life had nine seals with years on them side by side before. I laid every memorandum's seal against them, under the glass, ring by ring." She looked at Seln. "The newest issue is from this generation. The seventh falls between Greyvane's fourth renewal and its fifth. The oldest are older than any seal Greyvane has. I counted back from where they meet, ten years an issue, near enough, the way the seals change." She put the slip down. "The first memorandum is two hundred years old, give or take a decade."

"Two hundred years," said Lira.

"And the leaf is the same age as the first memorandum, on the same paper. The hand is the hand of the first one's top signature; I'd swear to that in front of Ilsev. Somebody sat down two hundred years ago, wrote out what the function was and what it was for, signed the first memorandum to every station, and put the note that explained it in the bottom of the box. That's the middle layer."

"Middle," said Cael.

"Middle." She touched the leaf's place on the table, though the leaf was in its sleeve in the case. "Read it again in your head: The function is appended to the reading and is not the reading. It does not alter what the reading shows. It's a note written by somebody who added something to a thing that was already there, and wanted it understood which part was his." She looked at Brom. "Think of your father's forge in the shed past the gardens, and the mill that must have stood on the estate's stream. If a millwright wants a wheel, he doesn't dig the river, because the river's there already. He cuts a race beside it, and puts his wheel in the race, and spends the rest of his life keeping the race clear of weed. That's maintenance, and that's what this leaf is: a millwright's note about a race. It doesn't say a word about who dug the river."

"Then who did?" said Lira.

"That's the question I said you'd ask," said Karis. "And there it is, and I'll come to it."

She went on.

"Under the policy there's something older: the reading, whatever it is that wakes behind your breastbone at Kindling and reads you. The function sits on it. It's older than the function by however long, and the case doesn't say how long, and I don't know." She laid her hand on the cloth. "But the case does show me one thing about what was there before the function came, because the first memoranda had to clear it out of the way. The first three issues, about eleven years apart, in the oldest paper. And they're not about the forty. They're about the old custom."

She looked at Cael.

"You know the margin I copied at Greyvane. The one in the old records, where an assessor once looked at somebody whose work went across many families, and couldn't fit him in any column, and wrote him down by what he could show instead, by judgment, with the old word." She did not drop her eyes. "I said it once, at Halcenvane, and closed it as a question. I'll say it once more, here, because I have to, and then not again. Unbound."

The word sat on the table among them.

"That was the old way," she said. "Before the policy. An assessor who met a reading that went across many families could write that, pending further study, and the person went on with his life under that word, and nobody corrected anything. It was a door the old system left open. And the first three memoranda shut it, in order. Each of them cites an article of the directive by its number, the same directive I sat over at Halcenvane." She counted on her fingers, slowly, one, two, three. "The first: close the door. No assessor may designate by judgment of what a person shows; a station enters what the reading gives, and only that. The second: remove the exit. The provisional custom, pending further study, is struck; there is to be no designation that waits on study. The third: delete the name. The old word is discontinued, and every person who carried it is to be re-entered under a flag."

She did not say which flag, and she did not have to. Cael's own schedule two had it, bracketed, under Path, on the instrument on his sill.

"That's the word your Arbiter said at Denvash," said Karis, quite gently. "It isn't a classification, Cael, and it never was. It's what they wrote where the old name used to be."

He had known it for a long time, in the way you know a thing you have never let yourself look at. He sat with it. It did not hurt the way he had thought it would. It was more like setting down something he had been carrying the wrong way round for years and finding that it was lighter the right way up.

Karis turned the second slip over.

"And that's where the case ends," she said. "So here is the limit."

She did not read it from the slip. She said it to the room, slowly, in the voice she kept for the last line of a finding, the line she would be held to.

"Here is the limit, and I am entering it as a limit and not a finding, because the difference is the whole of my discipline."

Nobody moved.

"I can tell you when the policy began, near enough, and that it was a policy, and that it's been kept since by forms. I can tell you that the oldest thing it did was shut a door the old way had left open, and take the name off the people who'd used it. I can't tell you what the old word was for, before. I can't tell you what the reading is, underneath the function, or how old, or how it came to be there to have a race cut beside it. Nothing in that case reaches down that far, not a line." She put the slip on top of the first one. "We've explained the middle of the story. Not the beginning. Entered as a limit."

It was quiet in the room for a long time. The lamp in the window burned at its usual height for the valley to see. The kettle had begun, very faintly, to sing.

It was Lira who spoke.

She had her chin on her fist and her eyes on the place on the table where the leaf had lain all week, and when she spoke it was slowly, the way she worked out a floor from the rail before a bout.

"They found it," she said.

Karis looked at her.

"The registry, or whoever sat at that desk. They didn't make the reading. Your leaf says so, as near as it can without saying it. It was there, and they found it." She lifted her chin off her fist. "Two hundred years is a long time to a registry. It's the whole of their paper. It isn't a long time compared to whatever's under it."

Nobody could answer her, and Karis did not try. She sat with her hands on the table and her eyes on Lira's face. Cael saw her decide not to write it down, and saw what it cost her not to.

The third slip was the shortest, and Karis read it almost at once, as if to get past it.

"I went through everything for the anomaly," she said to Cael, "for session nine. You asked me to, at Greyvane, and I've never forgotten that you asked." She did not look at the slip. "Anything in the forty that read across a family with nobody of that family near. Anything in the reports about a practitioner who took something from no one. Any memorandum that mentions Tide by name, or a reading at a distance, or one that came without an engagement. Anything in the leaf." She shook her head. "Nothing. Not one line in it touches session nine. The function works at Kindling, and session nine wasn't a Kindling. Whatever it is, the case didn't do it and doesn't know about it."

Cael took Hesk's book out of the satchel.

He opened it at the table, under the shaded lamp, at the clean leaf after Seln's terms, and wrote it there with all of them watching, because he wanted them to see it written. He had kept that one honest for three years and he was going to go on keeping it honest.

Not this either. Still open.

He blotted it and closed the book.

"That's all," said Karis. "That's the whole of the third."

"It's enough," said Cael.

For the fourth she did not unfold the slip at all. She took the grey notebook out of her coat instead and opened it at the inside of its front cover, where a few lines had gathered over two years that belonged to no case: the fielding clause, the squad rule, the charter's slip, Jent's answer on its plain card, and above them all, in her small hand, the line from the first night of the year. Cael knew it before she put her finger under it.

She read it aloud.

"They're trying to move him back inside the instrument." She moved her finger down a line. "I don't know why that distinction feels important. Noting it." She laid the open notebook on the cloth beside the slips. "Cael put a question mark beside it in his notebook. I saw him do it. I've owed him the answer since the first night."

"And now you've got it," said Brom.

"Now I've got it." She put her finger on the line. "The petition asks for one thing, compelled re-evaluation under standard protocol. It doesn't care about the provision or the house or the clause; it wants him in front of a reading again." She looked at the case on its shelf. "A re-evaluation is an evaluation. The memorandum covers every evaluation at which a reading is entered. If the reading reads him this time, older, with eight things in him instead of none, the function is waiting beside it with its advice, and the advice is entered, and the order comes down, and he's a column, whatever column it chooses: one family, first rank, margin not to be entered." Her voice was very steady. "And if the reading goes out again, the way it went out at Denvash, then there's no valid classification, and it's chapter fourteen, in sequence: nullification, suspension, restriction."

"Both doors," said Lira.

"Both doors open into the same room, and it doesn't matter to them which he walks through." Karis laid her hand over the open cover. "Re-evaluation isn't the test. It's the delivery."

Seln had not spoken all night except to agree to the eleven words. He spoke now, to the table, in his counter voice.

"That is why the road has gone quiet."

They looked at him.

"Nobody has come since the cut: no team, no knock, no rider at the gate. I have been reading the post for it every morning, and the lodge book, and the coats, and there is nothing." He moved one finger. "I thought at first they were counting what the road cost them, but that is not it. Why spend a team on a road, where things go wrong and a team goes home with nothing, when the seat will deliver him at the close of the year, by the book, in a room with a clerk? They don't need the hand when they have the instrument."

"Then it's not people," said Brom slowly, "is it? I keep looking for the person, somebody who decided."

"There were people," said Seln. "Two hundred years ago, one, at a desk. Since then there have been seventy-one people signing for coal, and keepers writing down margins, and clerks entering what they're told, and evaluators stamped enter at file, and a district clerk who told a father the truth and sent it up. None of them is wicked. Most of them are good at their work." He was quiet a moment. "A conspiracy can be exposed. A convenience cannot."

"It can't be filed either," said Karis.

She said it as if she had been carrying it for five nights and had only now found the place to put it down.

"I've thought about it every night this week, who you'd file it with. The seat runs on it, and so does the registry, and every evaluation office in the Compact sends its readings through it. You'd be filing a complaint about the corrections function with an office whose whole business is entering what it advises, and they'd find nothing irregular, because every form's been filled in properly for two hundred years." She took her hand off the notebook. "There's nobody to send it to who isn't standing on it."

Cael sat on the bench and looked at the four slips and the open notebook.

He thought of the first night of the year at his window, with the instrument on the sill and the pole written out in his best hand. The system has text, and text has held me every time the people failed. He had believed the people were the trouble and the text was the floor. Then the road had shown him that the room was never the system. He had thought, coming home over the bridge at dusk with his ribs strapped, that he had come to the bottom of it, that the system was broken somewhere he could not see, and that he was looking for the break.

There was no break; that was the whole of it. Every part of it was working.

He said it aloud. "It isn't broken. It's maintained."

Karis looked at him across the table. Then she closed the notebook on its cover, and gathered up the four slips and gave them to Seln, who unlocked the case on its shelf and put them in the lid's pocket beside the leaf and locked it again. The fifth slip she kept face down, without ever turning it over, and put it in her coat.

"That's all of it," she said. "Four findings and a limit."

"What's on the fifth?" said Brom.

"What I wrote on the first night, under the leaf, before I'd read anything." Karis buttoned the coat over it. "One word, and I was right. I'm not going to say it, because I wrote it before I had the paper, and a thing you write before the paper is a guess, even when it's right." She stood. "I'll burn it in the morning."

He went down the top stair behind Lira, at her pace, which was faster tonight than it had been. She went down standing now, one step at a time, with her hand on the wall and her right foot set down carefully but set down.

On the third-floor landing, where the top stair met the main one, she stopped and put her hand on the newel post's worn cap, and did not name it.

"So what's it for?" she said.

He knew what she meant.

"The case," said Lira. "If it can't be filed, if there's nobody to send it to who isn't standing on it. If we can't publish it without spending Seln, and we can't use it at the seat without the seat reading it as a forgery, and Karis won't take it a line past the paper." She looked down the main stair into the lamplit dark. "Twelve years on a shelf and five nights on her table, and it doesn't prove anything to anybody who matters. What's it for?"

He did not have an answer. He stood on the landing beside her and waited, because he could see she had one.

Lira took her hand off the post.

"It's not evidence. It's a map."

She started down the main stair, slowly, with her hand on the rail.

"Evidence is for a room," she said over her shoulder. "You carry it in and put it on a table and hope somebody reads it right, and we've done that all year, and the room was never the system." She went down another step. "A map's for walking. It doesn't have to convince anybody; it only has to be right about where the doors are." She stopped on the next landing and looked back up at him. "And now we know where they are, all of them, even the ones that open one way."

He came down the stair after her.

"Rail," she said to the rail, under her hand, quite seriously. "It goes all the way down. You can trust it."

He said it after her.

Chapter 40 — The Instrument

Cael said it on the Third-day night, in the reading room, before he could talk himself out of it.

"There's one man outside this room who's owed the case."

They were all there. They had come up by their three ways after supper as they did every evening now, without needing a floor schedule to tell them when. Karis had put the enrollment book back on Bracken's counter on the First-day before the second bell, as promised, and Bracken had weighed it on his palm and written it in. The case stood on its shelf between the grey boxes, and the lamp burned in the window.

They all knew who.

"He warned us," said Cael. "At Norhold, in a room that belonged to neither office, with forty clocks in it and nothing written down by either side. He told us to stop competing in public, and why, and he didn't have to. It cost him something to say it, and he said it anyway, and then he went back and was set aside for saying the same thing at the convening." He made himself go slowly. "And he's still the one evaluator in the Compact they need a sentence from. When the seat comes to re-evaluate me, somebody has to certify the protocol, and it'll be him they ask. He's going to be asked to sign the delivery, and he doesn't know what's being delivered."

"Seln paid twelve years for that case," Cael said, "and we've had it six nights. We can't file it, and we can't publish it, and we can't use it. But we can let one honest man inside the thing see what the thing is, before they hand him the pen." He looked at the cloth. "I think we owe him that, and I think it's the same debt as the stair. I don't know how to tell the difference."

"Then say the worst of it," said Lira, "all of us, in turn, before anybody puts a hand up." She looked round the table. "That's how we did the reach on the Second-day before the road. Everybody says the worst thing they can think of, out loud, so nobody's carrying one they didn't say."

Brom went first, because he was nearest the kettle and had been looking at it.

"He takes it up the stair the morning after," he said, "because that's what an honest man does with a paper he's been shown. He doesn't keep it in a drawer. He sends it to the office it concerns, with a covering note in his best hand, the way that clerk in the river town did." He did not look at the case. "And the stair eats it. And somebody at the top of the stair reads the covering note and asks where an Archmarshal saw forty copied orders in a surveyor's case, and the answer's a wing at Halcenvane. And Seln's gone by the end of the month, and none of us ever finds out where."

He sat back.

Karis went second.

"He verifies it," she said. "He's an evaluator; it's the whole of what he is. He doesn't believe a thing because it's on a table; he measures it. So he goes home and pulls a frame reading, or a station sheet, or a fresh reading on one of the forty, to see whether the case is true." She turned her pale fingers over on the cloth. "And the frame's theirs, and the station's theirs, and the reading runs through the function. Every instrument he could check it with comes back and says the case is wrong. And he believes his instruments, because he's believed them for forty years. And somewhere it gets minuted that a forgery was offered to the Archmarshal by persons connected with the respondent at Halcenvane."

She folded her hands.

Lira went third.

"He believes it," she said, "all of it, at once, the way you'd want him to, and it breaks him." She was looking at the case. "He's been measuring true for forty years because he thought true was the point. We show him the point was never true. And he goes home, and sits at his desk, and does nothing, because there's nothing he can do. He signs what he's given, or he doesn't, and either way he's a broken man signing things." She lifted her chin. "And we'd have done that to him. We'd have spent the one good man in the whole building for a bad night's sleep."

Seln went fourth. He did not take long.

"He is already theirs," he said. "Norhold was a knock, dressed as a kindness. A lent room, no paper, a warning that made you trust him. That is the third grade done well. And the case goes to the people it was taken from, by the hand of the one man you would have given it to."

He put his hands back flat on the table.

Cael went last, because he had proposed it.

"He reads it," he said, "and he asks about me. He's an evaluator, and I'm the one subject in the Compact he's never been able to read, and he's sitting across a table from the case and from me. He asks the natural question: why is the boy's file marked, what is he, how did the function fail on him." He made himself say the rest. "And somebody in the room answers, not because they mean to, but because it's the natural thing, and he asks well, and he's kind about it, and it's late."

Karis looked at him for a long moment.

"Then that's the rule," she said. "That's the one that matters. The rest are risks, and we can weigh them, but that one's a rule." She put both hands on the table. "He gets the case. Nothing about Cael. Say it, everybody, out loud. I want to hear it in every voice in this room, so that whoever's tired at the end of an afternoon in a strange room hears their own voice saying it."

"He gets the case," said Brom. "Nothing about Cael."

"He gets the case," said Lira. "Nothing about Cael."

Karis said it again, the third time, the same words.

"He gets the case," said Cael. "Nothing about me."

Seln was last. He sat with his hands flat on the cloth and looked at the shelf, at the dark leather between the grey boxes, for so long that Brom's kettle began to tick.

"He gets the case," said Seln. "Nothing about the boy."

"Hands," said Lira.

Brom's went up first, the right, because the left still did not like going over his shoulder. Then Karis's, with the pale fingers, and Lira's, and Cael's. Four hands stood up in the circle of the shaded lamp.

Seln's stayed flat on the table.

Nobody hurried him. They held their hands up and waited. It was his case and his twelve years and his name on a roll somewhere, and if his hand did not go up, then theirs would come down, and none of them would ever mention it again. Cael did not know which way it would go. He could have borne either, and that was new.

Seln lifted his hand off the cloth. He held it there a moment, a hand's breadth above the table, as if weighing it. Then he raised it.

"Five," said Lira.

Seln found the way in two days, and nobody asked him how until he had found it.

The wing posted station closures every week on a board behind the counter, because an enrollee could not be sent to a station for a frame reading on a day the station was shut. Nobody ever read the closures but the desk clerk, and the desk clerk only to answer a question. On the Fourth-day Seln read them, and there it was, in a district clerk's printed form: the river stations shut in turn for the Archmarshal's yearly inspection, which he walked himself, as he had walked it every year for a decade. The Ostrand station was down for the coming Seventh-day.

"He'll lie in Ostrand the night before," said Seln. "The inspection starts at the first bell. Officers of the Compact who are not of the seat lie at the inn on the wharf, the long low one where the seat's clerks eat in sitting weeks. They have done for as long as I have been in the trade."

"And then?" said Karis.

"And then a note." Seln took a small square of plain paper from his waistcoat pocket, the kind the wing used for marking places in ledgers, and laid it on the cloth, already written. "No name, no seal, no hand anybody would know. An address and an hour, and one line."

Cael leaned over and read it.

Four streets back from the seat, on the wharf side. The tall house with the brass plate. The third floor. The second bell after noon. Neither office's. Nothing written.

"He'll know it," said Seln. "It's his own note to you at Norhold, cut down to four words. Nobody saw that note but the people at the long table that night, and he knows that, and he'll know the line couldn't have come from anyone else."

"And the room?" said Brom.

"Is borrowed." Seln very nearly smiled. "A records administrator's, on the third floor of a leasehold building four streets back from the registry seat. He is on circuit in the hill stations for six weeks. His landlord's keeper lends the room by the morning or the afternoon to anybody with a reason and a deposit, and writes the reason in a book, and does not read it twice. My reason is a reading." He looked at the note. "I have used that kind of room before, but never that one."

"And if he doesn't come?"

"Then we go home on a Seventh-day," said Seln, "and nothing in the world is different, and we keep the case."

He took the note down the bluff road himself on the Fifth-day, in the house's ordinary post, with a dozen of the wing's letters, and left it at the inn on the wharf with the inn's boy in an envelope addressed in a copying hand to the officer of the river inspection. The coats at the foot of the road saw a clerk with the post. They had seen him with the post every week for two years.

They went down on the Seventh-day by five ways, because it was a Seventh-day and the whole hill went down to Ostrand on a Seventh-day by any way it liked.

Lira went with the program's carriers on the market cart at the first bell, because Rooke's program bought its tape and chalk at the chandler's by the bridge and somebody had to carry it, and she was not allowed to carry anything heavier. Brom walked, by the long road round the bluff, which took an hour and was the only exercise his shoulder would let him take. Karis took the house's errand to the fee office with a letter of Bracken's in her wallet. Seln went with the post. Cael went last, alone, by the ferry, because it was the way he always went when he went at all. He sat on the bench by the rail and let the coats at the landing look at him as they had looked at him for two years, and nobody wrote down anything but the hour.

The lane was narrow and steep, with a gutter down the middle and the backs of the warehouses on one side and a row of tall old houses on the other, let out floor by floor to clerks and factors and men who did a trade in paper. The building was the fourth along, with a door with a brass plate beside it listing its tenants, and a keeper's window, and a stair. Seln was at the keeper's window when Cael came in, writing his reason in the book, and did not look round.

The stair went up round a narrow well. On the second landing there was a clock on the wall, the building's own, an old round-faced thing in a box. Cael passed it on the way up and it said a quarter to the second bell.

It was a records administrator's room on the third floor of a leasehold building four streets back from the registry seat, with nothing of anyone's in it.

Cael stood in the doorway and looked at it in Seln's order before he knew he was doing it.

What the room had most of was absence. Along one wall the shelves still kept the outlines of the man's ledgers in the dust, clean oblongs of bare wood where his work had stood until a week or two ago, and above them on the plaster three paler squares showed where he had hung whatever he liked to look at. He had taken all of it on circuit with him, or locked it away, and left the shapes. What remained belonged to the building: a long scrubbed table, six chairs carried up from some store below and no two of them alike, an iron stove gone cold in the corner, and a brown door with a row of empty hooks on its back. The one tall window had small panes. Through them, across a lightwell and the wet slates of the lane, a green cupola stood four streets off, over the wool exchange where the seat sat.

"It's a good room," said Lira, from the chair by the stove. She had been there half an hour. "I've been counting, and there's nothing in it to count."

Brom had the chair with its back to the wall. Karis had the chair at the table's end, with the case on the floor at her feet, its lock still shut; Seln had carried it down inside the post satchel, between the wing's letters, and given it to her in the keeper's hall without a word. Seln came up last and locked the door behind him and gave the key to nobody. He did not sit. He went to the window and stood a little to one side of it, where the frame hid him from the lane, and looked down.

They waited.

Nobody talked. There was nothing to say that had not been said in the reading room, and nobody wanted to say anything in a room that was not theirs. The building made its sounds round them. Somebody on the floor below dropped a weight on boards. On the floor above, somebody was singing at his work. A cart went down the lane with its brake on, scraping. Through the open door of the room, across the landing, Cael could hear the clock in its box on the second landing below, ticking, slow and heavy, a building's clock that had nothing to do with any of them.

"Front stair," said Seln.

He said it quietly, to the glass. Then he stepped back from the window.

"He came in by the front, not the yard. He walked up the lane from the wharf end, on the gutter side, in grey, with nothing in his hands, and he stopped and read the brass plate by the door, and then he went in past the keeper's window, where the keeper could see him." Seln looked at the door. "By the clock on the landing, eleven minutes early."

They listened.

The steps came up the stair, single steps, not hurried, the whole first flight and then the second without a pause on the landing. They went past the clock and came up the third flight, and did not go on to the fourth, where the singing was. They stopped outside the door.

He knocked once.

Seln unlocked the door and opened it and stood aside.

Vastin stood on the landing in his plain grey coat with his hands empty at his sides, and did not come in at once. He looked at the room the way Seln had looked at the reading room on the birthday, the door and the window and the bare table and the shapes on the shelves, and then the five of them, one at a time. He did not let his eyes stay on any one of them longer than on the others, not on Cael, and not on the man who had opened the door to him.

Then he came in, and Seln shut the door and locked it.

"I was told nothing would be written," said Vastin.

"Nothing will be," said Karis.

He nodded. He bowed, not to any of them, but to the room, a short stiff bow from the waist of the kind evaluators gave a sitting before they took a chair. Then he took the chair across the table from Karis, the one with its back to the window, and sat down with his hands on his knees.

Karis lifted the case onto the table and turned it to face him.

Seln came to the table's other end and took the brass key from his waistcoat and opened the lock with its dry sound, and lifted the lid, and stepped back. He did not lay anything out this time. Karis did, in the order it had come out of the case on the first night, with the leaf in its sleeve last and a hand's width apart. When she had finished she sat down again in her chair and folded her hands.

Nobody said anything about anything.

Vastin read.

His left hand was the only part of him that moved for a long while. It lay on the wood beside the rows, and now and then, without his seeming to know it, it opened and closed twice, slowly, as a man tries a hand that has begun to dislike mornings. The rest of him read. A pile grew at his right elbow, face down, a pair at a time, each one turned over only when he had been through the station's record, the order clipped to it and the narrow slip pinned behind, in that order and never another.

Cael counted the pairs as they went face down. He could not help it.

At the twenty-third, Vastin found the letter. He unfolded the father's sheet, and read it, and unfolded the clerk's four lines inside it, and read those. Then he read the father's again from the top. He folded them both along their old folds, exactly as Lira had folded them, and slid them back under the clip, and laid the pair face down on the others. He sat with his hand on top of the face-down stack. Then he took the twenty-fourth.

He read all forty. He untied the pink tape, and read the twenty-three reports, and at the first one that carried Continue observation under its stamp he stopped. He stopped there for longer than he had stopped for the letter. He held the sheet a little nearer the window's light, and read the evaluator's line under the clerk's stamp twice, and put it down very carefully on the others. He went on.

He read the memoranda from the bottom, as Karis had, without being told. He read the seals. At the third issue he took out a small lens on a cord from inside his coat and looked at the seal through it, and at the seventh, and at the nineteenth, and put the lens away.

He came to the leaf last.

Karis took the cotton gloves out of her coat and held them out across the table without a word, and he looked at them, and at her, and took them, and put them on finger by finger as she had. He drew the leaf out of its sleeve by its edges and laid it on the table in the light from the window and read it.

He read it four times. Cael watched his lips not move.

The clock on the landing below struck the half after the second bell, and then the third bell, and then the half again. Nobody in the room had moved. Brom sat with his back to the wall and his eyes on the floor. Lira had her chin on her fist. Seln stood by the window, a little to the side, where the frame hid him.

Vastin put the leaf back into its sleeve, carefully, by its edges, and laid the sleeve on the table a hand's width from everything else, where Karis had put it. He took off the gloves and folded them and laid them beside it.

Then he sat back in the chair with his hands on his knees and looked at nothing.

The silence went on.

It went on past the point where silences end in rooms, past the point where somebody clears his throat or shifts in a chair or says a thing about the weather to let the room breathe. Nobody did any of those things. They had agreed, on the Third-day, without saying it, that whatever he did in the room would be his and nobody would help him with it.

The clock on the landing ticked. Through the floor came the sound of the weight on the boards again below, and somebody laughing, and a door. The singer on the floor above had stopped, and Cael did not know when. Out of the window, across the slate roofs, the green cupola of the wool exchange stood in the grey afternoon, four streets off, with a thin smoke going up behind it from somebody's chimney in a straight line, because there was no wind. Brom breathed, slow and even, the way he breathed in a long hold at the frames. The cold stove ticked once, the way iron does when the day changes round it. Cael's ribs, which the healer had called mended a week ago, reminded him where they had been.

Vastin did not move. His left hand lay on his knee, and once it opened and closed. His eyes were on the window, on the cupola, or past it, on nothing in particular, the way a man looks at the sky when he is listening for something a long way off. His face was quite still.

Cael could not look at it for long. He looked at the shapes of the ledgers on the shelf instead, the clean oblongs in the dust, and counted them, eleven, and then counted them again, and there were still eleven.

Then Vastin spoke. He said it to the window.

"I knew the system was imperfect. I didn't know it was designed to be."

When at last he turned from the window, his face had been tidied. Whatever had been in it was put away somewhere behind his eyes, as a careful man folds a letter he cannot yet answer and shuts it in a drawer, and he looked round the table at the five of them in turn, the first time he had let himself look at them since he began.

"Nobody here has asked me for anything," said Vastin. "I noticed that on the landing, and I have been noticing it for two hours." He laid his left hand on the scrubbed wood. "So I will save you the asking. There are three things I will not do, and you should go home knowing which."

He put one finger down on the table.

"The first is verification." His eyes did not go to the case. "I want to. I have wanted to since the twenty-third pair. I could ride home and send for a frame and a station's own sheet and a fresh reading on any one of those forty children, and watch the case come true under my own hand, and sleep." The finger stayed where it was. "But there is no instrument in the Compact I could test it with that does not run on the thing it accuses. The frames are theirs. The sheets come up the same stair. The reading passes through the very function on that leaf before anybody writes it down. Whatever I measured would be a play put on for my benefit by the defendant." He was quiet a moment. "And a play of that kind has a cast. A girl's name on a request, or a junior's on an order. I will not put a child in a ledger so that an old man can feel sure."

A second finger went down beside the first.

"The second is a report. I have sworn to every report I ever made, and the oath is made to the office that receives it." He looked at the memoranda, at the nineteen seals. "That office is the one that wrote these. I should be swearing, in my best hand, to the man who forged them, and he would read it with great courtesy and enter it and thank me."

The third finger.

"The third is certification." For the first time he looked at Karis, only at Karis, and Cael understood that the not looking at himself was being chosen, and chosen again, every moment. "Before this year is out the seat will send to my desk for my certificate on the protocol for a re-evaluation at Halcenvane. I have known it was coming since the convening. I meant to sign it, because the protocol is sound, and in forty years I have never refused my name to a sound protocol." He lifted his hand off the table. "When it comes, I shall decline. It is the only sentence I have left that they still need."

Nobody spoke. Down in the lane a dog barked twice at something and gave it up.

"I have made something over nine thousand evaluations," said Vastin, to the case, very quietly. "I counted them once, as a young man, and stopped counting when I stopped being one. Each of them I wrote down exactly as I found it, and sent up." His left hand opened on his knee and closed. "How many went into the registry as I wrote them, I don't know. I never shall. That is what I am taking home from this room. Not the paper. That."

Lira had been watching him all the while from her chair by the cold stove, her hands loose in her lap, her chin up off her fist now.

"Are you with us?" she said.

He gave her the whole of his attention before he answered. It was the look he had given the room from the doorway, slow and level and entire, the look of a man who has been sent to evaluate something and means to do it fairly even when the something is a girl with a turned ankle asking him a straight question.

"No. I am not with anyone."

There was no unkindness in it anywhere. Lira took it the way she took a panel's figure she had already worked out for herself, with a small nod, and something in her face that looked like respect for the man who had not rounded it up.

Vastin got to his feet.

For a moment he stood behind the chair with both hands on its rail, and his eyes went once round the borrowed room: the oblongs in the dust, the pale squares on the plaster, the stove gone cold, the cupola in the tall window with its straight thread of smoke. Then he made his bow again, the short stiff one from the waist, and made it to the room, and to nobody in it.

"Thank you," he said.

Seln turned the key for him. He went out onto the landing, and they heard him take the stair the way he had come up it, one even step after another, down past the old clock in its box and the keeper's window and out by the front door into the lane, where anybody at all could see him go.

Seln stood a little aside from the window and followed him down the lane with his eyes until the lane was empty.

Then he said, to the glass, "He was not managing us."

Karis had begun putting the case back in its order and did not raise her head. Brom was standing with his good hand on the rail of the chair Vastin had left, as though it might still hold some of the warmth.

Cael stayed where he sat, looking at the leaf in its sleeve, a hand's width apart from everything else on the table.

"He didn't join us. I'd have trusted him less if he had."

The Archmarshal sat at his desk high in the Compact's house, on the fifth morning after, with the window on his left and the porter feeding the pigeons in the paved court below from his paper bag, as he did every morning at the same hour, and did not look at the trays.

He had come back the night before from the river stations by the post road. He had walked all six in four days. Every frame was sound, though one had been shimmed and would read the damp no longer, and he had written that it would read the damp no longer, and signed it. His left hand had disliked the mornings on the river very much. His clerk had had a fire lit in the room before he came in, without being asked, which the clerk did perhaps twice a year, and had said nothing about it.

At the fourth station, a day upriver from Ostrand, the keeper had walked him through the frame room as keepers always did, proud of his brass, and at the end of it had opened a long drawer under the counter to show him the station's own sheets for the year. A keeper kept his sheets as a miller kept his tallies. They were the station's private record of what its frame had read on each child, before any clerk of entry had touched it, and this keeper wrote a good hand and wanted it seen.

"Every one since I came, sir," the keeper had said. "Margins and all. My predecessor never wrote the margins. I always have."

The Archmarshal had stood at the open drawer for what must have seemed to the keeper a very ordinary moment. The sheets lay in their order, a year of them, the top one in the keeper's careful hand. He could see from where he stood that there was something written at its margin.

He had not put his hand in the drawer. He had said that it was a very well-kept drawer, which it was, and that the keeper did his station credit, which he did, and he had watched the man close it with his own hands and turn the little key in it. Then he had signed the inspection book and gone out into the rain to the next station, and he had not been able to say afterward what the next station's frame looked like.

The three trays stood at his right hand in the order he had kept since before he had a desk worth the name. In, held, done.

He took the copy out of held.

It had lain there, under three other things, since the third evening of the junior's visit. A station's Kindling entry, four years old, for a girl in the northern district, her Path and her first rank in a station clerk's ordinary writing. The junior's notes beside it, in a hand still deciding what shape it meant to be: the frame, the clock, the bouts, the tables. The two recommendations they had settled between them. Second frame reading: within tolerance. And under the station's line, Continue observation.

He read it again, the whole of it, from the beginning.

It was exactly as it had been. Nothing on the page had changed, and he had known nothing would. She did everything her Path said she should, the junior had said, only as if the station had written down somebody a year younger. Inside tolerance every way he measured it. I still don't like it.

The Archmarshal read the station's line, and then he read the margin beside it. There was nothing in the margin; it was clean. The station clerk had written her Path and her first rank in a straight line and left the margin as clean as the oblongs of wood on a borrowed shelf.

He had read forty margins on a scrubbed table in a borrowed room in Ostrand. Every one of them had had something in it before it was cleaned.

He thought of the room in Ostrand, though he had told himself on the post road that he would not. Four young people and a man at a window. The man had stood a little to one side of the glass, where the frame hid him from the lane, the way the field service teaches its people to stand, and had copied forty orders in a round level hand that never once let itself be hurried. The Archmarshal had known what he was from the doorway. He had known, reading, roughly what the copying must have cost and how many years it had sat somewhere before it came to that table. He did not know the man's name, and he had been careful all the way home not to wonder it.

He would not write the man down. He would not write any of them down: not the girl with the turned ankle who had asked him a straight question, not the big one with the bad shoulder, not the researcher who had held out her gloves, not the boy he had not let himself look at. A description is a file with the name left off, and he had spent forty years learning how easily the name comes back.

Then, because it was what he was, he went back through it as he would have made a witness go back.

He could pull a third frame reading. The junior would do it on his word in a day. But he had stood some weeks ago in the house's frame shop and watched an old man in an apron put a shim into a river station's housing so that it would stop telling anybody about the damp. A frame could be made to stop telling. The frame shop would have no trouble telling him that a girl in the northern district was within tolerance, as it had told him twice.

He could ask for a fresh reading at her station. The reading would go up through the thing on the leaf and come back advised.

He could send to the station for its own sheet. A keeper writes at the margin of his own sheet, whatever the clerk of entry is told to enter, and the district clerk in the river town had said so in four lines. The sheet would be there, in a drawer in the north, with the keeper's hand on it. But a request from the Archmarshal's office for a station sheet goes in the dispatch ledger downstairs in his clerk's tidy upright hand, with a number and a date and a name, which would be her name. Then she would be a file, and somebody somewhere would read the ledger. There would be an order, clipped to a copy, and nine weeks of somebody watching her, and a slip on the back of it with nothing on it.

He could call the junior up the too-steep stair and tell him. He thought of the young man's face, nervous and good. He would make him a witness to a thing he could never afterward unknow, and send him back to a career of writing within tolerance under margins he would know had been cleaned.

Every road went the same way. Each of them was theater, and some of them had a victim.

In the middle of the afternoon there were steps on the too-steep stair, quick, the whole flight without a pause, and the junior put his head round the door.

He had a file under his arm, a different one, and a question about a guild hall's frame that took a minute to ask and a minute to answer. When it was answered he did not go. He stood in the doorway with the file against his chest, nervous and good, and looked past the Archmarshal at the tray.

"The northern girl, sir," he said. "I've been wondering. Should I ask for a third reading? I could have the frame shop send a man up. Or write to her station for its sheet." He coloured a little. "I still don't like it."

The Archmarshal looked at him, at the hand still deciding what shape it meant to be, at the young face that had not yet been told anything it could not unknow.

"No," he said. "Continue observation."

The junior waited, as if there might be a reason.

"Write what the instrument says," said the Archmarshal. "What you feel about it is information about you." He heard himself say it, the sentence every evaluator is told once, the sentence he had handed down to every junior he had ever had, and he heard for the first time what it would sound like to a man who knew what was on a leaf in a sleeve in a borrowed room in Ostrand. He did not take it back. It was the only safe thing he had to give the boy. "Keep her file as it is. Don't send for anything. If she does well, let her do well."

"Yes, sir," said the junior, and went down, and the Archmarshal listened to his steps go all the way to the bottom.

He had told a frightened young man to do the very thing the twenty-three evaluators in the pink tape had done, in the very words two of them had used, and he had done it to keep him safe. He sat with that a long while. It was, he thought, very probably how most of them had come to write it.

He did not take a slip of paper. He did not open the letter-book of fair copies in which everything that left the room had been entered for nineteen years. He did not open the lowest drawer, where the folder with its tab lay under his own hand, Pending a proceeding worth sending it to. He knew now that there was no proceeding, and never would be, and that the tab would stay as it was.

He did not write.

At the sixth bell his clerk stood in the doorway with the day's wallet against his chest, looking not at the desk but past it, at the window, where the evening had come in grey.

"Will you be getting home tonight, sir?"

"Yes," said the Archmarshal.

The clerk waited a moment, as if there might be more, and there was not, and he went down.

The Archmarshal looked at the copy a little longer. Then he put it back in held, under the three other things, exactly where it had been, and pushed the tray back to its place. He turned down the lamp. He took his coat from its hook and went down the too-steep stair at the ordinary hour. He crossed the paved court where the pigeons had gone to roost and went home.

It was the hardest thing he did that week, and nobody saw him do it, and nothing anywhere recorded that it had been done.

Chapter 41 — The Empty Hill

They came back up the bluff the way they had gone down it, by five ways, and nobody on the road could have said they had ever been together.

Cael came last again, by the ferry. The boat was low in the water with the term's last passengers, enrollees going home with their trunks roped and their boots tied round their necks by the laces, and he stood at the rail among them with his hands in his coat and let them talk over his head about mothers and roads and what they would eat first. Nobody looked at him twice. At the landing the two coats stood apart from each other by the bollards, as they always stood, and watched the trunks come off; they were counting trunks today, and he saw the nearer one's lips move.

He walked up the bluff road behind a carter's boy leading a mule with three trunks on its back, and let the mule set the pace.

At the top the house was emptying: the outer court was full of carts, and the lodge-man stood at his window with the arrivals book turned to its other face, the departures, writing a name for every trunk that went under the arch. Third-years shouted to one another across the flags about the next term as if it were a country. Somebody had left a cracked practice lath leaning against the capped well with a paper on it that said FREE, and nobody had taken it.

He went through to the north wall, because that was where he went, and sat on the coping by the third buttress, and watched the carts go down.

It took them until the light was going, a slow line down the switchbacks with the trunks swaying and the wheels loud on the turns, and at the foot of the road the coats stepped back against the chandler's wall to let them by. On the river the ferry made its crossing, and came back empty, and crossed again full. Four hundred and thirty enrollees lived on the bluff, and by dusk forty-one of them were left.

Four of the forty-one had signed their slips together, at the wing's counter, that morning before they went down.

The slips were the house's ordinary form for the recess, half a sheet, with a printed line for the enrollee's name and a printed line under it that said Remaining in residence. Reason:. Lira had written the program, and Brom the frames, and Karis had written research standing, per council, in her small upright hand, with the date of the council's sitting after it, because she could not leave a reason uncited. Cael had stood at the counter with the pen, and then written the proceedings.

It was the plainest reason of the four. Since the year's eighth day the registry had had a petition before its seat in the town below, asking that he be stood in a frame and read again. If the frame could not read him, the code had a chapter for that: his enrollment struck out, and after it, a letter at a time, everything else with his name on it. And a respondent who left the hill while the thing was pending would be entered as fled, with a note on three friends' files to say whose friends they were.

Seln had taken the slip from him across the counter, and read the one line, and blotted it.

"Mm," he had said, and put it with the others.

Nobody had needed to ask the four of them whether they would go home for the recess. The fifth was staff, and had no slip to sign.

Lira came out along the wall while the last carts were still on the upper switchback, walking at the careful pace she had kept all week, and sat down on the coping beside him with her right foot out along the stone. She had come up from the town on the program's market cart with the tape and the chalk, three hours before him, and she had plainly been waiting to see him come.

"Well?" she said, low, though there was nobody within forty yards.

"He went out by the front door. You saw."

"I saw. I mean after. On the ferry." She pulled her coat round her. A thin cold rain had begun to come in sideways off the river, hardly more than a wetness on the wind. "Did anybody look at you differently?"

"Nobody looked at me at all. They were counting trunks."

"Good." She watched the carts. "He never looked at you either. Two hours in that room, and he looked at everybody else exactly as long as he looked at the stove. I timed it. He was doing it on purpose, and it was the kindest thing I've ever seen anybody do with their eyes."

"I know."

"Six," said Lira, to the valley, as if she were trying the number on. "Six people carrying one thing. I've only ever kept a secret among three before, and I thought three was a lot." She got up, with her hand on the buttress. "I'm going in. It's wet, and I'm not allowed to be heroic about anything until Rooke says."

When the last cart had gone down he took Hesk's book out of the satchel and opened it on his knee in the last of the light. He did not write anything about Ostrand at first, but sat with the pen over the page and thought about what could go in a book and what could not.

Then he wrote three lines.

Seventh-day. Down by five ways, up by five. A man read something in a borrowed room and thanked the room, not us, and went home.

Six now. That's the whole of it.

The recess starts tomorrow. Nobody goes home.

Six people now knew what was in the case on Karis's shelf, and the sixth was an officer of the Compact who had read it through that afternoon and carried nothing away but the knowing. What it was, Cael did not write. It was not a thing that went into a book.

He blotted the page and read it back. It was true and it said nothing, and he understood with a small cold turn of the stomach that he had written it the way Seln wrote a return. He did not cross it out.

In his room, Hesk's clock on the shelf said ten minutes short of the eighth bell, and the lecture range had rung the eighth while he was on the stair. It had lost its usual minutes since the morning, in its usual direction. He set it right and wound it, and lay down, and was asleep before he had finished counting the things he did not have to do tomorrow.

The hill was a different place with nobody on it.

He learned it on the First-day morning, crossing the outer court to the refectory, when the fountain went up and came down and he could hear it do both. On an ordinary morning you could not hear the fountain at all; there were too many boots on the flags and too many voices under the covered walk, and somebody always shouting for somebody from a window. This morning there was the fountain, and the wind coming over the north wall off the river, and a pigeon on the lodge roof saying the same thing over and over, and nothing else.

The refectory had one table lit, for the cooks had put all forty-one of the house's remaining enrollees at the long table nearest the kitchen door, so that they would only have to carry the porridge one way, and the rest of the hall stood empty under its high windows with the benches turned up on the boards. The forty-one sat close together at their one table, as people do in a big room, and talked in low voices.

Lira was there already, in her program wraps, eating fast. She had been on the east hall's floor since before the first bell, or not on it, exactly, but at its rail, with Rooke's red book on her knee, watching.

"Rooke says the program doesn't stop for the recess," she said. "Rooke says the registry doesn't stop for the recess, so why should he." She pushed the honey toward him. "There are six of us. Me, the Current girl, the Force, the Stone, Rooke and the clerk. The clerk counts as one of us because she says so."

"And the ankle?"

"Is an ankle." She ate. "Ask me in a week."

Karis came in late with her coat buttoned wrong and a volume of the code under her arm, and sat, and opened the volume beside her bowl, and read it while she ate without once looking at what she was eating. Brom came in after her with Ephram, and the two of them sat at the end of the table with their elbows touching and ate enough for six and said almost nothing.

Cael had not known Ephram was staying.

"Somebody has to keep the frames honest," said Ephram, when he asked. "The springs go if nobody works them for a fortnight. I've seen it." He wiped his bowl with his bread. "Also I like the hill better with nobody on it. Don't tell the cohort."
